1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Design Thinking process is/are true?
o: It is a one-way pipeline: once Test is finished the process ends.
Test results can send the team back to Prototype or even Empathise.
During ideation, participants are asked to defer judgement.
The Define stage turns what you learned into a clear problem statement or point of view.
Once the requirements are written, there is no need to return to Empathise.
1.e: Design thinking is a loop: Test feeds back into earlier stages (A and E are false). Defer judgement is an Ideate rule, and Define synthesises research into a problem statement.
w: False: it is a loop; Test results often send you back to earlier stages.
True: findings from Test can send the team back to Prototype or even Empathise.
True: deferring judgement is an Ideate rule so early ideas are not killed.
True: Define turns research into a problem statement or point of view.
False: new findings often show you misread users, so you return to Empathise.

1.q: Which statement(s) about prototyping early and iterating are true?
o: Early prototypes expose unknowns while changes are still cheap.
Comparing several alternatives avoids fixating on the first idea.
A prototype must be polished before users can give any useful feedback.
A minimal version that tests the key assumption is a sound starting point.
Feedback should be collected only after the final milestone.
1.e: The course favours early, cheap prototypes, comparing alternatives and an MVP mindset. Waiting for polish or the final milestone delays learning.
w: True: prototypes expose unknowns while change is still cheap.
True: comparing alternatives avoids fixating on the first idea.
False: rough prototypes already expose concept and flow problems, and polish costs time and shifts feedback to surface detail.
True: a minimum viable version tests the key assumption with minimum effort.
False: feedback after the final milestone is too late and too expensive to act on.

1.q: Which statement(s) about usability and error prevention are true?
o: Poor usability can have safety consequences, not just cause annoyance.
Designers should prevent user errors by design rather than rely on users to avoid them.
Errors caused by a confusing interface are best fixed by training users more.
Reviewing an interface against usability heuristics can expose such problems early.
Interfaces should remove decisions so that users cannot make mistakes.
1.e: Error prevention is a design responsibility, not a user responsibility. Blaming users (C) or removing decisions (E) misses the point.
w: True: in safety-critical settings, a confusing interface can lead to harmful errors.
True: preventing errors by design beats relying on users never to slip.
False: training does not fix a confusing design. The interface is the cause of the errors.
True: a heuristic evaluation can find problems before release.
False: users still need to make decisions. Good design supports them instead of removing them.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about Fitts's Law and the Power Law of Practice is/are true?
o: The Power Law of Practice says performance improves quickly at first, then gains slow down.
The Power Law of Practice helps explain why QWERTY persists.
Fitts’s Law says that large, nearby targets are faster to hit.
Fitts’s Law says that small targets placed far away are faster to hit.
Because of the Power Law, changing an established interface costs users nothing.
1.e: Practice gives diminishing returns and makes users resistant to change. Fitts’s Law: time grows with distance and shrinks with target size.
w: True: the curve is steep for early trials, then flattens as each extra repetition gives less improvement.
True: people who have practised QWERTY for years would lose that speed on a new layout, so they resist switching.
True: movement time rises with distance and falls with target width, so big, near targets are quick.
False: a small, far target is the slowest case. It needs a long movement and a precise stop.
False: users must relearn, and the Power Law says their old skill took a long time to build, so the cost is real.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about good design is/are FALSE?
o: A well-designed BI dashboard adds as many elements as possible to look complete.
Gestalt principles such as similarity, proximity and common region help the eye group related elements.
Obsessive attention to detail and deliberate trade-off reasoning underpin minimalist design.
Technology that ignores users’ trust and feelings adds friction to the experience.
A good interface should be learned by users studying it before they can act.
1.e: Good dashboards remove non-essential elements; users should be able to act without having to study the interface first.
w: False statement: good dashboards remove non-essential elements; more is not better.
True statement: similarity, proximity and common region are Gestalt grouping cues.
True statement: minimalism comes from careful attention to detail and trade-offs.
True statement: ignoring users' trust and feelings creates friction.
False statement: a good interface lets people act without studying it first.

1.q: Which statements correctly order or describe the Design Thinking cycle?
o: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test.
Testing feeds back into Prototype or Empathise, so iteration is the point.
Once Test is finished the cycle is over and cannot be repeated.
Define comes before Ideate.
Prototype comes before Empathise.
1.e: The stages run Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test, and test results feed back into earlier stages.
w: True: it is the standard order of the five stages.
True: results from testing send you back to prototype or empathise again.
False: the cycle is iterative, so findings from testing are used to repeat earlier stages.
True: you frame the problem before generating ideas.
False: you learn about users before you build anything.

1.q: A dashboard looks cluttered. Which changes follow the course’s idea of good design?
o: Remove non-essential elements.
Use colour and font deliberately to direct attention to priorities.
Add as many charts as possible so nothing is missing.
Add context so raw numbers become meaningful.
Rely on users to study the interface before they act.
1.e: Good design is clean and value-focused, directs attention and tells a story with context. Users should be able to act without studying the interface first.
w: True: a clean design removes what is not essential.
True: colour and font should guide users to what matters.
False: more elements add clutter, not value.
True: context turns numbers into a story.
False: a good interface lets people act without having to study it first.

1.q: Which statements about human-centred design are true?
o: It designs around real user needs.
Those needs are discovered through empathy.
It starts from the designers’ assumptions about what users want.
It treats user research as unnecessary once a prototype exists.
It leaves error prevention to the user.
1.e: Human-centred design starts from real user needs found by empathy, and error prevention is the designer’s responsibility.
w: True: it designs around real user needs.
True: empathy is how the real needs are found.
False: designers do not automatically know what users want.
False: users have to be involved throughout, including after a prototype exists.
False: good design actively prevents errors rather than relying on users to avoid them.

1.q: A team builds a rough paper prototype in week one and revises it after every test. Which statements justify this approach?
o: A rough prototype is fast and cheap to change.
Early feedback exposes problems nobody thought to ask about.
A prototype should not be shown to users until it is polished.
Iterating on feedback is central to the course’s approach to design.
A first prototype is final, so revising it is wasted effort.
1.e: Prototype early, test with real users and iterate on the feedback.
w: True: rough prototypes are quick and cheap to change.
True: putting something tangible in front of users surfaces unknown problems.
False: early feedback is the reason to prototype early.
True: the course stresses iterating on feedback.
False: prototypes are expected to change.

1.q: Which statements about the Power Law of Practice and Fitts’s Law are true?
o: Performance improves predictably with repeated practice.
Bigger targets are acquired faster.
Closer targets are acquired faster.
Practice makes performance worse after the first few attempts.
Fitts’s Law says that target size does not matter.
1.e: The Power Law of Practice describes improvement with practice, and Fitts’s Law links acquisition time to target size and distance.
w: True: this is the Power Law of Practice.
True: larger targets take less time to hit.
True: closer targets take less time to hit.
False: performance improves with practice, with diminishing gains.
False: size and distance both matter.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about tacit knowledge is/are true?
o: It can be fully captured by simply asking people to describe their work.
Workarounds and hacks often reveal it.
It can spread by proximity, such as sitting next to an expert and watching them work.
Observation and master–apprentice learning help to uncover it.
Formal training is the only way it spreads.
2.e: People cannot always describe what they do automatically, so you watch and learn alongside them. Tacit knowledge spreads by proximity, not only by training.
w: False: people cannot always describe what they do automatically, so interviews alone miss it.
True: when users invent workarounds, they reveal knowledge the system does not capture.
True: people pick up tacit knowledge by being near experts, not only through formal training.
True: watching or learning alongside an expert exposes what they cannot easily state.
False: tacit knowledge also spreads by proximity and watching, not only through formal training.

2.q: Which of the following interview prompts is/are neutral and open-ended?
o: “Tell me about the last time you bought something online.”
“Don’t you find the checkout confusing?”
“Walk me through how you usually plan a delivery route.”
“Would you say the app is easy or hard to use?”
“Does your employer resort to trickery to defraud you?”
2.e: B and E are leading. D offers only two fixed answers, so it is closed. Open, neutral prompts invite stories.
w: True: an open prompt that invites a story.
False: leading question that pushes the answer.
True: an open prompt that invites a walkthrough.
False: closed: it offers only two answers.
False: loaded wording that presumes wrongdoing.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about documenting empathy research is/are true?
o: Video captures rich data but is time-consuming to review and transcribe.
Audio is less intrusive than video but still takes time to review.
Logs and diaries capture behaviour over time but rely on self-reporting.
Notes and photos preserve continuous context as well as video does.
Video analysis is always faster than reviewing notes.
2.e: Notes and photos capture critical incidents but lose continuous context; video is rich but slow to analyse.
w: True: video is rich but slow to review and transcribe.
True: audio is less intrusive than video but still slow to review.
True: logs and diaries show behaviour over time but rely on self-report.
False: notes and photos lose the continuous context that video keeps.
False: reviewing video takes far longer than reading notes.

2.q: Which statement(s) about choosing participants for user research are true?
o: Use whoever is easiest to reach, such as classmates.
Choose people who reflect the target user population.
Finding the right participants can take creativity and effort.
Test only with friends, since they give honest feedback.
Advanced users whose workarounds show unmet needs can be valuable participants.
2.e: Avoid convenience sampling; choose representative users and learn from lead users’ workarounds.
w: False: convenience samples may not represent your users.
True: findings only apply if participants resemble the target users.
True: the right participants may be hard to find, so recruiting needs ingenuity.
False: friends tend to be polite and unrepresentative.
True: advanced users' workarounds reveal needs the standard design does not meet.

2.q: Which of the following observations is/are strong empathy evidence (emotion + context + constraints) rather than a vague statement?
o: “Users are busy.”
“She worries about missing the delivery slot because customers rarely answer the phone while she is parking.”
“Users like the app.”
“He re-typed the address three times and sighed before giving up.”
“She checks the bus arrival in a Telegram group each morning because the official app is slow.”
2.e: The rubric asks you to avoid vague claims and collect specific emotion, context and constraints.
w: False: vague; it gives no emotion, context or constraint.
True: it names an emotion, a context and a constraint.
False: vague; says nothing specific.
True: a concrete observed behaviour plus an emotion.
True: it states a specific behaviour, context and the reason for it.

2.q: Theatre staff add numbered tape labels to switches on the panel that controls the stage lights. The handbook does not explain the labels. Which activities would help you understand why staff use them?
o: Observe staff using the panel and note how they use the labels.
Use only the handbook to explain why staff added the labels.
Ask a staff member to demonstrate how they use the labels.
Collect a 1–5 satisfaction rating, without any follow-up questions.
After observing, ask: “How does this label help you with this task?”
2.e: Empathy research needs real behaviour plus the user’s own explanation. The handbook does not explain the labels, and a bare rating cannot tell you why.
w: True: observation shows what people actually do with the labels.
False: the handbook does not explain the labels, so it cannot tell you why staff added them.
True: a demonstration shows the real use in context.
False: a rating without follow-up questions says nothing about why the labels are used.
True: a neutral follow-up question after observing links the behaviour to the user’s reason.

2.q: During an interview about how a team finds a table at the cafeteria, which questions are neutral and open?
o: “Can you walk me through how you looked for a table?”
“Why were you so slow?”
“How does that sign help you with this task?”
“Don’t you think the new layout is confusing?”
“What did you expect to happen when you pressed that button?”
2.e: Neutral, open questions explore what users did and why without suggesting a cause or a judgement.
w: True: it is open and asks for the user’s own account.
False: “why were you so slow?” blames the user and suggests a cause.
True: it asks about the user’s reason without leading.
False: it is a leading question that suggests the answer.
True: it asks about expectations without suggesting a cause.

2.q: A researcher watches a warehouse team and sees workers taping a handwritten step list to a scanner. Which interpretations are justified?
o: The note is a user-made artifact that may reveal a workaround.
It may show a gap between the documented process and actual practice.
It proves the scanner is broken.
It is irrelevant because it is not part of the official process.
It may be tacit knowledge the workers cannot easily put into words.
2.e: Workarounds and user-made artifacts show practice, which often differs from process. Do not conclude more than the evidence supports.
w: True: user-made artifacts are a tell-tale sign of workarounds.
True: process is the documented rule and practice is what people do when rules break down.
False: the note shows a need, not that the device is broken.
False: unofficial artifacts are exactly what ethnographic observation looks for.
True: knowledge held from experience is often hard to articulate.

2.q: A researcher observes users at their desks and notices they behave unusually carefully while watched. Which statements apply to observation?
o: The observer effect can change how people behave when watched.
Observation shows what people actually do.
Observing a few convenient friends gives a representative sample.
Longer time with users helps reduce the observer effect.
Observation always reveals motives directly.
2.e: Observation shows behaviour but can be affected by the observer, and the sample has to represent the target population.
w: True: people may behave differently when they know they are being observed.
True: observation shows behaviour, including workarounds.
False: a convenience sample is not representative.
True: spending extended time with users lets them relax.
False: interviews are better for motives, stories and opinions.

2.q: Which statements about slips and mistakes are true?
o: A slip is an execution error.
A mistake is a planning error.
Clicking an adjacent button by accident is a slip.
A slip happens when the user planned the wrong action.
Slips and mistakes are the same thing.
2.e: In a slip the plan was right and the execution went wrong. In a mistake the plan itself was wrong.
w: True: a slip is an error in carrying out the action.
True: a mistake is an error in the plan.
True: the goal was right and the finger landed on the wrong target.
False: a wrongly chosen plan is a mistake.
False: they differ in where the error occurs.

o: “The app must load in under 2 seconds” — non-functional
“A user can add a new payee” — functional
“The system stores the date and currency of each transaction” — data
“Users should find the app easy to learn” — functional
“A persona’s goals are the system’s functional requirements.”
3.e: Usability is a quality, not a function. Personas inform requirements but are not requirements themselves.
w: True: speed is a quality, so non-functional.
True: adding a payee is something the system does, so functional.
True: stored fields are data requirements.
False: ease of learning is a quality, not a function.
False: personas inform requirements but are not themselves requirements.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about personas is/are true?
o: They should be built from real research data.
Having too many personas dilutes the team’s focus.
They describe goals, behaviours and pain points, not only demographics.
Adding random hobbies makes a persona more useful.
A persona should mirror the designer’s own preferences.
3.e: Irrelevant details and designer self-projection weaken personas.
w: True: personas should come from real research.
True: too many personas dilute focus.
True: goals, behaviours and pain points matter more than demographics.
False: random hobbies add noise, not insight.
False: personas should reflect users, not the designer's preferences.

3.q: Which of the following describe(s) a scenario written early in design?
o: A narrative about a user’s goal and context.
A list naming the exact screens and buttons.
It keeps the user interface abstract.
A step-by-step specification of system behaviour.
It helps stakeholders discuss requirements in plain language.
3.e: Early scenarios avoid naming screens; step-by-step behaviour belongs to later specification.
w: True: a scenario is a narrative about a goal and context.
False: naming exact screens is too concrete for an early scenario.
True: early scenarios keep the interface abstract.
False: step-by-step system behaviour belongs to later specification.
True: scenarios let stakeholders discuss requirements in plain language.

3.q: Which of the following belong(s) to the Define stage?
o: A point-of-view statement linking user, need and insight.
A list of 50 feature ideas.
Prioritised user needs.
A high-fidelity prototype.
A persona based on research.
3.e: Idea lists belong to Ideate and prototypes to Prototype.
w: True: a point-of-view statement belongs to Define.
False: listing many ideas belongs to Ideate.
True: prioritising needs is part of Define.
False: prototypes belong to Prototype.
True: a persona synthesises research during Define.

3.q: Which statement(s) about happy paths and edge cases are true?
o: The happy path is the standard, error-free flow most users follow.
Edge cases are rarer flows that the design must still handle.
Edge cases can be ignored because most users follow the happy path.
Rare flows, such as changing a booking part-way through, belong to the happy path.
Scenarios can include edge cases to improve requirement coverage.
3.e: Ignoring edge cases leaves some users stranded. Rare flows are edge cases, not the happy path.
w: True: the happy path is the usual route with nothing going wrong.
True: edge cases are less common situations that still need handling.
False: even if few users reach them, those users get stuck, and edge cases often involve safety or payment.
False: a rare flow is by definition an edge case, not the standard route.
True: scenarios that include edge cases surface requirements the happy path alone would miss.

3.q: Students share project-task screenshots in Telegram. You observe a student using an older screenshot and starting a task a teammate has already completed. Members say: “Before we start, we need to know which tasks are still unfinished.” Which statements are correct?
o: Sharing screenshots is an observed behaviour.
The user goal is to share screenshots.
A user need is to know which tasks are still unfinished before starting work.
The users need a new app.
A breakdown is that an old screenshot leads a student to start an already-completed task.
3.e: Behaviour is what people do, a need is the information or support required, a goal is the desired outcome, and a breakdown is where the process obstructs the goal.
w: True: it is what people actually do.
False: sharing a screenshot is an action. The goal is to complete a needed task without duplicating completed work.
True: it is the information the members said they need.
False: this jumps to one solution before stating the need.
True: the old copy obstructs the goal of finishing needed work.

3.q: A community repair hub lends tool kits. Visitors photograph kit lists, find that some listed kits are unavailable, and ask volunteers to confirm pickup details. Which are well-formed requirements for a service to find, reserve and collect a kit?
o: Functional: support checking current kit availability.
Data: store kit IDs, availability, reservation status and collection details.
Make the service feel modern.
Functional: support reserving a kit and receiving confirmation.
Use a blue colour scheme.
3.e: Functional requirements describe what the service must support. Data requirements identify the information it must hold. Each should be traceable to the research.
w: True: it addresses the unreliable lists visitors currently photograph.
True: it names the information the service must keep current.
False: “modern” is vague and not tied to any research finding.
True: it helps visitors secure a kit and verify pickup details.
False: a colour choice is a design decision, not a requirement supported by the research.

o: “Search products by name” is functional.
“Loads in under 2 seconds” is non-functional.
“Store the user profile” is a data requirement.
“Users want to avoid re-entering their address” is a functional requirement.
“Used one-handed on a moving train” is a data requirement.
3.e: Functional means what the system does, non-functional means how well it does it, and data means what is stored. User and contextual requirements describe the user side.
w: True: it says what the system does.
True: it is a measurable quality of how well it works.
True: it names what data is stored.
False: it describes the user’s need, so it belongs on the user side.
False: it describes the context of use, which is a contextual requirement.

3.q: Which statements distinguish a scenario from a use case?
o: A scenario is an informal narrative of a specific situation.
A use case is a formal, concrete sequence of interactions.
An early scenario stays abstract about the user interface.
A use case is written before any research.
A scenario has to name every screen and button.
3.e: Scenarios are informal and UI-abstract narratives. Use cases are formal sequences of interactions between the user and the system.
w: True: scenarios are informal stories about a specific situation.
True: use cases are formal and concrete.
True: early scenarios do not commit to a user interface.
False: both are built from research findings.
False: that level of detail belongs to later, more concrete artefacts.

3.q: After interviews, a team writes a persona called “Sam, 34, loves cycling and sushi” with no link to its findings. Which of the following statements are true?
o: Details that are not supported by the research make the persona disconnected from the evidence.
A persona should be built from real data about a user group.
An empathy map (say, do, think, feel) can help synthesise observations into a persona.
Personas should include as many invented details as possible.
A persona should describe the system’s features rather than the user.
3.e: A persona is a realistic representation of a user group built from real data. Invented details undermine it.
w: True: unsupported details are invented, not evidence.
True: personas come from real data.
True: an empathy map turns observation into persona material.
False: invented details reduce the persona’s value.
False: a persona is about the person, not the system.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about brainstorming is/are true?
o: Diverge first (many ideas), then converge on the best.
Quantity leads to quality.
Build on others’ ideas.
Critique every idea immediately to avoid wasting time.
Time pressure always harms idea generation.
4.e: Defer judgement; time-boxing sessions helps keep energy and quantity up.
w: True: diverge for many ideas, then converge.
True: quantity tends to produce quality.
True: building on others' ideas extends them.
False: immediate critique stops ideas flowing; defer judgement.
False: time pressure is an IDEO technique that can help.

4.q: Which action(s) would reduce design fixation?
o: Sketch several different concepts in parallel.
Show a successful example solution before people start.
Reframe the problem away from existing features.
Draw inspiration from diverse existing designs.
Refine the first workable idea straight away.
4.e: Showing examples increases fixation, and refining the first idea is exactly the trap.
w: True: several concepts side by side stop one idea from taking over.
False: a sample solution makes people copy its features, which increases fixation.
True: describing the problem without referring to existing features opens new directions.
True: diverse sources broaden the set of options instead of anchoring on one.
False: refining the first workable idea is the definition of fixating on it.

4.q: Which statement(s) about fixation are true?
o: Functional fixedness is seeing an object only in its usual role, as in Duncker’s candle problem.
Design fixation means locking onto the first workable idea.
Participants shown a sample solution are less fixated than those shown none.
Fixation affects only novices.
Seeing an example solution can make people copy its features.
4.e: Sample solutions increase fixation. Fixation is common and affects experienced designers as well as novices.
w: True: people fail to see the box as a candle holder because they see it only as a container.
True: design fixation is sticking with the first workable idea without exploring alternatives.
False: those shown a sample were more fixated, because they copied its features.
False: fixation affects novices and experts alike.
True: examples anchor people on the example's features, which narrows the ideas they produce.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about using AI as a brainstorming partner is/are true?
o: It can produce many ideas quickly.
Teams may latch onto the first reasonable output, giving homogeneous results.
It removes the need for human judgement.
A sensible use is to widen the field with AI, then have humans converge.
AI-generated ideas are free of bias.
4.e: AI outputs carry bias and still need human selection.
w: True: AI can generate many ideas fast.
True: teams may latch on to the first output.
False: human judgement is still needed.
True: widen with AI, then have humans converge.
False: AI output carries bias.

4.q: Which of the following are rules that support productive brainstorming?
o: One conversation at a time.
Stay focused on the topic.
Judge ideas as they appear so weak ones are dropped early.
Adopt the leader’s idea to save time.
Defer judgement and encourage quantity.
4.e: Brainstorming rules postpone judgement and treat ideas as collective, with no lone genius deciding for the group.
w: True: a single thread at a time lets people build on each other instead of talking over one another.
True: a clear topic keeps the session productive and prevents drifting.
False: the rule is the reverse. Deferring judgement keeps people from self-censoring while ideas are generated.
False: ideas are collective. Adopting the leader's idea shuts down the group's contribution.
True: more ideas give more to choose from, and withholding judgement keeps them coming.

4.q: For the repair hub, a team proposes (1) a kit catalogue that starts from the equipment and (2) a repair-task guide that starts from the intended job and suggests suitable kits. Which claims are defensible?
o: These are two different concepts, not variations of one layout.
Pick the first idea to save time.
Each idea should be linked to a specific observation or interview finding.
“Add notifications” is specific enough as an idea.
Compare the alternatives against the needs and requirements before committing to one.
4.e: Ideation produces several genuinely different concepts, links each to research, and compares them before choosing.
w: True: they start from different things (equipment versus job).
False: alternatives should be compared before committing.
True: this keeps each idea grounded in the research.
False: it does not say who receives which update, or why.
True: comparing alternatives against needs is the point of ideating.

4.q: A team spends the first hour judging every idea as it is suggested. Which changes would support productive divergence?
o: Defer judgement while ideas are being generated.
Encourage wild ideas.
Aim for quantity of ideas first.
Converge only after the generation phase, using explicit criteria.
Stop as soon as one good idea appears.
4.e: Diverge first with many ideas and deferred judgement, then converge with explicit criteria.
w: True: judging early blocks idea generation.
True: wild ideas widen the solution space.
True: many ideas give more to choose from.
True: selection needs explicit criteria and comes after.
False: diverging means exploring a wide space before choosing.

4.q: A designer keeps adding features to the first sketch and never considers a different approach. Which statements apply?
o: This is design fixation on an early idea.
Generating several different concepts in parallel can reduce it.
Fixation can come from locking onto an object’s familiar use.
Fixation is good because it keeps the team focused.
Serial prototyping reduces fixation more than parallel prototyping.
4.e: Fixation locks onto an early idea or a familiar use. Parallel exploration reduces it.
w: True: locking onto an early design idea is design fixation.
True: several alternatives developed side by side reduce it.
True: functional fixation is locking onto the familiar use of an object.
False: fixation narrows the options and hides better ideas.
False: serial prototyping is more fixation-prone than parallel.

4.q: Which statements about creative confidence and play are supported by the course?
o: Early criticism can create lasting creative blocks.
Fear of judgement stops people from sharing ideas.
Brainstorming works best as a low-stakes, playful activity.
Only “creative types” can generate useful ideas.
Play is a distraction from innovation.
4.e: Creative confidence is the belief that everyone can think creatively, and play is a legitimate route to innovation.
w: True: negative feedback early on can suppress later idea generation.
True: fear of judgement stops people from sharing.
True: play in a safe sandbox supports brainstorming.
False: creative confidence is the belief that everyone can think creatively.
False: play is framed as a route to innovation.

4.q: A team has 40 ideas and must choose three to prototype. Which approaches are sound?
o: Agree explicit selection criteria first.
Compare ideas against the user needs and requirements.
Choose the idea the loudest person prefers.
Prototype the best few and test them.
Prototype only one idea to save time.
4.e: Converge using explicit criteria tied to needs, then prototype the best few.
w: True: criteria make the choice defensible.
True: needs and requirements are what the ideas must satisfy.
False: volume of voice is not a criterion.
True: the best few go to prototype and test.
False: several alternatives are better than one.

5.q: Which of the following is/are low-fidelity prototyping methods?
o: Paper sketches.
Storyboards.
Wizard of Oz, where a human secretly simulates the system.
A fully coded app with a working back end.
A polished, interactive high-fidelity mock-up.
5.e: Low-fidelity methods are cheap, quick and easy to change.
w: True: paper sketches are cheap and quick.
True: storyboards are low-fidelity.
True: Wizard of Oz fakes the system with a human.
False: a coded app with a back end is high-fidelity.
False: polished interactive mock-ups are high-fidelity.

5.q: Which statement(s) about serial versus parallel prototyping are true?
o: Parallel prototyping produces more diverse designs.
Serial prototyping refines one idea at a time.
Parallel prototyping produces worse results than serial prototyping.
Serial prototyping reduces fixation.
Parallel prototyping tends to give better final designs and more confidence in them.
5.e: Parallel prototyping reduces fixation and improves outcomes.
w: True: comparing alternatives side by side led to more varied solutions.
True: the serial approach builds one prototype, gets feedback and iterates on that one idea.
False: parallel prototyping gave better outcomes than serial.
False: serial prototyping encourages fixation on the single idea being refined.
True: comparing alternatives gives better designs and more confidence in the final choice.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the purpose of prototypes is/are true?
o: They reveal known unknowns.
They can uncover unknown unknowns.
They should be complete and polished.
They should be easy to change and short-lived.
They should first cover the parts that are cheapest to change.
5.e: Prototypes are incomplete by design. Prototype first the parts whose cost of change will rise, not the cheapest ones.
w: True: a prototype lets you test specific questions you already know you have.
True: users do things the team never predicted, which reveals problems nobody asked about.
False: prototypes are meant to be incomplete. Polish is costly and makes people defend the design.
True: if they are cheap to change and discard, teams learn and move on quickly.
False: the priority is the parts whose cost of change will rise later, not the cheapest ones.

5.q: Which statement(s) about prototype fidelity are true?
o: A prototype need not be built to scale or contain a working product.
Fidelity should match the question being tested.
Full fidelity is always necessary to get useful feedback.
A rough mock-up can answer one key question, such as how people would browse content.
Low-fidelity prototypes cannot reveal interaction problems.
5.e: Prototype fidelity should match the question being tested, and low-fidelity prototypes can still reveal important problems.
w: True: prototypes are incomplete by design.
True: if the question is about navigation, a rough mock-up is enough.
False: high fidelity is costly, and many questions can be answered with rough prototypes.
True: a prototype can be built to answer a single key question.
False: paper and storyboard prototypes can reveal interaction and flow problems.

5.q: Which statement(s) fit the minimum-viable-product mindset?
o: Build the smallest version that tests the key assumption.
Learning from many cheap prototype versions beats waiting for a perfect one.
Prototyping early is wasteful when requirements are unclear.
A good plan means no prototypes are needed.
Fail often so you succeed sooner.
5.e: Unclear requirements are the best reason to prototype. The MVP mindset treats each version as a way to learn.
w: True: a minimum viable product tests the key assumption with the least effort.
True: each cheap version produces evidence that shapes the next one.
False: when requirements are unclear, prototypes are how you find out what they should be.
False: planning is essential, but a plan cannot replace testing assumptions with a prototype.
True: quick, cheap failures teach the team faster.

5.q: The repair-hub team tests both the finding flow and the reserving flow with paper screens. Which statements are true?
o: A low-fidelity paper prototype lets you compare interaction approaches cheaply before committing to one.
A paper prototype must look polished to give valid feedback.
The team should state what participants do and what is being tested.
Keeping kit and pickup details visible and showing a clear confirmation lets users verify the result.
A paper prototype cannot be used to test navigation.
5.e: A low-fidelity prototype is fast and cheap, and it is useful only if you state the task and what is tested.
w: True: low-fidelity prototypes are quick to change and cheap to discard.
False: polish is not needed for early feedback on flows.
True: without a task and a question, “use paper prototypes” says nothing about what is tested.
True: visible details and confirmation support the verifiable-result rationale.
False: screens on paper can be swapped by hand to test navigation.

o: A paper sketch of each screen.
A storyboard of the user’s journey.
A navigation diagram.
A fully coded and styled app.
A pixel-perfect mock-up with real content.
5.e: Storyboards, paper and navigation diagrams are low-fidelity. Polished mock-ups and coded apps are high-fidelity.
w: True: paper is the classic low-fidelity method.
True: storyboards are low-fidelity.
True: navigation diagrams are low-fidelity.
False: a fully built app is high-fidelity.
False: a polished mock-up is high-fidelity.

5.q: Which statements about Wizard of Oz prototyping are true?
o: A hidden human operator fakes the system’s intelligence.
It lets the team test an interaction before building the technology.
It is a low-fidelity method.
It requires the system to be fully built first.
Participants are always told about the operator before the session.
5.e: In Wizard of Oz testing a person behind the scenes plays the system, so the idea can be tested cheaply before the technology exists.
w: True: a human plays the system.
True: the interaction is tested before the technology is built.
True: it is listed among the low-fidelity techniques.
False: the point is to test without building the system.
False: the illusion is normally kept for the session.

o: A form prototype explores look and feel.
A function prototype explores what the product does.
An experience prototype explores the end-to-end feel of use.
Every prototype must test all three at once.
A prototype’s goal is chosen after it is built.
5.e: Prototypes can aim at form, function or experience, and the goal decides the fidelity and what is tested.
w: True: form means look and feel.
True: function means what it does.
True: experience means how the whole use feels.
False: a prototype is usually built to answer a specific question.
False: the goal is set before building so it determines what to build.

5.q: A team is exploring concepts on day one and has two hours. Which choices are sensible?
o: Use paper or storyboards.
Build several prototypes in parallel.
Build one polished high-fidelity app first.
Keep each prototype minimal, just enough to test one key assumption.
Wait until the product is finished to prototype.
5.e: Early on, quick low-fidelity prototypes in parallel are cheap and surface problems that nobody thought to ask about.
w: True: paper is fast and cheap for exploring concepts.
True: parallel prototypes give more divergent ideas.
False: a polished first build is slow and encourages fixation.
True: a minimal prototype can be built within the two hours and still answers the riskiest question.
False: prototyping is meant to happen early.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true?
o: The implementation model is how the system actually works.
The conceptual model is what the designer intends users to understand.
The mental model is what users believe about the system.
Problems occur when the user’s mental model matches the conceptual model.
Users’ mental models are always accurate.
6.e: Problems appear when the models diverge, which is why designers try to make the conceptual model visible through the interface.
w: True: this is the real inner workings, such as code and hardware, which users rarely see.
True: the designer's intended understanding, communicated through the interface and its labels.
True: users form their own beliefs from experience, whether or not they are right.
False: when the user's model matches the designer's, interaction goes smoothly. Trouble arises when they diverge.
False: mental models are often incomplete or mistaken, which is a major source of user error.

6.q: Which statement(s) about the gulfs of execution and evaluation are true?
o: The gulf of evaluation is when users cannot tell what state the system is in or whether an action worked.
The gulf of execution is when users cannot work out how to perform the action they want.
A progress bar reduces the gulf of execution.
Clear affordances and natural mapping reduce the gulf of execution.
Immediate visible feedback reduces the gulf of execution.
6.e: Execution is about working out how to act: affordances and mapping help. Evaluation is about judging what happened: progress bars and feedback help.
w: True: users cannot judge the result of their action, which is the gulf of evaluation.
True: users cannot work out how to perform the action, which is the gulf of execution.
False: a progress bar shows what is happening, so it helps evaluation, not execution.
True: affordances signal what can be done and natural mapping shows which control does what, helping people act.
False: feedback after an action helps users interpret it, so it reduces the gulf of evaluation, not execution.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about interaction styles is/are true?
o: Command-line interfaces rely on recall of syntax.
Menus rely on recognition.
Direct manipulation uses physical, reversible, incremental actions with immediate feedback.
Direct manipulation is best for repetitive batch operations on many objects.
Natural-language interfaces eliminate all mapping problems.
6.e: Command lines can batch repetitive work better.
w: True: command lines need recalling syntax.
True: menus let you recognise options.
True: direct manipulation is physical, reversible, incremental with feedback.
False: command lines suit repetitive batch work better.
False: natural language does not remove every mapping problem.

6.q: Which statement(s) about interface metaphors are true?
o: Metaphors let users apply knowledge of familiar objects, such as a shopping cart or a trash can.
Metaphors can mislead where the metaphor breaks down, such as dragging a disk to the trash to eject it.
Metaphors never need to change over time.
A metaphor works best when it is followed literally in every detail.
Metaphors may need to adapt as technology and users’ familiarity change.
6.e: Metaphors help learning but can mislead where they break, and they adapt over time.
w: True: familiar objects give users a ready-made understanding of how things work.
True: the trash can suggests deletion, so users fear losing the disk when they eject it.
False: metaphors need to change as technology and users' familiarity change.
False: following a metaphor literally makes interfaces clumsy, since digital things can do more than physical ones.
True: as users learn new conventions, old metaphors can be dropped or extended.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about slips and mistakes is/are true?
o: Pressing the wrong knob although you know which is right is a slip.
Choosing a knob because a misleading layout made it seem right is a mistake.
Slips are best handled with clarifying explanations.
Mistakes come from pressing a control by accident.
Natural mapping reduces such errors.
6.e: Prevent slips by design, for example with clear spacing or confirmation, and reduce mistakes by clarifying the system so users form the right plan.
w: True: the knowledge is right but the execution goes wrong, so it is a slip.
True: the layout led the user to a wrong plan, which is a mistake.
False: explanations do not stop an accidental action. Slips are prevented by design such as spacing or undo.
False: pressing a control by accident is a slip. Mistakes come from wrong goals or plans.
True: when the layout of controls matches the layout of what they affect, users choose correctly more often.

6.q: After renewing an equipment loan, the portal returns to the home page with no confirmation. To check the loan, the borrower must remember an equipment code from the previous screen. Which statements are justified?
o: This is a gulf of evaluation: the borrower cannot perceive, interpret and evaluate the outcome.
This is a gulf of execution.
Showing “Loan renewed until 27 November” beside the equipment name gives concrete feedback.
Showing the equipment name, code and due date together supports recognition rather than recall.
Naming the three evaluation stages without applying them is a complete answer.
6.e: The borrower has already acted, so the problem is in evaluating the result. Concrete feedback and visible information fix it.
w: True: nothing tells the borrower whether the renewal succeeded, failed or is still processing.
False: the borrower has already performed the action, so execution is not the problem.
True: it states what happened and gives a due date the borrower can verify.
True: the information is visible instead of having to be remembered from an earlier screen.
False: the stages must be applied by saying what the borrower cannot do at each one.

6.q: A shopping app lets customers return parcels at a locker. Experts inspect a prototype. Later, a user says “I know I can change the locker, but where?” and opens three menus. Which statements are justified?
o: An inspection proves users can complete returns successfully.
The incident suggests a gulf of execution.
Record the task context, actions and comment as a critical incident.
Show the correct path immediately whenever a user hesitates.
A visible “Change locker” action is a plausible improvement to test.
6.e: The user knows the goal but cannot find the action, which is a gulf of execution. Record the incident and test a visible control.
w: False: an inspection finds likely problems, not proof that users succeed.
True: the goal is clear, but the way to carry it out is not visible.
True: a critical incident keeps the context, actions and comment together.
False: stepping in each time hides what the user would really do.
True: it addresses the obstacle, and it should be tested rather than assumed.

6.q: Which pairings of interaction style and example are correct?
o: Instructing: typing a command or choosing a menu item.
Conversing: a chat interface or voice assistant.
Manipulating: dragging a resize handle on an object.
Exploring: typing commands one way to the system.
Direct manipulation: commands with fixed syntax and no immediate feedback.
6.e: Instructing is one-way commands, conversing is a two-way exchange, manipulating acts on represented objects, and exploring is moving around a represented space.
w: True: commands and menu selections are instructing.
True: a two-way exchange is conversing.
True: acting directly on represented objects is manipulating.
False: exploring means moving around within a represented space.
False: direct manipulation has continuous representation, immediate feedback and reversible actions, with no command syntax.

6.q: Which statements about mental, conceptual and implementation models are correct?
o: A mental model is what users believe about the system.
A conceptual model is the designer’s intended model of how the application works.
The implementation model is how the system actually works internally.
The conceptual model should align with the user’s mental model.
The implementation model is what users see and must learn.
6.e: The designer builds a conceptual model that should match what users believe. The implementation model is internal.
w: True: it is what users believe.
True: it is the intended user model of how the application is organised.
True: it is the internal workings.
True: alignment is the goal.
False: users do not need to learn the internal workings.

6.q: Which statements about Norman’s action cycle and the two gulfs are correct?
o: The gulf of execution is the gap between a goal and the actions available.
The gulf of evaluation is the gap between the outcome and the user’s understanding of it.
The cycle runs from intention, specifying and performing an action to perceiving, interpreting and evaluating the result.
A missing confirmation after a task is a gulf of execution.
Evaluation comes before the user states a goal.
6.e: Execution is how to do it, and evaluation is whether it worked.
w: True: “How do I do it?” is the gulf of execution.
True: “Did it work?” is the gulf of evaluation.
True: this is Norman’s action cycle.
False: a missing confirmation is a problem with evaluating the outcome.
False: the user compares the outcome with the goal, so the goal comes first.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Model Human Processor is/are true?
o: The visual image store holds roughly 7–17 chunks for about 100–1000 ms.
Working memory holds about 4 ± 1 chunks.
Long-term memory has a small, strict capacity.
The auditory image store holds about 4–6 chunks for a few seconds.
Working memory retains information indefinitely without rehearsal.
7.e: Working memory decays rapidly without rehearsal, while long-term memory is effectively unlimited.
w: True: this brief, large buffer means screen detail fades within about a second unless attended.
True: working memory is small, which is why long lists and codes overload users.
False: long-term memory has a vast capacity. The bottleneck is getting information in.
True: the auditory buffer is smaller than the visual one but lasts a few seconds, so spoken input lingers briefly.
False: without rehearsal working memory fades in seconds, which is why information needs to stay visible.

7.q: Which design choice(s) reduce(s) working-memory load?
o: Showing recently used items so users can recognise them.
Requiring users to remember a code from the previous screen.
Splitting a long number into chunks.
Showing a progress indicator or breadcrumb trail.
Hiding all options behind unlabelled gestures.
7.e: Recognition beats recall: keeping options visible means the interface stores the information, not the user.
w: True: users can pick a familiar item from the screen instead of remembering it.
False: remembering a code across screens loads working memory, and it is forgotten if attention shifts.
True: grouping digits turns many items into a few chunks that fit in working memory.
True: showing where the user is and how far they have gone offloads tracking to the interface.
False: unlabelled gestures must be recalled, which adds the load recognition would remove.

7.q: Which statement(s) about chunking and expertise are true?
o: Experts remember more because they group items into meaningful chunks.
A chunk is a stimulus that has become familiar through repeated exposure.
Experts have a larger raw working-memory capacity than novices.
Chunking only helps with numbers, not with other kinds of information.
When material is random and unfamiliar, experts lose much of their advantage.
7.e: The experts' advantage is organisation of familiar patterns, not raw memory.
w: True: familiar patterns collapse many items into a few chunks that fit in working memory.
True: a chunk is built through repeated exposure.
False: the advantage comes from familiar patterns, not from a bigger raw capacity.
False: chunking applies to any familiar patterns, including words, images and layouts.
True: without familiar patterns to chunk, experts perform like novices.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about practice and long-term memory?
o: Performance improves quickly at first and then more slowly.
Practice moves a skill towards long-term (procedural) memory.
Reading instructions once guarantees long-term retention.
Consistent interface patterns leverage practice users already have.
Changing an established layout has no retraining cost.
7.e: Retention needs repetition, and established habits make users resist change.
w: True: the Power Law of Practice describes steep early gains that flatten over time.
True: repeated use turns deliberate steps into automatic, procedural skill.
False: reading once does not guarantee retention. Repetition is what stores skills.
True: reusing familiar patterns means users do not have to learn from scratch.
False: users must unlearn the old layout, and years of practice make that costly.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about attention is/are true?
o: Performance is best at moderate attentional load.
Too little load can under-engage attention.
Stripping an interface to the minimum is always best.
Colour, size and position can direct attention to key elements.
Multitasking increases working-memory capacity.
7.e: Interfaces need helpful structure. Too little stimulation under-engages people, too much overloads them.
w: True: performance follows an inverted U, peaking at moderate load.
True: with too little to engage them, people lose focus and make careless errors.
False: over-stripping can remove cues that help people find and understand things.
True: visual emphasis guides the eye to the element that matters.
False: multitasking splits a fixed capacity, so performance on each task usually drops.

7.q: A booking form makes people remember a reference code from an earlier screen and type a 16-digit number in one block. Which changes reduce working-memory load?
o: Show the reference code on the current screen.
Keep requiring the code from the earlier screen.
Split the long number into chunks.
Rely on a training manual instead of the interface.
Show a progress indicator or breadcrumb trail.
7.e: Working memory holds only a few chunks, so interfaces should show needed information, chunk long strings and show where the user is.
w: True: recognising a visible code is easier than recalling it.
False: it makes users hold the code in working memory.
True: chunking groups digits into fewer items.
False: a manual does not reduce the load while using the interface.
True: it shows where the user is, so they need not remember it.

7.q: Which statements about working memory are true?
o: It holds about 4 ± 1 chunks.
Information decays quickly without rehearsal.
It is the bottleneck behind many memory-related usability problems.
It has a large, durable capacity.
It stores information indefinitely without attention.
7.e: Working memory is small and decays rapidly, which is why interfaces should not tax it.
w: True: its capacity is small, about four chunks.
True: without active rehearsal it decays rapidly.
True: its small size and rapid decay cause many usability problems.
False: that describes long-term memory.
False: it needs attention or rehearsal to hold information.

7.q: Which statements about presenting a phone number are correct?
o: Three or four chunks: area code, prefix, line number.
Ten unseparated digits.
Grouping the digits into meaningful units.
Showing the number only once and then hiding it.
Requiring users to retype it from memory on the next screen.
7.e: A chunk is a single meaningful unit that groups raw pieces. Groups are easier to hold than ten separate digits.
w: True: a few chunks fit within working memory.
False: ten separate digits exceed working memory.
True: meaningful groups are chunks.
False: hiding the information forces recall.
False: forcing recall from an earlier screen loads working memory.

7.q: Which statements about memory strategies and design implications are correct?
o: Attention is needed: information that is not attended to is rarely remembered.
Rehearsal helps move information into long-term memory.
Interfaces should favour recognition over recall.
Interfaces should require users to recall codes from earlier screens.
The Power Law of Practice says that skills never improve once learned.
7.e: Direct attention with clear representations and avoid taxing working memory.
w: True: unattended information is rarely remembered at all.
True: repetition supports long-term storage.
True: recognition is easier than recall.
False: that taxes working memory.
False: it describes rapid early improvement that slows as a skill automates.

7.q: Which design features reduce reliance on memory?
o: A visible breadcrumb trail.
Showing recently used items.
Presenting information in chunks.
Hiding options behind unlabelled gestures.
Making users remember each step of a long task.
7.e: Showing where the user is, offering recognisable items and chunking information all reduce the load on working memory.
w: True: it shows where the user is, so they need not remember.
True: users can recognise items instead of recalling them.
True: chunks fit working memory.
False: hidden options must be remembered.
False: that increases the load.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about Fitts’s Law is/are true?
o: Larger targets are faster to hit.
Screen corners are effectively infinite targets for a mouse.
On a touchscreen the control–display ratio is 1:1.
Moving frequently used controls farther away speeds them up.
Pointing time depends on distance only.
8.e: Pointing time depends on both distance and target size.
w: True: a larger target allows a faster, coarser movement, so time falls as width rises.
True: the cursor stops at the corner, so you cannot overshoot and the target is effectively infinitely deep.
True: your finger touches the content directly, so one unit of finger movement equals one unit on screen.
False: moving frequent controls farther away increases pointing time. Frequent controls should be near.
False: target size matters too. Time depends on distance and size together.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about direct and indirect pointing is/are true?
o: A touchscreen is direct pointing.
A mouse is indirect pointing with a variable control–display ratio.
A trackpad is direct pointing.
Direct mapping implies a 1:1 control–display ratio.
Indirect devices cannot apply gain.
8.e: A trackpad moves a separate cursor, so it is indirect. Indirect devices can apply gain, which is how they get their variable C-D ratio.
w: True: you touch the target itself, so there is no separate cursor.
True: you move the mouse on a desk and the cursor moves on a screen, with software controlling the ratio.
False: a trackpad moves a separate cursor, so it is indirect.
True: with direct pointing the finger and the display coincide, so the ratio is 1:1.
False: gain is exactly what indirect devices apply, such as pointer acceleration.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about text entry is/are true?
o: QWERTY encourages alternating hands.
Dvorak places the most common letters on the home row.
QWERTY persists because it is the fastest layout.
QWERTY persists through network effects and training inertia.
On-screen keyboards can never be redesigned.
8.e: QWERTY is dominant, not fastest. It stays because of habit and the cost of retraining, and screens make new layouts possible.
w: True: many common English letter pairs sit on opposite hands, which helps typing flow.
True: Dvorak puts the most frequent letters under the strongest fingers on the home row.
False: QWERTY persists but is not the fastest layout.
True: everyone already knows it, devices ship with it and retraining is costly.
False: on-screen keyboards are software, so they can be redesigned (e.g. swipe and predictive layouts).

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about touch input is/are true?
o: The fat-finger problem arises from occlusion and imprecision.
Hover is fully available on touch.
Larger touch targets help.
Multi-touch gestures allow richer input.
Touch is always more accurate than a mouse.
8.e: Touch lacks hover and is less precise than a mouse, but gestures give it richer input.
w: True: the finger hides the target and is wide relative to small buttons.
False: a finger cannot hover, so hover tooltips and previews do not work on touch.
True: bigger targets are easier to hit with a wide, imprecise fingertip.
True: pinch, swipe and rotate use several fingers for richer input than a single cursor.
False: touch is generally less precise because of finger width and occlusion.

8.q: Which design change(s) follow Fitts’s Law?
o: Enlarge a frequently used button.
Place a frequent control near where the pointer or finger finished the previous step.
Make two different buttons identical and adjacent.
Move a frequently used button to a far corner of the screen.
On a desktop, place a frequently used toolbar at the screen edge.
8.e: Confusable adjacent buttons raise errors, and far-away targets take longer to reach.
w: True: bigger targets are quicker to hit.
True: a shorter distance reduces movement time.
False: identical adjacent buttons cause slips. That is an error-prevention issue, not Fitts's Law.
False: moving a frequent control farther away increases the distance, so it slows reaching.
True: the cursor stops at the edge, so the edge acts as an infinitely deep target.

8.q: A designer is deciding where to place a frequently used button. Which statements about Fitts’s Law are true?
o: Larger targets are faster to hit.
Moving a frequently used control farther away speeds it up.
Screen edges and corners are effectively very large targets for a mouse.
Pointing time depends on distance only.
Pointing time grows with distance and shrinks with target size.
8.e: Fitts’s Law says that the time to acquire a target depends on both its distance and its size.
w: True: a larger target is acquired faster.
False: a longer distance increases the pointing time.
True: the cursor stops at the edge, so edge targets are easy to hit.
False: target size matters as well as distance.
True: this is the distance and size relationship in Fitts’s Law.

8.q: Which statements about text entry techniques are true?
o: Gesture typing recognises a continuous stroke as a word by its shape.
Speech recognition is fast, but spoken language differs from written text.
Soft keyboards have less tactile feedback than physical keys.
Mobile multi-tap puts little load on the user.
QWERTY is the fastest possible layout.
8.e: Each technique has trade-offs. QWERTY persists through network effects and training inertia, not speed.
w: True: a swipe across the keyboard is matched to a word.
True: noise, privacy and the structure of speech are constraints.
True: on-screen keys give lower tactile feedback.
False: multi-tap has a high cognitive and motor load.
False: QWERTY persists through training inertia, not because it is fastest.

8.q: Which statements about Fitts’s Law and the index of difficulty are true?
o: ID = log₂(D/W + 1).
The index of difficulty rises as distance D increases.
The index of difficulty falls as target width W increases.
Pointing time is independent of target size.
A smaller target always makes pointing faster.
8.e: Difficulty grows with distance and shrinks with target width.
w: True: this is the formulation given in the course.
True: longer distance means more difficulty.
True: a wider target is easier to hit.
False: size matters in Fitts’s Law.
False: smaller targets are harder to hit.

8.q: Which statements about the control–display (C-D) ratio and pointing are correct?
o: It relates physical device movement to cursor movement.
A touchscreen is direct pointing with a 1:1 mapping.
A mouse is indirect pointing, and its ratio can vary.
A trackpad is direct pointing.
Indirect devices cannot apply gain.
8.e: Direct devices map the finger to the screen, while indirect devices can apply gain.
w: True: this is the definition of the C-D ratio.
True: direct mapping is 1:1.
True: indirect pointing can use a variable ratio.
False: a trackpad is indirect, since the pad is not the screen.
False: indirect devices can apply gain.

8.q: Which statements about touch input are true?
o: The fat-finger problem arises from imprecision and the finger occluding the target.
A callout-based technique such as Shift helps with occlusion.
Larger targets reduce touch errors.
A finger is more precise than a mouse pointer.
Touch has hover available as a fallback.
8.e: A finger is imprecise, covers what it touches and cannot hover.
w: True: the finger is imprecise and hides the target.
True: it shows the covered area in a callout.
True: a larger target is easier to hit.
False: a mouse pointer is more precise than a finger.
False: a finger cannot hover.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about density-independent units (DP on Android, PT on iOS) is/are true?
o: The operating system converts DP/PT to the right number of physical pixels.
A 100 × 100 px image appears physically smaller on a higher-PPI screen.
Using raw pixels guarantees a consistent physical size across devices.
A design specified in DP/PT renders at a consistent physical size across densities.
A higher-PPI screen shows the same pixel dimensions at a larger physical size.
9.e: Raw pixels vary in physical size with density.
w: True: the OS converts DP/PT to physical pixels.
True: the same pixels cover less physical size on a higher-PPI screen.
False: raw pixels change physical size with density.
True: DP/PT keeps a consistent physical size.
False: higher PPI makes the same pixels physically smaller.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about mobile usability patterns is/are true?
o: Give immediate visual feedback after actions.
Ask for a permission at the moment it is needed.
Ask for all permissions on first launch.
Bottom, thumb-reachable navigation supports one-handed use.
Small, dense layouts are preferred.
9.e: Context makes a permission request understandable.
w: True: immediate feedback reassures users.
True: ask for a permission when it is needed and understandable.
False: asking for everything at launch is confusing.
True: thumb-reachable navigation supports one-handed use.
False: small dense layouts hurt touch accuracy.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about mobile context is/are true?
o: Mobile use is frequently interrupted.
Devices are location-aware and sensor-rich.
Users usually have long uninterrupted focus.
Hover can be used for tooltips on touch screens.
Testing on real devices is recommended.
9.e: Touch screens have no hover, and mobile attention is fragmented by interruptions.
w: True: users are on the move, so sessions are short and often cut off.
True: GPS and sensors let apps use location and context.
False: attention on mobile is fragmented, with short sessions and interruptions.
False: a finger cannot hover, so tooltips that rely on hover will not appear.
True: real devices expose touch, performance, glare and context problems that emulators hide.

9.q: Which of the following are sound principles for designing mobile apps?
o: Show the value of the app upfront.
Allow ‘go back’ in one step.
Differentiate ‘sign in’ from ‘sign up’.
Hide the search field in a menu.
Require registration before showing any content.
9.e: Prominent search and delayed registration are recommended, so hiding search and forcing early sign-up are wrong.
w: True: users decide quickly, so the benefit should be clear before they commit.
True: a clear way back reduces frustration and abandonment.
True: confusing returning and new users causes drop-off, so label them clearly.
False: search should be prominent, not hidden in a menu.
False: forced registration before value drives users away, so it should come later.

9.q: Which approach(es) suit adapting a desktop website for mobile?
o: Prioritise the primary tasks and disclose detail progressively.
Shrink the desktop layout proportionally.
Use large touch targets.
Keep hover-only menus.
Use overview → scan → detail zoom.
9.e: Shrinking and hover menus break on touch, while prioritising and large targets suit small screens.
w: True: small screens force you to put the main tasks first and reveal extra detail on demand.
False: shrinking everything makes text and targets too small and the layout cramped.
True: fingers are wide, so larger targets cut errors.
False: touch has no hover, so those menus cannot be opened.
True: show an overview first, then let users scan and zoom in to detail.

9.q: A tool tip appears only when the cursor hovers over a control. The team plans to ship the same screen on phones. Which claims are defensible?
o: Touch has no hover, so hover-only tooltips cannot be opened.
Larger touch targets reduce fat-finger errors.
Mobile attention is fragmented by interruptions, so prioritise content.
A finger is more precise than a mouse pointer.
Hover-only menus are fine on mobile.
9.e: A finger cannot hover, covers the target and is imprecise, and mobile use is interrupted.
w: True: a finger cannot hover.
True: larger targets cut errors caused by finger occlusion and imprecision.
True: mobile use is short and interrupted, so prioritise content.
False: a finger is less precise than a mouse pointer.
False: those menus cannot be opened on a touchscreen.

o: Use often happens while moving or multitasking.
Attention is short and frequently interrupted.
Devices are location-aware and sensor-rich.
A mobile device should be treated as a desktop that moves.
Mouse clicks are the dominant input.
9.e: Mobile is not a small desktop: context, fingers and attention all change.
w: True: users often multitask and move.
True: interruptions are common.
True: location services and sensors such as GPS and accelerometers are available.
False: the course warns against this mindset.
False: touch, gesture and voice dominate on mobile.

9.q: Which are mobile usability patterns the course recommends?
o: Immediate visual feedback after actions.
Overview, scan, then detail zoom.
Asking for a permission at the moment it is needed.
Asking for every permission at first launch.
Placing all navigation at the top, out of thumb reach.
9.e: Patterns reduce memory load and fit one-handed, interrupted use.
w: True: it confirms the action registered and shows system status.
True: it lets users narrow their focus progressively.
True: in-context requests explain why the permission is needed.
False: up-front requests lack context.
False: bottom-oriented, thumb-reachable navigation supports one-handed use.

9.q: Which statements about density-independent units (DP on Android, PT on iOS) are true?
o: They adapt to the screen’s pixel density.
They help one design look similar across devices.
They are device-independent design units.
A pixel-based size looks the same physical size on every screen.
They make touch targets irrelevant.
9.e: DP and PT keep physical size roughly constant across screens with different pixel densities.
w: True: they adapt to PPI.
True: they support cross-device consistency.
True: they are device-independent units.
False: the same number of pixels is physically smaller on a denser screen.
False: target size still matters on touch.

9.q: A desktop website is being adapted for phones. Which approaches fit?
o: Show only what is needed right now.
Prioritise the primary task and keep navigation simple.
Minimise the input effort required.
Keep hover-only menus.
Shrink the desktop layout without changing it.
9.e: Mobile needs priority content, simple navigation and little input effort.
w: True: it reduces load.
True: the primary task should come first.
True: typing on a phone is costly.
False: touch cannot hover.
False: a shrunken desktop layout ignores mobile constraints.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about how people read online is/are true?
o: Text-heavy pages are often scanned in an F-pattern.
Low-text pages with a single call to action often suit a Z-pattern.
Most people read every word.
Viewers tend to follow another person’s gaze in a photo.
Eye-tracking shows attention stays at the page centre.
10.e: The baby-face study showed attention following the gaze of the person in the photo.
w: True: people read the first lines across, then scan down the left edge as interest fades.
True: the eye moves along the top, diagonally down, then across, which suits sparse pages.
False: most people scan online and skip much of the text.
True: viewers look where the person in the picture looks, so gaze can steer attention to a call to action.
False: attention follows the content layout and hierarchy, not a fixed spot.

10.q: Which of the following increase(s) information scent?
o: Descriptive link labels such as ‘Compare pricing plans’.
Generic links such as ‘Click here’.
Bulleted lists and highlighted keywords.
Dense paragraphs that enumerate options.
Meaningful headings that summarise sections.
10.e: Vague links and dense text weaken scent, so users cannot judge where a path leads.
w: True: the label tells users what is behind the link, so they can choose confidently.
False: 'Click here' gives no clue about the destination.
True: lists and highlighted keywords make the relevant words easy to spot while scanning.
False: dense paragraphs hide the options, so users cannot see which path to follow.
True: informative headings tell users what each section contains before they read it.

10.q: Which of the following practice(s) violate(s) data integrity?
o: Truncating a bar chart’s y-axis to exaggerate differences.
Cherry-picking a time window that supports a claim.
Using different y-scales across small multiples without saying so.
Labelling units and sources.
Using the same colour for the same category in every chart.
10.e: Labelling and consistency support integrity. Distorting scales, selecting data and hiding scale differences mislead readers.
w: True: a truncated axis makes small differences look large.
True: choosing a convenient window hides the broader trend.
True: readers assume the scales match, so comparing multiples with hidden different scales misleads.
False: labelling units and sources lets readers interpret and verify the data.
False: consistent colour meaning helps readers compare charts. Inconsistent colour is what causes confusion.

10.q: Which chart choice(s) fit the purpose?
o: Small multiples to compare many similar charts.
A treemap to show a trend over time.
A line chart for trends over time.
A pie chart to compare 15 categories precisely.
A scatter plot to show a relationship between two variables.
10.e: Pies fail with many categories, and treemaps show part-to-whole hierarchies, not time.
w: True: repeating the same chart makes differences between panels easy to see.
False: a treemap shows part-to-whole hierarchy by area. A line chart suits trends over time.
True: a line connects points in sequence, which makes direction and change over time clear.
False: with 15 slices, angles are hard to compare, so a bar chart would be more precise.
True: each point plots two variables, so patterns and correlations show up.

10.q: Which of the following improve(s) the scannability of a long document?
o: One idea per paragraph.
Highlighting keywords.
Using lists instead of paragraphs that enumerate options.
Starting with a long introduction before any content.
Overly promotional wording to attract attention.
10.e: Promotion and long intros hurt scanning, because readers skim for the content they came for.
w: True: scanners can read the first words and decide whether to continue.
True: keywords stand out and let readers pick out meaning quickly.
True: a list makes each option a separate, visible line.
False: a long introduction delays the content readers want.
False: promotional language lowers credibility and makes readers skip the text.

10.q: Visitors cannot find application deadlines. The page has vague labels, equally prominent headings and status shown only by colour. Select all defensible changes.
o: Rename “More” to “Application deadlines” if that is its destination.
Use heading sizes to distinguish sections from body text.
Group related information using proximity and consistent styles.
Use text or symbols alongside colour to communicate status.
Increase saturation so colour alone communicates status.
10.e: Specific labels, a clear hierarchy, grouping and redundant cues all help. Colour alone excludes users who cannot distinguish the colours.
w: True: a specific label tells people where the link goes.
True: size shows hierarchy.
True: grouping and consistent styles show what belongs together.
True: text or symbols mean status does not depend on colour alone.
False: stronger colour alone is still colour alone.

10.q: Which writing practices make web text scannable?
o: Highlight keywords.
Use meaningful sub-headings.
Use bulleted lists and one idea per paragraph.
Use promotional language to attract attention.
Write long paragraphs so nothing is missed.
10.e: Users scan rather than read. Promotional language imposes a cognitive burden.
w: True: highlighted keywords draw the eye.
True: sub-headings should be meaningful, not clever.
True: lists and short paragraphs scan well.
False: users have to filter out the hyperbole.
False: extra ideas in a paragraph are skipped.

10.q: Which statements about the F-pattern and the Z-pattern are correct?
o: The F-pattern suits text-heavy pages such as articles.
The Z-pattern suits low-text pages with a call-to-action.
In an F-pattern the user scans down the left-hand edge.
The Z-pattern is best for long articles.
Both patterns mean users read every word.
10.e: F is for text-heavy pages and Z is for simple pages with one call-to-action.
w: True: text-heavy pages are scanned in an F shape.
True: landing pages place the call-to-action along the Z.
True: after the top lines the user scans down the left side.
False: the Z suits low-text layouts.
False: users scan, they do not read word-by-word.

o: Link labels that predict what is behind them.
Clear, specific headings.
Navigation cues that tell users whether they are getting closer.
Vague labels such as “More”.
Clever slogans in place of descriptive headings.
10.e: Information scent is how well navigation cues predict where relevant content is.
w: True: good labels predict the destination.
True: specific headings give a stronger scent.
True: scent is about cues that predict where content lies.
False: vague labels give a weak scent.
False: clever wording hides what the heading is about.

10.q: Which chart choices fit their purpose?
o: A line chart for change over time.
A bar chart for comparing categories.
A scatter plot for the relationship between two numeric variables.
A pie chart with twenty thin slices to compare values precisely.
A truncated axis that exaggerates a small difference.
10.e: Choose the chart by what you want people to see, and keep the data honest.
w: True: lines show trends over time.
True: bars compare categories.
True: scatter plots show relationships.
