False: twenty slices are hard to compare.
False: a truncated axis misrepresents the data.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about colour in visualisation is/are true?
o: Ordered quantities are best encoded with lightness.
Limit qualitative categories to about six hues.
Use twelve hues to distinguish categories.
Supplement colour with shape, position or size for colour-blind users.
Red and green alone are safe for everyone.
11.e: Too many hues are indistinguishable; red-green is problematic.
w: True: lightness encodes order well.
True: about six hues is a sensible limit.
False: twelve hues are hard to tell apart.
True: add shape, position or size for colour-blind users.
False: red-green alone is a problem for many.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about colour theory is/are true?
o: RGB is additive and used on screens.
CMYK is subtractive and used in print.
Complementary colours sit opposite each other.
Analogous colours are opposite each other.
A triadic scheme uses two colours next to each other on the wheel.
11.e: Analogous colours are neighbours, and a triadic scheme spaces three colours evenly around the wheel.
w: True: screens emit light, so mixing red, green and blue gives white.
True: inks absorb light, so more ink gives a darker result.
True: opposite hues give maximum contrast.
False: analogous colours are neighbours on the wheel.
False: a triadic scheme spaces three colours evenly around the wheel, not next to each other.

11.q: Which Gestalt principle(s) is/are correctly matched?
o: Common region — items inside a shared border are grouped.
Proximity — things close together seem related.
Similarity — things that look alike seem related.
Closure — items that are close together seem related.
Gestalt principles are decoration only.
11.e: Gestalt principles guide how people perceive and group elements, so they affect layout.
w: True: a card or box makes its contents read as a unit.
True: spacing alone can create groups.
True: shared colour, shape or size suggests a relationship.
False: that describes proximity. Closure is about completing an incomplete shape, as in progress rings.
False: they describe how perception works, so they shape layout.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about typography is/are true?
o: Typography is functional, not just aesthetic.
Tiny, low-contrast print can make critical information easy to miss.
Serif fonts always signal informality.
More fonts always improve readability.
Consistent font use reduces eye strain.
11.e: Too many fonts hurt readability, and serif fonts tend to signal authority rather than informality.
w: True: type choices affect whether people can read and understand the content.
True: small, faint text is overlooked, especially when it carries the key information.
False: serif faces are associated with authority and respect, not informality.
False: too many fonts hurt readability.
True: consistent letterforms are easier on the eyes.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about colour meaning is/are true?
o: Red signals good luck in Chinese culture but danger or ‘stop’ in Western culture.
Blue is often associated with calmness and trust.
Colour meanings are universal.
Never rely on colour alone to convey information.
Colour perception is identical for everyone.
11.e: Colour meanings are cultural and perception varies, so colour alone should never carry the message.
w: True: culture shapes what red means.
True: blue is widely linked to calm and trust.
False: meanings differ by culture.
True: always add another cue such as shape, text or position.
False: colour perception varies, for example with colour blindness.

11.q: Which design choices use Gestalt principles correctly?
o: Put related fields inside one card or bordered box (common region).
Squeeze unrelated fields close together to save room (proximity).
Style all links in one colour (similarity).
Align items in a row or column so they read as a sequence (continuity).
A progress ring with a small gap will be read as incomplete and broken (closure).
11.e: Proximity groups things that sit close together, and closure makes us complete small gaps.
w: True: a shared boundary makes its contents read as one group.
False: elements that sit close together are read as related, so this groups unrelated fields.
True: things that look alike are seen as related.
True: elements along a line or smooth curve read as a sequence.
False: closure means we fill in small gaps and see a whole shape.

11.q: Which statements about the Gestalt principles are correct?
o: Closure: we fill in small gaps to see a complete shape.
Figure/ground: we separate a stable figure from the background, such as blurring the background behind a dialog.
“Enclosure” and “common region” are two different principles.
Proximity: closer elements are grouped and separated from those that are farther away.
Similarity groups items only if they are enclosed in a box.
11.e: Enclosure is the older name for common region, and similarity needs no boundary.
w: True: progress rings and loaders rely on this.
True: the blur pushes the background back so the foreground reads as the figure.
False: they are the same principle under two names.
True: this is the proximity principle.
False: similarity depends on shared shape, colour or size, not on a box.

11.q: A form has labels far from their inputs, and every button looks the same. Which changes apply Gestalt principles?
o: Place each label close to its input (proximity).
Style the primary action differently from secondary actions (similarity and contrast).
Use many different fonts and colours so every element stands out.
Put related fields in one bordered section (common region).
Remove all whitespace to reduce scrolling.
11.e: Gestalt grouping needs distance, shared styles and shared regions that match the real relationships.
w: True: closeness shows which label belongs to which input.
True: like items look alike, and the primary action is made distinct.
False: too many styles break the groups instead of showing them.
True: a shared boundary groups the fields.
False: whitespace helps separate groups.

11.q: Which statements about colour schemes and colour use are correct?
o: A monochromatic scheme uses one hue.
An analogous scheme uses adjacent hues.
A complementary scheme uses opposite hues.
Ordered values are best shown with distinct, unrelated hues.
Colour alone is enough to communicate status.
11.e: Use hue for categories and lightness for ordered values, and never rely on colour alone.
w: True: one hue, with variations in lightness.
True: adjacent hues on the colour wheel.
True: opposite hues on the colour wheel.
False: ordered values should use a lightness gradient, and hues suit categories.
False: colour should be paired with text or symbols.

11.q: Which statements about fonts and affordance are correct?
o: Serif fonts signal authority and professionalism.
Script fonts signal enthusiasm and creativity.
Sans-serif fonts signal simplicity and modernity.
A button should look as if it can be pressed.
Affordance is about the system’s internal code.
11.e: Fonts carry associations, and visual affordance shows what action is possible.
w: True: serif fonts carry that association.
True: script fonts carry that association.
True: sans-serif fonts carry that association.
True: affordance is the appearance signalling what action is possible.
False: affordance is a property of an object’s appearance, not its code.

12.q: Which of the following describe(s) a cognitive walkthrough?
o: Experts step through task actions with four prescribed questions
It focuses on learnability for new users
One question is ‘Will the user recognise which visible action is correct?’
It requires real users to perform the tasks
It evaluates whether the database will scale
12.e: A cognitive walkthrough is an expert, task-based method that looks at learnability for new users. It does not need real users and is not a technical test.
w: True: the experts follow the user's route through each step and ask the same four questions at every action.
True: the method asks whether a first-time user could work out what to do, so learnability is the aim.
True: the question is whether users will recognise that the visible action is the right one.
False: it is an inspection, so it does not need real users to perform tasks.
False: it evaluates usability, such as whether people can find and understand actions, not technical scalability.

12.q: Which pairing(s) of finding and heuristic is/are correct?
o: Greying out unavailable dates — error prevention.
A ‘you are here’ map — error prevention.
Check-in counters at a hotel’s front — consistency and standards.
Showing the raw term ‘UTF-8’ instead of a cart icon — violates match with the real world.
Undo and redo — help and documentation.
12.e: A 'you are here' map shows status, and undo and redo belong to user control and freedom.
w: True: users cannot pick an invalid date, so the error is prevented.
False: a 'you are here' map tells users where they are, which is visibility of system status, not error prevention.
True: familiar layouts follow conventions users already know.
True: jargon the user does not understand breaks the match between system and real world.
False: undo and redo belong to user control and freedom.

12.q: Which factor(s) determine the severity of a usability problem?
o: How frequently it occurs.
Its impact on the user.
How persistent it is.
Whether the evaluator likes the design.
The number of lines of code needed to fix it.
12.e: Severity is frequency, impact and persistence.
w: True: frequency counts.
True: impact counts.
True: persistence counts.
False: evaluator preference is not a severity factor.
False: fix effort is not a severity factor.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about heuristic evaluators is/are true?
o: Different experts find different problems.
Adding evaluators brings diminishing returns.
Evaluators should work individually first, then debrief.
Evaluators should work together from the start.
One expert is enough because experts are unbiased.
12.e: Evaluators work individually first and then debrief, because independent judgements find more problems than one expert or a group working together.
w: True: each evaluator notices different things, which is why one person is not enough.
True: the first few evaluators find most problems and each extra one adds fewer new ones.
True: working alone first gives independent views before the group combines them in a debrief.
False: starting together makes people anchor on the first views, so independence is lost.
False: one expert misses many problems and brings their own biases.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about inspection is/are true?
o: Experts may miss problems that real users hit.
In this lecture, ‘expert’ means a member of the target user group.
Inspection can be cheap and early.
Inspection can replace usability testing entirely.
Experts bring their own biases.
12.e: 'Expert' here means a UX expert, not a typical user. Inspections are cheap and early, but they cannot replace testing with real users.
w: True: experts judge from knowledge and may not anticipate what real users do.
False: here 'expert' means a UX expert, not a typical member of the user group.
True: inspections can be done on early designs without recruiting users, so they are cheap and quick.
False: inspections cannot replace user testing, because only real users reveal some problems.
True: experts have their own habits and assumptions, which colour what they notice.

12.q: Which claims about heuristic evaluation (an inspection method) are defensible?
o: Several evaluators find more problems than one.
It can replace user testing.
It suggests likely problems but does not prove users can succeed.
Pairing double experts (usability and domain) beats single experts.
Evaluators have to be real users.
12.e: An inspection is done by experts, so it is used in addition to, not instead of, user testing.
w: True: different evaluators find different problems.
False: only real users reveal some problems, so inspection cannot replace user testing.
True: experts are not real users.
True: knowing both usability and the domain finds more.
False: inspection involves experts, not users.

12.q: Which statements about the cognitive walkthrough are true?
o: It evaluates learnability for a first-time user.
Experts walk through a scenario step by step.
Four questions are asked at each step.
It requires real users to complete the tasks.
Its main output is a rating of overall aesthetics.
12.e: A cognitive walkthrough is an inspection method, so experts, not users, walk through the task.
w: True: it focuses on a first-time user’s learnability.
True: it follows a task scenario.
True: four questions are asked per step.
False: it is an inspection method, so no real users take part.
False: its output is a list of problems per step.

12.q: Which statements about heuristic evaluation are correct?
o: Experts compare the interface against Nielsen’s 10 heuristics.
Several evaluators are used, with diminishing returns for each extra one.
Problems are given a severity based on frequency, impact and persistence.
It uses real users as the evaluators.
One evaluator finds nearly every problem.
12.e: Heuristic evaluation uses several experts, because each finds different problems and the gains diminish.
w: True: those heuristics are the basis of the evaluation.
True: more evaluators find more, but each extra one adds less.
True: severity combines how often, how much and how persistent.
False: the evaluators are experts, not users.
False: one evaluator misses many problems.

12.q: Which pairings of a finding and a Nielsen heuristic are correct?
o: The system shows no loading indicator after Submit: visibility of system status.
An error message says only “Error 42”: help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors.
Users must remember a code from a previous screen: recognition rather than recall.
A button looks different on every page: error prevention.
A required help page is missing: aesthetic and minimalist design.
12.e: Match each problem to the heuristic it violates.
w: True: feedback about system status is missing.
True: the message does not help users diagnose or recover.
True: it taxes memory instead of showing information.
False: that is a consistency and standards problem.
False: that is help and documentation.

12.q: Which statements about the use of experts in inspection are justified?
o: “Expert” here means a UX expert, not someone from the target user population.
Experts can miss problems that only real users would hit.
Experts are often easier to recruit than real users.
Experts flag only serious problems and never trivial ones.
Experts are free from bias.
12.e: Inspection is quick and cheap, but experts are not real users and they carry biases.
w: True: it is a stand-in evaluator with usability knowledge.
True: real users hit problems experts do not.
True: recruiting is easier and the feedback is easier to process.
False: experts often flag many trivial issues.
False: they carry their own biases.

13.q: Which of the following statement(s) about evaluation strategies is/are true?
o: A field study offers high realism but low control.
A laboratory study offers high control but lower realism.
A survey is easy to run at scale but relies on self-report.
Inspection offers the highest realism.
Experiments maximise realism.
13.e: Inspection involves experts rather than realistic use, and experiments maximise precision, not realism.
w: True: you see real behaviour in context, but you cannot control what happens.
True: a laboratory setting controls distractions but is artificial.
True: you can reach many people, but they report what they recall or think.
False: inspection is done by experts, so it does not capture realistic use.
False: experiments maximise precision by controlling variables, which reduces realism.

13.q: Which of the following are quantitative usability metrics?
o: Task completion time.
Number of errors.
A quotation from a think-aloud session.
Task success rate.
A participant’s story about their frustration.
13.e: Quotations and stories are qualitative.
w: True: time is a number measured on each task.
True: the number of errors is counted, so it is quantitative.
False: a quotation is words, so it is qualitative.
True: success rate is the proportion of successful attempts, a number.
False: a story about frustration is a narrative, so it is qualitative.

13.q: Which of the following statement(s) about usability task cards and success criteria is/are true?
o: A task card lists the goal, task, data to collect and apparatus.
A task card should list the exact buttons the participant must press.
A good success criterion is measurable and set before testing.
‘Users like it’ is a well-formed success criterion.
The data field says what you will record during the task.
13.e: A task card = Goal, Task, Data, Apparatus. Success criteria must be objective, measurable and set before testing.
w: True: these four parts define what to achieve, what to do, what to collect and the equipment.
False: tasks should state a goal, not the path. Listing buttons tells the participant what to do.
True: a measurable criterion, set before testing, avoids choosing the target after seeing the results.
False: 'like' is subjective and cannot be checked against a threshold.
True: the data field names what you will measure or record, such as time or errors.

13.q: Which of the following statement(s) about moderated usability testing is/are true?
o: A facilitator is present and can probe why a participant did something.
It is usually run as a survey of hundreds of participants.
A small number of participants can reveal the major, frequent problems.
It records what people say they would do rather than what they actually do.
Thinking aloud commonly accompanies it, to reveal reasoning.
13.e: Moderated tests are small and observed, so you can see behaviour and ask why.
w: True: the facilitator can ask follow-up questions in the moment.
False: moderated tests are small and observed. Surveys reach hundreds.
True: five to eight participants usually find the major, frequent problems.
False: usability testing observes behaviour. Self-report is what surveys capture.
True: think-aloud lets you hear the participant's reasoning.

13.q: Which of the following illustrate(s) triangulation?
o: Combining a heuristic evaluation, a laboratory study and an A/B test.
Using methods whose blind spots differ.
Relying on one large survey because large samples are enough.
Observation plus an experiment.
Asking the same question three times in one survey.
13.e: Triangulation combines different methods so that their blind spots differ.
w: True: inspection, user behaviour and live comparison look at the product in different ways.
True: the point is that what one method misses another can catch.
False: a large survey still has one blind spot, self-report, so more people do not fix it.
True: observation shows real behaviour and an experiment adds control.
False: repeating a question does not add a different method, so it adds no new view.

13.q: The repair-hub team plans three evaluations: an inspection of labels, navigation and feedback against usability principles; a laboratory study where representative borrowers find and reserve a kit; and a randomised web A/B test of the two implemented versions. Which statements are correct?
o: The inspection gives likely problems to address early, but does not prove users can succeed.
The laboratory study shows actual task success, time and observed confusion.
The A/B test gives evidence of the effect on reservation completion.
All three answer the same question, so one is enough.
The inspection shows how users behave in the real world.
13.e: The methods answer different questions, so each contribution has to be explained. Combining them (triangulation) covers each one’s blind spot.
w: True: experts find likely problems cheaply, but they are not real users.
True: users are observed doing real tasks in a controlled setting.
True: a randomised comparison of versions measures the effect on reservations.
False: each method answers a different question.
False: inspection is done by experts, not by users in real use.

13.q: Which statements about the four evaluation strategies are correct?
o: Inspection has low realism and low effort.
Field studies have high realism and low control.
Laboratory studies have high control and medium realism.
Surveys give behaviour in real contexts.
An experiment is a fifth, separate strategy.
13.e: The four strategies are Inspection, Field studies, Laboratory studies and Surveys, and an experiment is a special type of user study.
w: True: it uses experts, so realism is low and the effort is low.
True: real context but little control.
True: a controlled environment with moderate realism.
False: surveys give opinion, not behaviour.
False: an experiment is a user study with two or more conditions, run within a laboratory study or online.

13.q: Which statements about usability metrics and success criteria are correct?
o: Effectiveness, efficiency, safety, utility, learnability and memorability are six usability metrics.
Success criteria should be measurable and set before testing.
“The design should be liked” is a measurable criterion.
A satisfaction questionnaire such as ASQ is a post-task measure.
PSSUQ is a post-task measure.
13.e: Define measurable criteria before testing, and use the right questionnaire for the right moment.
w: True: these are the six metrics.
True: measurable targets keep the evaluation objective.
False: “liked” is subjective and cannot be checked against a threshold.
True: ASQ is asked after each task or scenario.
False: PSSUQ is a post-study questionnaire.

13.q: A team combines an inspection, a laboratory study and a survey for the same product. Which statements justify this?
o: Each method has a different blind spot.
Combining methods is called triangulation.
One method is enough if it is the most realistic.
The methods’ results cannot be compared.
Inspection removes the need for any user data.
13.e: Triangulation combines methods so that the weaknesses of one are covered by another.
w: True: inspection misses real users, laboratory studies are artificial and surveys are opinion.
True: using more than one method is triangulation.
False: no single method covers every blind spot.
False: results from different methods can complement and be compared.
False: only real users give actual behaviour data.

13.q: Which statements rebut the argument “we are the experts, so we do not need to test with users”?
o: You cannot tell how good a UI is until users try it.
Designers do not automatically know what users want.
Even experienced designers need validation.
Real users can never reveal unexpected problems.
Evaluating with users is always cheaper than inspection.
13.e: Real-user evaluation is costly but is the only source of actual behaviour data.
w: True: real use reveals real reactions.
True: expertise in design is not knowledge of the users.
True: validation is needed whatever the experience.
False: real users uncover unexpected issues.
False: user studies are more costly and time-consuming than inspection.

14.q: Which of the following is/are qualitative data?
o: Think-aloud transcripts.
Time on task.
Likert ratings.
A count of how many users met an issue.
Themes drawn from open comments.
14.e: Times, ratings and counts are numbers, so they are quantitative. Transcripts and themes are descriptive.
w: True: words describing thoughts are qualitative.
False: time is measured as a number, so it is quantitative.
False: ratings are numbers on a scale, so they are quantitative.
False: a count is a number, so it is quantitative.
True: themes summarise what people said, which is qualitative.

14.q: Which of the following statement(s) about coding is/are true?
o: Clustering is informal grouping.
Coding is formal categorisation with defined criteria.
Inter-coder reliability checks whether independent coders classify the same way.
Affinity mapping uses statistical tests to sort codes into themes.
Open coding always yields only a few codes.
14.e: Open coding can produce very many codes, and affinity mapping groups codes into themes by hand.
w: True: similar items are grouped without strict rules.
True: coding uses defined categories and criteria.
True: agreement between independent coders shows the scheme is reliable.
False: affinity mapping is a manual grouping technique and does not use statistical tests.
False: open coding can generate thousands of codes before they are merged.

14.q: Which of the following statement(s) about observations and questions is/are true?
o: Observations are generally more reliable than self-reports for actions.
Questions remain useful for demographics and subjective assessments.
People are fully aware of what they do.
Closed questions are best for exploring unexpected insights.
Open-ended questions give richer, unexpected insights.
14.e: People are not fully aware of their actions, which is why observation matters.
w: True: people forget, rationalise or misreport what they do.
True: age, role and opinions are things only the person can tell you.
False: much behaviour is automatic, so people cannot describe it accurately.
False: closed questions limit answers to options you provided, so they cannot surface surprises.
True: people use their own words, which reveals issues you did not anticipate.

14.q: Which approach(es) are sensible for analysing hours of recordings?
o: Mark timestamps and critical incidents.
Always transcribe everything.
Transcribe key quotes only.
Use AI for first-pass coding and verify it by hand.
Skip human verification.
14.e: Humans still verify, because AI can miss or misread nuance.
w: True: timestamps let you jump back to important moments.
False: complete transcripts rarely repay the time spent.
True: key quotes carry the evidence you need for reporting.
True: AI can speed up the first pass, but a person must check the results.
False: unchecked AI coding can introduce errors and miss context.

14.q: Which of the following statement(s) about survey questions is/are true?
o: A Likert range gives more information than a binary easy/hard question.
A 5-point rating is qualitative.
Open-ended questions produce qualitative data.
‘Why do you think AI will help?’ is neutral.
‘Rate from 1 to 5’ is a closed question.
14.e: Ratings are quantitative, and the 'Why' question presumes that AI helps, so it is leading.
w: True: a range tells you how strongly someone agrees, not just which side they are on.
False: a numerical rating is quantitative.
True: open answers are in words, so they are qualitative.
False: it presumes that AI will help, which makes it a leading question.
True: the participant must choose from a fixed set of numbers.

14.q: After a laboratory study, the team has notes from observations and comments. Which steps are good qualitative analysis?
o: Put each relevant observation or comment on a separate note and keep its task and participant context.
Group related notes and label the recurring issue, keeping contradictory cases.
Treat a theme as proof of causation.
Discard contradictory cases to keep the themes clean.
Use a theme to propose a clearer design and retest it.
14.e: Themes guide explanations and design changes. They do not alone prove causation.
w: True: context is needed to interpret the note.
True: contradictory cases are kept, not hidden.
False: themes guide explanations but do not alone prove causation.
False: contradictory cases are evidence and should be preserved.
True: revise and test again.

14.q: Which statements about open and closed questions are correct?
o: Open questions are answered in the participant’s own words.
Closed questions are answered from fixed options.
Open questions can capture unexpected insights.
Closed-question responses are analysed for themes and patterns.
“What did you like about the UI?” is a closed question.
14.e: Open questions give qualitative data and closed questions give quantitative data.
w: True: participants answer in their own words.
True: the options are fixed.
True: they allow unexpected insights.
False: closed responses are counted and analysed statistically.
False: it invites a free answer, so it is open.

o: Critical incidents.
Think-aloud data.
Participant comments.
Time spent on a task.
Number of clicks.
14.e: Descriptions are qualitative and numbers are quantitative.
w: True: it is a description of what happened.
True: it is spoken description.
True: comments are words.
False: time is a number.
False: a count is a number.

14.q: Which statements about clustering and coding are correct?
o: Clustering groups comments into themes.
Coding formally labels items into categories.
Inter-coder reliability checks agreement between two independent coders.
Coding should be done by one person only, with no check.
Clustering and coding are the same thing.
14.e: Cluster into themes, code each item, then check agreement between coders.
w: True: grouping into themes is clustering.
True: coding is labelling into categories.
True: agreement is checked between independent coders.
False: a second coder is used to check reliability.
False: they are different steps.

14.q: Which statements about observations and questions are correct?
o: Observations are generally more reliable than self-reported answers.
People are often not fully aware of their own actions.
Questions are still useful for demographics and subjective views.
People always report their behaviour accurately.
Thinking aloud guarantees correct answers.
14.e: People often behave differently from what they report, but questions capture what observation cannot.
w: True: people are not always able to describe their actions accurately.
True: awareness of one’s own actions is limited.
True: observation cannot capture age or opinions easily.
False: self-reports are often inaccurate.
False: if you ask a question people will always give an answer, even if it is unrelated to facts.

15.q: Which of the following statement(s) about running a laboratory study is/are true?
o: In a pilot you may help participants.
In the main study you should follow the protocol and avoid interfering.
Materials include task cards, consent forms and questionnaires.
You recruit participants after running the study.
After analysis, fix every problem equally in the order found.
15.e: Recruitment comes before the sessions, and fixes should be prioritised by severity.
w: True: a pilot tests the protocol, so help reveals where it needs improving.
True: following the protocol keeps participants comparable.
True: these are the standard materials you prepare before running sessions.
False: you need participants before you can run the study, so recruit first.
False: fix severe problems first, rather than treating all problems equally.

15.q: Which statements about designing tasks and running the main study are true?
o: “Update your phone number in your account.”
“Click the Settings gear, then press Edit next to phone.”
Every participant gets the same tasks
If a participant is stuck in the main study, give hints
Tasks should be realistic
15.e: Good tasks state the goal, not the path.
w: True: it states what the participant wants to achieve without telling them how.
False: it spells out the buttons, so you cannot see whether the participant could find the way.
True: identical tasks make participants' results comparable.
False: hints in the main study bias results, so use pre-set intervention criteria instead.
True: realistic tasks show how people behave in real use.

15.q: Which of the following statement(s) about thinking aloud is/are true?
o: It reveals reasoning.
It can make tasks 25–100% longer.
Timing metrics are unaffected because participants talk in their own time.
It is the best way to measure speed.
It helps explain why problems happen.
15.e: Thinking aloud explains problems but distorts timing, so use other measures for speed.
w: True: you hear how participants interpret the interface.
True: talking while working slows people down.
False: because tasks take longer, timing data are distorted.
False: it distorts timing, so other measures are better for speed.
True: verbalised thoughts show what confused them.

15.q: Which of the following statement(s) about ethics is/are true?
o: Participation is voluntary and participants can stop at any time.
Stress that ‘we are testing the design, not you’.
Participants may become distressed, so facilitators must be supportive.
Recording should be hidden from participants.
Privacy need not be considered.
w: True: ethics requires voluntary participation and the right to withdraw.
True: this reminds participants that mistakes are the design's fault, which reduces anxiety.
True: tasks may be stressful, so facilitators should be supportive and ready to stop.
False: hidden recording breaks informed consent. It must be disclosed.
False: privacy must be respected, with anonymised data and secure storage.

15.q: Which of the following statement(s) about participants is/are true?
o: About 5–8 participants often find the major frequent problems.
Recruit people who represent the target users.
A convenience sample of classmates is ideal.
Prior experience can act as a confound.
More than 100 are required to find problems in qualitative tests.
w: True: five to eight users usually reveal the major, frequent problems.
True: results only apply if participants resemble the target users.
False: classmates are a convenience sample and may not represent real users.
True: prior experience can change how participants behave and distort comparisons.
False: qualitative tests look for problems, not statistical significance, so 100 participants are not needed.

15.q: A team runs a laboratory study where representative borrowers find and reserve a kit. Which statements are true?
o: Recruit participants who represent the target users.
A pilot with people outside the team checks that the prototype and the method work.
A laboratory study is more realistic than a field study.
A study protocol is the step-by-step procedure for a session.
“Measure usability” is a sufficient success definition.
15.e: A laboratory study trades realism for control. It needs observable measures, a protocol and a pilot.
w: True: results only transfer to users like the participants.
True: a pilot finds problems with the setup before the real sessions.
False: a field study is more realistic, a laboratory study gives control.
True: it fixes the tasks and steps for every participant.
False: it needs an observable definition such as correct reservation and time to correct confirmation.

15.q: Which lists give the six steps of a laboratory study in order?
o: Plan, Recruit, Prepare, Run, Analyse, Recommend.
Plan, Recruit, Prepare, Run (pilot first), Analyse, Recommend.
Recruit, Plan, Run, Prepare, Recommend, Analyse.
Analyse, Plan, Recruit, Prepare, Run, Recommend.
Plan, Run, Recruit, Analyse, Prepare, Recommend.
15.e: Order matters: the plan decides everything else, and a pilot comes before the real sessions.
w: True: it is the correct order.
True: it is correct, and the pilot is part of the Run step.
False: recruiting and preparing precede running, and analysis precedes recommending.
False: analysis comes after running.
False: running comes after recruiting and preparing.

15.q: Which statements about thinking aloud are true?
o: The participant verbalises their thoughts while performing a task.
It does not guarantee correct answers.
It can reveal why users struggle.
It never changes how the participant works.
It replaces the need for a task.
15.e: Think-aloud gives insight into reasoning, but it can be unreliable and it can change behaviour.
w: True: that is the method.
True: people will give an answer even when it has nothing to do with facts.
True: it shows reasoning and confusion.
False: speaking aloud can affect how people work.
False: participants still perform tasks.

15.q: Which statements about participants in a laboratory study are correct?
o: About 5–8 users reveal the major problems.
About 10–12 users reveal rarer problems.
About 15 or more users are needed for statistics.
One participant is enough to prove a design works.
Participants should be recruited from whoever is nearest, not from the target users.
15.e: Sample size depends on the goal: problems or statistics.
w: True: a few users reveal the major problems.
True: more reveal the rarer ones.
True: statistics need larger samples.
False: one person cannot generalise.
False: they should reflect the target users.

15.q: Which statements about ethics and the laboratory environment are correct?
o: Participants should give informed consent.
A quiet office without interruptions suits a laboratory study.
Realism elements can improve ecological validity.
A laboratory study is more realistic than a field study.
Ethics only matters for field studies.
15.e: A laboratory study trades realism for control, and the participants’ rights still apply.
w: True: consent protects participants.
True: it cuts distractions and keeps conditions consistent.
True: adding realistic elements balances control with authenticity.
False: a field study is more realistic.
False: it applies to every study with people.

16.q: Which of the following statement(s) about UI standards is/are true?
o: They enable innovation by reducing reinvention.
They inhibit innovation in the dimension they fix.
A standard fixes one dimension of a design so that effort can go elsewhere.
They make all innovation impossible.
Familiar patterns force users to learn a new mental model for each app.
16.e: Standards fix one dimension so effort can go elsewhere, and familiar patterns let users reuse what they already know.
w: True: designers do not have to reinvent basic parts, so effort goes elsewhere.
True: in the dimension the standard fixes, there is little room to innovate.
True: like a standard screw thread, fixing one dimension frees effort to innovate around it.
False: standards limit one dimension, not all innovation.
False: familiar patterns let users reuse their existing mental models.

16.q: Which of the following statement(s) about threshold and ceiling is/are true?
o: MS Word has a low threshold and a low ceiling for web pages.
JavaScript has the highest threshold and the highest ceiling of the three.
A high threshold means the tool is easy to start.
For a demo tomorrow, a low threshold fits best.
Ceiling means how hard a tool is to learn.
16.e: Threshold = ease of starting; ceiling = maximum capability.
w: True: Word is easy to start with (low threshold) but cannot do much for web pages (low ceiling).
True: JavaScript is harder to start with but can build almost anything.
False: a high threshold means the tool is harder to start with.
True: for a demo tomorrow, speed to a prototype matters more than capability.
False: ceiling is how much the tool can do, not how difficult it is to learn.

16.q: Which of the following statement(s) about UI tools is/are true?
o: They speed up development.
They can make non-standard widgets harder.
They can discourage change.
They remove the need for design skills.
Integrating several tools is usually seamless.
16.e: Tools do not replace design skill, and combining several tools can be discouraging.
w: True: ready-made components save time.
True: the standard components are easy, and anything unusual takes extra effort.
True: because the default path is easy, changing direction is less appealing.
False: design skills are still needed to decide what to build.
False: integrating several tools is often discouraging, and fixes can break workarounds.

16.q: Which of the following statement(s) about platform ecosystems are true?
o: Platform owners publish design guidelines that apps are expected to follow.
Different platforms have different conventions and guidelines.
Platform rules and store policies shape what apps can do.
Beta testing is done the same way on every platform.
Following a platform’s guidelines has no effect on how familiar the app feels to its users.
16.e: A platform owner controls its design guidance and store, so the rules differ between platforms and affect what an app can do.
w: True: owners provide guidelines for their platform.
True: conventions are platform-specific.
True: the owner controls the store, so its rules shape which apps and features are possible.
False: each platform has its own tools and services for beta testing.
False: familiar patterns let users reuse mental models they already have.

16.q: Which of the following statement(s) about generative UI is/are true?
o: It depends on design-system standards as constraints.
Goals and constraints matter most.
It removes the need for standards.
It can generate interfaces dynamically.
Humans have no role.
16.e: Standards still constrain generation, and people still set the goals.
w: True: standards keep generated interfaces consistent.
True: you specify goals and constraints, and the system assembles an interface.
False: standards still constrain generated UI.
True: interfaces can be assembled on the fly for the context.
False: humans still set the goals and review the results.

16.q: A student must choose a UI tool for a demo tomorrow and for a larger product later. Which statements about tool choice are true?
o: Threshold is how hard a tool is to learn or start using.
Ceiling is the limit on how sophisticated a result the tool can produce.
A good prototyping tool has a high threshold and a low ceiling.
Ask whether it supports the intended UX, how easily you can iterate and whether it allows user testing.
UI tools remove the need for user testing.
16.e: Choose a tool by its threshold, its ceiling and whether it supports the experience, iteration and testing.
w: True: a low threshold means it is easy to start.
True: a high ceiling means more sophisticated designs are possible.
False: that is the worst combination, hard to start and limited in what it can do.
True: these are the three questions for choosing a tool.
False: tools do not replace user testing.

16.q: Which statements about types of UI tools are correct?
o: A toolkit is mostly a library of components.
A framework is a coherent architecture and is harder to combine with others.
An IDE integrates toolkits and frameworks and often includes a UI builder.
A UI builder is a WYSIWYG editor.
Toolkits are always faster than frameworks, with no trade-off.
16.e: Each tool type has trade-offs between flexibility, speed and ease of combining.
w: True: toolkits are libraries of components.
True: frameworks are hard to combine.
True: IDEs bring tools together.
True: builders are WYSIWYG editors for the libraries.
False: toolkits are flexible but more work.

o: Efficiency, as streamlined processes save time and cost.
Compatibility, as interoperable parts give wider market access.
Consumer protection.
Standards make all innovation impossible.
A standard has no effect on competition or pricing.
16.e: A standard fixes one dimension of a design so effort can go elsewhere.
w: True: it saves time and cost.
True: it gives wider market access.
True: it supports safety, durability and fair markets.
False: a standard inhibits innovation in one area and enables it in another.
False: more suppliers keep standardised parts cheap.

16.q: A team needs a prototype by tomorrow, then a long-lived product. Which statements apply to tool choice?
o: For tomorrow, a low-threshold tool fits.
For the long-lived product, a higher ceiling matters.
A high ceiling means the tool is easy to learn.
Tool choice has no effect on iteration speed.
Choose the tool with the highest threshold in every case.
16.e: Threshold is how easy it is to start, and ceiling is the maximum capability.
w: True: you need to start quickly.
True: the product needs capability to grow.
False: ceiling is about maximum capability, not ease of learning.
False: a tool’s fit affects how easily you can iterate.
False: a high threshold means a tool is harder to start with.

16.q: Which statements about UI tools are correct?
o: They can speed up development.
They can make non-standard widgets harder.
They can discourage change.
They remove the need for design skills.
Integrating several tools is always seamless.
16.e: UI tools bring speed and consistency at the cost of flexibility.
w: True: they save effort.
True: a UI builder can limit non-standard widgets.
True: they can lock in early choices.
False: design skills are still needed.
False: integration is often hard.

17.q: Which of the following statement(s) about A/B testing is/are true?
o: The control is the unchanged baseline.
Assignment of users should be random.
Change several things at once to save time.
HiPPO stands for Highest Paid Person’s Opinion.
Senior staff intuition should override test data.
17.e: Changing many things at once confounds the result, and data should outweigh opinion.
w: True: the baseline lets you see what the change did.
True: random assignment makes the groups comparable.
False: several changes at once mean you cannot tell which one caused the effect.
True: HiPPO is the Highest Paid Person's Opinion, which testing aims to replace with data.
False: A/B testing exists to replace opinion with evidence about user behaviour.

17.q: Which statement(s) about changing several things at once in an A/B test are true?
o: If the new version does worse, you cannot tell which change caused it.
Bundling changes can hide a harmful change behind helpful ones.
Bundled changes can be separated afterwards by looking at the overall result.
It is a good way to save time without losing information.
The lesson is to test one change at a time, or use a multivariate design.
17.e: Bundled changes confound the result, so test one change at a time or use a multivariate design.
w: True: with many changes, the result cannot be traced to any one of them.
True: a harmful change can be masked by a helpful one, or the reverse.
False: bundled changes cannot be separated after the fact.
False: the time saved is lost, because you cannot learn which change mattered.
True: either isolate one change, or use a design that tests combinations on purpose.

17.q: Which of the following statement(s) about metrics is/are true?
o: Conversion rate is the percentage of visits that include a purchase.
A North Star metric guides the product.
Adding an item to a wishlist is a micro conversion.
A wishlist addition is a macro conversion.
Page views are always the best dependent variable.
17.e: Macro conversions are the final goal.
w: True: conversion rate = visits with a purchase divided by visits.
True: a North Star metric is the single measure the product aims to improve.
True: adding to a wishlist is a small step towards the final goal, so it is a micro conversion.
False: a wishlist addition is a micro conversion. A macro conversion is the final goal, such as a purchase.
False: page views may not reflect real value, so they are not always the best dependent variable.

17.q: Which of the following statement(s) about advanced experiment designs is/are true?
o: Ramp-up starts with a tiny share of users.
Auto-abort stops a bad test automatically.
Multivariate testing tests several variables and interactions.
A multi-armed bandit splits traffic equally for the whole test.
Multivariate testing needs less traffic than A/B.
17.e: A bandit shifts traffic toward better variants, and multivariate tests need far more traffic than A/B.
w: True: starting small limits exposure to a harmful change.
True: if metrics get worse, the system ends the test without waiting for a person.
True: it varies several things together to find their effects and interactions.
False: a bandit moves traffic towards variants that are performing better.
False: more combinations need far more traffic.

17.q: Which of the following statement(s) about experimentation culture are true?
o: Small changes, such as removing an unnecessary form field, can change conversion substantially.
A simple, cheap experiment can overturn a senior person’s opinion.
A test result should be ignored if it contradicts expert opinion.
Local context, such as accepting cash where cards are uncommon, can matter for adoption.
A required field always improves data quality without hurting conversion.
17.e: Data should outweigh opinion, and small friction points can have large effects.
w: True: removing a confusing field can reduce friction and raise conversion.
True: experiments replace opinion with evidence about real behaviour.
False: ignoring a contrary result brings back opinion over data.
True: adapting to local payment habits can unlock growth.
False: required fields add friction and can reduce completion, so the trade-off must be tested.

17.q: The repair-hub team runs a randomised web A/B test of a catalogue-first version A and a repair-task-first version B. Which statements describe a sound design?
o: Randomly assign eligible visitors and keep each visitor on the same version.
Run A in a quiet week and B in a busy week to save time.
Run both versions concurrently.
Define the outcome (reservation rate) before collecting data.
H0: pA ≠ pB.
17.e: H0 is no difference (pA = pB). Time-based differences are a confound, which concurrency and random assignment control.
w: True: this limits selection bias and keeps conditions comparable.
False: the difference could come from the week, not from the version.
True: concurrency limits a time confound.
True: deciding the outcome first avoids picking it after seeing the data.
False: H0 says the two versions are equal (pA = pB). The difference is H1.

17.q: Which statements about A/B testing and multivariate testing are correct?
o: A/B testing compares exactly two whole designs, control (A) against treatment (B).
It is the simplest randomised controlled experiment.
Multivariate testing tests every combination of several design variables.
Multivariate testing needs less traffic than A/B testing.
A/B testing compares many combinations of variables at once.
17.e: Multivariate testing needs significantly more traffic than A/B testing.
w: True: it compares control and treatment.
True: it is the simplest randomised controlled experiment.
True: every combination is tested.
False: every combination needs significantly more traffic.
False: that describes multivariate testing.

17.q: A manager insists on launching a redesign because “I have seen enough of these.” Which statements rebut this decision made by authority?
o: Decisions made by the highest-paid person’s opinion (HiPPO) are decisions by authority, not by data.
Data should trump intuition.
A small change can have a large effect, such as removing an unnecessary form field.
Senior opinions are always more accurate than test data.
A/B tests cannot measure the effect of small changes.
17.e: Decide with data, not authority. Small changes can be detected and can matter.
w: True: it is authority, not evidence.
True: testing gives evidence rather than opinion.
True: an unnecessary field is friction that every user has to consider, and a test can measure its effect.
False: authority is not evidence.
False: small changes are exactly what A/B tests can detect.

17.q: Which statements about conversion metrics and safeguards in online experiments are correct?
o: A macro conversion is the primary success metric.
Micro conversions are frequent smaller actions that lead to it.
Ramp-up gradually increases the traffic given to the treatment.
Auto-abort stops the test automatically on a negative signal.
The experiment should send all traffic to the treatment on day one.
17.e: Ramp up gradually and abort automatically on a negative signal to limit harm.
w: True: the macro conversion is the main outcome.
True: smaller actions lead to the macro conversion.
True: it limits risk by starting small.
True: it protects users and the business.
False: starting with all traffic removes the safeguard.

17.q: Which statements describe where web analytics sits among evaluation methods?
o: It is an empirical method.
It is the least obtrusive empirical method.
It observes real behaviour without users knowing they are studied.
Inspection is more empirical than web analytics.
It is the most obtrusive method.
17.e: Methods differ in how obtrusive they are and whether they are empirical or theoretical.
w: True: it measures real behaviour.
True: users do not notice it.
True: that is why it is unobtrusive.
False: inspection sits toward the theoretical end.
False: it is the least obtrusive.

18.q: Which statement(s) about independent and dependent variables are true?
o: The independent variable is what the experimenter manipulates.
The dependent variable is what the experimenter measures.
The independent variable is the measured outcome.
A variable that changes with the condition but is not manipulated can confound the result.
The dependent variable is the number of conditions.
18.e: The IV is what you vary; the DV is what you measure.
w: True: the experimenter deliberately sets the levels of the independent variable.
True: the dependent variable is the measured outcome.
False: the measured outcome is the dependent variable.
True: an uncontrolled factor that varies with the condition gives an alternative explanation.
False: the number of conditions is a design choice, not the measured outcome.

18.q: Which of the following statement(s) about validity is/are true?
o: Internal validity asks whether X really caused Y.
External validity asks whether the design was implemented correctly.
Using only students as participants threatens external validity.
Uncontrolled confounds mainly threaten external validity.
Holding the task constant raises internal validity but may lower external validity.
18.e: External validity is about generalising, and confounds threaten internal validity.
w: True: internal validity concerns cause and effect within the study.
False: external validity asks whether results generalise to other people, designs and situations.
True: results from one group may not apply to other users.
False: confounds threaten internal validity, because they give alternative explanations.
True: control reduces noise and raises internal validity, but artificial tasks may not generalise.

18.q: Which of the following statement(s) about between- and within-subjects designs is/are true?
o: Within-subjects needs fewer participants.
Within-subjects risks order and carryover effects.
Counterbalancing can use a Latin square.
Between-subjects controls individual differences better.
In between-subjects each participant sees every condition.
18.e: Within-subjects controls individual differences, and in between-subjects each participant sees only one condition.
w: True: each participant provides data for all conditions.
True: experience from one condition can influence the next.
True: a Latin square rotates the order so each condition appears in each position equally often.
False: within-subjects controls individual differences, because each person is their own control.
False: in between-subjects each participant sees one condition only.

18.q: Which of the following could be confounds?
o: Testing A in the morning and B in the evening.
Group A being more skilled.
Different devices between conditions.
Random assignment of participants.
Using the same instructions for every participant.
18.e: Randomisation and standard instructions are controls, not confounds.
w: True: time of day differs by condition, so fatigue or traffic could explain the difference.
True: skill differences would affect results independently of the design.
True: device differences would affect speed or accuracy independently of the design.
False: random assignment spreads unknown differences evenly, so it controls confounds.
False: identical instructions keep conditions comparable, so they are a control.

18.q: Which of the following are classic threats to internal validity?
o: History, such as UI changes during the study.
Maturation.
Selection.
Counterbalancing the order of conditions.
Participants being paid.
18.e: Counterbalancing is a control, and payment is not a classic threat.
w: True: events during the study can change results independently of the manipulation.
True: participants may change over time, for example by learning or tiring.
True: groups may differ because of how people were chosen.
False: counterbalancing is a way to control order effects, not a threat.
False: payment is not one of the classic threats.

18.q: Twelve editors use layout A, then layout B, to correct the same caption. B is faster. Which claims are justified?
o: This is a within-subjects design.
B must be better because each person is their own control.
Practice or remembering the answer may make B appear faster.
Counterbalance the order and use matched tasks.
Treat the 24 observations as independent participants.
18.e: Within-subjects designs are exposed to order and carryover effects. The 24 observations come from only 12 people.
w: True: every editor uses both layouts.
False: being your own control does not remove order effects.
True: this is an order or practice effect.
True: half do A then B, half B then A, with tasks of equal difficulty.
False: the observations are paired, not independent.

18.q: In a between-subjects A/B experiment, which statements about validity are correct?
o: Random assignment from the same visitor stream reduces selection bias.
If A runs on a well-stocked day and B on a day with few kits, availability could explain a difference.
Running both versions concurrently and monitoring the availability shown under each condition is a matching mitigation.
“Randomise to solve validity” is enough without naming a threat.
Evidence from one quiet week proves the result holds at busy events.
18.e: A good answer names a specific threat, explains an alternative cause and states the matching control. Generalisation is a separate question.
w: True: visitors have the same chance of either version.
True: availability is a competing explanation for any difference.
True: it controls the time confound the threat names.
False: it has to name the threat and explain the control.
False: external validity would need broader contexts or replication.

18.q: Which statements about independent and dependent variables are correct?
o: The independent variable is what the experimenter manipulates.
The dependent variable is what is measured.
An example independent variable is the interface version.
An example dependent variable is the time to complete a task.
The dependent variable is the one the experimenter assigns to groups.
18.e: The independent variable is the condition, and the dependent variable is the outcome.
w: True: it is the condition being manipulated.
True: it is the outcome that is measured.
True: versions are the conditions.
True: time is the outcome.
False: the experimenter assigns the independent variable.

18.q: Which statements distinguish a user study from an experiment?
o: A user study measures data from real users and is descriptive.
An experiment has two or more conditions and tests a hypothesis.
The comparison gives a measurement a reference point.
A plain study of one design can show that it is better than another.
An experiment is one of the four evaluation strategies.
18.e: An experiment is a special type of user study with a comparison structure.
w: True: it measures, for example, error counts without a comparison.
True: its conditions allow a hypothesis to be tested.
True: “how few errors is few enough?” needs a comparison.
False: it cannot support a comparison with another design.
False: an experiment is a type of user study, not a fifth strategy.

18.q: Which statements about internal and external validity are correct?
o: Internal validity asks whether X really caused Y.
External validity asks whether the results generalise to other people, designs and contexts.
A confounding variable changes systematically with the independent variable.
A confound strengthens internal validity.
External validity is about the study’s design and confounds.
w: True: it is about causation.
True: it is about generalisability.
True: it varies along with the condition, so it can explain the result.
False: it weakens it.
False: that describes internal validity.

19.q: Which of the following statement(s) about p-values is/are true?
o: If p < α you reject the null hypothesis.
If p = 0.03, a result this extreme would occur about 3% of the time if H0 were true.
p is the probability that H0 is true.
19 heads in 20 fair flips has a probability of about 0.004% (p ≈ 0.00004, two-tailed).
p measures the size of the effect.
19.e: p is not the probability of H0 or an effect size.
w: True: p below alpha means a result this extreme would be unlikely if H0 were true.
True: p = 0.03 means about 3% of the time under H0.
False: p is a probability of the data given H0, not the probability that H0 is true.
True: 19 or more heads, or 1 or fewer, in 20 fair flips happens only about 4 times in 100,000.
False: p does not tell you how big the effect is. Effect size is a separate measure.

o: Between-subjects, interval, not normal — Mann–Whitney U.
Paired nominal success/failure — McNemar’s test.
Between-subjects, interval, normal — independent t-test.
Likert data as ratio data.
Within-subjects, interval, normal — independent t-test.
19.e: Likert data is ordinal, and a within-subjects design needs a paired test.
w: True: Mann–Whitney U is used for two independent groups when normality does not hold.
True: McNemar's test is for paired binary outcomes.
True: two independent groups with normal interval data suit the independent t-test.
False: Likert data is ordinal, not ratio.
False: the same people in both conditions need a paired t-test, not an independent one.

19.q: Which of the following statement(s) about measurement levels is/are true?
o: Likert scales are ordinal.
Ratio data has a true zero.
Task success (yes/no) is nominal.
Interval data has a true zero.
Task time is ordinal.
19.e: Interval data lacks a true zero, and task time is a ratio measure.
w: True: responses are ordered, but the gaps are not equal.
True: a true zero means 'none of the quantity', which allows ratios.
True: pass/fail are categories without order.
False: interval data does not have a true zero, as with temperature in °C.
False: time has a true zero and equal spacing, so it is ratio data.

19.q: Which of the following statement(s) about tests is/are true?
o: A two-tailed test is the default.
A one-tailed test needs a justified direction.
A bimodal histogram suggests perfect normality.
The t-test assumes roughly normal data.
Run more tests until p < 0.05.
19.e: Repeating tests until p < 0.05 is bad practice, and a bimodal histogram suggests two different effects.
w: True: you rarely know in advance which way the effect goes.
True: choosing the direction after the data are in would not be legitimate.
False: a bimodal histogram has two peaks, which suggests two subgroups or effects.
True: the t-test assumes the data are approximately normal.
False: repeating tests until one is significant inflates false positives.

19.q: A t-test gives p = 0.007586 and α = 0.05. Which conclusion(s) is/are justified?
o: Reject the null hypothesis.
The difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone.
Design B is certainly better in all contexts.
The probability that H0 is true is 0.7586%.
The result is statistically significant.
19.e: p is not the probability of H0.
w: True: p = 0.0076 is below alpha = 0.05, so you reject the null hypothesis.
True: chance alone is an unlikely explanation for the observed difference.
False: one study does not show that Design B is better in all contexts.
False: p is the probability of the data under H0, not the probability that H0 is true.
True: the result is statistically significant, since p is below alpha.

19.q: A help centre compares search layouts A and B. Forty different visitors use one version each, 20 per version. Search times are strongly skewed, and three B users take unusually long. Which statements are justified?
o: Mann–Whitney U fits independent, skewed observations.
A paired t-test is appropriate.
An independent t-test is appropriate without checking the skew.
H0: equal outcome distributions. H1: different distributions.
Drop the three slow B users without explanation.
19.e: The visitors are different (between-subjects), so a paired test is wrong. Skewed data calls for a non-parametric test, and exclusions must be explained.
w: True: it compares two independent groups without assuming normality.
False: the visitors are different, so the observations are not paired.
False: a t-test assumes roughly normal data, and these times are strongly skewed.
True: these are the hypotheses for a Mann–Whitney U test.
False: unexplained exclusions are a common error.

19.q: Which test choices fit the design?
o: Each participant tries both interfaces and says which they prefer: binomial test.
The same users’ task success (yes/no) before and after a change: McNemar’s test.
Task success (yes/no) in two independent groups with small samples: Fisher’s exact test.
Likert ratings from two groups: independent t-test, treating the ratings as ratio data.
The same people in both conditions, interval and normal: independent t-test.
19.e: Pick the test by the variable type and the design: nominal data with paired or independent groups, or ordinal and non-normal data.
w: True: a preference between two options is nominal, and each participant provides one choice, tested against 50/50.
True: McNemar’s test compares paired yes/no outcomes.
True: Fisher’s exact test is for nominal data from independent groups with small samples.
False: Likert data is ordinal, so Mann–Whitney U is the independent-groups test.
False: the same people in both conditions need a paired t-test.

19.q: Which statements about null and alternative hypotheses and p-values are correct?
o: The null hypothesis states that nothing unusual is happening.
The alternative hypothesis states that the effect is real.
A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if H0 is true.
p < α means the result is statistically significant.
p is the probability that H0 is true.
19.e: p is the probability of the data under H0, not the probability of H0.
w: True: H0 attributes differences to chance.
True: H1 states a real effect.
True: it is a probability about the data.
True: p below α is the decision rule.
False: p says nothing about the probability that H0 is true.

19.q: Which are correct levels of measurement?
o: Likert ratings are ordinal.
Task success (yes/no) is nominal.
Task completion time is ratio.
Temperature in °C is ratio.
Blood type is ordinal.
19.e: Levels run from nominal to ordinal to interval to ratio.
w: True: they are ordered with unequal gaps.
True: categories without order are nominal.
True: time has a true zero.
False: °C is interval because its zero is arbitrary.
False: blood type has no order, so it is nominal.

19.q: A researcher wants to compare two means. Which statements about the t-test are correct?
o: It compares means of two groups of interval or ratio data.
It assumes roughly normally distributed data.
The paired version suits within-subjects data and the independent version suits between-subjects data.
It is the right test for yes/no data.
A one-tailed test is the default.
19.e: Check normality, and use the version that matches the design.
w: True: it is for interval or ratio data.
True: a large sample or roughly normal data is needed.
True: the pairing depends on the design.
False: yes/no data is nominal.
False: the two-tailed test is the default.

20.q: Which of the following is/are good pitch-video advice?
o: Show the interface with powerful visuals.
Use few compelling facts, given space to stand out.
Use as many facts as possible.
Speak to logic and emotion.
Read your slides verbatim.
20.e: Less is more: a short pitch should be visual, focused and spoken, not read.
w: True: seeing the real interface makes the idea concrete.
True: a few strong facts are remembered, while many blur together.
False: too many facts blur the message.
True: logic gives reasons and emotion makes people care.
False: reading slides loses the audience.

20.q: Which statement(s) about storytelling in a pitch are true?
o: Starting with why gives the audience a reason to care.
A very short story can still carry a clear message.
Include every feature to be complete.
Problem and why it matters come before the solution.
Hide the problem statement until the end.
20.e: Lead with the problem, and keep the story focused.
w: True: starting with why gives the audience a reason to care before the details.
True: a very short story can still carry a clear message.
False: including everything dilutes the story.
True: the audience needs to understand the problem before the solution makes sense.
False: hiding the problem leaves the solution without a purpose.

20.q: Which of the following is/are sound?
o: A pitch video has little time to grab attention.
Keep text on screen minimal.
Play unrelated loud music for energy.
Show the real interface.
Postpone the main message to the end.
20.e: Relevance beats noise, and the main message belongs up front.
w: True: viewers decide in seconds whether to keep watching.
True: viewers cannot read and listen at once.
False: unrelated loud music distracts from the message.
True: real screens make the idea credible.
False: the main message belongs up front because attention fades.

20.q: Which statements describe the two-part structure of a pitch?
o: State the problem and explain why it matters and why the audience should care.
Explain how you solved it.
Say explicitly what makes your solution unique compared with alternatives.
Start with a long list of features and finish with the problem.
Skip the problem and present only the interface.
20.e: A pitch tells a story: what the problem is and how you solved it.
w: True: it states the problem and why it matters.
True: the solution is the second part.
True: uniqueness is part of the solution.
False: a feature list does not tell a story.
False: the problem gives the solution its reason.

20.q: A pitch could lead with purpose before the product. Which statements about structuring a pitch are correct?
o: Communicate the underlying purpose or belief (why) first.
Then explain the approach (how).
Then present the product itself (what).
Lead with product features before the purpose.
This is a replacement for stating the problem and the solution, so those can be dropped.
20.e: Leading with purpose is a complementary storytelling lens, not a replacement for the problem and solution structure.
w: True: purpose comes first.
True: the approach follows.
True: the product comes last.
False: that is the opposite order.
False: it complements the problem and solution structure.

20.q: Two products are technically comparable, but one wins because its pitch engages the audience emotionally while the other lists only features. Which points does this illustrate?
o: A technically comparable product can lose if its story fails to engage.
A pitch should speak to emotion as well as logic.
Facts and logic still matter.
A feature list alone wins audiences.
Emotion has no place in a design pitch.
20.e: Speak to both logic and emotion.
w: True: story and emotion can decide the outcome.
True: a purely logic-driven pitch is weaker than one that also engages emotion.
True: facts still matter.
False: a feature-only pitch can lose to one that tells a story.
False: a pitch should engage emotion too.

20.q: Which choices suit a short pitch video?
o: Show the interface visually at a high level.
Keep the video short, about 60 seconds.
Use powerful visuals rather than describing the interface in words.
Walk through a detailed evaluation in the video.
Fill the video with text so nothing is left out.
20.e: Less is more: show the interface, and save the deep evaluation for elsewhere.
w: True: it gives an impression of the design.
True: the guideline is about 60 seconds.
True: show it rather than describe it.
False: the deep evaluation belongs elsewhere in the presentation or report.
False: filling it with uninteresting words drives audiences away.

20.q: Which statements about telling a story in a pitch are true?
o: A story needs few words, so a short, clear message is better than a long one.
The video must grab attention in the first 60 seconds.
Avoid walls of text.
Over-explain until the audience loses interest.
Facts speak to emotions on their own.
w: True: a short story can be told in very few words.
True: you have about 60 seconds.
True: walls of text push audiences away.
False: ending while interest is still high is better.
False: facts and logic matter, but you also need to speak to emotions.

20.q: Which statements about sharing UX research insights are correct?
o: Let people hear you talk, rather than only posting findings.
Avoid walls of text.
Present the most compelling facts and give them space to stand out.
Show every finding at equal size so nothing is emphasised.
A document with every detail replaces a spoken pitch.
20.e: Share insights in a way people will actually take in.
w: True: hearing the speaker helps audiences engage.
True: walls of text are ignored.
True: space makes the key facts stand out.
False: emphasis helps priorities stand out.
False: a spoken, visual story engages people better.

20.q: Which items belong to the pitch structure given in the lecture’s summary?
o: Grab attention in 60 seconds.
Explain the problem and why it matters.
Present your solution and what is unique about it.
End so that people want more.
Start with the solution, then add the problem at the end.
20.e: The flow is attention, problem, solution, uniqueness, then leaving them wanting more.
w: True: the opening has to grab attention.
True: the problem comes next.
True: the solution and its uniqueness follow.
True: ending with interest left is the final step.
False: the problem comes before the solution.

21.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the course review is/are true?
o: It recaps experts vs. users, field vs. lab, study vs. experiment and qualitative vs. quantitative.
The GUI empowered mainstream users beyond experts.
Working memory is large and permanent.
The design process is a one-way line from vision to release.
Systems appear when a vision meets reality.
21.e: Working memory is small and temporary, and the design process is a cycle.
w: True: these contrasts help you choose an evaluation method.
True: graphical interfaces made computers usable by everyone.
False: working memory is small and temporary. Long-term memory is the large store.
False: the design process is a cycle, with feedback leading to more iteration.
True: quality depends on the vision and how it adapts to reality.

21.q: Which of the following contrast(s) is/are correct?
o: Inspection uses experts; user testing uses real users.
Field studies are realistic; laboratory studies give control.
Experiments describe what users do in daily life without manipulating anything.
Qualitative data is numbers; quantitative data is themes.
Qualitative data helps explain why.
21.e: Experiments manipulate variables, and qualitative and quantitative data are reversed in the false option.
w: True: experts judge from knowledge, users reveal real behaviour.
True: you trade realism against control.
False: experiments manipulate conditions to compare them. Observing daily life without manipulation is a field study.
False: qualitative data is descriptive and quantitative data is numeric.
True: descriptions and quotes show reasons that numbers alone do not.

21.q: Which statements about the course review are correct?
o: It re-walks the Empathise, Prototype and Evaluate cycle, equivalent to the Design Thinking cycle.
The design cycle is fundamental to everything in the course.
Systems appear when a vision meets reality.
Quality depends on how beautiful the vision is and how well it adapts to reality.
The review introduces an entirely new design method.
21.e: The review revisits earlier material and adds some refinements.
w: True: the lecture walks the same cycle.
True: the iterative cycle underlies the course.
True: that is how the review puts it.
True: both the vision and its adaptation matter.
False: the review mainly revisits earlier material.

21.q: Which statements about the review’s memory-store figures are correct?
o: The visual image store holds about 7–17 letters.
The auditory image store holds about 4.4–6.2 letters.
Long-term memory has unlimited associative capacity and is stable.
Working memory is the bottleneck.
Long-term memory decays within seconds.
21.e: The review gives more precise figures, and the point that working memory is the bottleneck stands.
w: True: visual store: 7–17 letters.
True: auditory store: 4.4–6.2 letters.
True: long-term memory is large and stable.
True: working memory has the smallest capacity and fastest decay.
False: long-term memory has no decay.

21.q: The review asks “is there a problem with this process?” and then shows AI prototyping trends. Which statements are justified?
o: The question bridges into the AI lecture.
The implied gap is that AI acts as an active participant, not just a passive tool.
AI prototyping is reported to make iteration from lo-fi to hi-fi 50–70% faster.
Designers are reported to shift from creators to curators of AI output.
Human empathy and evaluation are no longer needed.
21.e: Human-centred empathy and evaluation are still required however much prototyping AI assists.
w: True: it leads into Lecture 22.
True: the classical cycle does not account for AI as an active participant.
True: those are the trend figures quoted.
True: designers curate AI output.
False: the review reminds us that empathy and evaluation are still required.

21.q: Which contrasts from the course are correct?
o: Inspection uses experts, while laboratory studies observe users.
Between-subjects gives each participant one condition, while within-subjects gives each participant all conditions.
Internal validity is about causation, while external validity is about generalisation.
A slip is a planning error, while a mistake is an execution error.
The independent variable is what is measured, while the dependent variable is what is manipulated.
21.e: Check each pair against its definition.
w: True: inspection is the strategy in which experts judge the design.
True: that is the definition of each design.
True: one is about X causing Y, and the other about generalising.
False: a slip is an execution error and a mistake is a planning error.
False: the independent variable is manipulated and the dependent variable is measured.

21.q: Which pairs of evaluation concepts does the Test part of the review contrast?
o: Experts versus users.
Field versus laboratory.
Study versus experiment.
Qualitative versus quantitative data.
Memory versus perception only.
21.e: The review lists these contrasts under Test.
w: True: inspection versus testing with users.
True: realism versus control.
True: descriptive study versus comparison.
True: words versus numbers.
False: that is not one of the Test contrasts.

21.q: Which statements about the review’s closing debate are supported?
o: It asks whether all this user-centred work is really necessary.
It asks whether such work could be harmful.
It cites a view that user-led innovation cannot create breakthroughs.
It concludes that testing with users is never useful.
It says the design cycle can be dropped.
21.e: The debate is posed as an open question, not a settled conclusion.
w: True: the debate asks about necessity.
True: it asks about possible harm.
True: a view that user-led innovation cannot create breakthroughs is cited.
False: it is posed as an open question.
