False: the cycle is described as fundamental.

21.q: Which statements about the four headings of the review are consistent with the course?
o: Design includes observation, requirements, and models, memory, input and mobile.
Prototype includes quantity versus quality, colour and font, and parallel prototyping.
Test includes experts versus users and field versus laboratory.
The map covers only the Empathise stage.
Prototype includes only data analysis.
21.e: Each heading maps onto a stage of the cycle.
w: True: they are listed under Design.
True: they are listed under Prototype.
True: they are listed under Test.
False: the map covers the whole cycle.
False: data analysis belongs to Test.

21.q: Which statements about how the review treats earlier lectures are correct?
o: It mostly revisits material from earlier chapters.
It gives refined, more precise memory-store figures.
It includes a new discussion question that leads into AI.
It adds a new unrelated chapter topic.
It replaces the earlier lectures.
21.e: The review revisits, refines and bridges.
w: True: concepts named in the map are covered in earlier chapters.
True: the figures refine Lecture 7.
True: the discussion question leads into Lecture 22.
False: it does not add an unrelated topic.
False: it does not replace the earlier lectures.

22.q: Which of the following statement(s) about AI in design evaluation is/are true?
o: Synthetic users should be treated as hypotheses to test.
AI moderation suits structured, well-defined questions at scale.
AI thematic analysis should be a first pass, verified by humans.
AI can fully replace real users.
A multi-armed bandit keeps traffic split 50/50 throughout.
22.e: Real users cannot be replaced, and a bandit shifts traffic to better variants during the test.
w: True: synthetic users generate ideas to check, not facts.
True: it gives consistency and scale for well-defined questions.
True: the first pass saves time, but people verify it.
False: AI lacks real emotion and context, so it cannot replace real users.
False: a bandit shifts traffic towards better variants rather than keeping a fixed split.

22.q: Which statement(s) about agent-based (LLM persona) A/B simulation are true?
o: Vendor accuracy claims should be treated with caution until independently verified.
Simulations use many LLM persona agents to imitate user behaviour.
Simulations are final proof.
Synthetic users reproduce real emotion and context exactly.
External validity is limited because the users are synthetic.
22.e: Simulated users lack real emotion and context, so simulations are for screening, not proof.
w: True: marketing figures for accuracy need independent evidence.
True: each agent plays a persona and acts as a simulated user.
False: simulations are not final proof. Real users are needed to confirm.
False: synthetic users lack real emotion and context, so they do not reproduce them exactly.
True: results from simulated people may not generalise to real users.

22.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true?
o: AI ideation risks fixation on the first output.
Use AI to diverge, then humans converge.
Generative UI relies on constraints.
Humans need not review AI output.
AI removes the need for empathy.
w: True: people may anchor on the first AI output, so ideas converge.
True: AI can generate a wide range of ideas, and humans select and refine.
True: generated interfaces depend on constraints such as design-system standards.
False: people must review AI output to catch errors and bias.
False: AI lacks real empathy, so human understanding of users remains essential.

22.q: Which pairings of a design stage and AI support are correct?
o: Empathise: synthetic users, as a supplement only.
Ideate: an AI partner, watching for fixation.
Prototype: prompt-to-UI.
Test: AI heuristic evaluation, moderation and analysis.
Empathise: synthetic users, as a full replacement for real users.
w: True: synthetic users supplement real research.
True: AI can help ideation but teams may latch onto its first output.
True: prompt-to-UI tools generate designs.
True: AI can support several parts of testing.
False: synthetic users supplement, never substitute, real research.

22.q: Which statements about AI in ideation are correct?
o: AI as a “naïve expert” can reduce early fixation by asking unexpected questions.
Teams may latch onto the first reasonable AI output.
The role shifts from idea generator to creative curator.
Humans define problems and constraints and evaluate and refine.
AI removes the need for human judgement.
22.e: The risk is convergent homogeneity, and judgement stays with people.
w: True: an outsider’s questions can break fixation.
True: that risk is called convergent homogeneity.
True: curation becomes the human role.
True: people own the judgement.
False: human judgement stays essential at every stage.

22.q: Which statements about AI prompt-to-app design tools are correct?
o: A plain-language prompt can generate both the UI and its logic.
Existing design frames can be converted into a functioning coded interface.
They can reference published design guidelines to keep generated elements on-brand.
They output real frontend code, bridging designers and engineers.
They remove the need to review or refine the generated design.
22.e: AI proposes and humans decide, so the output still has to be reviewed and refined.
w: True: text-to-app tools turn a prompt into UI and logic.
True: design-to-code reads layout, typography and colour from a design.
True: design system integration keeps the output consistent.
True: the output is real code such as React and CSS.
False: human judgement stays essential at every stage.

22.q: Which statements about AI design tools that turn prompts or sketches into designs are correct?
o: They can turn prompts, wireframes or screenshots into editable UIs and code.
Portable design rules can be encoded in a file with accessibility checks built in.
They let the designer refine by chat, comments, direct edits or sliders.
They can export to common formats or hand off to a coding tool.
The tools are so different that they cannot be compared.
22.e: The tools are comparable alternatives aimed at the same prompt or sketch to working design workflow.
w: True: prompt, wireframe or screenshot to editable UI is the core workflow.
True: design rules can be portable and validated for accessibility.
True: refinement happens interactively.
True: export and hand-off are part of the workflow.
False: they are positioned as comparable alternatives.

22.q: Which statements about AI in the test stage are correct?
o: Well-established, visually inspectable heuristics are likely to be automated.
LLMs make large-scale qualitative analysis feasible for small teams.
Algorithms can optimise an experimental plan for efficient design-space exploration.
AI makes human interpretation of results unnecessary.
AI can always replace moderators with no loss.
22.e: Humans stay in the loop to judge and interpret.
w: True: those checks can be automated.
True: content analysis and affinity diagramming become feasible.
True: AI can plan experiments efficiently.
False: human judgement is still required.
False: an AI moderator is less nuanced than a human who can adapt.

22.q: A team uses AI personas to simulate users in place of interviews. Which statements are justified?
o: Synthetic users can supplement real research.
Synthetic users should never substitute real research.
Real users can reveal what you did not know you did not know.
Simulated users are as reliable as real observation, so interviews can be skipped.
AI-simulated users have no limitations.
22.e: Treat synthetic users as a supplement and still do real empathy research.
w: True: they add inexpensive input.
True: they are simulated by AI.
True: real research reveals unexpected needs.
False: real observation is still needed.
False: simulation cannot reveal unknown unknowns.

22.q: Which statements does the consolidated AI map across the design stages support?
o: AI can support every stage of the cycle.
Human judgement stays essential at every stage.
Testing still feeds back to earlier stages.
AI replaces the Design Thinking cycle.
Each stage needs a different AI tool by definition.
w: True: the map has AI branches for all five stages.
True: that is the throughline.
True: the cycle remains iterative.
False: AI augments the cycle.
False: tools differ, but no single tool is required by definition.

23.q: Which of the following statement(s) about Human–AI interaction is/are true?
o: Good AI interfaces make uncertainty and adaptation visible.
Human-in-the-loop means a person can review or correct output before it acts.
Transparency and explainability are new AI-specific heuristics.
Users should assume AI behaves deterministically.
Users who assume AI is deterministic trust it more.
23.e: AI is not deterministic, and users who expect determinism struggle to trust it.
w: True: showing confidence helps users calibrate trust.
True: a person can intervene before the output has consequences.
True: users need to understand why an AI behaves as it does.
False: AI output can vary, so assuming otherwise leads to surprises.
False: users who expect determinism lose trust when the AI behaves differently.

23.q: Which design choice(s) help users judge how far to trust an AI assistant’s answer?
o: Show uncertainty so users can calibrate trust.
Hide that AI was used.
Let users correct the output.
Offer an explanation where feasible.
Never ask users to verify output.
23.e: Transparency and user control matter, and users should be encouraged to verify output.
w: True: showing confidence tells users how much to rely on the answer.
False: hiding AI use removes transparency and erodes trust.
True: user correction improves outcomes and keeps users in control.
True: explanations help users judge whether the output is reasonable.
False: verifying important output is part of using AI responsibly.

23.q: Which mental-model shifts does the lecture give for AI?
o: Deterministic to probabilistic.
Rule-based to learning-based.
Transparent to opaque.
Fixed to adaptive.
Probabilistic to deterministic.
23.e: Good AI interfaces make uncertainty and adaptation visible.
w: True: answers are likely, not certain.
True: strengths and blind spots depend on training.
True: it may not show how it decided.
True: it changes as the user interacts.
False: AI moves away from determinism.

23.q: Which examples show how an AI interface can signal uncertainty?
o: A text-completion feature shows its suggestion in light grey, so it reads as a suggestion and not committed text.
A medical tool displays a confidence score with its result.
A response gives a likely answer and says that it might be wrong.
Presenting every output as certain.
Hiding all uncertainty to look reliable.
23.e: Visible uncertainty helps users calibrate trust.
w: True: grey text signals a suggestion.
True: a confidence score shows how sure the system is.
True: it matches the “likely answers” reframing.
False: false certainty misleads users.
False: hidden uncertainty harms trust calibration.

23.q: Which are reasons users who treat AI as deterministic struggle?
o: They expect it to always behave the same predictable way.
They have difficulty with trust.
They have difficulty understanding its explanations.
They have no mental model at all.
Probabilistic outputs are always identical.
23.e: An outdated model of how software behaves harms use of an AI system.
w: True: that is the deterministic expectation.
True: trust suffers when outputs vary.
True: explanations do not fit the assumed model.
False: they have an outdated model, not none.
False: probabilistic outputs can vary.

23.q: Which are examples of learning-based and collaborative AI interaction?
o: Like and dislike buttons that shape later recommendations.
A learning app that adjusts difficulty to the learner’s performance.
A code assistant whose suggestions the developer can accept, modify or reject.
A fixed rule set that never changes.
A tool that offers no way to reject a suggestion.
23.e: Human-in-the-loop interaction keeps the person in control.
w: True: feedback shapes later recommendations.
True: difficulty adapts to the learner.
True: the person stays in the loop.
False: that is rule-based and fixed.
False: a lack of control breaks user control and freedom.

23.q: Which are AI-specific readings of Nielsen’s heuristics?
o: Visibility of system status: display progress, typing indicators or model confidence.
User control and freedom: provide undo, retry and corrective flows.
Error prevention: flag low-confidence outputs and possible hallucinations.
Consistency and standards: maintain a consistent tone, controls and invocation method.
Error prevention: hide uncertainty so users do not worry.
23.e: The AI readings extend the original heuristics.
w: True: progress and confidence indicate status.
True: users need to undo and retry.
True: low-confidence outputs should be flagged.
True: consistency applies to the AI’s behaviour.
False: hiding uncertainty is the opposite of prevention.

23.q: A team designs a chat assistant. Which choices fit good Human–AI interaction?
o: Make uncertainty and adaptation visible.
Offer understandable reasons even if the internal workings are opaque.
Let users edit a prompt and reject a suggestion.
Imply that the assistant is always right.
Remove any explanation of how it works.
23.e: Effective AI acts as a partner while being open about how it reaches outputs.
w: True: visible uncertainty supports calibrated trust.
True: reasons help even when the model is opaque.
True: control and freedom apply.
False: false certainty misleads.
False: transparency about how it works supports trust.

23.q: Which statements about the status of the Human–AI interaction lecture are correct?
o: The source marks it as supplementary and optional.
It is not tested in the IS211 final examination.
It should be deprioritised relative to the main chapters when studying for the exam.
It is the most heavily tested lecture.
It replaces Nielsen’s heuristics.
w: True: the notes say it is supplementary.
True: the source says it is not tested.
True: study the main chapters first.
False: it is not tested.
False: the heuristics still apply and are reimagined.

23.q: Which statements about traditional HCI versus Human–AI interaction are correct?
o: Traditional HCI is deterministic, rule-based and transparent.
Modern Human–AI interaction is probabilistic, learning-based and adaptive.
Human–AI interaction requires new mental models from the user.
Traditional HCI is probabilistic and adaptive.
Human–AI interaction can rely on the old mental model of fixed software.
23.e: The shift in assumptions changes what interfaces must communicate.
w: True: those are its characteristics.
True: those are the AI characteristics.
True: users have to adjust their expectations.
False: that describes AI, not traditional HCI.
False: the old model strains with AI.

lessons.title: Introduction & Design Thinking
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersEverything in this course hangs on one idea: design for real people, and keep looping until it works for them.
🧠 Memory hookE-D-I-P-T — Every Designer Iterates, Prototypes, Tests. Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test, and Test sends you back.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
What makes design "good" or "bad"?The five course values (design philosophy)The Design Thinking process (Stanford d.school)AI-powered Design Thinking (overview)
⚡ At a glance — the Design Thinking cycle
Empathise→Define→Ideate→Prototype→Test
↺ Test feeds back into Prototype or Empathise — iteration is the point.
1.1What makes design "good" or "bad"?

Good design is judged from two angles that show up repeatedly through the course:

  • The user's angle: the interface should be easy to use and hard to misuse — the user should be able to act without needing to consciously study the interface first.
  • The developer/designer's angle: the design should actively prevent user errors rather than relying on the user to avoid making them (i.e. error prevention is a design responsibility, not a user responsibility).

A worked illustration used in the slides is a BI (business intelligence) dashboard: a well-designed one is clean and polished because non-essential elements are removed, colour and font are used deliberately to direct attention to priorities (an application of Gestalt principles — similarity, proximity, common region — which group related elements so the eye parses them as one unit), and it tells a story by adding context so raw numbers become meaningful.

Gestalt principles (added context): these are perceptual rules describing how humans automatically group visual elements — similarity (things that look alike are seen as related), proximity (things placed close together are seen as related), and common region (things inside a shared boundary are seen as one group). The full set of six is listed in §11.5. (Lecture 1, slide 2 calls the third one enclosure; it is the same idea as common region in Lecture 11.) They recur later under Visual Design (§11) and are why "add a border/background" or "align things into columns" is a real design decision, not decoration.

📍 CASE FILE

“Jenny” — when bad UI costs a life

The setting

A hospital used patient-charting software that nurses had to operate while caring for very ill patients. It is the course's high-stakes example of why usability matters.

What happened

Nurses were distracted by trying to work out the software and missed a young cancer patient's requirement for three days of hydration. She died of toxicity and dehydration.

The lesson

Usability is a safety issue, not decoration. A quick review of an interface against common-sense rules (a heuristic evaluation, Lecture 12) is a cheap way to catch such problems.

More from the lecture

A UI critique warm-up asks you to list good/bad parts of a bad error dialogue box, using a heuristic worksheet (heuristic / description / does the design do a good or bad job?).

The activity is a heuristic evaluation — applying common-sense knowledge of good design to judge a design against an acceptable standard (formalised in §12). The high-stakes illustration: a hospital patient-charting UI where nurses, distracted by figuring out the software, missed a young cancer patient's three-day hydration requirement

She died of toxicity and dehydration. Source of the statement that 75–95% of industrial accidents are attributed to human error — but "how is it that so many people are so incompetent? They aren't. It's a design problem." (cf. §1.1: error prevention is the designer's responsibility.)

1.2The five course values (design philosophy)

The course is built around five values, each with its own theoretical grounding. These aren't just course admin — they define the vocabulary the rest of the module uses.

# Value What it means Grounded in
1 Design is for people Design should empower users (human-centred design). Cited examples: the 1984 Macintosh ("The Computer for the Rest of Us") pairing an affordable GUI + mouse to enable mainstream computing; smartphones being usable even by very young children. Empathy
2 Prototype Build tangible, low-cost representations of ideas early, and iterate them based on feedback, rather than jumping straight to a finished product. Cited examples: the Wright brothers and SpaceX both iterated many prototypes before their first full success; paper prototypes let you rapidly and cheaply test interface ideas and visualise a GUI for stakeholders before writing any real code. Prototype (low-fidelity → high-fidelity)
3 Compare alternatives Plan evaluation strategies by their accuracy vs. cost trade-off: define goals, what data to collect, who the testers are, and what metrics you'll use; then choose a method — field study, laboratory study, or survey — and a technique — think-aloud, A/B test, focus group. Evaluate
4 Iterate Deliver incremental improvements (minimum viable product mindset), moving from low-fidelity prototypes (fast, inexpensive, rough — used to test concepts) to high-fidelity ones (detailed, realistic — used to test polish/final feel). Empathy → Prototype → Evaluate cycle
5 Principles Ground design decisions in established theory rather than guesswork. Key examples introduced here (each expanded later in the course): Fitt's Law (a bigger/closer target is acquired faster — so make important, frequently-used controls large and close to the likely cursor/finger position), the Power Law of Practice (repeated practice builds long-term procedural memory — performance improves predictably with repetition, which is why "recognition over recall" and consistent placement matter), and an early preview of heuristic evaluation (see below). Learn from experience/theory

Why this matters: these five values map directly onto the Empathy → Prototype → Evaluate cycle that recurs as the backbone of the whole module (see the diagram in §1.3).

Heuristic evaluation was previewed (not yet taught in full — expanded in Lecture 12: Inspection) with these early bullet points, attributed to Jakob Nielsen: visibility and clear feedback; match the users' language and mental models; give the user control (exits, undo, redo); consistency and standards; prevent errors and support recovery from them; favour recognition over recall (e.g. visible menus/shortcuts over memorised commands); keep the design simple and clean, with help available when needed.

Other framing examples

Poor wayfinding signs ("Where is the mall?") and an app where the camera/QR-scan entry point is hard to find show that essential actions must be immediately discoverable. An architecture analogy extends the point: when a building doesn't work well we blame the users — but poor design is the problem, not the people. Scale matters too: Facebook's like/share buttons are viewed ~22 billion times a day, so a tiny tweak can cause global outrage or help millions (Margaret Gould Stewart's three rules for design at scale). Counter-example of poor external consistency: the Windows 8 Start screen (2012) was found confusing by usability experts on a desktop PC.

Users are not like you

Designers/engineers know more about the design than users do, so cannot rely on their own intuition. Latency also matters (even tiny delays to search results measurably change behaviour).

🧩 Pause & recall — Which sequence lists the five Design Thinking stages in order?
Answer: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test
Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test, with iteration looping back from Test.
1.3The Design Thinking process (Stanford d.school)

Design Thinking is an iterative (not strictly linear) process for designing and innovating, built from five stages:

Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test → (loop back as needed)

  • Empathise — discover what people actually need (not what you assume they need).
  • Define — turn that raw understanding into a clear point of view, typically expressed as a persona (a representative user) and scenarios (concrete situations that user is in).
  • Ideate / brainstorm — generate a wide range of candidate ideas.
  • Prototype — make ideas tangible, quickly, specifically in order to learn from them (the prototype is a learning tool, not a finished product).
  • Test — refine the prototypes and learn more about the users from how they respond.

This 5-stage process is a more detailed version of the 3-stage "Empathy → Prototype → Evaluate" cycle used elsewhere in the course: Define + Ideate sit inside/before "Prototype," and "Test" corresponds to "Evaluate." Both describe the same underlying loop at different levels of granularity — don't treat them as two different frameworks.

flowchart LR
    A[Empathise] --> B[Define]
    B --> C[Ideate]
    C --> D[Prototype]
    D --> E[Test]
    E -.iterate.-> A
    E -.refine prototype.-> D

Caption: The Design Thinking cycle — note the two feedback loops: Test can send you all the way back to Empathise (you learned something new about the user) or just back to Prototype (you just need to refine the current design).

📍 CASE FILE

IDEO redesigns the shopping cart

The setting

IDEO, a leading design firm, was filmed taking on a deliberately ordinary object — the supermarket trolley — in a few days. This film is the course's showcase of design thinking in action.

What happened

The team had no titles or permanent roles, so anyone could contribute. They split up to watch and talk to shoppers, shoppers with kids, professional shoppers and even the staff who maintain the carts. Back together they brainstormed under strict rules (one conversation at a time, defer judgement, encourage wild ideas, build on others' ideas), built quick prototypes, got reactions from experts and refined them.

The lesson

Design is not a flash of genius but a loop: empathise → define → ideate → prototype → test. It shows the course values of empathy, diversity and iteration working together.

More from the lecture

Worked example — shopping cart redesign

  • (used in the slides to illustrate the process in action, drawn from an IDEO case study video): a team was asked to redesign the shopping cart.
  • Notable process observations from the case: the team had no titles and no permanent roles (an expression of diversity — anyone can contribute any kind of idea), they learned quickly from users and experts by going out and observing/interviewing them directly (an expression of empathy), and they operated under a set of "innovation mantras" that describe a brainstorming mindset: one conversation at a time; stay focused on the topic; encourage wild ideas; defer judgement; build on others' ideas; embrace "focused chaos"; embrace trial and error
  • Value success over rigid planning
  • No lone genius (ideas are collective); work under time constraints
  • Fail often so you succeed sooner.

David Kelley's framing: human-centred innovation integrating human needs, technological possibilities and business requirements, through empathy, experimentation and iteration. IDEO's process highlights, beyond the mantras in §1.3: fluid structure (no permanent titles/assignments → diversity of thought), expert integration (quickly bring in domain experts and users), "thinking with your hands" (rapid prototyping surfaces unexpected insights). Mapping the shopping-cart video onto the design process: (1) start with a problem proposal

(2) empathise with distinct user groups (shoppers, shoppers with kids, professional shoppers, cart maintenance staff) (3) brainstorm from the observed breakdowns and prototype (4) test the prototypes as you build; (5) iterate.

Gotcha: "Defer judgement" and "encourage wild ideas" are Ideate-stage mindset rules, not Evaluate-stage ones — during ideation you deliberately do not filter/critique ideas yet, because premature judgement kills the volume and diversity of ideas you need before you move to prototyping and testing. Don't confuse this brainstorming discipline with the later evaluation stage, where critical judgement is exactly what you want.

Further worked case: future-of-grocery-store concepts (Amazon Dash Cart, Alibaba Hema, Walmart's metaverse experiments, a FairPrice smart-trolley trial, an SMU "Pick & Go" unmanned-checkout prototype) were shown as inspiration for how empathy + technology can reshape an everyday interaction (e.g. Dash Cart uses a camera and weight sensors so the cart itself checks items in/out and skips a checkout queue entirely). (These are illustrative inspiration examples, not something you need to reproduce the specifics of for an exam — the teaching point is "observe an everyday interaction and ask what technology could remove friction from it.")

A generic design process (Dix et al.)

All the popular process models emphasise empathising with users, ideating solutions, quick prototyping, evaluation and iteration. Common attributes: ideate UI designs and interaction models that satisfy the requirements quickly build prototypes that demonstrate the interactions

plan and execute evaluations that assess users' responses and show paths to improvement. Practical workflow: go back and forth between empathising and testing

Use cheap tools (pen and paper) for lo-fi prototypes early, then move to hi-fi interactive prototypes via wireframe tools. The d.school "bootleg" version in four verbs: understand users by observing and engaging → brainstorm many solutions → build quick versions to test → get feedback to improve. The textbook (Preece et al.) presents another process model.

📍 CASE FILE

NTUC FairPrice self-checkout (Singapore, 2017)

The setting

FairPrice launched self-checkout counters in October 2017 as a technology upgrade to speed up shopping.

What happened

Scanned items had to be placed on a weight-sensitive pad (the system effectively ‘didn't trust’ customers) and every self-service counter still needed a staff member. Customers complained, but nothing changed.

The lesson

Technology that ignores how people feel and behave adds friction instead of removing it. The moral: get inspiration by researching real users.

More from the lecture

Worked inspiration cases — retail.

  • Smart carts with cameras + weight sensors + account-linked dashboards (checkout-free)
  • Mobile barcode scanning with recommendations
  • Walmart metaverse/VR shopping (built by Mutual Mobile for SXSW 2017); AI-powered unmanned stores
  • Computer vision for product recognition.
  • A design failure to learn from: NTUC FairPrice self-checkout (launched Oct 2017) required scanned items to be placed on a weight-sensitive pad ("don't trust you") and every self-service counter still needed a staff member — customer feedback but no change.
  • Moral: "get inspiration — research."

Obsessive attention to detail: Steve Jobs spent two weeks deliberating over a washing machine, weighing wash-time vs. softness/longevity trade-offs before choosing a German-made Miele; he reportedly had the Macintosh cooling fan removed (and the motherboard redesigned) because it sounded "noisy and clumsy". Lesson: deliberate trade-off reasoning plus zero tolerance for mediocrity underpins minimalist design — "it takes a lot of hard work to make something simple".

1.4AI-powered Design Thinking (overview)

The course maps generative-AI tools onto each Design Thinking stage. This is only introduced as an overview here; each item is developed in depth much later (Lecture 22).

Design Thinking stage AI-powered technique introduced
Empathise Synthetic users; AI-assisted requirements gathering; conversational interaction
Ideate AI-assisted ideation
Prototype AI prototyping / generative UI; data visualisation
Test Heuristic evaluation (AI-assisted); AI usability testing; thematic analysis; A/B testing; hypothesis testing

(See §22 for the full treatment once that lecture is added to this file.)

⚡ Quick examples
Good visual design basics
PointClean, polished, value-focused design uses colour, typography and Gestalt principles.
ExampleA checkout page with one clear 'Pay now' button and ample whitespace.
ExplanationReducing clutter lets users find what matters quickly.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Design is a loop of five stages: Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test.
  • Design for people: be empathic, principles-based, and iterate on feedback.
  • Compare alternatives and prototype for feedback.
  • Start with a Minimum Viable Product covering core functions, then improve through feedback cycles.
  • Clean, polished, value-focused design uses colour, typography and Gestalt principles.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Human-centred designtap to flip
Designing around real user needs, discovered via empathy
Fitt's Lawtap to flip
Bigger & closer targets are acquired faster
Power Law of Practicetap to flip
Performance improves predictably with repeated practice
Low-fidelity prototypetap to flip
Fast, cheap, rough representation used to test concepts early
High-fidelity prototypetap to flip
Detailed, realistic representation used to test final polish
Design Thinking cycletap to flip
Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test (iterative)
Gestalt principlestap to flip
Similarity, proximity, closure, common region, continuity, figure/ground — perceptual grouping rules
Heuristic evaluation (preview)tap to flip
Nielsen's usability heuristics; full treatment in Lecture 12
➡ Where next? To design for people you first have to understand them — that is the Empathise stage.

lessons.title: Empathy
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersPeople can't always tell you what they do, because much of it is automatic. So you watch first, then ask.
🧠 Memory hookTacit = Can't Tell. If someone can't explain it, observe it. Observe → Ask → Immerse.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Tacit knowledgeRecording empathyHow to interview (engaging users)ImmersionWorked example: evidence rubric (avoid vs. collect)
⚡ At a glance — ways to learn about users
TechniqueGets youWatch out for
Observation (field / controlled / “deep hanging out”)What people actually do, incl. workaroundsObserver effect, sampling
InterviewsMotives, stories, opinionsLeading questions; people don’t report tacit knowledge
Immersion (contextual inquiry, master–apprentice, diaries)Tacit knowledge in contextTime-consuming

Empathy is the foundation of human-centred design — it is the "Empathise" stage of the cycle introduced in §1.3, and its purpose is to reveal what you didn't know you didn't know about users. The lecture organises empathy work into four sub-skills: tacit knowledge, recording empathy, interviewing, and immersion.

2.1Tacit knowledge

Tacit knowledge (added context definition): knowledge people hold from internalised experience that they cannot easily put into words or write down — "we can know more than we can tell." It is surfaced through ethnographic methods, informally called "deep hanging out": spending extended time with users rather than just asking them questions.

  • Ethnographic observation reveals undocumented practices — what people actually do, which is often not the same as the officially defined process (see Process vs. Practice below).
  • It also reveals workarounds and hacks: informal fixes people invent to bypass a system's limitations. A concrete tell-tale sign to look for is user-made artifacts — e.g. a post-it note with step-by-step instructions taped to a machine, a reminder for information the system doesn't surface, or tape covering a button that's easy to press by accident.
  • Agile methodology relies on tacit knowledge: teams get their speed partly because they rely on shared tacit understanding within the team rather than writing everything down in formal plans (attributed to Barry Boehm).
📍 CASE FILE

Jack Whalen & the call-centre technicians (Xerox PARC)

The setting

Researcher Jack Whalen studied how technicians in a call centre fixed customers' copier problems. Everyone assumed the most experienced technician would be the best performer.

What happened

The second-best performer turned out to be not the second-most-experienced person but the one who physically sat next to the expert. Knowledge spread by overhearing and watching, not by manuals or training sessions.

The lesson

This is tacit knowledge: people absorb a lot without being able to explain it. That is why you observe users in context instead of only asking them.

More from the lecture

Worked example — Jack Whalen & the call centre (Xerox PARC): Researchers studying call-centre repair technicians expected the most experienced technician to be the best performer. Instead, the second-best performer was consistently the person who physically sat next to the expert — not the second-most-experienced person by tenure.

This is offered as direct evidence for how tacit knowledge actually spreads: through proximity and informal observation/absorption, not through formal training or experience alone.

Process vs. Practice — a key conceptual pair:

Aspect Process Practice
Definition Defined rules and standard workflow What people actually do when the rules break down
Documentation Documented, easy to find Often undocumented, but equally important
Basis Repeatable across teams Experience-based judgement in context (knowing when to bend the rules)

Common mistake: treating "the process" (what's written down) as the whole story. The practice — the workarounds people invent because the process doesn't cover every real situation — is exactly the material empathy research is meant to surface, and it is often the richest source of design opportunities.

Errors during observation — Slips vs. Mistakes (this pairing recurs later, e.g. under Evaluation — cross-reference when it reappears):

Aspect Slip Mistake
Definition An execution error that prevents completing an otherwise-correct plan A planning error — the user's plan itself was wrong, and they can't self-correct it
Example fix Small physical/interface design improvements (e.g. bigger button, clearer icon) Provide clearer information; better align the interface with the user's mental model

Worked micro-examples from the slides' "evidence rubric": a slip is pressing the wrong icon by mistake (the user knew what to do, execution failed); a mistake is a user misunderstanding what "Clear cache" actually does (the user's plan/understanding itself was wrong).

Tacit knowledge — extra examples

"Being a student" involves vast unconscious practical knowledge (e.g. the socially acceptable thing to do on walking into a crowded SMU lecture room — obvious to insiders, opaque to outsiders).

Researcher Genevieve Bell calls discovering this "deep hanging out". In the Xerox PARC call-centre case, the neighbour of the top technician absorbed things manuals can't capture — e.g. how the expert arranged manuals on the desk for quick access and the rhetorical strategies used to resolve ambiguity over the phone.

Process vs. Practice — wording

Process = easy to discover (manuals), "how work should be done"; Practice = how people handle exceptions and extemporise when rules fail, how work is actually done, "experts knowing when to break rules". Great design accounts for both; the gap between them reveals the key insights.

2.2Recording empathy

Observation takes time — plan for repeated sessions, and take care to find and recruit the right people to observe (e.g. to validate a startup idea against real target users, not just whoever is convenient).

Gotcha — sampling: avoid convenience sampling (using whoever is easiest to reach); prefer representative sampling (people who actually reflect your target user population). The slides use Moen's showerhead redesign as an example of the value (and the difficulty) of finding the right people to observe.

Documentation formats and their trade-offs:

Format Pros Cons
Notes & camera (photos) Fast, captures critical incidents Loses continuous context
Video Rich data (captures everything) Time-consuming to review and transcribe
Audio Smaller files, less intrusive than video Still time-consuming to review/transcribe
Logs & diaries Captures behaviour over time, longitudinal Relies on user self-reporting

Synthetic users (AI-generated simulated users) for usability testing: they can produce simulated thoughts/needs/experiences, but they cannot replace real user research — they tend to give shallow or overly favourable feedback. The course's position: use synthetic users to supplement, not substitute real research, and specifically for desk research and generating hypotheses — not for final decision-making.

Gotcha: don't confuse this cautious framing of synthetic users (an early caution, Lecture 2) with the fuller AI-powered empathy toolset previewed in §1.4 and expanded in Lecture 22 — the course consistently treats AI tools in this space as supplements to real user contact, not replacements.

Validating a startup idea — who to validate with matters. Two idea-generation strategies were contrasted:

Strategy Approach
Market first Start with a market you're interested in, then identify a specific problem within it
Experience ripe for improvement Find an everyday consumer experience that should clearly be better
Problem first Start from a clear, specific problem statement

Airbnb's Brian Chesky is cited for the framing: focus on "100 people who love you," not a million who merely like you — i.e. depth of enthusiasm from a small, well-understood user group beats broad, shallow approval.

A related validation tool given directly, the "disappointment" test: ask users "How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]?" (very disappointed / somewhat disappointed / not disappointed / N/A no longer use it). If over 40% answer "very disappointed," the product likely has sustainable, must-have-level demand. This matters because scaling a startup too early — before this signal is present — can kill it.

📍 CASE FILE

Moen finds the right people for a shower head

The setting

Moen (2009) wanted to redesign the shower head, which meant observing how people really shower.

What happened

The team recruited naturists to observe, and the resulting product won design awards. Their point: with ingenuity you can almost always find the people you need.

The lesson

Choose representative participants for the behaviour you study, not just whoever is easiest to reach (avoid convenience sampling).

More from the lecture

Observing people showering is hard to arrange; Moen (2009) recruited nudists as participants and the resulting shower head won design awards. Lesson: "with a little ingenuity you can almost always find people." The best people to observe/interview are subject matter experts — target users with the most experience of the task. Find real experts so you learn faster.

Recording — extra tips

  • Notebook + still camera are invaluable
  • Write down everything half-interesting
  • Pictures of critical ideas/actions
  • Video is rich but slow to process
  • transcribing everything is rarely worth it — note the time of interesting events/quotes and transcribe only those
  • Audio is easier than video and often gets "good quotes".
  • Ask the observee to think-aloud while working so you can record thoughts
  • Over-the-shoulder video captures software use. Documentation list: timestamped field notes, photos of environments, audio, video, sketches of workarounds.

Startup-idea validation channels

Validate with direct feedback from the right people; use personal, professional and online platforms; mine public feedback and online forums for pain points. Anecdotes: Airbnb's product lead (listen to the customer — e.g. why Airbnb doesn't let you sort by price); Doordash/Facebook's Brian Hale (put login teams inside security rather than growth).

🧩 Pause & recall — A team interviews users and learns only what users say they do. What kind of knowledge is likely to be missed?
Answer: Tacit knowledge: workarounds, hacks and undocumented practices
Tacit knowledge is what people do without being able to easily articulate it, so observation and immersion are needed.
2.3How to interview (engaging users)

Core principle: the questions and methods you choose materially change the answers you get. Prefer open-ended, unbiased questions, especially early in design.

Gotcha — not all open-ended questions are equally useful. "Tell me a story about yourself" is technically open-ended but too vague — people struggle to produce a relevant story on demand and default to a flat summary (e.g. Q: "How is your day?" A: "It is fine."). A deeper, more specific prompt elicits a step-by-step narrative instead — e.g. "Tell me about your day, starting from arriving at work" successfully prompts a concrete walk-through.

Avoiding biased/leading questions — worked example, showing progressive improvement:

  1. Biased/leading: "How angry do you feel when an online transaction fails?" — presumes the emotion is anger.
  2. Better: "Recall a failed online transaction. How did you feel?" — removes the presumed emotion, but still only asks about feeling.
  3. Best: "Recall a failed online transaction. What did you think or feel?" — neutral, and captures both cognitive and emotional response.

Similarly, "Do you like the UI?" asked by the project team itself is biased because it invites polite agreement — reword to a neutral question that doesn't signal the "correct"/hoped-for answer.

The framing effect (added context, cognitive-bias background used to justify neutral wording): identical facts described in positive vs. negative terms shift people's choices. Classic study cited: given a hypothetical treatment for 600 people with a deadly disease, 72% chose it when it was framed as "saves 200 lives"

Only 22% chose the same outcome framed as "400 people will die." Lesson for interviewing/surveys: how you word a question can bias the answer even without an explicit leading question — pay attention to positive/negative framing, not just obvious bias.

Interview structure types:

Type Description Best for
Structured Ask only a predefined, fixed set of questions Comparability across many participants
Semi-structured Scripted core questions, but diverge/probe when useful Depth while keeping some consistency
Unstructured Interviewer chooses questions on the fly during the interview Maximum depth/flexibility, least comparability

Use focus groups specifically when group dynamics are the thing you want to observe (not just individual answers).

Planning an interview: set goals and prioritise them (you likely can't cover everything); prepare questions but ask what matters most rather than rigidly working through a full list in order; anticipate likely responses and prepare follow-up probes; practise beforehand. Also: be comfortable with silence — let the interviewee speak into a pause rather than filling it yourself ("silence is golden" / mnemonic: "silent" and "listen" share the same letters).

Why engage with users

Our minds automatically filter out information, so empathy tools give "a fresh set of eyes". Engaging directly lets you: uncover needs people may not be aware of; identify the right users to design for; discover the emotions that guide behaviour.

What people say they do — even when it differs from what they actually do — reveals deeply held beliefs.

You also need your own personal experience in the design space (immerse yourself). Qualitative observation/interview reveals how people interact with technology, what challenges they face, and how they work around them.

Interview technique — extra points

  • Binary vs open: "Do you exercise regularly?" (bad: yes/no) → "How often do you exercise in a week?" (a little better; "a lot") → "When was the last time you exercised?" (much better; elicits a story). Broad prompts like "Tell me about challenges you face" are hard to answer quickly — break questions down and prepare interviewees.
  • "Tell me a story" rarely works: people stammer ~45 s, then offer an uninteresting, possibly rehearsed story (cf. the "How is your day?" example in §2.3).
  • Biased wording — the Bradburn/Sudman/Wansink example: "Does your employer resort to trickery to defraud you of your earnings?" (words "trickery", "defraud" signal the asker's opinion; attributed to Karl Marx's survey of workers) vs. neutral "Are you fairly compensated?". The UI analogue: "Do you find that you make more mistakes with interface A than with B?" Better than "Do you like the UI?": "What are your initial impressions of the UI?" or "What challenges, if any, did you experience?"
  • Framing effect — complete setup (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981): 600 people; Treatment A = 400 die (≡ "saves 200"); Treatment B = 1/3 chance nobody dies, 2/3 chance everybody dies. Positive wording ("saves 200 lives" vs. "33% chance of saving all 600") → 72% chose A; negative wording → far fewer. (extends §2.3.)
  • Strategic silence: gives space to reflect; premature interjections lead the interviewee; uncomfortable silence prompts users to share motivations/frustrations.
  • Setting up: set goals (otherwise you feel lost); never use all questions in order; trial run with colleagues/friends to iron out redundancies/inconsistencies; introduce yourself and purpose ("the interview is about them, not you"); ask the question then let them answer; follow up; adapt to earlier answers; use their language; ask for examples; interview in their setting (or ask for a tour) so they can show rather than tell.
  • Unstructured = interviewer has full control; ideal for exploratory research.
2.4Immersion

Strategies for immersing yourself in the user's real context, beyond a single interview:

Method What it is
Contextual inquiry (Contextual Design) Observe users in their real context while asking questions to explain behaviour as it happens; learn tasks via a master–apprentice relationship
Lead-user innovation Study advanced/expert users' own workarounds and adapt user-created solutions into prototype ideas
Diary studies Users record their own experiences as they happen, over time — supports longitudinal, indirect observation
Master–apprentice pairing Learn a task step-by-step directly from an "expert" user, the way an apprentice learns a trade
📍 CASE FILE

William Whyte watches the plaza

The setting

William H. Whyte, an urban researcher, studied how people really use public plazas in his book The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces, using film and direct observation rather than questionnaires.

What happened

Watching where people stood, sat and gathered revealed behaviour that planners had not designed for: people favoured ledges and steps over purpose-built seating.

The lesson

Observation shows what people do, which often differs from what they say or what designers assume.

More from the lecture

Several slides reference embedded video clips illustrating these methods (a research-interview walkthrough contrasting a "bad" driving-experience interview with a better one; a UX persona interview clip; William H. Whyte's The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces on observing public-space use). The videos cannot be watched from the PDF; their accompanying bullet takeaways are captured above/below as source content.

Contextual inquiry — the four principles

Context (observe their environment), Partnership (work with them to understand), Interpretation (validate interpretations with participants), Focus (don't get distracted). Diary studies: best when the entry is recorded at the moment of experience

Keep entries fast (time, activity, location, people, equipment) or people stop. Lead users (von Hippel, 1986) meet needs months/years before the general market and build their own solutions Studying them anticipates future needs and gives early validation.

2.5Worked example: evidence rubric (avoid vs. collect)

The slides give a direct "what good empathy evidence looks like" rubric — useful as a checklist when writing up findings:

Concept Avoid (weak evidence) Collect instead (strong evidence) Example
Empathy Vague statement, e.g. "Users are busy" Emotion + context + constraints "Worried about missing the bus during the UTown–COM2 rush"
Tacit knowledge Only a verbal description of the workflow Shadow the user directly; capture physical artifacts Screenshots of bus-ETA checks shared via Telegram
Slip vs. mistake Labelling every error simply as "a user problem" Classify as slip or mistake; prevent slips, explain/clarify for mistakes Slip = wrong icon pressed; mistake = "Clear cache" misunderstood

Workarounds — extra evidence to look for

Handwritten notes on devices/monitors, personalised cheat sheets, unofficial shortcuts; tape across easily-pressed buttons. When designing a replacement system, existing hacks are evidence of breakdowns the new design can fix (e.g. Xerox usage tips on post-its → better help system or redesign the copier).

Slip vs. Mistake — additional worked examples

Aspect Example Suggested fix
Slip 1 Hands slip off a door handle Larger/easier-to-grab handle
Slip 2 Wrong menu item chosen four levels deep Flatten the menu hierarchy
Mistake 1 Believing Kofu is under the SIS building when it is under the SMU Library Signs pointing the way
Mistake 2 Looking for auto-correct in Preferences when it lives in Options Easier help on "auto-correct", or merge the two dialogs

Another definition of a slip: the user has the right idea of how to interact but errs in execution (mis-clicking, missing a notification).

📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Leading vs. neutral question (Bradburn, Sudman & Wansink)

The setting

A classic survey-methodology example of how wording steers answers.

What happened

“Does your employer resort to trickery to defraud you?” pushes the respondent towards a damning answer; “Are you fairly compensated?” asks the same topic without loading it.

The lesson

In interviews, ask neutral, open questions and avoid leading ones, or you collect your own opinion back.

⚡ Quick examples
Immersion techniques
PointContextual inquiry, master–apprentice learning, lead-user innovation, diary studies.
ExampleA researcher apprentices with a chef to learn kitchen ordering; users log meals for a week in a diary.
ExplanationLearning from the expert or over time reveals what snapshots cannot.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Watch people in context; field observation = natural setting, controlled = lab.
  • Users hold knowledge they cannot easily articulate: habits, workarounds, hacks.
  • Ask open-ended, unbiased questions; value silence; plan and practise.
  • Contextual inquiry, master–apprentice learning, lead-user innovation, diary studies.
  • Recruit participants who represent target users.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Tacit knowledgetap to flip
Experience-based knowledge people can't easily articulate
Process vs. Practicetap to flip
Documented rules vs. what people actually do when rules break down
Slip vs. Mistaketap to flip
Execution error (slip) vs. planning error (mistake)
Representative samplingtap to flip
Recruiting observees who reflect the real target population (vs. convenience sampling)
Synthetic userstap to flip
AI-simulated users; supplement, never substitute, real research
"40% very disappointed" testtap to flip
Startup product-viability signal from a disappointment survey
Framing effecttap to flip
Same facts, positive vs. negative wording, shift choices
Structured / semi-structured / unstructured interviewtap to flip
Fixed script / scripted-with-probes / fully improvised
Contextual inquirytap to flip
Observe + question users in their real context (master–apprentice)
Lead-user innovationtap to flip
Study & adapt advanced users' own workarounds

User self-records experience over time
➡ Where next? Your research is now a pile of observations. Next you turn it into a clear problem and needs.

lessons.title: Requirements
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersResearch is only useful once it becomes a sharp statement of who the user is and what they need.
🧠 Memory hookPersona = WHO. Scenario = WHAT HAPPENS. Personas give a face to the user; scenarios tell their story.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
The Define stageRequirements: system needs vs. user needsPersonasScenariosAI and establishing requirements (preview)
⚡ At a glance — requirement types
SideTypesExample
SystemFunctional · Non-functional · Data“Upload photo” · “loads in < 2 s” · “store user profile”
UserUser · ContextualNeeds, goals, environment, constraints
Observe→Synthesise persona→Write scenarios→Derive requirements
📛 Exact names — know these word for word: requirement types
NameWhat it coversTell it apart
Functional requirementsWhat the system does“Search products by name”
Non-functional requirementsHow well it does it (measurable)“Loads in under 2 seconds”
Data requirementsWhat data is stored and how“Store the user profile”
User requirementsUser goals, needs and pain pointsAbout the person, not the system
Contextual requirementsThe context and conditions in which the product is usedUser-side, with user requirements

The first three describe the system; the last two describe the user side.

This lecture covers the Define stage of Design Thinking (§1.3) — the step where raw empathy findings are turned into a clear design direction — plus the concrete artefacts (personas, scenarios) used to capture requirements.

3.1The Define stage

Define means to clarify and reframe the design problem: synthesise empathy findings into insights, and frame opportunities for design alternatives. Its key outputs are personas and scenarios, plus a clear Point of View (POV) — a synthesised, insight-driven statement of the real problem to solve (as opposed to an assumption-driven one).

Worked example — Whyte's public-space study, revisited for insight extraction: The same Social Life of Small Urban Spaces footage introduced in §2 is used here to demonstrate turning observation into insight: people use public space to participate, not to escape (i.e. they want social contact, not just solitude) People adapt/repurpose designed spaces to fit their own needs

Informal features (steps, ledges/edges) are often used more than purpose-built seating

Social activity increases where there is seating, food, and cues inviting interaction. A second worked example (HDB Smart Planning) draws the insight that smart-technology initiatives should focus on people and lived experience, not on the technology itself.

Point of View (POV) statement and its test

  • Template: "___ (persona) needs to (function) ___ because ___ (insight)." A POV reframes a design challenge into an actionable problem statement that launches generative ideation.
  • A good POV: provides focus and frames the problem
  • Is a reference for evaluating competing ideas
  • Empowers team members to decide in line with high-level goals
  • Fuels brainstorms by suggesting "How Might We" statements; captures hearts and minds
  • Saves you from solutions "all things to all people"
  • Is revisited and reformulated as you learn. HDB smart-planning take-away: "It is about the people, not the technology."
3.2Requirements: system needs vs. user needs
Category Sub-type Covers
System requirements Functional What the system must do; required behaviours
Non-functional (measurable) Performance, usability, scalability, security, reliability, maintainability
Data What data must be stored, and how (e.g. which database)
User requirements — User goals, needs, and pain points

Gotcha: non-functional requirements are frequently forgotten because they're not about what the system does but about how well — but they are explicitly called out as measurable (e.g. "loads in under 2 seconds," "supports 10,000 concurrent users"), so they should be written as testable criteria, not vague adjectives.

Requirements — examples and a three-way framing

Functional example: "The system shall allow users to search for products by name, category or price range." Non-functional example: "Must use HTTPS and encrypt user data." Good requirements combine types in one sentence — e.g. "The system allows the user to book [functional] a holiday plan [data] while allowing all family members to discuss the plan [contextual]." (Cooper, About Face p.116.) Persona vs. user requirement contents: user needs = problems to solve

User goals = what users want to accomplish.

🧩 Pause & recall — Which is a non-functional requirement?
Answer: The page must load in under 2 seconds
Non-functional requirements describe qualities/constraints (performance, security, usability), not specific functions.
3.3Personas

Persona (formal definition, reproduced from source): "User characteristics that represent a group of users, described as a realistic individual" / a set of characteristics that "represent a target group and bring them to life."

Key principles:

  • A persona is grounded in real data — it is synthesised from real user research, not invented from assumptions, and is explicitly not a real person.
  • It describes behaviours, goals, and motivations — not a stereotype, a job role/title, a "profile," or a market segment.
  • It's brought to life with a name, background, goals, frustrations/pain points, and short stories, so the team can reason about "what would [persona] do here?" concretely.

Characteristics used to build a persona include: ability, background, and attitude to technology; economic status, habits and preferences; and behaviour range:

Behaviour dimension Low end High end
Expertise Novice — needs step-by-step guidance, constrained choices Expert — wants flexibility, shortcuts, power-user access
Frequency of use Infrequent — needs clear instructions (e.g. menu paths spelled out) Frequent — wants shortcuts and efficiency
Skills e.g. platform familiarity (iOS vs Android)

Persona types — a comparison table, since these are easy to conflate:

Type Definition Example
Primary The most important persona; the core user the system is designed for The buyer in a marketplace app
Secondary Lower-priority or additional users who still interact with the system The seller in a marketplace app
Supplemental Needs already covered by primary/secondary personas; introduces no new requirements A payment provider
Customer Purchases the software but does not personally use it A manager or purchasing officer
Served Affected by the system but neither uses nor buys it The end-customer being supported by staff who use the system

Steps for creating personas (given as a 7-step process; note the slide numbering is non-sequential in the source — sequence given here is the intended logical order):

flowchart TD
    S1["1. Identify behavioural variables<br/>(activities, attitudes, motivations, skills, roles)"] --> S2["2. Map behavioural range<br/>(e.g. Novice–Expert; Price–Quality conscious)"]
    S2 --> S3["3. Identify behavioural patterns<br/>(cluster users with similar behaviours)"]
    S3 --> S4["4. Synthesise characteristics<br/>(environment, routines, goals, frustrations)"]
    S4 --> S5["5. Check redundancy & gaps<br/>(ensure coverage, spot missing behaviour)"]
    S5 --> S6["6. Expand the description<br/>(add detail and visual cues)"]
    S6 --> S7["7. Designate persona types<br/>(primary, secondary, supplemental)"]

Caption: the persona-creation pipeline — note it starts from raw behavioural data (step 1–3, essentially clustering real observations), only then writes a rich description (steps 4–6), and only assigns primary/secondary/supplemental status last (step 7), once you know how the personas relate to each other.

Tips for personas (practical constraints): Prioritise only the highest-impact personas — avoid creating one for every low-impact edge case Include just enough detail relevant to the problem (balance depth against time available) Check for and remove redundant/inconsistent personas, keeping only genuinely differentiating features

When user data is limited, create a provisional persona and use it to plan further research rather than treating it as final. This directly supports the summary's listed common pitfalls: too many personas, and personas that are too detailed.

Empathy map: a collaborative visualisation tool used to synthesise raw observations into a persona (i.e. it's the intermediate step between empathy data and a finished persona). It structures notes into four quadrants:

Quadrant Captures
Say What the user said — key quotes and phrases
Do What the user did — observed actions and behaviours
Think What the user might be thinking — inferred beliefs/assumptions
Feel What emotions the user might be experiencing

It helps identify goals and pain points, aligns the team/stakeholders on a shared understanding, and directly feeds the persona's characteristics.

Extra persona-creation detail

Typical behavioural variables for the case studies: age group, price-vs-quality orientation, purpose of use, assistive device, mode of transport, computing-device use frequency, tech fluency, expertise, casual-vs-power use, supervised vs. self-practice (rehab case). Step 1 = collect & organise data (e.g. in an empathy map/table)

Step 2 = map participants to variables Step 3 = identify significant behaviour patterns (cluster, e.g. "users 1, 4, 5") Step 4 = synthesise characteristics and goals into brief bullets

Steps 5–7 refine. Step 5 (redundancy/completeness) → step 6: expand bullets into a third-person narrative and research any behaviour missing from the ranges. A persona should have a clear scope — an app for diverse users with different goals increases cognitive load and navigational overhead (Cooper, About Face 4th ed., p.62). Provisional personas are also useful for designing the qualitative data-gathering process

Definition: built from historical/anecdotal/statistical knowledge rather than patterns seen directly in user research.

Persona risks with AI

personas built from synthetic data can amplify biases, misrepresent groups, overlook cultural nuance and fail to capture individual characteristics. (cf. §2.2 synthetic users, §22.3 sycophancy.)

3.4Scenarios

Scenario (formal definition, reproduced from source): "An informal narrative about a specific situation involving an IT system," grounded in a persona so the story reflects real user goals and pain points. Scenarios are used early, deliberately keep UI and implementation details abstract, and focus on clarifying what the product should do rather than how it looks.

Gotcha — Scenarios vs. Use Cases (easy to conflate; the slides pose this explicitly as a discussion question):

Aspect Scenario Use Case
Formality Informal narrative Formal sequence of actions and system responses
Focus User goals and context System behaviour and interactions
UI/system detail Kept abstract Concrete
Best used for Understanding user needs; framing requirements (requirements discovery) Software design and implementation

Rule of thumb: reach for a scenario when you're still figuring out what problem you're solving; reach for a use case once you know the goal and need to specify exactly how the system will behave step by step.

📍 CASE FILE

Jason and Home Bake Delivery

The setting

The course carries one example through persona, scenario and requirements. Jason is a 24-year-old business-admin student who delivers cakes for his mother's home bakery part-time.

What happened

His persona records goals (support the family business, save for a start-up, do more deliveries per day, keep customers happy) and pain points (time spent planning routes, obscure drop-off points, expensive parking, customers who can't be reached, last-minute changes). He uses Google Maps and WhatsApp. The scenario then tells his afternoon in plain language: he imports orders, follows a suggested route, adapts on the fly and completes the drop-offs, without naming a single screen.

The lesson

A persona gives the team a face and real needs; a scenario shows the context and flow. Together they turn research into requirements without prescribing the interface.

More from the lecture

Worked example — Home Bake Delivery (Jason), carried through all three levels:

  • Persona: Jason, 24, business-admin student, delivers for his mother's home bakery part-time; uses Google Maps and WhatsApp; goals include supporting the family business, saving for his own start-up, completing more deliveries/day, keeping customers happy; pain points include route planning time, finding obscure drop-off points, affordable parking, uncontactable customers, and last-minute changes.
  • Scenario (narrative, UI abstract): a plain-language walkthrough of Jason's afternoon using a delivery app (imports orders, follows a suggested route, adapts on the fly, completes drop-offs).
  • Use case (formal, concrete): the same scenario rewritten as a numbered system/user interaction sequence (system displays input options → user imports orders → system shows recommended route → … → system confirms completed order → loop until all orders delivered).

This progression — user story → scenario → use case — mirrors a real design pipeline: user stories capture what the user wants and why; scenarios expand that into a contextual narrative; use cases formalise the narrative into precise system interactions. Each stage adds structure and precision, moving from raw user needs toward an implementable spec.

Scenario types (a second, more detailed scenario taxonomy — don't confuse this "scenario" with the "context/key/validation" set below; they describe stages of refinement of the same story, not alternative techniques):

Type Also called Detail level UI Focus Used when
Context scenario "Happy path," easy case Early-stage, brief Kept abstract User goals and context Start of design
Key scenario "Happy path," detailed Detailed and structured Concrete Critical paths through the system Deriving use cases
Validation scenario Edge case, "what if things go wrong?" Shorter than a key scenario — Breakdowns and exceptions Testing and evaluation, often after detailed design

The "hard" version of the Home Bake Delivery scenario (Jason hunting for cheaper parking, a customer asleep and unreachable, a last-minute reschedule request, an accident triggering a reroute, and difficulty finding a unit resolved via an AR wayfinding feature) is the slides' worked example of a validation scenario: every beat is a plausible breakdown/exception the system needs to gracefully handle.

Worked persona/scenario case studies in the other decks

Case Persona (summary) Scenario / insight
AccessTrip Joe, 35, wheelchair user and research scientist planning a conference trip to Osaka; wants accessible hotels. Derived from interviews with mobility-impaired participants (cane/walker/scooter users) Scenario narrates searching hotels by location/dates/accessibility; abstract about the UI.
RehabCoach Maria, 58, post-stroke survivor, no smartphone, wants ≥3 exercise sessions/week; pain points: forgets sessions, can't perform exercises 100% correctly, low motivation (Lee et al. 2022) Context (happy-path) scenario: schedules sessions → service reminds her → detects incorrect form and suggests fixes → reports progress over three sessions.
RoadRunner delivery Jason: part-time delivery 3 days/week; goals: efficient routes, customer loyalty; pains: manual route planning, uncontactable customers, revisits Easy scenario ("smooth delivery day": plan → coordinate → deliver → complete) vs. hard scenario (parking too expensive, customer unavailable/changes time, accident blocks route, drop-off hard to find).
Will & Well Adaptive clothing for disabled users (Elisa Lim): wheelchair users, drawstring pants with caregiver zip, eating-ice-cream pains Example of requirements discovered through lived experience.

The hard scenario asks "what additional requirements do these situations reveal?" — complications become new requirements. Scenario template: When / Where / What happens? and "what happens as they try to achieve it?"; these goals and pain points should appear in the scenario.

User stories vs. scenarios vs. use cases

User story format: "As a [type of user], I want to [action] so that [goal/benefit]" (e.g. "As a customer, I want to track my delivery in real time so that I know when to be available"). Scenarios are longer narratives and often contain several user stories; user stories are brief structured statements. Use cases suit developers needing the precise user↔system sequence (e.g. "user chooses building list, system provides list…").

Scenario Use case
Focus on user experience and context Focus on system functionality and logic
Goals abstract and generalised; UI abstract UI concrete and detailed
Informal narrative Written in structured format
3.5AI and establishing requirements (preview)

As AI systems act more like goal-driven agents rather than fixed tools, and interfaces are increasingly generated dynamically based on user intent/context, requirements shift away from specifying fixed screens and toward specifying: user goals, decision boundaries, and constraints/trust requirements.

Consequences for personas and scenarios: personas should capture intent, trust, and delegation (how much the user is willing to let the AI decide on its own) Scenarios should describe human–AI collaboration, not just single-user actions

Designers define what must be resolved, not how it visually looks. (Expanded fully in Lecture 22.)

⚡ Quick examples
Types of requirements
PointSystem side: functional, non-functional, data. User side: user and contextual.
ExampleFunctional 'upload a photo'; non-functional 'loads under 2 s'; data 'store profile'; contextual 'used one-handed on a train'.
ExplanationSeparating types makes sure you capture both what the system does and how well and where it must work.
Persona pitfalls
PointDon't make too many personas or over-detailed ones.
ExampleTen personas for a simple booking app dilute focus; knowing Mei's favourite food adds nothing.
ExplanationA few focused personas are usable; excess detail is noise.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • System side: functional, non-functional, data. User side: user and contextual.
  • A persona is a synthesised archetype with behaviour patterns backed by data — not a real person.
  • Don't make too many personas or over-detailed ones.
  • Scenarios narrate how a persona reaches a goal, keeping the UI abstract.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Point of View (POV)tap to flip
Insight-driven statement of the real design problem (Define output)
Functional / non-functional / data requirementstap to flip
What system does / how well it does it / what & how data is stored
Personatap to flip
Realistic-individual representation of a user group, from real data
Primary / Secondary / Supplemental / Customer / Served personatap to flip
Persona-type taxonomy by role relative to the system
Empathy map (Say/Do/Think/Feel)tap to flip
Tool synthesising raw observation into a persona
Scenariotap to flip
Informal, UI-abstract narrative of a specific situation
Use casetap to flip
Formal, concrete sequence of system/user interactions
Context / Key / Validation scenariotap to flip
Early abstract / detailed critical-path / edge-case scenario
Persona vs. scenario (extra)tap to flip
Persona = data-backed behaviour patterns (not one interviewee/celebrity); scenario narrates goal achievement
➡ Where next? With the problem defined, it is time to generate lots of ways to solve it.
