lessons.title: Ideate
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersGood ideas come from many ideas. Creativity is a method, not a mood.
🧠 Memory hookDiverge, then Converge. Go wide (quantity, defer judgement) before you go deep (choose).
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Creative confidence & playQuantity & quality (divergence and convergence)Functional/design fixationInspirationGuidelines & brainstorming processAI-powered ideation
⚡ At a glance — diverge → converge
Diverge: many ideas, wild ideas, defer judgement→Converge: select with explicit criteria→Prototype the best few

Ideate is the brainstorming stage of Design Thinking: explore a wide solution space, go beyond the obvious, and pull on diverse team perspectives to generate ideas from unexpected places. The lecture organises this into five guidelines.

4.1Creative confidence & play

Brainstorming works best as a low-stakes, playful activity ("play in a safe sandbox") rather than a high-pressure evaluation exercise.

Two supporting cases: David Kelley's TED talk on creative confidence describes how a teacher once shut down a student's creative confidence (illustrating how early negative feedback can suppress people's willingness to generate ideas later in life), and describes Doug Dietz's redesign of a GE MRI machine — reframing a frightening medical scan into a "pirate ship adventure" for child patients, an example of empathy-driven reframing solving a problem no purely technical fix could.

Stuart Brown's "play is more than fun" talk frames play (curiosity, social play, rough-and-tumble, imaginative/story play) as a legitimate route to innovation, not a distraction from it.

Creative confidence — extra detail

  • Kelley: many people divide the world into "creative types" and "practical types"
  • Early criticism creates lasting creative blocks
  • Fear of judgement stops people sharing ideas
  • creative confidence = belief that everyone can think creatively given the right environment. Doug Dietz's MRI redesign: children were terrified of his technically excellent machine
  • Theming it as adventures cut sedation rates from ~80% to under 10%. Practices: psychological safety to take risks
  • Playful elements/toys reduce inhibitions
  • Treat "failed" ideas as learning. A contrast case: a child X-ray device designed without empathy.
4.2Quantity & quality (divergence and convergence)

Core claim: quantity is the path to quality. Cited evidence — the "quantity vs quality" ceramics class experiment (Bayles & Orland, Art and Fear): one group was graded purely on the quantity of pots produced, the other purely on submitting one "perfect" pot.

The quantity group ended up producing the highest-quality work, because they learned iteratively from many attempts, while the quality group spent their time theorising about the ideal pot and had little to show for it. Similarly, IDEO's Paul Bradley built 80 foam models while designing the Microsoft mouse.

Design ideation therefore proceeds in alternating phases:

flowchart LR
    D1[Diverge:<br/>generate many ideas] --> C1[Converge:<br/>select best ideas]
    C1 -->|Second pass| D2[Diverge again]
    D2 --> C2[Converge again]

Caption: divergence generates breadth (many candidate solutions); convergence narrows that breadth down to the strongest candidates. A single diverge→converge pass can still miss good ideas hiding outside the initially explored space — so the cycle should be iterated, re-diverging from the converged result rather than stopping after one pass, to reach solutions that a single pass would have missed.

Quantity — how IDEO builds it in

Three reasons multiple alternatives matter in design; the first is building dozens of prototypes to understand the design space (Paul Bradley's 80 foam mouse models). Each iteration explores different aspects of ergonomics, usability and aesthetics; the final design combines elements from several prototypes — "no single model was perfect". Buxton: design has two core activities — generating multiple solutions (divergence) then selecting desirable ones (convergence).

Why one diverge–converge pass is not enough (iteration detail)

Pass Role
Pass 1 Establishes understanding of the problem space, obvious solutions and constraints; builds creative momentum/team dynamics; breadth over depth
Pass 2 Diverges in more promising directions using lessons from pass 1; strong ideas are combined/transformed

Converging only incrementally improves your existing good ideas, so you can miss better ones; a better approach is to start with brainstorming and make big variations early, saving small improvements for later iterations.

🧩 Pause & recall — Which statement best captures 'quantity leads to quality' in ideation?
Answer: Generate many ideas, then converge on the best
Alternate divergence (many options) and convergence (selection).
4.3Functional/design fixation

Functional fixation (formal definition, added context from cognitive psychology): The tendency to see an object or a concept only in terms of its most familiar use, which blocks you from seeing alternative uses or approaches. Classic demonstration: Duncker's candle problem (1945) — given a candle, matches, and a box of tacks, the task is to attach the candle to the wall so wax doesn't drip on the table

📍 CASE FILE

Duncker's candle problem (1945)

The setting

A classic psychology experiment on functional fixedness: people are given a candle, matches and a box of tacks and must fix the candle to a wall so wax does not drip on the table.

What happened

Most people fail because they see the box only as a container for tacks. The solution is to empty it, tack it to the wall and use it as a platform for the candle.

The lesson

Functional fixation is seeing an object only in terms of its familiar use. In design it appears as design fixation: sticking with your first workable idea.

Most people fail to see that the tack box itself can be emptied and used as a candle-holder platform, because they perceive the box only as "a container for tacks," not as "a potential platform."

Design fixation Is the same phenomenon applied to a design task: once a designer generates or is given one workable idea, they tend to lock onto it and refine it rather than exploring alternatives.

Worked example — the egg-drop design task (Dow et al., 2009): participants who had already settled on one approach (e.g. a parachute) described being unable to see any other option ("I don't see any other," "I am not a very good outside-the-box thinker...

📍 CASE FILE

The egg-drop study (Dow et al., 2009)

The setting

Researchers asked participants to design a way to protect a dropped egg, then examined how they thought about the problem.

What happened

Those who had settled on one approach (for example a parachute) said they could not see any other option, even when better designs existed. Participants shown a sample solution beforehand were more fixated than those given none.

The lesson

Showing examples can increase fixation. Generate many alternatives and defer judgement before choosing.

I kinda just had one idea"), even when better designs existed.

Gotcha — providing examples increases fixation, it doesn't reduce it. Participants shown a sample solution before designing showed more fixation in their own designs than a control group given no samples at all — they anchored on the example. The control group's fixation instead came from anchoring on their own first self-generated idea.

Lesson: giving your team a "reference example" for inspiration can backfire by narrowing the idea space rather than widening it — introduce examples carefully, and only after a first independent round of ideation, if at all.

Related risk: ego investment. Once a designer has invested effort into a single idea (e.g. "their" egg-drop design), anxiety about having that idea critiqued affects their performance and willingness to consider alternatives — reinforcing why "defer judgement" (§4.5) is a deliberate ideation-stage rule, not just etiquette.

Design fixation — more findings

In the egg-drop task most participants settled quickly on one approach, many on cushioning like existing packaging; few explored radically different ones. Seeing examples first: designs resemble the examples, often copying unnecessary features that don't address the core problem (Leahy, Daly, McKilligan & Seifert).

Cause of attachment Description
Ego investment Emotional attachment to initial concepts
Anxiety Fear of failure → clinging to "safe" solutions
Cognitive economy The brain conserves energy by reusing familiar patterns
Confirmation bias We notice evidence supporting existing ideas

Designers working in parallel respond more positively to critique (negative feedback on one of several ideas isn't read as "I'm a bad designer"); a serial participant described feeling "I'm a failure at this" after feedback on his single design — anxiety harms performance.

Anti-fixation techniques: develop several distinct concepts in parallel; add artificial constraints ("How would you solve this without electricity?", "What if it had to fit in a pocket?"); anonymise ideas during critique to remove ego; set strict time limits so you don't polish one idea.

4.4Inspiration

It's acceptable — encouraged, even — to draw inspiration from existing designs, provided sources are cited and not plagiarised ("Good artists borrow, great artists steal" — Picasso, illustrated by Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon drawing visible influence from 19th-century Fang/African sculpture).

Gotcha — tension with §4.3: "draw inspiration from existing designs" (guideline 4) sits in direct tension with "providing examples increases fixation" (guideline 3, §4.3). The resolution implied by the ordering of the guidelines: use existing designs as background inspiration/citation after you've already generated your own independent ideas — not as a starting template handed to the team before they've ideated on their own.

Inspiration — nuance

All new ideas build on existing ones, but too much exposure to current solutions limits thinking; research existing solutions after initial ideation, to refine not define.

Picasso studied African masks/sculptures, absorbed their abstract representation of the human form and used it to create Cubism — "find someone to imitate who hasn't been imitated before".

Take inspiration from outside your domain; cite sources. User hacks/DIY solutions reveal unmet needs and priorities (cf. §2 workarounds).

4.5Guidelines & brainstorming process

Guideline summary: focus on the topic, but entertain wild ideas; defer judgement; go for quantity.

Setting up a brainstorming session:

Element Guidance
Setting Stand up, use whiteboard space, capture every idea (whiteboard/sticky notes), keep toys/mock-ups on hand
Participants Diverse viewpoints; include non-decision-makers; limit group size to 6–8 people
Topic Not too broad, not too narrow; frame the prompt provocatively

Session process:

  1. Prelude — a warm-up activity.
  2. Brainstorm — go for quantity; defer judgement; encourage wild ideas; build on others' ideas; everyone writes on sticky notes (be visual, share the pen).
  3. Postlude — each person votes for their favourites; capture everything (don't discard ideas even if unvoted).

(The slides also reference IDEO U's "7 Rules for the Perfect Brainstorming Session" as further reading, without listing all seven explicitly.)

Purpose in practice: brainstorming is used to address specific breakdowns identified during user observation (i.e. it follows directly from the empathy work in §2) — it is a core technique for generating out-of-the-box ideas to help users overcome those breakdowns.

Brainstorm session set-up — extra points

Standing space, ample writing surfaces, physical objects/toys, sticky notes for all; include people of different expertise; limit decision-makers to prevent premature evaluation; 6–8 people; consider including users/stakeholders.

Frame topics as "How might we…", breaking complex problems into focused topics. Prelude warm-ups shift from analytical to creative thinking and build energy Sticky notes give everyone an equal voice and a visual record

Stay visual (quick sketches), and avoid a dominator. Brainstorming targets breakdowns — frustration points, workarounds, pauses/confusion, expectations vs. reality

Each breakdown is an opportunity and may have several solutions. In practice you iterate between writing scenarios and ideating solutions.

SCAMPER prompts with app examples

A structured idea-generation checklist, illustrated with products:

Move Guiding question / examples
Substitute Replace the manual process with automation — Google Pay (contactless for cash), CamScanner (phone camera for scanner), Grammarly (AI for proofreading)
Combine WeChat (messaging + payments + ride-hailing + shopping), Strava (fitness + social), Notion (notes + databases + collaboration)
Adapt Duolingo (gaming for language learning), Apple Watch (medical devices for health), Uber Eats (ride-hailing logistics for food)
Magnify/Modify Facebook Lite (low bandwidth), Instagram Stories (ephemeral content as core), Google Maps offline
Put to another use Slack (game chat → workplace tool), Pinterest (wishlist → visual discovery), Zoom (business → education)
Eliminate Instagram removing non-photo features from Burbn; Google's minimalist homepage; Dropbox focusing only on syncing/sharing
Reverse/Rearrange Airbnb (homeowners as hoteliers), TikTok (feed before account creation), Spotify Discover Weekly

(The slide listing is partially extracted; the mapping of examples to SCAMPER letters follows the guiding questions shown and is marked (inferred) where the heading was not shown.)

4.6AI-powered ideation

AI is framed as a brainstorming partner, not a replacement: it amplifies divergence by generating many ideas quickly, exploring a wider possibility space and reducing early fixation, acting as a kind of "naïve expert" that proposes unexpected ideas a human might not think of. This implies a redefined designer role: the human defines the problem and constraints, the AI generates options, and the human curates, judges, and refines.

Caution (explicitly flagged in the source): AI can introduce its own new fixation (e.g. converging on similar, low-novelty ideas across many prompts), so human judgement remains essential — don't treat AI-generated idea volume as automatically equivalent to genuine divergence.

Purpose of ideation — "flaring, not focusing"

Ideate = going wide in concepts and outcomes; the goal is a wide solution space with both fluency (volume) and flexibility (variety), to harness team perspectives, uncover unexpected areas, and "get obvious solutions out of your heads". It is the transition from identifying problems to exploring solutions.

Worked ideation example

From a persona's goals, restate them as "successfully book a wheelchair-accessible hotel room" / "find accessible transport", ask "how could we address the challenges / help people achieve their goals", then list solutions (e.g. accessibility-aware hotel search with filter-by-ability

Behaviour-pattern analysis for an exercise reminder system Intuitive priority graphics with explanations).

For each solution, think how you could implement it. each member produces ≥5 ideas on sticky notes (10 min) → group related ideas and assess (5 min) → present. With "How might we…" for 1–3 key pain points Present (2 min share + 3 min discussion), then redo with feedback.

⚡ Quick examples
Diverge then converge
PointGenerate many options (diverge), then select with explicit criteria (converge).
ExampleSketch 20 ways to show bus arrivals, then pick the top 3 by speed to understand.
ExplanationQuantity raises the chance of a great idea; criteria keep selection fair.
AI as a brainstorming partner
PointAI can amplify divergence but may introduce its own fixation.
ExampleTeams accept the first reasonable ChatGPT idea and all end up similar.
ExplanationHumans must curate and challenge AI output rather than defer to it.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Generate many options (diverge), then select with explicit criteria (converge).
  • Focus on the topic, entertain wild ideas, go for quantity, defer judgement, use sticky notes.
  • People lock onto early or provided concepts.
  • AI can amplify divergence but may introduce its own fixation.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Divergence / Convergencetap to flip
Generate many ideas / narrow to the best
Functional / design fixationtap to flip
Locking onto an object's familiar use / onto an early design idea
➡ Where next? Ideas are cheap but unproven — so make them tangible and test them quickly.

lessons.title: Prototype
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersA prototype is a question you can hold in your hand. It lets you learn before you build.
🧠 Memory hookFail early, fail cheap. Low-fidelity to learn, high-fidelity to polish.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Why prototype: known unknowns vs. unknown unknownsDesign is a choice (Bill Buxton)Strategy: serial vs. parallel prototypingGoals: form vs. function vs. experienceMethods: low, medium, and high fidelity
⚡ At a glance — prototype fidelity
FidelityExamplesUse when
LowStoryboard, paper, navigation diagram, Wizard-of-OzExploring concepts fast and cheaply
MediumPowerPoint, POP, BalsamiqTesting flow and layout
HighFigma, Justinmind, Axure, AI generators (Claude Design, Stitch)Testing look, feel and detailed interaction
Serial = one after another (risks fixation)→Parallel = several at once (better, more divergent)
5.1Why prototype: known unknowns vs. unknown unknowns

Prototyping is a strategy for efficiently dealing with things that are hard to predict. The lecture distinguishes:

  • Known unknowns — things you know you don't know (you can plan research to answer them directly).
  • Unknown unknowns — things you don't even know you don't know. Prototyping is specifically valuable for surfacing unknown unknowns, because building something tangible and putting it in front of real use/users exposes problems no one thought to ask about in advance.

This directly extends course value #2 from §1.2 (prototype for feedback) and connects back to the "gulf" concepts covered later in §6.4.

5.2Design is a choice (Bill Buxton)

Quoted directly: "Design is choice, and there are two places where there is room for creativity: 1) the creativity that you bring to enumerating meaningfully distinct options from which to choose[;] 2) the creativity that you bring to defining the criteria, or heuristics, according to which you make your choices (metrics)." — Bill Buxton. Point 2 (defining measurable goals/criteria) is called out as hard but important work — you cannot meaningfully compare prototypes without first deciding, in advance, what "better" means for this project.

🧩 Pause & recall — Why prototype early?
Answer: To learn about known unknowns and uncover unknown unknowns cheaply
Prototypes are a strategy for dealing efficiently with things that are hard to predict.
5.3Strategy: serial vs. parallel prototyping

Claim: more divergence leads to better design. Comparison, evidenced by an ad-design study:

Aspect Serial prototyping Parallel prototyping
Structure One design, iterated repeatedly with feedback between each iteration Several distinct designs developed alongside each other, each getting feedback, before converging
Study setup 6 iterations on one design 3 iterations on three designs
Click-through rate 398 / million 445 / million
Time on site (avg, s) 21 28
Expert rating (0–50) 22 24
Similarity (0–7, 7 = most similar to each other) 3.18 2.78 (parallel designs stayed more distinct from each other)

Parallel prototyping outperformed serial prototyping on every measured outcome. A serial-condition participant's quote illustrates why: "I tried to find a good idea, and then use that idea and keep improving it and getting feedback. So, I pretty much stuck with the same idea" — i.e. serial prototyping is highly prone to the design fixation already introduced in §4.3, because each iteration reinforces commitment to the first idea rather than exploring alternatives.

Cross-reference: parallel prototyping is the prototyping-stage embodiment of the same "quantity/divergence before convergence" principle taught for ideation in §4.2 — the same underlying lesson (don't commit early) recurs at two different stages of the process.

📍 CASE FILE

Designing ads for Ambidextrous (Dow et al.)

The setting

Designers were asked to create banner ads for the Stanford student journal Ambidextrous and were split into serial and parallel prototyping groups.

What happened

The parallel group made several designs at once (3, then 2, then a final one) and received feedback on all of them; they produced more diverse designs than the serial group, who refined one idea at a time.

The lesson

Prototyping several options in parallel reduces fixation and gives better results than refining a single idea.

More from the lecture

Designers made online ads for the Stanford student journal Ambidextrous (a zoo ad brief in the slide) and received structured feedback so it was comparable. Serial = make one design at a time with feedback after each (6 designs).

Parallel = create 3 designs, get feedback on all; create 2, get feedback; create a final design. Both groups had the same total time and feedback. Metrics: click-through rate (clicks through to the magazine), time on client site, expert ratings.

Parallel also showed lower similarity between designs (more diverse). The serial designers' interviews echoed the egg-drop fixation comments; serial iterations showed minimal variation.

5.4Goals: form vs. function vs. experience

A prototype should be built to test a specific one (or more) of three goal types:

Goal Tests Example from source
Form Look & feel — physical/visual appearance A furniture design competition focused on form
Function Role / what it actually does (implementation) The same furniture competition also needs function — this course focuses primarily on form
Experience The end-to-end feel of using the thing in context Boring Company's Las Vegas tunnel using Tesla FSD (an experience prototype of what riding through it feels like, distinct from the actual engineered implementation — the "Vegas Loop")

Additional worked examples used to practice classifying a prototype's goal: the iGlass AR-glasses concept design, and Apple's Vision Pro OS — asking "is this prototype demonstrating form, function, or experience?" for each.

Why prototypes matter beyond testing: they also communicate with stakeholders — colleagues, clients, users, and even yourself (a prototype clarifies your own thinking).

Where to prototype (cost/time/resource vs. learning trade-off): the guidance is to stay as early/cheap as possible for as long as possible — i.e. favour the point that maximises learning per unit of cost/time spent, rather than jumping straight to an expensive, resource-heavy prototype.

A prototype, regardless of fidelity, should be: incomplete (it doesn't need to do everything the final product will), easy to change (low cost of revision), and (disposable/short-lived) — thrown away once it has answered its question, rather than treated as precious.

What a prototype is, and why

A simple experimental model of a proposed solution used to test/validate ideas and assumptions quickly and cheaply so designers can refine or change direction. Benefits: streamlines development by focusing on important interface elements Gives the client a complete idea of the end result

Exposes unnecessary elements early; avoids global changes later Involves the customer. Alternative definition: an early sample, model or release built to test a concept or process

A wireframe is a basic outline of a digital experience, like an app or website. Prototypes let you learn what works with minimal cost. Houde & Hill identify three goal types for prototypes (form/function/experience) — see "What Do Prototypes Prototype?".

📍 CASE FILE

IDEO's camera back (1990s)

The setting

In the 1990s, when digital cameras were new (cf. the Kodak DC210), IDEO wanted to test the experience before any real product existed.

What happened

They built a mock-up camera back, not to scale, tethered by a thick cable to a desktop that ran the graphics and logic. It did not even take pictures. What mattered was having the right inputs and co-located input and output, so users could browse the pictures they had taken.

The lesson

A prototype only needs to answer one question. Choose the fidelity that tests that question, and no more.

More from the lecture

In the 1990s (cf. Kodak DC210, 1998) IDEO built a mock-up camera back: not to scale, tethered by a thick cable to a desktop that ran graphics/logic, and it didn't even take pictures. What mattered was the right inputs and co-located input/output, so users could experience it as a camera — specifically browsing the pictures they had taken, the key difference from film cameras. Exploring experience questions this way matters more as computing leaves the desktop.

Measurable prototype goals

Define specific, measurable criteria; think of 3–5 goals a prototype should help you evaluate. Measurable goals also reveal when goals conflict, so you can set priorities and trade-offs.

Functional fixation explains why novices stumble on one design "that seems to work" and argue for it. (Buxton's point #2 = this goal-setting.) Plans vs planning: "Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face" Eisenhower: *"Plans are worthless

But planning is everything."* Design Thinking rejects the rigid project-planning mindset yet keeps a flexible plan.

The prototype value equation

A prototype has no value except what it teaches: ask "what can this prototype teach me?"; maximise learning while minimising cost/time/resources; stop improving a prototype once it has taught you all it can; avoid over-building features not tied to a learning goal; don't get attached — be willing to start fresh.

5.5Methods: low, medium, and high fidelity
flowchart LR
    subgraph Low["Low Fidelity"]
        L1[Navigation Diagrams]
        L2[Storyboards]
        L3[Paper Prototypes]
    end
    subgraph Med["Medium Fidelity"]
        M1[PowerPoint]
        M2[POP]
        M3[Balsamiq]
        M4[Figma]
    end
    subgraph High["High Fidelity"]
        H1[Figma]
        H2[JustinMind]
        H3[Axure]
        H4[Partial implementation]
    end
    Low --> Med --> High

Caption: fidelity increases left→right; note Figma spans medium-to-high fidelity depending on how it's used.

Method Fidelity What it's for
Navigation diagram (sitemap / flow diagram) Low Sitemap = hierarchical view, doesn't need to show all navigation; flow diagram = shows the decision process, focused on the main flow only. Rule of thumb: whichever works, as long as each "view"/screen appears exactly once.
Storyboard Low Quick, versatile, powerful way to depict a sequence of use in context
Paper prototype Low Read the scenario as-is and show the corresponding UI; change the UI freely without touching the scenario; keep separate pages for separate UI states/dialogs/pop-ups; focus on the big-picture goal, avoid polishing specific visual details (colour, font, alignment)
Wizard of Oz Low → High (technique, not a fidelity level) The system's "intelligence" is faked by a hidden human operator behind the scenes — at low fidelity, a paper UI where the designer manually shows the effect of an action; at medium/high fidelity, a fixed-path map, a pre-written "static" AI reply, a static video, or a Figma-triggered video standing in for real functionality
PowerPoint prototype Medium Draw/shape design (format, shapes/buttons, images) plus interactivity via slides, hyperlinks, mouseover effects, animation/transitions
Marvel POP Medium Turns a sketch or photo of a UI into an interactive, clickable prototype
Balsamiq Medium Wireframing focused on structure and content — colours/visual details deliberately deferred
Justinmind High Life-like, responsive/adaptive prototypes; conditional navigation, forms, and data lists
Figma Medium–High Wireframes; shareable/commentable; has an "html to design" plugin and a Dev Mode with conditional logic; Figma AI/"Figma Make" can generate a working prototype directly from an AI prompt or from pasted design frames
Axure RP10 High Full prototype-to-developer transition tool: diagrams/customer journeys/wireframes, dynamic content, conditional logic, adaptive views, code export, automated redlines

AI-powered prototyping tools (added structure over the raw slide list):

  • The deck also covers newer AI-generative design tools that go beyond traditional wireframing software — Claude Design (Anthropic
  • Describe → generate → refine → export
  • Auto-applies an existing brand system
  • Exports to Canva/PDF/PPTX/HTML or hands off to Claude Code), Google Stitch (+ Design.md
  • AI-native "vibe design" canvas
  • Prompts/wireframes/screenshots → editable UI + production code
  • Includes a DESIGN.md file format for portable design rules with WCAG accessibility validation), and Figma Make (text-to-app prompting, design-to-code from pasted Figma frames, iterative natural-language prompting, and real React/CSS code generation). The broader AI prototyping trend: "prompt-to-prototype" (natural language → interactive prototype), AI agents that directly create/modify canvas components using existing design systems, and "code-to-canvas" (paste code → editable design components).
  • Reported impact figures: 50–70% faster prototyping cycles, and 78% of designers reporting efficiency gains. The slides pose this as an open discussion question rather than a settled conclusion: does AI prototyping help or hinder learning — i.e. does offloading prototype-building to AI reduce the designer's own hands-on learning about the problem?

Fidelity spectrum — wording and caveat

Low = simple, quick, inexpensive, core concepts and basic interactions; high = detailed, refined, closer to final, includes visual design/interactivity, more resource-intensive. Start low and increase detail only to answer specific questions. The tools placed in "medium fidelity" are considered low-fidelity by some; the categories are fuzzy — "higher fidelity" means closer to the look and feel of the final app.

Navigation diagrams

Sitemap = hierarchical organisation of screens/content (architecture view); flow diagram = decision process, user pathways and conditional navigation. Sitemaps are tricky when a view is reachable several ways: usually show only the most common/important route. Example: an app with home pages for three roles — group them as "role-specific pages" and list the rest under "shared pages".

📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

The Wright brothers and SpaceX

The setting

Both are used in the course to illustrate prototyping and iteration.

What happened

The Wright brothers built and tested many versions of their aircraft; SpaceX flew many Starship prototypes and learned from each failure instead of waiting for a perfect one.

The lesson

Fail early and cheaply. Learn from each prototype rather than aiming for a perfect first release (the MVP mindset).

⚡ Quick examples
Why prototype
PointPrototyping is a strategy for dealing with things hard to predict.
ExampleTest a paper mock of a booking flow before coding.
ExplanationIt exposes unknown problems at the lowest cost.
Good prototypes
PointBe incomplete, easy to change, and short-lived, with an explicit goal (form, function or experience).
ExampleA prototype that only tests whether users find the 'cancel' button.
ExplanationA focused goal maximises learning for minimal time.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Prototyping is a strategy for dealing with things hard to predict.
  • Build several prototypes in parallel rather than one after another.
  • Low: storyboard/paper/Wizard-of-Oz. Medium: PowerPoint, Balsamiq. High: Figma, Axure, AI tools.
  • Be incomplete, easy to change, and short-lived, with an explicit goal (form, function or experience).
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Serial vs. Parallel prototypingtap to flip
One design iterated repeatedly (fixation-prone) vs. several developed alongside each other (better outcomes)
Prototype goal types: Form / Function / Experiencetap to flip
Look & feel / what it does / end-to-end feel of use
Low / Medium / High fidelitytap to flip
Rough & fast / structured wireframe / near-final realistic
Wizard of Oztap to flip
Faking system "intelligence" with a hidden human operator
Serial vs. parallel prototyping studytap to flip
Parallel prototyping yields better designs/less fixation than serial
➡ Where next? Before choosing how things should work, we need to know how people think and perceive — the human factors.

lessons.title: Interaction Models
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersUsers act on the mental model in their head. When it doesn't match the system, they get lost.
🧠 Memory hookTwo gulfs, two questions: “How do I do it?” (execution) and “What just happened?” (evaluation). Good design bridges both.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Mental, conceptual, and implementation modelsConceptual models: objects, lexicon, metaphorInteraction stylesNorman's Action Cycle and the two gulfsAI-assisted conversation interaction (preview)
⚡ At a glance — Norman’s gulfs
Goal→Plan→Specify action→Execute→Perceive→Interpret→Compare with goal
↺ Gulf of Execution = goal → action; Gulf of Evaluation = outcome → understanding.
📛 Exact names — know these word for word: interaction styles
NameWhat it doesExample
InstructingOne-way verbal/textual commandsTyped commands, menu selections
ConversingTwo-way exchangeChat interfaces, voice assistants
ManipulatingActing directly on represented objectsDragging a resize handle
ExploringMoving around within a represented spaceNavigating the space itself

Direct manipulation is a specific form of Manipulating: continuous representation, immediate feedback, incremental and reversible actions, no command syntax. The two gulfs are the Gulf of Execution (goal → action) and the Gulf of Evaluation (outcome → understanding).

6.1Mental, conceptual, and implementation models

Mental model (formal definition, reproduced from source, attributed to Jakob Nielsen): what users believe about a system. Designers separately build a conceptual model: a high-level description, the intended user's model of how the application is organised and operates. There is also an implementation model: how the system actually works internally.

flowchart LR
    IM[Implementation Model<br/>how it actually works] -.should inform.-> CM[Conceptual Model<br/>designer's intended user model]
    CM -.should align with.-> UM[User's Mental Model<br/>what the user believes]

Caption: three distinct models exist simultaneously. Good interaction design works to close the gap between the conceptual model (what the designer intends the user to understand) and the user's actual mental model (what they really believe) — problems occur whenever these two diverge.

📍 CASE FILE

“The refrigerator from hell”

The setting

Norman's classic example of a fridge with two controls that do not do what users expect.

What happened

One dial controls airflow to the fridge and freezer compartments and a separate valve controls compartment routing, but the labelled ‘temperature control’ does not map to a single temperature. A change takes up to 24 hours to show and the user gets no immediate feedback or visible system state.

The lesson

The user's mental model (‘one dial = temperature’) does not match the implementation model, so users cannot predict results. Good mapping and feedback close the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

More from the lecture

Worked example — "the refrigerator from hell": A fridge's temperature dial is unclear about what it actually controls; a setting change takes up to 24 hours to take effect.

Three concrete failures: unclear mapping between the control and its outcome; no immediate feedback after adjusting it; and the labelled "temperature control" doesn't actually correspond 1:1 to a single temperature value.

Underneath (the implementation model), one dial (R) controls airflow to the fridge/freezer compartments and a separate valve (F) controls compartment routing — with no visible system state exposed to the user at all.

The user's mental model ("turning this dial sets the temperature") does not match the implementation, and the interface gives no feedback to help them correct that mental model.

6.2Conceptual models: objects, lexicon, metaphor

A conceptual model specifies: the objects users interact with; each object's visible attributes; the actions a user can perform; and the relationships between objects (type hierarchies/inheritance, and part/whole containment).

Worked example — an animation tool (K-Sketch): objects are drawing items with colour attributes Actions include move, rotate, scale, set timing, move relative, appear/disappear, trace, repeat/copy motion, define cels, interpolate, move forward/back, deform, move limb, orient to path.

Lexicon (naming) consistency:

  • Use one consistent term per concept throughout both the interface and the documentation, and use the users' own language, not developer jargon — this requires deliberate team agreement and discipline.
  • Example gotcha from K-Sketch: is the action called "Move," "Translate," or "Position"?
  • "Rotate," "Spin," or "Orientation"?
  • "Scale," "Resize," or "Grow/Shrink"?
  • Picking one term per concept and using it everywhere reduces the user's cognitive burden of relearning synonyms.

Interface metaphors

  • Map an unfamiliar system concept onto a familiar real-world experience (e.g. a spreadsheet mapped to a ledger; the Xerox Star's desktop metaphor mapping files/folders/trash to a physical desk).
  • Worked example — the shopping cart metaphor: objects = product, cart, shopping list, money
  • Product attributes = quantity, price, reviews, discount
  • Actions = add product, check out, pay
  • Relationships = "add product" maps to "put product into cart" (clicking the button = the physical action), "check out" maps to "calculate total" (clicking the button surfaces the cart total).
Metaphor pros Metaphor drawbacks
Leverages users' existing, familiar knowledge (desktop, trash bin, file cabinet, tree view) Can mislead — e.g. dragging a mounted disk to the desktop trash bin actually ejects it, not deletes it, which contradicts the trash-can metaphor
Supports explanation and discussion of complex functionality Doesn't scale well — a "shopping cart" is conceptually meant for imminent purchase, but real shoppers often repurpose it as a general "save for later" list, which the metaphor doesn't naturally support
— Degrades over time / across contexts — e.g. on small mobile/touch screens, cart abandonment rises, and mobile carts need extra animation or clear visual feedback just to confirm an "add to cart" action actually registered
📍 CASE FILE

VisiCalc → Xerox Star → Windows 8

The setting

Three milestones in how interface metaphors help (and sometimes hinder) people.

What happened

VisiCalc, the first spreadsheet, used the ledger sheet to make calculation accessible. The Xerox Star (1981) used the desktop with files, folders and trash. Mac OS and Windows 3.1 followed it; Windows 8's tile interface departed from the metaphor and Windows 10 brought desktop elements back.

The lesson

Metaphors give users a head start by leveraging familiar knowledge, but they can mislead and must adapt over time.

More from the lecture

VisiCalc (first spreadsheet) used the ledger sheet metaphor to make calculation accessible to non-programmers, establishing the rows/columns/cells structure.

Xerox Star (1981) used the desktop metaphor (files, folders, documents, trash) with directly manipulable objects arranged spatially. Evolution: Mac OS 1 (1984) and Windows 3.1 (1992) followed the metaphor

Windows 8's tile interface departed from it and Windows 10 re-incorporated desktop elements — metaphors adapt over time while keeping core concepts. Metaphors also give users a common vocabulary to talk about the system

Drawbacks: suggesting functionality that doesn't exist, poor scaling as systems evolve, and degrading as the original referent becomes unfamiliar to new users.

🧩 Pause & recall — Which model is the designer's/system's view of how it actually works?
Answer: Implementation model
The implementation model is how the system really works; the user holds a mental model; the conceptual model is what you present.
6.3Interaction styles
Style Description
Instructing One-way verbal/textual commands (typed commands, menu selections)
Conversing Two-way verbal/textual exchange (chat interfaces, voice assistants)
Manipulating Interacting directly with represented objects
Exploring Moving around within a represented space

Direct manipulation interfaces (a specific realisation of the "manipulating" style) are characterised by: continuous visual representations of the objects being acted on; immediate, visible feedback; actions that are incremental and reversible; and no command syntax required. They are often built on top of a metaphor (e.g. resizing a shape via a drag-handle in PowerPoint).

Direct manipulation — extra detail

Three key properties as listed (continuous representation, immediate feedback instead of command syntax, rapid/reversible/incremental actions) It reduces cognitive load by letting users act on visible objects rather than translating intentions into commands

Requires handles/affordances (e.g. the rectangle's resize/rotate handles). Calendar trip-date picker is the worked example: instantly highlighted selection matches the mental model; the alternatives would be instructing (type dates in a format) or conversing (answer questions) — likely less intuitive.

Effective interfaces often combine interaction styles.

6.4Norman's Action Cycle and the two gulfs
flowchart TD
    I[1. Form intention] --> S[2. Specify action]
    S --> P[3. Perform action<br/>input device]
    P --> Sys["4. System changes state"]
    Sys --> Per[5. Perceive system state<br/>display]
    Per --> Int[6. Interpret result]
    Int --> E[7. Evaluate outcome]
    E -.compare against.-> I
    I -.-|"Gulf of Execution"| P
    Per -.-|"Gulf of Evaluation"| E

Caption: worked example from the source — turning off a stove. (1) "I should turn off the stove after cooking." (2) "I will turn off the stove by twisting the knob." (3) Twist the knob. (4) The stove turns off. (5) Perceive: no gas, no more fire. (6) Interpret: "I see the fire is gone." (7) Evaluate: "I understand that I have turned off the stove." The Gulf of Execution is the gap between forming an intention and knowing how to actually perform it on this specific interface ("how do I specify what I want?"); the Gulf of Evaluation is the gap between the system changing state and the user understanding that it did what they wanted ("did I get what I wanted?").

Reducing both gulfs — design strategies:

Gulf Reduced by
Execution Clear affordances (an object's design visibly signals what action is possible on it — e.g. a raised/shaded button shape signals "clickable"); logical mapping from intention to the physical input action; making the required action easy to perform
Evaluation Visible system state; clear feedback that connects system state back to an interpretation; a meaningful (interpretable) outcome

Worked example of poor mapping: a stove with four burners and four knobs arranged in a row gives no clue which knob controls which burner; the fix is a spatially congruent layout — arranging the knobs in the same 2D layout as the burners they control, so the mapping is immediately obvious without needing labels.

Gotcha — Slips vs. Mistakes, revisited (cross-reference §2.1): This lecture reuses the same slip/mistake distinction on the stove example, now tied explicitly to the Gulf of Execution: a slip is a correct intention but the wrong action (e.g. pressing the wrong knob due to poor mapping)

A mistake is a wrong intention in the first place (e.g. deciding "I should blow out the fire" — a fundamentally incorrect plan for turning off a gas stove).

Slips are Gulf-of-Execution problems (interface/mapping issues); mistakes are upstream planning/understanding problems (see §2.1's fix: clearer information, better-aligned mental model).

Slips vs. mistakes — Norman-style examples

Slip: typing "teh" for "the", or pushing a pull door. Mistake: using the wrong formula, or misunderstanding how a system works. Norman doors — "It's not you. Bad doors are everywhere." (Don Norman): doors giving incorrect visual cues (pull handles on push doors). Fix: pull handles for pulling, flat plates for pushing, so the visual cue aligns with the required action.

6.5AI-assisted conversation interaction (preview)

Conversational/chat-based AI interfaces stress both gulfs in new ways: the Gulf of Execution widens because users often don't know "what to ask" an AI system, so interfaces need scaffolds — suggested prompts, examples, guardrails; the Gulf of Evaluation widens because AI responses can be uncertain or hallucinated, so interfaces need verification affordances (citations, confidence cues, "show your work"), making human-in-the-loop review a default safety pattern rather than an optional extra.

⚡ Quick examples
Norman's two gulfs
PointGulf of Execution: 'How do I do what I want?' Gulf of Evaluation: 'Did I get what I wanted?'
ExampleUnclear buttons widen execution; no confirmation after submit widens evaluation.
ExplanationGood design reduces both: clear affordances and visible feedback.
Slips vs. mistakes
PointA slip is the right goal with wrong execution; a mistake is a wrong goal/plan from a faulty model.
ExamplePressing K instead of L (slip); deleting only a shortcut thinking the file is gone (mistake).
ExplanationSlips need prevention/undo; mistakes need better models and feedback.

  • Metaphors help learning but can mislead.
  • Gulf of Execution: 'How do I do what I want?' Gulf of Evaluation: 'Did I get what I wanted?'
  • A slip is the right goal with wrong execution; a mistake is a wrong goal/plan from a faulty model.

lessons.title: Memory
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersHuman memory and attention are small and leaky. Design must not overload them.
🧠 Memory hookShow, don't make them remember. Recognition beats recall; chunk information.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
The Model Human Processor (MHP) and memory storesMemory strategiesDesign Implication 1 — use representations to direct attentionDesign Implication 2 — avoid taxing working memory
⚡ At a glance — memory stores
Sensory (very brief)→Working memory (small, seconds)→Long-term memory (large, durable)
↺ Design implications: direct attention with representations · avoid taxing working memory (recognition over recall).
7.1The Model Human Processor (MHP) and memory stores

The Model Human Processor models human cognition as a pipeline of stores connected by a cognitive processor:

Store Approx. capacity Approx. decay
Visual image store 7–17 chunks 100–1000 ms
Auditory image store 4.4–6.2 chunks 1–3 s (short term)
Working (short-term) memory ~4 ± 1 "chunks" Rapid decay without active rehearsal
Long-term memory Large, associative capacity Stable over time

Working memory is the bottleneck — its small size and rapid decay are the direct cause of most memory-related usability problems, which motivates the two design implications in §7.3–7.4.

A "chunk" (added context, standard cognitive-psychology term used throughout): a single meaningful unit that groups multiple raw pieces of information (e.g. a phone number is easier to hold in working memory as three or four chunks — area code, prefix, line number — than as ten separate digits).

7.2Memory strategies
Strategy What it does
Attention Focus on the relevant information — information not attended to is rarely remembered at all
Rehearsal Repetition supports moving information into long-term memory (e.g. Preview–Question–Re-read–Study–Test study technique)
Chunking Group related items using visual cues (colour), verbal cues (acronyms, rhymes), or spatial cues (physical grouping/layout); organise via categorisation and structure
External aids Offload memory onto tools outside your own head (appointment books, memos, timers, even a string tied around a finger as a physical reminder)

Performance is optimal at moderate cognitive load — not minimum, and not maximum. Too little load under-engages attention; too much load overwhelms working memory's ~4±1-chunk capacity. This is why interfaces shouldn't be stripped to the point of losing helpful structure, nor packed with more simultaneous information than a user can actually hold in mind.

Power Law of Practice (cross-reference §1.2, now given its mechanism): Performance improves rapidly with early practice, then improvement slows as the skill becomes automated (proceduralised into something closer to long-term memory/muscle memory, requiring less conscious working-memory effort each time).

This is explicitly used to explain resistance to change for the QWERTY keyboard layout: because so many typists have already automated QWERTY through years of practice, even an objectively faster layout carries a huge retraining cost, so the incumbent layout persists.

Power Law of Practice — design implications

Rapid early gains then diminishing returns; explains QWERTY persistence; highlights the difficulty of changing established interfaces; suggests the value of consistent interface patterns.

📍 CASE FILE

Chess masters and chunking (Chase & Simon)

The setting

Researchers asked chess players to look at a real game position of about 25 pieces for 5–10 seconds and reproduce it.

What happened

Masters recalled about 90% of the pieces, weaker players about 25%. When the pieces were placed randomly, the masters fell to novice level.

The lesson

Experts do not have better raw memory; they have better organised chunks. Designers can lower memory load by grouping information into meaningful chunks.

More from the lecture

Participants saw a position of about 25 pieces for 5–10 seconds and reproduced it. A chunk = any stimulus that has become familiar through repeated exposure and is recognised as one unit.

Masters ≈ 90% vs. weaker players ≈ 25%; with random placement the expert falls to novice level — superior organisation of stimuli, not superior visual memory.

The deck draws a hypothesis for prototyping: expert designers rely on chunking before building a prototype so that they build the right kind of prototype and ask the right questions.

Working-memory rules of thumb

Capacity 5–9 chunks, decay 5–226 s; requires conscious attention; display rather than require recall; recognition over recall; clear information hierarchies.

🧩 Pause & recall — In the Model Human Processor, which store has very limited capacity and short duration?
Answer: Working memory
Working memory is small and brief; long-term is large and durable.
7.3Design Implication 1 — use representations to direct attention

Expertise = pattern recognition, built through chunking. Worked example — chess board memory: experts correctly recall ~90% of piece positions from a real, meaningful game configuration, but drop to the same ~25% as novices when the same number of pieces are placed in a random (non-meaningful) arrangement.

This shows experts aren't simply "better at memory" in general — they've chunked familiar, structured patterns into fewer, larger memory units, and that advantage disappears when the structure isn't real (i.e. isn't something their chunks apply to).

Board configuration Experts Novices
Meaningful (actual game) ~90% ~25%
Random arrangement ~25% ~25%

Design Implication 1: representations shape what users notice — good representations reveal structure and meaning; poor representations hide what matters.

Supporting concepts:

  • Cues support memory in three channels: visual (icons, colour, layout — e.g. MRT line colours), verbal (acronyms, labels, rhymes — e.g. "LOL"), and spatial (position/grouping — e.g. grouping MRT lines that interchange). Cues specifically help users recognise, not recall — this directly reinforces Nielsen's "recognition over recall" heuristic previewed in §1.2.
  • Isomorphic problems can feel very different in difficulty depending on representation, even when mathematically identical. Worked example: a number game (two players alternately pick cards 1–9, goal = any 3 summing to 15) feels genuinely hard, but it is structurally identical to Tic-Tac-Toe (the numbers 1–9 map onto a magic square whose rows/columns/diagonals all sum to 15) — Tic-Tac-Toe's spatial layout makes the winning patterns visually obvious, while the numeric version hides the same structure behind arithmetic. A parallel example: the algebraic identity a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b) is far easier to see as true from a geometric diagram (subtracting a smaller square from a larger one) than from the symbols alone.
  • Software abstraction as representation (added context, connecting to CS if relevant to the reader): primitive data types (int, string, bool) direct attention to what raw data matters; abstract data types (Stack, Queue, Map) hide implementation detail behind meaningful operations; object orientation models real-world entities; design patterns are reusable representations of recurring solution shapes; APIs/frameworks abstract complexity so developers can focus on structure rather than low-level detail. Quoted: "The purpose of abstraction is not to be vague, but to create a new semantic level in which one can be absolutely precise." — Edsger W. Dijkstra.
  • Colour choice for data representation: hue (e.g. arbitrary colour categories) does not imply order and is hard to visually compare, whereas intensity/saturation of a single hue (e.g. darker blue = more water depth) is easy to compare visually and should be preferred whenever the underlying data is ordered/quantitative.

Representations and cues

Representations influence what users notice/remember: they guide attention, facilitate recognition of patterns/relationships, and support efficient processing; colour, size, position and contrast direct attention. Memory aids: visual cues highlight elements, consistent patterns cut learning, mnemonics give memorable shortcuts, metaphors link new to existing knowledge (e.g. Do-Re-Mi — "Do, a deer, a female deer…" — uses concrete objects to remember abstract notes).

Isomorphic game — the number version

Two players alternately say a number 1–9 (no repeats); first to hold three numbers summing to 15 wins. Plotted on a 3×3 magic square, three numbers sum to 15 iff they lie in a straight line, so it is Tic-Tac-Toe — useful for programming the game by mapping grid squares to magic-square numbers.

Colour for height — the cartography argument

Hue has a physical order (wavelength) and everyone knows the rainbow, yet the visual system struggles to treat hue as ordered: "Where is above ground? Below? What's the highest point?" are hard to answer; saturation is nearly impossible. Sets varying by luminance/intensity are easy to order: two colour sets (browns above ground, blues below), darker = deeper/higher — "cartographers have done this for 2000 years". First decide categorical (under water or not), then use intensity for how much.

7.4Design Implication 2 — avoid taxing working memory

Working memory is limited and fragile — do not force users to remember things; externalise information into the interface instead.

  • Worked example — subway map design: a literal, geographically-accurate map forces the rider to hold a lot of irrelevant detail in mind
  • An abstracted schematic map (like the MRT or Tokyo Metro diagrams) discards true geographic scale/shape and keeps only the information relevant to the task (which stations connect, in what order, where to interchange), directly reducing working-memory load.
  • Comparing SMRT's older vs. current (2023) platform-information design shows the same principle applied to wayfinding signage.
  • Recommendations drawn from this example: prioritise the rider's current journey information
  • Remove redundant or irrelevant detail
  • Use abstraction instead of full/literal maps
  • Group information by task and context
  • Show only what the user needs right now (e.g. showing only the next few stops rather than the entire line, and showing simple left/right exit directions rather than full multi-storey exit diagrams).

Abstraction in maps — diagram vs. map

The first schematic subway map showed that a transit map need not follow the exact track path — only direction and stops matter ("you don't need to know the little wiggles"). Geographic maps preserve distance, direction and route shape (better for locations; higher load for route planning); schematic diagrams simplify connections and emphasise topology over geography (optimised for route planning; lower working-memory load).

Singapore design-critique lessons: Don't show less information than users need; every element should have a purpose; avoid superfluous animation. A redesign proposal (Wilson Chew) targets readability (fonts), removing redundant map elements/useless landmarks (use announcements instead), only essential info, better animation/fonts. Signage critique: "Stand in the circle. Do not sit in the circle." — inconsistent instructions (both should say stand/sit, or neither).

⚡ Quick examples

ExampleYou can hold a phone number for seconds but forget it unless you rehearse it.
ExplanationInterfaces must not rely on users holding much in working memory.
Attention and load
PointPerformance peaks at moderate attentional load (Yerkes–Dodson).
ExampleA dashboard with a few key numbers works; one with 50 alerts overwhelms.
ExplanationToo little or too much load hurts; aim for the middle.

  • Chunking groups items into meaningful units; practice builds expertise.
  • Performance peaks at moderate attentional load (Yerkes–Dodson).
  • Use representations to direct attention; avoid taxing working memory.

lessons.title: Input
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersSpeed and accuracy of acting depend on physical facts you can calculate, not guess.
🧠 Memory hookFitts' Law: Bigger + Closer = Faster. Time grows with distance, shrinks with target size.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Framing questions for input devicesText entryPointing devices and Fitts's LawMulti-touch and touchscreen interaction
8.1Framing questions for input devices

Before evaluating any input device or technique, ask: what tasks must the user actually perform with it? Which actions are fast vs. error-prone on this device? What interactions does the device enable, and what does it restrict?

Framing questions

What low-level tasks are users trying to accomplish? How can we conceptualise the space of possible input devices? What interaction techniques does a device encourage or discourage?

8.2Text entry
Technique Notes
Keystroke / physical keyboard Array of physical buttons; one- vs two-handed use; QWERTY is highly standardised despite being suboptimal for raw speed — its layout was originally designed to reduce mechanical typewriter jamming and to encourage alternating hand use, and frequently used letters are not all placed centrally, yet it persists due to the Power-Law-of-Practice "resistance to change" effect covered in §7.2
Mobile multi-tap (legacy) Multiple presses per numeric key to reach a letter; high cognitive/motor load; ambiguity resolved via dictionary lookup or T9 predictive text
Soft/on-screen keyboards (dominant on mobile today) Flexible layouts and languages; lower tactile feedback than physical keys; input via touch or stylus
Gesture typing (swipe/glide) A continuous stroke across the on-screen keyboard, recognised as a word by its shape; faster than discrete tap-typing once learned, but requires practice and more visual attention
Handwriting recognition (stylus/finger, e.g. iPad + Apple Pencil) AI-based pattern recognition, ≈97% accuracy in lab settings; slower than typing for long text, but well suited to diagrams, maths, and quick notes
Speech recognition / dictation Fast (~130–150 wpm); used in assistants (Google Assistant, Siri, Bixby, Alexa); a key gotcha is that speech ≠ written language — spoken content differs in structure from print-ready text, ambient noise and privacy are real constraints, and speaking in well-formed, print-ready sentences is itself cognitively demanding

A comparison prompt from the slides ("which is fastest?") notes stenographers can reach ~200 words per minute using a specialised shorthand keyboard, faster than any general-purpose consumer text-entry method listed.

QWERTY vs. alternatives — comparison

QWERTY was designed with mechanical typewriters in mind; modern assessment: awkward finger motions, fingers must jump over rows, one hand (left) does a lot of the work, but it encourages alternating hands.

Alternatives (e.g. Dvorak) place the most common letters on the easiest (home) row and the least common on the bottom row, with predominantly right-handed key distribution.

QWERTY persists through network effects and training inertia. Keyboard fact set: array of buttons in many shapes/layouts, compact to full size; the two-handed full keyboard is relatively standardised.

Mobile text entry — pros/cons

Method Pros Cons
Multi-tap (multiple presses per letter) and dictionary/T9 (one press per letter + lookup) Dominated early phones High effort, ambiguity
Soft keyboard Adaptable layouts/languages; no parts to wear out; screen space reclaimed when unused; dynamic suggestions No tactile feedback; takes screen space; easier errors without key boundaries; slower than physical for experts
Handwriting Natural motions; intuitive for pen-and-paper users; supports hard-to-type character sets (e.g. Chinese); sometimes faster for some languages Accuracy depends on clarity; recognition errors frustrate; slower than keyboard for Latin scripts
Gesture typing (Swype, ShapeWriter, Microsoft SwiftKey) Draw a word by sliding across letters; less precise targeting; easier one-handed use; comfortable Needs practice

Speech

Dictation faster than typing (~100 wpm here; §8.2 cites ~130–150 — the sources differ by deck/year), minimal physical effort, accessible to users with motor disabilities, hands-free, natural for conversation. Limitations: speech differs from written language; privacy concerns

Disruptive in quiet shared spaces; accent/dialect recognition Editing/correction is cumbersome. Text-entry speed ordering shown: stenographers (specialised shorthand keyboard) > proficient QWERTY typists > mobile soft keyboard > multi-tap with dictionary.

🧩 Pause & recall — Fitts's Law predicts that pointing time depends on:
Answer: Target distance and target size
Longer distance and smaller targets increase movement time.
8.3Pointing devices and Fitts's Law

Pointing device types: mouse, trackball, joystick, pointing stick, touchpad, touchscreen, tablet/stylus.

Key properties for comparing pointing devices:

  • Mapping — direct (finger touches the object itself, e.g. touchscreen) vs. indirect (moving the device moves a separate cursor, e.g. mouse).
  • Control–Display (C-D) ratio — for one unit of physical movement, how far does the on-screen cursor travel? Direct touchscreen input has a C-D ratio of 1:1. For indirect devices, the ratio can vary dynamically with speed/gain (formally: xₜ = max(0, min(sw, xₜ₋₁ + dx·r_{c-d}))), meaning a fast flick of the mouse can move the cursor proportionally further than a slow, precise movement — a deliberate design feature that trades off speed against precision.
  • Device acquisition time — how quickly a user can switch to/from this device from another (e.g. from keyboard to mouse and back).

Fitts's Law: predicts the time to point at a target from distance D with target size W, via an Index of Difficulty, ID = log₂(D/W + 1), and pointing time Tₚₒₛ = a + b·log₂(D/S + 1) (S = target size). Interpretation: larger, closer targets are faster to acquire; only the relative precision (D relative to W) matters, not absolute distance alone. This directly formalises the informal statement of Fitt's Law given back in §1.2.

Worked applications of Fitts's Law (why the mouse dominates, and UI-design consequences): The mouse is judged the fastest general-purpose pointing device because it supports optimised eye–hand coordination and a mix of large ballistic movements plus small corrective movements, matching natural human motor bandwidth. Interface implications: a pie menu (options arranged as wedges around a central point) is faster on average than a rectangular list menu, because every option sits at a similar, short distance from the centre with a comparatively large "size" (angular width) — lower ID for every item. Screen edges and corners act as effectively infinite-sized targets (the cursor can't overshoot past the physical screen edge), making them the fastest possible targets to acquire — this is why OS menus (the classic Mac OS X Apple menu, the Windows Start button) are placed in screen corners. Microsoft's Office Ribbon exploits the same idea: grouping larger targets together lets them be clicked faster, and placing the most-used button (Office/File) in the "magic corner" (upper-left) and a mini toolbar close to the current cursor position both minimise D.

Direct vs. indirect devices

Direct = pointer space and screen space unified (touchscreen, light pen); indirect = a change in pointer causes a change on screen (mouse, rotary encoder, joystick). Without direct mapping, the C-D ratio can change with speed (jerky moves send the pointer further). The classic study showing the mouse fastest for text selection: Card, English & Burr (1978).

Fitts's Law — intuition via ballistic movements

The Index of Difficulty reflects the number of ballistic movements; e.g. D/S = 12/4 = 3 and 6/2 = 3 give the same difficulty — the ratio D/S matters more than distance alone.

The constants a (start/stop time) and b (bandwidth of the human muscle group and the device) define a line per device, enabling comparison graphs (horizontal = bits, vertical = time).

The mouse is nearly optimal because it uses wrist and fingers; the limiting factor is eye–hand coordination. Pie menus are faster than rectangular lists, but rectangular menus scale to many options.

Corners are "magic" — details

Four places are effectively infinitely wide and tall: the corners; acquiring them needs almost no fine motor control. Mac puts the menu bar at the top of the screen (a Fitts win); Windows puts menus at the top of each app window for historical reasons. Pre-Windows-2000 the Start button had a single dead pixel on its left/bottom edge, causing missed clicks and slower acquisition (Jensen Harris, "Giving You Fitts"). Office 2007's ribbon applies the same ideas.

8.4Multi-touch and touchscreen interaction

Key distinctions to keep straight (each pair is easy to conflate but describes a different axis):

Pair Distinction
Touch-tablet vs. touchscreen A tablet is a separate touch-sensitive surface not co-located with the display; a touchscreen combines the touch surface and the display in the same physical location
Single-finger vs. multi-finger Whether the interaction uses one point of contact or several simultaneously (e.g. pinch-to-zoom)
Multi-point vs. multi-touch Multi-point = multiple simultaneous distinct touch points can be sensed; multi-touch specifically enables gestures combining those points (not just detecting them)
Multi-user vs. multi-touch Multi-touch = many contact points from possibly one user; multi-user = the surface can distinguish and support several different people interacting concurrently
Points vs. gesture Whether the system reads touches as static positions, or as a shaped motion/gesture over time
Hands vs. objects Whether the sensing technology (e.g. capacitive vs. computer-vision-based) can also recognise non-finger objects placed on the surface

The "fat finger" problem and occlusion: A fingertip covers a much larger screen area than a mouse cursor's point, both reducing precision (you can't reliably hit small targets) and physically occluding (blocking your own view of) the exact spot you're touching, which is especially disruptive right after the tap when you'd want visual confirmation.

The Shift technique is cited as one mitigation: it displays a callout showing a zoomed, un-occluded copy of the area under/above the finger so the user can see and confirm the exact target before committing to the touch.

Touch terminology (Buxton)

Touch exactly where the thing is → touch screen/display; touching a surface not overlaid on the screen → touch tablet/pad. Two fingers of one user ≠ one finger from each of two users; systems may sense pose (not just position) and what object, where, which orientation.

Multi-touch supports two or more simultaneous commands (e.g. pinch-to-zoom). Many surfaces (iPhone/iPad) track point centres but not the full contact region

Some apps (e.g. SandCanvas) need full contact regions, achieved with FIR (frustrated internal reflection) displays. Gesture example: Minority Report-style interfaces.

"Fat finger" errors with real consequences. Examples cited: a Tokyo trader's mistaken order overturning orders worth ¥67.78 trillion (£381bn) — largely cancellation, so fallout limited; UBS in 2009 ordering ¥3 trillion instead of ¥30 million of Capcom bonds; a 2005 trader intending to sell 1 J-Com share at ¥610,000 but selling 610,000 shares at ¥1 (Mizuho lost ¥27 bn; the TSE head later resigned). Lesson: input precision is a safety issue — pair with error prevention/confirmation (§12.4 #5).

Occlusion fixes — full Shift walkthrough and a hardware alternative

  • Shift (Vogel & Baudisch, CHI 2007): (a) on contact, Shift detects whether occlusion is a problem
  • (b) it shows a callout containing a copy of the occluded area with a pointer at the finger's selection point
  • (c) keeping the finger down, the user makes corrective movements until the pointer is over the target
  • (d) lifting the finger selects
  • (e) the callout disappears. Back-of-device interaction (LucidTouch, Wigdor et al. UIST 2007
  • PlayStation Vita): rear touch sensors give zero occlusion, no reaching, a clean display
  • Drawbacks: no visible fingers, a learning curve, extra hardware.
  • Useful for very small devices.
📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Apple's menu bar vs. Windows'

The setting

Two operating systems place menus differently: Apple fixes the menu bar to the top of the screen, while Windows attaches it to each window's title bar.

What happened

When you move the mouse up to the screen edge on a Mac, the cursor cannot overshoot, so the bar behaves as if it were infinitely tall. A Windows menu has a finite height and you must stop precisely on it.

The lesson

Fitts' Law: movement time falls as targets get larger and closer. Screen edges and corners are very fast targets.

📍 CASE FILE

QWERTY vs. Dvorak

The setting

The QWERTY layout dates from mechanical typewriters; Dvorak puts the most common letters on the home row.

What happened

QWERTY is awkward (fingers jump rows, the left hand does a lot of the work), yet it persists through network effects and training inertia: millions have automated it through practice.

The lesson

The Power Law of Practice means people resist even objectively better layouts because retraining costs too much.

⚡ Quick examples
Text input
PointKeyboards, touch, stylus and speech; QWERTY dominates but isn't fastest.
ExampleGesture typing trades some speed for flexibility on phones.
ExplanationFamiliarity often beats theoretical speed.
Pointing devices
PointMouse is the fastest pointing device; also trackball, stick, tablet, touchscreen.
ExampleDesigners get faster precise selection with a mouse than a touchpad.
ExplanationDevice choice affects speed, precision and fatigue.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Keyboards, touch, stylus and speech; QWERTY dominates but isn't fastest.
  • Mouse is the fastest pointing device; also trackball, stick, tablet, touchscreen.
  • Pointing time depends on target distance and size.
  • The 'fat-finger' problem: fingers are imprecise and occlude the target.
