lessons.title: Mobile Devices
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersMobile is not a small desktop. Context, fingers and attention all change.
🧠 Memory hookOne hand, one eye, one moment. Design for thumbs and interruptions.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Why mobile interaction differs from desktopMobile usability patternsScreen density and cross-device design (DP/PT)Beyond touch: gesture and sensor-based interaction
9.1Why mobile interaction differs from desktop

Mobile use happens while moving and multitasking, producing short, frequently interrupted attention spans; screens are small with limited input precision; devices are location-aware and sensor-rich; and the dominant interaction modalities are touch, gesture, and voice rather than mouse clicks. Direct usability consequences: only show what's needed right now, prioritise the primary task, keep navigation simple, and minimise required input effort.

This is a direct application of §7.4's "avoid taxing working memory" principle to a context (mobile) where attention itself is already scarce and interrupted — the mobile constraints amplify, rather than introduce, memory-load design pressure.

Mindset

"Don't think of your mobile device as a desktop that moves." Users multitask (watching TV, socialising), micro-task with frequent interruptions, focus on primary tasks; mobile adds location-based services (LBS), touch/gesture, and sensors (accelerometer, GPS). Yelp example: the mobile version keeps only the most important parts and adds mobile-only features — a navigation screen and map-based search that uses the current location.

📍 CASE FILE

Google's 25 mobile-app principles (Jenny Gove)

The setting

Google tested 100 mobile apps with 100 participants, each spending 90 minutes on 6 apps, half iOS and half Android, using think-aloud tasks.

What happened

The study produced 25 principles, such as show the value of your app upfront, allow ‘go back’ in one step, differentiate sign in from sign up, keep a prominent search field and make filtering easy.

The lesson

Mobile usability can be studied systematically, and the same small frictions (login, search, navigation) recur across apps.

More from the lecture
  • 100 mobile apps; 100 participants × 90 minutes × 6 apps; half iOS/half Android; think-aloud tasks.
  • Principles quoted on the slide include: show the value of your app upfront
  • Frictionless transitions between app and mobile web
  • Prominent search field with good indexing; provide filter and sort
  • Differentiate "sign in" from "sign up"
  • Organise/label menu categories; allow "go back" in one step
  • Make it easy to change location manually
  • Show previous search/purchase info
  • Allow reviews to be viewed and filtered; enable comparison shopping
  • Multiple third-party payment options
  • Show clear utility before asking users to register
  • Frictionless password authentication; user-friendly forms
  • Communicate form errors in real time
  • match the keyboard to the required input
  • Provide helpful in-context form info
  • Speak the same language as your users. (Fits Nielsen #2, #5, #6.)
9.2Mobile usability patterns
Pattern Why it matters
Immediate visual feedback after actions Confirms the action registered, shows system status, indicates progress/delays, reduces uncertainty and errors — especially important because mobile interaction is easily interrupted mid-task
Overview → scan → detail zoom Lets users progressively narrow focus rather than needing everything visible (and memorised) at once
User-controlled zoom The user, not the system, decides how much detail to see at a given moment
In-context permission requests Ask for a permission (camera, location, etc.) at the moment it's actually needed, not up-front, so the user has the context to understand why
Bottom-oriented, thumb-reachable navigation Supports one-handed mobile use and gesture-based interaction, though some users still prefer/expect a top navigation bar (a "resistance to change" effect, cf. §7.2's QWERTY example)
Persistent, glanceable system feedback (e.g. Dynamic Island) Context-aware, glanceable information that supports multitasking without forcing a full interruption

Overview/detail split

On mobile, overview and detail that shared one screen on desktop become separate screens.

Top vs. bottom search bar (iOS 15 Safari)

Safari moved the address bar to the bottom: important controls closer to the thumb, one-handed browsing, swipe left/right on the tab bar to switch tabs; many sites show how to revert — a resistance-to-change signal. Dynamic Island: proximity sensor under the display, pill-shaped cutout with the camera circle; used for maps, Apple Pay confirmation, music controls, Lyft ETA, privacy indicators, call length, timers, sports scores, AirPods status.

🧩 Pause & recall — Why use DP (Android) or PT (iOS) instead of raw pixels?
Answer: It makes layouts independent of screen density
Density-independent units keep sizes consistent across devices.
9.3Screen density and cross-device design (DP/PT)

The problem with pixels (PPI ≠ physical size): a fixed pixel count (e.g. a 100×100 px image) occupies a different physical size depending on the device's pixel density (pixels per inch, PPI) — the same pixel dimensions render smaller, with finer detail lost, on a higher-PPI screen. Mobile devices span a wide PPI range (roughly 163 up to 476–515 PPI for common Android/Apple devices, vs. a ~72 PPI historical web-design baseline).

Solution: design using device-independent units , not raw pixels — Android's DP (density-independent pixels) or iOS's PT (points).

The OS itself converts a DP/PT value to the correct number of physical pixels for that specific screen's density, so one design specification renders at a consistent physical size across devices with different PPI. General principle: screen size, resolution, and PPI are three independent variables that don't move together — design in DP/PT, then test across a range of real densities, and plan for genuine device diversity rather than assuming one reference device.

Responsive design for the web extends the same idea to browsers/layouts adapting to viewport size (referenced tools: Twitter Bootstrap / CSS responsive grids, and browser-based resizing test tools).

Density — how to reason

Display sizes averaging 1024×768 give ≈85 ppi on desktop; wide variance in density across devices means pixel size affects design; "expect and manage diversity".

DP = device-independent pixel (Android); PT = point (Apple) — essentially the same. Example: a "Jim" icon 44×44 DP/PT with 20 DP/PT padding is specified once regardless of PPI; always use resolution-independent values for spacing, more so as screens vary.

Also consider aspect ratio (width:height). (The deck itself flags one claim about 200 ppi as "is this true?"; treat the densities in §9.3 as the authoritative figures.)

Responsive design

Content rearranges to the available browser space (resize the desktop window to see it). It lets you build one application for all devices, but is tricky: media queries are powerful but need planning — "RD is a strategy, not a silver bullet". Compare with native apps.

Standards and design systems

External consistency = align with industry standards, using common UI components such as cards and navigation menus. Internal consistency = achieved by design systems: shared components giving everyone the same foundation, and pre-built reusable elements (colours, typography) that keep projects uniform (Spotify's design system as the cited example). (cf. §16.1 standards.)

9.4Beyond touch: gesture and sensor-based interaction
  • Apple Watch AssistiveTouch: uses the watch's built-in gyroscope, accelerometer, and heart-rate sensor to recognise hand gestures without any touch input — e.g. a "pinch" (index finger to thumb) as "next," a "clench" (loose fist) as "confirm" (which can even be used to accept an incoming call).
  • Project Soli (radar-based gesture sensing): a miniature radar sensor that reads human motion at multiple scales, from a heartbeat up to full-body movement, as an alternative to camera-based gesture recognition; demonstrated for touchless hand-gesture control such as a volume slider, paired with haptic feedback.

Takeaways

design for multitasking/interrupted attention; optimise for touch with suitable target sizes, gestures and feedback; leverage LBS; use density-independent measures and responsive principles; explore gesture control (e.g. Google ATAP Soli).

⚡ Quick examples
Touch ≠ click
PointNo hover, imprecise, occlusion.
ExampleA tooltip that appears on hover is unreachable on a phone.
ExplanationDon't rely on hover; use bigger targets and visible controls.
Small, dense screens
PointPrioritise content; use DP (Android) or PT (iOS) units, not pixels.
ExampleA 48dp button is the same physical size on any phone.
ExplanationDensity-independent units keep layouts consistent.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Mobile use is contextual and interrupted.
  • No hover, imprecise, occlusion.
  • Prioritise content; use DP (Android) or PT (iOS) units, not pixels.
  • Expect many screen sizes and test on real devices.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
DP (Android) / PT (iOS)tap to flip
Device-independent design units that adapt to screen PPI
➡ Where next? Whatever the device, people must find and understand information — information design.

lessons.title: Information Design
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersPeople scan rather than read, and follow the trail that looks most promising.
🧠 Memory hookScan → Scent → Select. Give strong scent so users never wonder where to go next.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
How people read onlineThe Information Design pipelineInformation scentData integrity and misrepresentationVisualisation types by categoryAI-powered data visualisation
10.1How people read online

Direct quote/paraphrase attributed to Jakob Nielsen: people scanning web content generally "don't [read]" in the traditional sense — they scan. Scannable text requires: highlighted keywords (hyperlinks), meaningful sub-headings, bulleted lists, one idea per paragraph, leading with the conclusion, and roughly half the word count (or less) of equivalent print writing.

Eye-tracking research reveals two dominant scanning patterns:

Pattern Shape of attention Best suited to
F-pattern View the top line fully, then a shorter second horizontal pass, then scan down the left-hand vertical edge Text-heavy pages (articles, search results)
Z-pattern Eyes trace a Z shape across a low-text layout Simple pages where a single call-to-action is the priority (e.g. a landing page — "simplicity is a priority and call-to-action is the main takeaway")
📍 CASE FILE

The baby-face eye-tracking test

The setting

An advertisement with a photo of a baby was A/B tested while eye-tracking recorded where viewers looked.

What happened

When the baby looked straight at the viewer, the heat map showed the baby's face as the hottest area. When the same baby looked towards the headline, viewers' attention followed the gaze and shifted onto the headline.

The lesson

People automatically look where others appear to look, a factor on top of F- and Z-shaped scanning. You can direct attention with gaze and cues.

More from the lecture

Worked eye-tracking example (baby-face ad, A/B tested): When a baby in an ad photo looks directly at the camera/viewer, the heat map shows the baby's face as the hottest (most-attended) area When the same baby is repositioned to look toward the headline text instead, viewer attention follows the baby's gaze and shifts onto the headline.

This demonstrates a general human tendency to automatically look where another person (even a photographed one) appears to be looking — a factor independent of, and compounding with, plain F/Z scanning patterns.

Nielsen's writing guidance — specifics

Web pages need scannable text: highlighted keywords (hyperlinks, typeface variation, colour), meaningful (not "clever") subheadings, bulleted lists, one idea per paragraph (users skip extra ideas not caught by the first words).

Nielsen's research found that combining the three writing styles — concise, scannable, objective — improved usability by 124%; promotional language imposes a cognitive burden because users must filter out the hyperbole.

People read word-by-word only when really interested. Credibility cues (quality graphics, good writing, references) and no overly promotional writing make text scannable.

Eye tracking — how and why

Specialised cameras track pupil movement/gaze to create heat maps; cheap equipment makes collecting saccade data from many users feasible.

Three design questions: where do the eyes go first? what influences where they go next? can we control focus to guide users to our goal? F-pattern = a horizontal read across the upper content, a shorter second horizontal movement lower down, then a vertical scan down the left edge

Common on text-heavy pages (articles, blogs, news) — put key information in the most-scanned spots, use short catchy headlines and bold headers.

Z-pattern = top-left → top-right → diagonal to bottom-left → bottom-right; suits low-text pages with a clear CTA (landing pages), with the call-to-action placed along the Z path; it serves branding, call-to-action, structure and hierarchy.

Visual hierarchy = the item that first grabs attention is at the top, each next one subordinate. The deck cautions that F/Z are structural aids, and that creating a visual hierarchy (including gaze cues like the baby example) matters more.

10.2The Information Design pipeline
flowchart LR
    DS[Data Source] --> DA["Data Analysis & Mining<br/>(inspect, clean, transform, model for decisions)"]
    DA --> DV["Data Visualisation<br/>(present analysed data — facts, figures, findings)"]
    DV --> VD["Visual Design<br/>(aesthetics: size, colour, contrast, alignment,<br/>repetition, proximity, whitespace, font, layout)"]
    VD --> ID["Information Design<br/>(present clear, accessible, accurate data<br/>to meet a need or solve a problem)"]

Caption: raw data passes through analysis, then visualisation, then visual-design polish, arriving at "information design" — presenting the result so it's clear, accessible, and accurate for a real user need. Visual Design itself is expanded fully in Lecture 11.

Information design vs. data visualisation

Data visualisation = usually an objective presentation of facts/figures that leaves room for the audience to make up its own mind (encyclopaedias, textbooks, performance reports).

Information design = helps users meet a specific need or solve a problem, or presents subjective findings/predictions/conclusions (instruction manuals, recipes, opinion pieces). Its core purpose is to help people process information better/faster with less frustration

Ronnie Lipton: it "begins and ends with understanding the people who will use the content". Examples: a recipe with icons/lists/diagrams Airport wayfinding signage.

🧩 Pause & recall — How do most people read web content?
Answer: They scan, often in F- or Z-patterns
Eye tracking shows scanning patterns; write concisely and scannably.
10.3Information scent

Information scent (added context: the term borrows from information foraging theory, which treats online information-seeking as analogous to an animal foraging for food by following environmental cues). A strong scent — e.g. clear, specific menu labels — lets users navigate directly to what they need.

A weak scent produces recognisable symptoms: users can't find what they want, waste time searching (feeling increasingly frustrated), and eventually give up and leave the site entirely.

Worked example: trying to find "iPod rechargeable batteries" through vague category labels fails, while a more specific, stronger-scent label succeeds — though very specific/verbose labelling of every possible sub-category doesn't scale to a large catalogue, so scent needs to be tuned to the actual scope of the content.

Information foraging — detail

Users estimate the useful information available on a path, then compare the outcome with their prediction; when the scent stops getting stronger they switch source. Scent cues: link text, navigation labels, images and other UI elements. Strong scent reduces cognitive load; weak scent "creates a poverty of attention".

Weak-scent symptoms Remedy
High bounce rate (visit and leave without acting); abandoned tasks; frustration; poor satisfaction/brand perception Give users more context to choose the best option
Users fall back on call centres/offline resources; people give up from decision pages (home/section pages) rather than content pages A high-scent label pattern: one clear word with more words under it; a horizontal menu with clear categories that exposes secondary navigation while keeping hierarchy
Overlapping sections (an iPod could be under "Audio and TV" or "Computing") A "fudged" fix — multiple listings — is fine for a few high-use items but quickly clutters the site

Related myth: "all pages should be reachable in 3 clicks" is a UX myth (clarity of scent matters more than click count). Prior research cited: strong scent made information easier to find by 124%.

10.4Data integrity and misrepresentation

Design implication: avoid misrepresenting data. Use clear, thorough labels to prevent ambiguity, and make sure a chart shows genuine data variation, not an artefact of design/formatting choices (e.g. a truncated y-axis, or inconsistent bar widths, can visually exaggerate a difference that isn't actually that large in the underlying numbers).

Tufte's six principles of graphical integrity

The five shown on the slide: (1) the representation of numbers, as physically measured on the graphic, should be directly proportional to the quantities (2) clear, detailed, thorough labelling to defeat distortion and ambiguity, with explanations written on the graphic and important events labelled

(3) in time-series of money, use deflated, standardised monetary units rather than nominal (4) the number of information-carrying (variable) dimensions depicted should not exceed the number of dimensions in the data

(5) graphics must not quote data out of context. Ethics summary: avoid misrepresentation (don't manipulate scales), prevent distortion (consistent scales, axis labels), eliminate ambiguity, maintain consistency.

10.5Visualisation types by category
CategoryTypeWhat it encodes & key detail
Keyword-basedWord cloud / tag cloudFont size ∝ word frequency (also size, colour, font, layout; colours may mark themes; layout random or shaped). Limitation: no context or semantic meaning — frequency alone doesn't show relationships. Cost-effective alternative to paid coding tools for open-ended text, but unsuitable if the data isn't optimised for context.
RelationshipNetwork diagramNodes and connecting edges (e.g. computer networks)
Tree diagramHierarchical parent/child relationships (e.g. a family tree)
Chord diagramMany-to-many relationships around a circle (e.g. mixed-reality design relationships)
Radar chartMultiple attributes on radiating axes from a shared centre (e.g. a UX-skills profile)
Tree mapNested rectangles for hierarchical part-to-whole data: size = magnitude, colour = value (e.g. red negative, green positive). Captures individual values and hierarchy; example sizes sectors by market cap and shows the reaction to an interest-rate speech (26 Aug 2022).
Temporal / time-seriesLine chartTrend of a value (often a percentage) over continuous time (e.g. inflation); label axes/units, use distinct colours and a legend, annotate events
Stream graphStacked area graph displaced around a central axis: layered flowing bands over time (e.g. colour = artist, width = popularity)
Heat mapColour intensity across a 2-D grid of two time levels (e.g. monthly temperature); spots “hot spots”
Animated scatter plotPoints move over time as an added dimension; shows transitions, not just end-points; improves retention
Other time chartsStacked area chart, bar chart (grouped/stacked), Gantt chart (horizontal bars of work vs allotted time; Henry Gantt), polar area diagram (cyclical data; sectors differ by how far they extend from the centre, not by angle)
ComparativeSmall multiplesSame chart repeated with one variable changed, so viewers compare shape/pattern across panels. Also called trellis/lattice/grid/panel charts; same scale and axes across panels; popularised by Edward Tufte; raises information density; best for many related datasets, similarities/differences and outliers. UN population example: shared horizontal scale (1950–2100), vertical scales from zero with differing maxima.
GeographicGeographic mapSnow’s map of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak

Historic firsts

Charles Minard (1781–1870): quantitative data on a map depicting the shrinking of Napoleon's army in the 1812 Russian campaign. William Playfair (1759–1823): a bar chart of Scotland's 1781 imports/exports with 17 countries — the first quantitative visualisation not plotted against time or geographic space.

10.6AI-powered data visualisation

Trend: natural-language-to-chart generation — a user asks a plain-language question (e.g. "Show revenue by region") and an AI pipeline handles pattern detection, anomaly highlighting, chart-type selection, and predictive insight, producing an auto-generated real-time dashboard without the user needing to manually pick a chart type, map axes, or format anything.

Market size cited: US$5.75B in 2026, at a 14.7% CAGR. Cited impact: it lets non-technical users build dashboards without SQL or design skills, AI-assisted eye-tracking can predict viewer fatigue/cognitive load, and over 50% of organisations reportedly already use AI for automated insight generation (Gartner, 2026).

Named risks (explicitly flagged in the source), not just benefits: reduced human awareness of bias in how data is being presented, and over-reliance on AI-selected charts/insights without independent verification — directly analogous to the AI-ideation caution in §4.6 and the AI-conversation caution in §6.5: AI accelerates a stage of the process, but doesn't remove the need for human critical judgement.

⚡ Quick examples
Visual hierarchy
PointSize, contrast and position set what is seen first.
ExampleA large bold headline then smaller body text then a coloured button.
ExplanationHierarchy guides attention and reading order.
Information foraging
PointUsers follow 'scent' cues to decide whether a path leads to their goal.
ExampleA link labelled 'Pricing' has strong scent; 'More' has weak scent.
ExplanationStrong labels keep users on track; weak scent makes them leave.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • People scan in F- or Z-patterns rather than read fully.
  • Size, contrast and position set what is seen first.
  • Users follow 'scent' cues to decide whether a path leads to their goal.
  • Do not misrepresent data.
  • Word clouds, tree maps, network diagrams, time series, small multiples.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Information scenttap to flip
How well navigation cues predict where relevant content lies
F-pattern / Z-patterntap to flip
Two dominant eye-tracking reading patterns for web content
➡ Where next? Findable is not enough; it also has to look clear and readable — visual design.

lessons.title: Visual Design
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersType, colour and layout silently tell users what matters and what is clickable.
🧠 Memory hookThe eye groups by Gestalt. Near, similar, connected or enclosed things read as one. Never rely on colour alone.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Where Visual Design sits in the bigger pictureText, fonts, and typographyColourAffordance (visual design lens)Gestalt principlesAI in Visual Design: Generative UI
📛 Exact names — know these word for word: Gestalt principles
NameWhat it doesExample
SimilarityThings that look alike are seen as relatedAll links share one colour
ProximityCloser elements are grouped; farther ones are separatedSegments of a progress bar
ClosureWe fill in small gaps to see a whole shapeA partly drawn logo still reads as complete
Common regionElements inside the same bounded area are grouped (older name: enclosure)Items in one card or bordered box
ContinuityElements along a line or smooth curve are seen as relatedItems in a row or an aligned column
Figure/groundWe separate a stable “figure” from the backgroundBlurred background behind foreground content
11.1Where Visual Design sits in the bigger picture
👁 SEE IT — each strategy, shown rather than described
Colour
The bright one catches the eye first.
Size
The larger element dominates attention.
Contrast
low contrasthigh contrast
Stark differences draw the eye.
Proximity
Close items read as one group.
Whitespace
Space separates groups from each other.
Alignment
Left: aligned = expected position. Right: ragged = looks accidental.
Repetition
Repeated elements build a pattern; the breaker stands out.
Texture / style
A distinct theme helps chunking.

Extending the Information Design pipeline from §10.2, this lecture places Visual Design within the wider family of design disciplines:

Discipline Focus
Data Analysis & Mining Inspect, clean, transform, model data for decision-making
Data Visualisation Present analysed data (facts, figures, findings) for exploration
Visual Design Aesthetics — size, colour, contrast, alignment, repetition, proximity, whitespace, texture, fonts, typography — grounded in principles: Gestalt, space, hierarchy, scale, dominance, similarity
Information Design Present clear, accessible data to meet a need or solve a problem
Interaction Design (IxD) User engagement and dialogue
UI Design Create the visual elements of an application
Product Design Design products to meet user needs and drive business growth
UX Design The umbrella covering information, visual, interaction, UI, and product design

Visual design strategies map onto Gestalt-style perceptual effects, each drawing the eye or supporting grouping in a specific way: colour (bright colours catch the eye), size (larger elements dominate attention), contrast (stark differences draw the eye), proximity (group related elements together), whitespace (separates groups from each other), texture/style (distinct themes aid chunking, cf. §7.3), alignment (users expect elements in consistent positions), and repetition (repeated elements draw the eye and build visual rhythm).

Basic elements of visual design

Lines (connect two points; define shapes, divisions, textures), shapes (self-contained areas), colour (differentiates items, creates depth/emphasis, organises information), texture (repeated element → pattern; can attract or deter attention), typography (font, size, alignment, colour, spacing), form (3-D volume and mass). Successful visual design doesn't take away from content/function but enhances it, building trust and interest in the brand.

11.2Text, fonts, and typography
👁 SEE IT — what the terms look like
Serif vs sans-serif vs script (and what each “says”)
SerifRapid Hamburgefonts 2025authority · professional · respect
Sans-serifRapid Hamburgefonts 2025simple · minimal · modern
ScriptRapid Hamburgefonts 2025enthusiasm · creativity · adventure
Anatomy: baseline, x-height, cap height, ascender, descender
Weight: thin → black
ThinLightRegularMediumBoldBlack
Bold/medium for emphasis; black hurts body readability.
Italics: Roman, Oblique (fake), true Italic
RomanQuick fox, agile
ObliqueQuick fox, agilejust slanted
ItalicQuick fox, agileredrawn letterforms
Tracking (group) and leading (line spacing)
TightTRACKING EXAMPLE
NormalTRACKING EXAMPLE
WideTRACKING EXAMPLE

Tight leading packs the lines together and the paragraph feels dense and heavy to read.

Generous leading gives each line room to breathe, so the paragraph is easier to read.

Kerning is the same idea between just two letters (e.g. A–V).
Capitals, small caps and numerals
All capsNASA AND THE HTML SPECuse only to start a line
Small capsNASA and the HTML specsubtler emphasis
Lining1 234 567 890tables & data
Old-style1 234 567 890blends into running text
Layout: centred vs asymmetric (Tschichold)
Left: centred blocks feel arbitrary. Right: asymmetric, aligned to an edge — purposeful.
Grid: align to lines, not centres
Elements snap to grid lines → rhythm, and content can reflow at other screen sizes.
Applied: the party invitation, before and after
party saturday come join us at stacy s house 7pm rsvp and bring some food call stacy
Stacy’s Party
When Saturday, 7 pm
Where Stacy’s house
Bring some food
RSVP → call Stacy
Hierarchy (size), alignment, grouping and white space make it scannable.

Font properties:

Property Notes
Serif vs. sans-serif "Serif" likely derives from the Dutch schreef ("stroke"/"line") — the small line finishing a letter's strokes. Cultural association (from the logo-branding example, §11.5): serif ≈ authority/professionalism/respect; sans-serif ≈ simplicity/minimalism/modernity; script ≈ enthusiasm/creativity/adventure.
Line spacing Controls vertical density/readability of a text block
Weight Thin → bold; used to create emphasis/hierarchy
Italics Three distinct forms: Roman (normal upright), Oblique (a "fake" italic — Roman letterforms mechanically slanted), and true Italic (a separately designed, more cursive letterform)
Small capitals Capital-shaped letters set at roughly x-height, used for a subtler kind of emphasis than full caps
Lower-case (old-style) numbers Digits designed with ascenders/descenders like lowercase letters, sitting more quietly within a line of text, as opposed to uniform-height uppercase (lining) numbers

Typography (layout) — two named approaches:

  • Asymmetric layout (Jan Tschichold, 1928): contrasted against the older convention of schematically, thoughtlessly centring text blocks (described as "ugly"). Tschichold's asymmetric arrangement of the same blocks within the same type area is instead constructive, meaningful, and economical ("beautiful") — and narrow columns of text are noted as difficult to read regardless of layout style.
  • Grid systems: a key pattern for implementing rationality, modernism, and asymmetry; importantly, no elements are centred. Grid systems are also where the proximity Gestalt principle shows up structurally — e.g. related radio buttons placed closer together within the same grid cell/region. Found in modern design tools (Sketch) and web frameworks (Bootstrap).

Typography vocabulary

Term Meaning
Typeface vs. font Typeface = the design family; font = a specific size/weight instance
Baseline The invisible line upon which most letters rest
x-height Height of the main body of lowercase letters ("x")
Ascender / descender Parts extending above x-height / below baseline (their lengths contribute to a font's style)
Cap height Height of capitals from the baseline
Kerning Adjusts space between two letters
Tracking (letterspacing) Adjusts spacing of a group of letters: tight = dense, may reduce readability; normal = optimal; wide = airy/emphasis
Leading (line spacing) Vertical distance between lines; tight = density, generous = readability
Type size Measured from the top of the ascender to the bottom of the lowest descender

Typographic hierarchy expresses organisation of content, emphasising some elements and subordinating others, so readers know where to enter/exit and what to pick (Lupton, Thinking with Type). Serif history: until ~1900 most typefaces were serif; modernists use sans-serif; designers realised a typeface could come in two versions to convey information.

Serif vs. sans-serif legibility is not settled. One hypothesis: serifs are easier to read for long text because they act as anchors that guide the eye; the competing hypothesis is familiarity — "legibility, in practice, amounts simply to what one is accustomed to" (Eric Gill, 1931). Other course material notes there is no real support for the anchor hypothesis. Serif examples: Times New Roman, Georgia, Baskerville; sans-serif: Arial, Helvetica, Calibri (better for digital displays).

Typography details

  • Font weight: thin/light (delicate, large headings), regular (body), medium (subtle emphasis), bold (strong emphasis/hierarchy), black/heavy (dramatic, hurts body readability); CSS controls weight.
  • Italics uses: emphasis, titles of works, foreign/specialised terms, contrast/hierarchy; true italics nearly always look better than oblique.
  • Capitals: use all-caps only to start a line; don't use them for emphasis (hard to read) — use small caps instead. "Fake" small caps (scaled-down capitals found in many DTP programs) look wrong because the stroke weight is off; true small caps are specially designed (acronyms, abbreviations, section headings, running titles).
  • Numerals: lining (uppercase) figures — uniform height on the baseline, best for tables/headings/technical data; old-style (lowercase) figures — ascenders/descenders, blend into body text and are easier to read. Babbage (1827) found uniform-height figures more legible — later research contradicted this.
  • Text alignment (left / centre / right) is "a fundamental typographic act".
  • Tschichold (1928): "Asymmetry is the rhythmic expression of functional design"; centred layouts pre-Bauhaus placed photos centrally with text flowing around, which was harder to read; asymmetry feels more dynamic.

Grid systems — what they buy you

Consistent alignment and spacing; coherent structure; rhythm that guides the eye. Elements are aligned to grid lines, not centred. Gestalt in practice: alignment connects elements, consistency/repetition builds recognition, white space builds hierarchy

E.g. a "Find" label is easy to see in a column of its own, spacing between buttons is consistent, similar things (radio buttons) are closer, the bottom buttons are spaced differently because they're different.

Grids also let content reflow across screen sizes, speed design/development, and establish visual importance via consistent size relationships; the Sketch overlay of red vertical stripes shows content aligned even when asymmetric.

🧩 Pause & recall — Which colour property should encode ordered quantitative values?
Answer: Lightness/tint/shade
Use lightness for sequential data; hues for categories.
11.3Colour
👁 SEE IT — the colour ideas, with real colour
Colour wheel
Opposite hues (red↔cyan-green, blue↔orange-yellow) give maximum contrast. Black, white and grey are neutrals, not hues.
HSL — drag the sliders
Hue = which colour · Saturation = purity/intensity · Lightness = light↔dark.
Tint · Tone · Shade (same hue)
pure hue
tint
+ white
tone
+ grey
shade
+ black
Monochromatic
One hue; varying tints/tones/shades → calm, cohesive, but can turn monotone.
Analogous
Neighbouring hues; one dominant, others as highlights. More vibrant than monochrome.
Complementary
Opposite hues: high impact — good for call-to-action; pure pairs can vibrate.
Triadic
Three evenly spaced hues: one dominant, two accents.
Split-complementary
A hue plus the two neighbours of its complement: contrast, less tension.
Square (two complementary pairs)
Four evenly spaced hues.
Warm vs cool
warm → sun, energy, cosiness
cool → water, calm, isolation
Simultaneous contrast — same grey, different background
The three middle squares are the identical grey (#808080). Always judge colour in context.
Contrast checker (WCAG)
Sample text 16px
Aim for ≥ 4.5 : 1 for body text, ≥ 3 : 1 for large text.
Colour blindness simulator
colour only — can you tell red from green?
✕✓colour + icon — still clear
Never rely on colour alone: add icons, labels, patterns, or brightness differences.
Palettes for data
Qualitative (categories)
Sequential (low → high, by lightness)
Diverging (around a meaningful centre, e.g. 0)
About 6 categories is the safe limit for telling colours apart.

Colour properties:

Model What it describes
Colour wheel (primary/secondary/tertiary) The base structure for identifying contrasting colours (e.g. blue/yellow, red/green as complementary pairs)
HSL (Hue–Saturation–Lightness) Hue = which colour; Saturation = intensity/purity of that colour; Lightness = how light/dark it is
TTS (Tint–Tone–Shade) Tint = colour + white (lighter); Tone = colour + grey (muted); Shade = colour + black (darker)
Colour blindness Most common forms are red-green and blue-yellow blindness — never rely on colour alone to convey information; add redundant cues (brightness, location, shape)

Colour schemes (relationships between wheel positions):

Scheme Structure Effect
Monochromatic One base hue in varying tints/tones/shades Reduces visual complexity; sets a consistent mood
Analogous Adjacent hues on the wheel More vibrant than monochromatic; one dominant hue, others as highlights
Complementary Opposite hues on the wheel One dominant hue, others as high-contrast highlights
Triad / Split-complementary / Rectangle / Square Evenly spaced hues, or complementary pairs, around the wheel Various dominant/accent balances — e.g. triad = one dominant + two accents; square = two complementary pairs
Cool vs. warm Every hue has warm and cool undertone variants Warm evokes sun/energy/coziness; cool evokes water/serenity/isolation

Emotional and cultural colour associations: Red = energy/adventure/passion/danger; blue = calmness/tranquility/stability/honesty; green = growth/nature/freshness; yellow = happiness/playfulness; brown = stability/earthiness; black = solemnity/mystery/power.

Associations are culturally specific and not universal — e.g. red signals good luck/celebration in Chinese culture, but excitement/danger/love/"stop" in Western culture (and is also associated with Christmas when paired with green, and with Valentine's Day). Perception of colour can also differ between men and women.

Contrast checkers can be misleading — trust your visual judgement too. A contrast-ratio tool can report a passing ratio for, e.g. white text on a very high-luminance background, even where the practical result still reads poorly — the numeric ratio doesn't capture every real perceptual factor.

Colour for data (cross-references and extends §10.4's data-integrity guidance):

Data type Correct colour property Example
Qualitative (categories, with or without inherent order — e.g. country, race, gender, grade, rank) Hue — distinct hues for distinct categories, limited to roughly 6 hues for clarity, since more than six become hard to visually differentiate —
Sequential (quantitative) (numerical data with inherent order — e.g. temperature, test scores, time, income) Lightness — lighter shades = lower values, darker = higher values —
— Continuous sequential Lightness varied continuously Allows precise association with the actual value
— Discrete sequential Lightness varied in a few fixed steps/buckets Reduces cognitive load via broad, discrete patterns rather than fine gradation
Diverging (data with a meaningful zero/ratio point, spanning two directions) Hue for the categorical split + tint for positive, shade for negative E.g. a diverging palette split around a "0" midpoint

Worked before/after example (cross-references §7.3's identical sea-level map case): using arbitrary hues to represent sequential sea-level depth is a bad example — hard to distinguish sea from land or read any ordering, and more than six hues become indistinguishable; the good version uses hue only for the qualitative split (brown = land, blue = water) and lightness for the sequential value (darker = further from sea level).

Colour guideline summary (as given in source): Use hues for qualitative data (limit to ~6, drawing on primary/secondary/tertiary colours) and choose a colour scheme deliberately (monochromatic, analogous, complementary, etc.), factoring in mood, dominant colour, cultural/emotional associations, contrast, and consistent colour use across all charts in a set

Use lightness/tint/shade for quantitative data Use hue within a diverging palette specifically to separate categories (e.g. land vs. sea) And always attend to colour blindness by supplementing colour with shape, location, and size cues.

Colour for data — palette details

Qualitative palette for categorical variables (distinct hues; rule of thumb here ≤ ten colours vs. the six used elsewhere — both appear in sources; ≈6 is the safer limit for distinguishability).

Sequential palette for numeric/ordered values — the most prominent dimension is lightness (lower values lighter, higher darker).

Diverging palette = two sequential palettes sharing an endpoint at a meaningful central value (e.g. zero), each with a distinct hue. Discrete vs. continuous: discretisation reduces cognitive load (colour is weaker than position/length for exact values), allows unequal ranges to handle outliers, but loses comparison within a bin. Rainbow scales have no natural order and fail colour-blind users

The improved map uses brown for land and blue for water (qualitative) with darker = deeper/higher.

11.4Affordance (visual design lens)
👁 SEE IT — does it look like what it does?
Visual affordance: button vs plain text
Save
Left looks pushable (shadow, fill). Right looks like a label.
Slider and text box
A slider invites sliding; a text box invites typing — before you touch them.
Explicit and pattern affordance
Click here
☰🔍⋮
Explicit = it tells you. Pattern = familiar icons signal standard behaviour.
Four kinds, one line each
  • Physical — shape suggests action (door handle)
  • Visual — shadow/fill (button)
  • Pattern — familiar conventions
  • Explicit — a label tells you

Affordance (cross-reference §6.4, now given the visual-design treatment): a property of an object's appearance that shows the user what action is possible, ideally perceived intuitively, without deliberation — a button should visually look pushable; a slider should visually invite sliding; a text box should visually invite typing. The practical evaluation question posed by the slides: for each interactive element, "are the actions obvious?"

Affordance types

Physical (shape suggests action, e.g. door handle), visual (button shadow), pattern (familiar patterns suggest standard behaviour), explicit ("Click here"). Norman: "When affordances are taken advantage of, the user knows what to do just by looking." Check: slider needs to slide? text box needs text?

Mapping the action cycle to a UI task

Goal: "I want more screen so I can see the content better" → intention: "I will maximise my browser window" → action: "drag the mouse to the maximise button and click". The recap also restates Fitts's Law ("time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target") with ID = D/S exercises (e.g. S = 2, D = 8 → 4) and contrasts screen-edge hot corners with an on-screen "Go" button. (These recap slides re-apply §6.4 and §8.3.)

11.5Gestalt principles
👁 SEE IT — the six Gestalt principles, drawn
Similarity
Things that look alike (same colour or shape) read as one set.
Proximity
Same dots, but the gap makes two groups.
Closure
Your eye completes the circle (useful for progress rings and loaders).
Common region
Things inside the same card/box read as related.
Continuity
Dots along a smooth curve read as one flowing line.
Figure / ground (Rubin’s vase)
Vase or two faces? We seek a stable figure. Light text on a dark ground uses this.
Logo fonts + colour carry meaning
Heritagemodern →Power
Serif = authority · sans + arrow = forward · bold caps = strength. Blue = trust, red = energy/urgency.

Building on §1.1's brief introduction, the Gestalt principles are given full treatment here, describing how people perceive structure, logic, and patterns. These are the standard names used everywhere in this guide: Similarity, Proximity, Closure, Common region, Continuity, Figure/ground.

Principle Description Example
Similarity Elements that look alike (shape, colour, size) are seen as related; dissimilar elements are seen as separate groups Links styled in one colour read as one group of links
Proximity We group closer-together elements and separate them from elements that are farther away A progress bar's segments read as one connected sequence because they sit close together
Closure We prefer complete shapes and automatically fill in small gaps to perceive a whole A partially drawn shape or logo is still read as complete
Common region We group elements that share the same enclosed or bounded region (older name: enclosure) Elements inside the same card or bordered box are read as related
Continuity Elements arranged along a line or smooth curve are perceived as related (good continuation) Items in a row or aligned column read as a sequence
Figure/ground We dislike ambiguity and seek solid, stable items to perceive as the "figure" against a background An iOS blur/focus effect pushes the background out of focus so the foreground reads clearly

Source conflict, resolved. The lecture slides use two different lists. Lecture 1 (slide 2) names similarity, enclosure, proximity; Lecture 11 (slides 46–48 and the closing summary) teaches four: Closure, Common region, Figure/ground and Proximity. “Enclosure” and “Common region” are the same principle, so this guide uses Common region. Lecture 11’s overview slide also lists “similarity” among the principles behind visual design, and the Notion notes add Continuity, so Similarity and Continuity are in the table even though Lecture 11 does not teach them in full. Two further grouping principles appear in Lecture 10 / Notion Ch. 9: symmetry and periodicity (Weinschenk, 2011).

Logo/branding worked example ties fonts and colour choices together deliberately: serif fonts signal authority/professionalism, script fonts signal enthusiasm/creativity, sans-serif fonts signal simplicity/modernity; blue signals trust/security/strength/wisdom, red signals energy/excitement/urgency, yellow signals happiness.

Gestalt — extra detail

Developed in the 1920s by German psychologists; the brain is wired to see structure, logic and patterns.

Figure/ground (multi-stability, Rubin's vase): we look for solid stable items; use it to contrast light text (figure) on dark ground; iOS uses blur, semi-transparent overlays and shadows; Material design uses Z-axis elevation.

Proximity (emergence): closer elements form one entity (e.g. the Girl Scouts logo's clustered faces). Closure: remember it when designing loading indicators/progress bars. Similarity: elements that look alike are seen as related — e.g. one colour for every link. Continuity: elements along a line or smooth curve read as a sequence — e.g. an aligned column of items.

📍 CASE FILE

The 2017 Oscars envelope

The setting

At the 2017 Academy Awards, presenters opened an envelope card whose layout was the problem.

What happened

The card put the category (‘Best Actress’) at the bottom in small print and gave the logo prominence, so the wrong envelope was read and ‘La La Land’ was announced for Best Picture. A better layout puts the category at the top, the logo at the bottom and the winner largest.

The lesson

Typography is functional, not just aesthetic: size, position and contrast decide what people read first.

More from the lecture

Typography failures have real consequences — the 2017 Oscars envelope card. The card's poor typography put the category ("Best Actress") at the very bottom in small print and gave the logo prominence, so the presenters read the wrong envelope ("La La Land" named Best Picture). A better layout moves the category to the top, the logo to the bottom, and makes the winner (Emma Stone) the largest element. Lesson: typography is functional, not just aesthetic.

11.6AI in Visual Design: Generative UI

AI-generated ("generative") UI creates context-aware interfaces in real time; teams using AI design tools reportedly ship 40–60% faster. Cited AI capabilities: automatic contrast checks and WCAG accessibility-compliance auditing (colour, legibility, assistive readiness)

Personalisation, where a full UI path adapts per individual user (cited McKinsey figure: +40% revenue for top-performing personalised experiences)

And a shift in the designer's role toward curation rather than manual construction — but the underlying Gestalt and colour-theory principles above remain essential, since curating AI output still requires the same judgement this lecture teaches.

📛 Exact names — know these word for word: the two inspection methods
NameWhat it doesUse it for
Heuristic evaluationExperts compare the UI with Nielsen’s 10 heuristics and rate severityGeneral usability problems
Cognitive walkthroughExperts walk through a scenario step by step, asking four questions per stepLearnability for a first-time user

Inspection is one of the four evaluation strategies (Inspection, Field studies, Laboratory studies, Surveys). It is the only one where experts judge the design instead of real users.

This lecture is the Test stage of Design Thinking, specifically the sub-branch of testing that uses UX experts rather than real users.

12.1The Test stage, and why use experts

Design Thinking's Test principle: "Prototype as if you are right, test as if you are wrong." Testing exists to make ideas better, to learn about users by sharing prototypes and observing reactions, to refine your Point of View (§3.1), and to potentially uncover unexpected insights that send you back to redefine or reframe the problem.

Terminology gotcha: in this lecture, "expert" does not mean someone from the target user population — it means a UX expert with strong general usability/domain knowledge, used as a stand-in evaluator. This is a completely different meaning of "expert" from the "expert vs. novice" behaviour-range axis introduced for personas in §3.3 — don't conflate the two.

Why use experts instead of real users? They're often easier to recruit, their feedback is easier to process (more structured, expert-framed), and there are fewer ethical/practical concerns than running studies with real users. Trade-offs: experts with genuine domain+UX knowledge aren't always easy to find; they can be expensive; they can miss important problems that only real users would hit; conversely they often flag many trivial issues; and they carry their own biases.

12.2Two types of inspection
Type What it does
Cognitive walkthrough Experts walk through each task step, answering four prescribed questions, to identify interface challenges specifically for new/first-time users
Heuristic evaluation Experts apply broad usability rules of thumb (heuristics — e.g. Nielsen's 10) to evaluate the interface generally

A general caveat applies to both: evaluation quality depends on the accuracy of the underlying theory and the skill of the expert applying it — inspection is not a mechanical, bias-free process.

🧩 Pause & recall — A cognitive walkthrough primarily evaluates:
Answer: Learnability from a new user's perspective
It follows tasks step by step asking four questions about a first-time user.
12.3Cognitive walkthrough

Procedure: give experts a UI prototype and a set of scenarios; tell them the assumed user population, context of use, and task details; the experts then walk through the prototype against each scenario, guided by four fixed questions:

  1. Will the user really want to do this action (does it align with a plausible goal)?
  2. Will the correct action be visible to the user?
  3. Will the user recognise which visible action is the correct one (as opposed to a similar-looking wrong one)?
  4. Will the user correctly interpret the feedback they get after performing the action?

These four questions are explicitly framed as addressing mental models, memory, and attention — i.e. cognitive walkthrough is essentially applying §6 (interaction models) and §7 (memory) concepts systematically, scenario by scenario, rather than as an independent new theory. Worked example given: applying the four questions to a paper prototype of a video-recording app, question by question, for a specific recording scenario.

Definitions

A cognitive walkthrough evaluates the learnability of a system from a new user's perspective; unlike user testing it involves no users (so is relatively cheap); like heuristic evaluation it relies on expert reviewers who, in a highly structured manner, walk a task and assess the interface. Inputs: a UI prototype of any fidelity + clearly defined assumptions (user population, context, task).

12.4Heuristic evaluation

Definition (reproduced from source, attributed to Jakob Nielsen): "Heuristic evaluation involves having a small set of evaluators examine the interface and judge its compliance with recognised usability principles (the 'heuristics')." It's a quick, affordable expert-evaluation method: test the UI guided by the heuristics, record problems, and rank them by severity.

Nielsen's 10 Heuristics (reproduced faithfully, since these are formal named principles likely to be tested verbatim):

# Heuristic Definition (reproduced)
1 Visibility of system status The system should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time. Example: a "you are here" map.
2 Match between system and the real world Speak the users' language, with words, phrases and concepts familiar to the user, rather than system-oriented terms. Follow real-world conventions, making information appear in a natural and logical order. Example: a shopping-cart metaphor is easier to recognise than a raw technical term like "UTF-8."
3 User control and freedom Users often choose system functions by mistake and need a clearly marked "emergency exit" to leave the unwanted state without an extended dialogue. Support undo and redo.
4 Consistency and standards Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform conventions. Example: check-in counters usually sit at a hotel's front — matching a real-world convention.
5 Error prevention Even better than good error messages is a careful design which prevents a problem from occurring in the first place — eliminate error-prone conditions, or check for them and offer a confirmation. Example: graying out unavailable date-selection options.
6 Recognition rather than recall Minimise the user's memory load by making objects, actions, and options visible; the user should not have to remember information from one part of the dialogue to another. Cross-reference §7.3: this is the same recognition-over-recall principle Nielsen's heuristics are named for. Example: a ribbon UI with visible commands beats a command-line interface requiring memorised syntax.
7 Flexibility and efficiency of use Accelerators, unseen by novice users, may speed up interaction for expert users, so the system can cater to both; allow users to tailor frequent actions. Example: Amazon's "1-click" ordering; keyboard shortcuts. Cross-reference §3.3's "novice vs. expert" persona behaviour range.
8 Aesthetic and minimalist design Dialogues should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed — every extra unit of information competes with the relevant ones.
9 Help users recognise, diagnose, and recover from errors Error messages should be in plain language (no codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution. Example: a "no search results" message that offers useful next-step guidance, rather than just stating failure.
10 Help and documentation Ideally the system needs no documentation at all; if needed, it should be easy to search, task-focused, list concrete steps, and not be too large. Example: contextual tooltips/info icons.

Common mistake — mixing up which heuristic a problem violates. Since several heuristics can superficially look similar (e.g. #3 "user control/freedom" vs. #9 "recover from errors" both relate to getting out of a bad state), a useful discriminator: #3 is about escaping an unwanted state the user caused by mistake (undo/exit), while #9 is specifically about communicating and recovering from an error condition once it's occurred.

The slides pose a direct practice prompt — "do these violate any heuristic?" using a bottom-of-screen mobile UI element that can be accidentally swiped away — as an exercise in correctly identifying which heuristic(s) apply.

Heuristic evaluation process (three stages):

  1. Briefing — gather experts, introduce the prototype (let them explore it once, then assign a representative task), present the project goals and the heuristics being used.
  2. Evaluation — each expert independently evaluates the interface and generates their own list of usability violations.
  3. Debriefing — experts discuss findings together and merge them into a single, prioritised list of problems.

Severity rating scale (used to prioritise the merged list):

Rating Meaning
0 Not a usability problem at all
1 Cosmetic — fix only if extra time available
2 Minor — low fixing priority
3 Major — important, should be given high priority
4 Catastrophic — imperative to fix before the product can be released

How many experts is enough? Nielsen found 3–5 experts offers the best cost-benefit ratio — different experts consistently find different problems, so using more than one expert catches more issues, but the marginal benefit of adding still more experts diminishes (not all researchers agree this exact number generalises to every context).

Choosing heuristics: you can adopt an existing published set — Nielsen's 10 (most common in this course), Gerhardt-Powals's 10 Cognitive Engineering Principles, Connell & Hammond's 30 Usability Principles, Smith & Mosier's 944 UI Design Guidelines — or develop your own project-specific heuristics.

Heuristic examples

# Extra good/poor examples and notes
1 Good: you-are-here maps; predictable interactions build trust in product and brand. Communicate system state — no consequential action without informing users; give feedback ideally immediately.
2 Poor: "UTF-8" options in settings. Never assume your understanding of words matches users'. Natural mapping = controls follow real-world conventions and correspond to outcomes
3 Good: prominent Cancel button; poor: hidden/unclear exit makes users feel trapped; easy back-out fosters freedom/confidence
4 Jakob's Law: people spend most of their time on other products, which set their expectations; inconsistency raises cognitive load. Consistency is internal (within app) and external (outside app); same fonts, colour scheme, layout
5 Grey out unavailable calendar dates; Twitter character counter; highlight problems before submission. Avoid slips with helpful constraints and good defaults; prevent mistakes by removing memory burdens, supporting undo and warning users (e.g. MS Word save/undo)
6 Good: comparison tables, MS Word ribbon; poor: command line. Humans have limited short-term memory
7 Experienced users bypass standard checkout; keyboard shortcuts for power users, menus for beginners; multiple ways to do the same thing (e.g. search); personalisation
8 Poor: cluttered design; good: clean design; think signal-to-noise ratio. Doesn't require flat design — keep content/visuals focused on the essentials
9 Helpful no-results search with alternatives vs. unhelpful technical codes/generic errors; style errors so users notice them
10 Amazon's help centre (organised, searchable, task-focused); info icons, tooltips, in-context help at the moment of need

Process wording and prototype-testing steps

Briefing (show the prototype, explain assumptions/context, let the evaluator explore once) → Evaluation (assign specific tasks, e.g. "find X" or a series of actions

The evaluator applies heuristics and documents problems) → Debriefing (discuss findings, rate and prioritise). In the course project each team invites one evaluator at a time, explains problem context/persona/easy scenario, runs the prototype via Wizard-of-Oz (follow the scenario or free explore), records every problem the evaluator states per heuristic, repeats with more evaluators (≈30 min), then compiles a heuristic-evaluation chart with columns Severity | Heuristic type | Description. Example problems logged: "P1: No visible help for commands", "P2: No shortcut for repetitive tasks".

Severity — the three factors (Nielsen)

Severity combines frequency (common or rare?), impact (easy or difficult to overcome?) and persistence (a one-time problem or repeatedly bothersome?). Ratings allocate fixing resources and indicate the need for further usability effort: if several catastrophic problems remain, don't release

If all are cosmetic, you may release. Different experts find different problems, which is why more than one evaluator is needed. Domain-specific heuristics should be clearly defined and measurable.

12.5AI-powered heuristic evaluation

Multimodal LLMs can scan UI screenshots directly to flag heuristic violations (Baymard's UX-Ray 2.0 is cited at 95% accuracy across 207 guidelines)

LLMs can also run synthetic cognitive walkthroughs, simulating user task flows in a way shown to align with human cognitive-walkthrough findings in at least one study (Zhong et al., 2025).

Implication: faster, cheaper first-pass evaluation is possible, but generic (non-domain-trained) prompts are only 50–75% accurate, so AI augments, but does not replace, expert evaluators.

Heuristic evaluation — more on the method

An analytical evaluation (by analysis of an interface rather than observing people), a "discount" usability technique — fast, no user recruitment. The exact heuristic set is not set in stone

Nielsen compiled the ten in the late 1990s from the best ideas of the time (Nielsen–Molich). Controversy: HE is best done prior to and in addition to user testing Using it instead of user testing is poor practice Pairing "double experts" (usability + domain) beats single experts

Its effectiveness is debated.

📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Exam-style scenario: the mobile banking app (hypothetical)

The setting

A heuristic evaluation of a banking app finds two issues: users cannot locate the logout button, which is hidden in a submenu under Settings, and the app shows ‘Error 404’ when connectivity drops.

What happened

Match each issue to a heuristic: the hidden logout is a problem of user control and freedom (a clear exit); ‘Error 404’ breaks match between the system and the real world (technical jargon) and also helps users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors.

The lesson

Heuristic evaluation means naming the specific heuristic that is violated and giving a concrete example of the issue.

ExampleAn evaluator reviews a prototype before any user testing.
ExplanationFast feedback, but they can miss real-user issues and have bias.
Cognitive walkthrough
PointEvaluate learnability for a new user by walking tasks and asking four questions.
ExampleWill the user try to do this? Will they notice the button? Will they recognise it as right? Will they see progress?
ExplanationIt exposes steps where a first-time user would get stuck.

  • Brief → evaluate individually → debrief → rate severity.

lessons.title: Evaluating Designs
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersDifferent questions need different evidence, so choose the method to fit the question.
🧠 Memory hookMatch the method to the question. Then measure what matters (performance, preference, perception).
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Why evaluate with real users at all?The four evaluation strategies, comparedUsability metrics
⚡ At a glance — four evaluation strategies
MethodRealismControl / precisionEffortBlind spot
InspectionLowMediumLowMisses real users
Field studiesHighLowHighUncontrolled, may see nothing useful
Laboratory studiesMediumHighMediumArtificial setting
SurveysLowLowLowOpinion, not behaviour

Combine methods (triangulate). Set measurable success criteria before testing.

📛 Exact names — know these word for word: the four evaluation strategies
NameWhat it doesStrengthWeaknessUse when
InspectionExperts analyse the system (heuristic evaluation)Easy to run, no users to recruitExperts aren’t real users, so less reliableYou need quick, cheap checks of common problems
Field studiesObserve users in their real contextRealisticLess precise: no experimental controlContext and real-world use matter most
Laboratory studiesObserve users in a controlled environmentPreciseLess realistic than field studiesYou need precise data on specific interactions or a comparison
SurveysAsk people questions instead of observing tasks (interview / web experiment)Easy to run at scaleSelf-report, less realistic and less reliableYou need attitudes and opinions

An experiment is not a fifth strategy. It is a special type of user study with two or more conditions (Chapter 18), so it can be run inside a laboratory study or, as a web experiment / A/B test, online (Chapter 17). Combine methods to triangulate.

This lecture zooms out from expert-only inspection (§12) to the full landscape of evaluation methods, including — critically — testing with real users.

13.1Why evaluate with real users at all?

Two justifications given directly: designers/experts don't automatically know what users want (despite being "the expert" in domain knowledge), and it's genuinely hard to predict what real users will do — a plausible-sounding design intuition can still fail in practice. The trade-off acknowledged: real-user studies are more costly, time-consuming, and can carry more subjectivity than inspection, but they're the only source of actual user behaviour data.

Sceptic's arguments for *not* evaluating with users

"We're the experts"; "it's too costly and time-consuming"; "too many differing opinions". Rebuttal: you can't tell how good a UI is until users try it; other methods rely on evaluators who may know too much about design or too little about tasks and users' environments; even experienced designers need validation. Real-user evaluation is the only way to know how users actually react and uncovers unexpected issues/opportunities.

13.2The four evaluation strategies, compared

"Goals determine your study method." Four approaches sit on trade-offs between realism, precision/control, and cost/ease of running:

Method Approach Pros Cons
Inspection (heuristic evaluation, §12) Experts analyse the system Easy to run; no need to recruit users Experts aren't real users — less reliable
Field studies Observe users in their real context Realistic Less precise — no experimental control
Laboratory studies Observe users in a controlled environment Precise Less realistic than field studies
Surveys (interview / web experiment) Ask people questions rather than observe them doing tasks Easy to run Less realistic than field or laboratory studies — less reliable 
flowchart LR
    A[Inspection] -->|more realistic, less easy| B[Surveys]
    B --> C[Laboratory Studies]
    C -->|more realistic, less control| D[Field Studies]

Caption: a rough realism/control gradient across the four methods — inspection is furthest from real user behaviour but cheapest to run; field studies are the most realistic but sacrifice experimental control; laboratory studies (expanded fully in §15) and surveys sit in between on different trade-off axes.

Emerging fifth method — AI-moderated usability testing: an AI moderator runs structured usability sessions using a pre-set protocol. Pros: scalable (many concurrent sessions), can compress weeks of scheduling into hours. Cons: evaluation quality depends heavily on how well the protocol itself was designed, and it's less nuanced than a human moderator who can adapt on the fly.

Triangulation: studies typically combine more than one method (e.g. observation and an experiment together) rather than relying on a single method alone, precisely because each method above has a different, non-overlapping blind spot.

The methods — extra pros/cons and when to use

Method Extra points
Inspection (theory-based) Experts apply established principles; easy/quick; finds many common problems; may miss contextual issues; less reliable for innovative interfaces; theories can't capture everything but describe aspects of behaviour in detail
Field study Deploy a system in its actual environment for a prolonged period; you exert very little control; reveals actual usage patterns; hard to standardise; time-intensive; behaviour may be uninteresting. Use when contextual factors and real-world use are critical
Laboratory study Precise measurement; artificial environment may affect behaviour; needs a dedicated space. Use when you need quantitative data on specific interactions or comparison between alternatives
Survey Easy to administer at scale; good for attitudinal feedback; self-reports can be unreliable; doesn't capture actual behaviour; response biases; if participants are well chosen results generalise to all users

Summary lines: inspections quick but miss user perspective; field = realistic but less controlled; lab = precise but artificial; surveys easy but less behaviourally accurate — combine methods to triangulate. Early prototypes can also be tested through unmoderated, qualitative, observational sessions.

🧩 Pause & recall — Which evaluation method offers the highest realism but least control?
Answer: Field study
Field studies observe real contexts with little control.
13.3Usability metrics

Before evaluating, define success criteria and how you'll measure them. Six standard usability metrics:

Metric Question it answers
Effectiveness How well does the product do what it's supposed to do?
Efficiency How well does the product support users in carrying out tasks (with reasonable speed/effort)?
Safety Does the product protect users from dangerous conditions and undesirable situations?
Utility Does the product provide the right functionality for actual user needs?
Learnability How easy is the system to learn (for a first-time user)?
Memorability How easy is it to remember how to use the product after some time away?

These reappear directly as the basis for goal-setting in laboratory studies (§15.2). A referenced example is Nielsen's longitudinal "Web UX 2016 vs 2004" study, which planned sites/users/tasks/attempts against success and emotional metrics over time.

Usability testing — what it is and the task card

  • Collect data from members of the target user group, usually in a controlled setting (usability lab or quiet office); you moderate (e.g. one task at a time).
  • You are testing the technology, not the users. Key planning questions: what hypotheses, which quality metrics matter most?
  • Establish evaluation criteria before testing
  • Metrics should be objective, measurable and tied to user goals and business outcomes. Task card: Goal (what users should achieve), Task (realistic actions), Data (quantitative — time, errors, completion
  • Qualitative — observations), Apparatus (prototype, devices, recording tools).
  • The scenario can be just the goal/task statement or a short story that adds motivation. Participants: recruit a representative sample; simple random sampling recruits randomly from a list of all potential participants.
  • Control environmental factors and devices for experiments. Testing formats and methods include web A/B experiments.

Metric-to-task worked example

A grid of "What does it mean here? → What task measures it? → What data? → How would you know it's good?": Efficiency — "a user can send money to a recipient quickly" → ask them to transfer money via the app → record time and number of steps → duration and steps within acceptable limits. Memorability = recall after periods of non-use. Data types: ordered and nominal data are non-numerical ("categorical").

Case study — Web UX evolution 2004–2016

A 12-year tracking study (Nielsen Norman): consistent methodology across years, same tasks and metrics, a mix of new and returning participants; success rates (task completion) rose and frustration fell over time.

13.4Worked case study — Tullis & Albert, Measuring the User Experience §10.2

(Usability evaluation of a speech-recognition IVR, reported by J. R. Lewis; answers the four reading questions set in the Lecture 13 participation task.)

  • Who / how many? 6 participants; a formative (problem-discovery) study of a speech-recognition interactive voice response system (find stores/service centres, buy accessories/products).
  • What did they do? Four tasks: (1) find the nearest service location, (2) find an accessory and a nearby store, (3) buy an accessory, (4) order a new product. The text does not state the test room explicitly; participants read each task, asked for clarifications and signalled when ready — the study was run as a moderated session with the experimenter.
  • Metrics collected. Task level: completion time (all task means < 3 min; 90% CIs), success rate with 90% binomial confidence intervals, and satisfaction via the ASQ (After Scenario Questionnaire: 3 items, 1–7, lower = better). Study level: PSSUQ (16 items, 7-point, lower = better; subscales SysUse, InfoQual, IntQual; overall mean ≈ 2.0 ± 1.1, well below midpoint → favourable). Qualitative: three most-/least-liked attributes per participant (liked: easy to understand/use, good recognition, repeat function; disliked: confusing main-menu wording (3 participants), phone numbers spoken too fast, barge-in unreliable, no keypad (DTMF) input, unforgiving recognition).
  • Results. Tasks 2–4: 100% success. Task 1 failures: two participants chose "Find a store" instead of "Find service". Task 4 satisfaction slightly poorer because 5 of 6 were confused by one menu option's wording.
  • Severity score formula. Severity = frequency (% of participants who hit the problem) × impact weight, where impact levels carry weights Level 1 = 10, Level 2 = 5, Level 3 = 2, Level 4 = 1 (max 1,000). Level 2 = "required more than one minute to recover". Top problem: asked for store rather than service (33% × 10 = 333). Compare the frequency/impact/persistence view in Chapter 12.
  • Sample-size adequacy (Lewis 2006). 12 problems found by 6 users; problem-discovery rate p̂ = 0.278, adjusted 0.134 → expected proportion found = 1 − (1 − 0.134)^6 ≈ 0.578 → ≈ 21 problems available (12 / 0.578). Later participants would each add roughly one new problem, diminishing thereafter; low discovery rate and low severities suggest a well-designed UI.
  • Recommendations (design alternatives). (1) Reorder/reword the main menu so "Find service" isn't confused with "Find a store" (place "Find service" first; callers barge in one option late); (2) replace the confusing menu option with alternative wording; (3) slow TTS speech rate, especially for phone numbers; (4) consider allowing zip-code entry via keypad.
  • Lessons. A formative study can still cheaply yield standard metrics (time, success, satisfaction) usable as benchmarks for later versions; report CIs to show measurement limits with n = 6; tabular presentation works well for development teams.
📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Tullis & Albert: the speech-recognition phone system

The setting

A usability evaluation of an interactive voice response (IVR) system, reported by J. R. Lewis, is the Lecture 13 reading case.

What happened

Six participants tried tasks with the system in a moderated study. Two of them picked ‘Find a store’ instead of ‘Find service’, the biggest failure found.

The lesson

It shows how a small, moderated study can find real problems, and how to combine task success with observation. (Full details are in the case section below.)

⚡ Quick examples
Why test with real users
PointUsers reveal what experts can't.
ExampleExperts approve a form; real users repeatedly miss the optional 'Company' field's purpose.
ExplanationOnly real use shows how people actually react.
McGrath's trade-off
PointEvidence balances generalisability, precision and realism.
ExampleA laboratory study is precise but less realistic; a field study is realistic but less controlled.
ExplanationYou can't maximise all three at once.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Users reveal what experts can't.
  • Inspection, field, lab, survey — each trades realism, control and cost.
  • Evidence balances generalisability, precision and realism.
  • Test the technology, not the users; use goal, task, data, apparatus.
  • Make them objective and measurable.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Inspection / Field study / Laboratory study / Surveytap to flip
Four evaluation strategies trading realism vs. control vs. ease
Effectiveness / Efficiency / Safety / Utility / Learnability / Memorabilitytap to flip
Six usability metrics
McGrath trade-offtap to flip
Evidence maximises generalisability, precision, realism — never all three
Task cardtap to flip
Goal, Task, Data, Apparatus for a usability test
ASQ / PSSUQtap to flip
Post-task / post-study satisfaction questionnaires (lower = better in Tullis)
➡ Where next? Much of what users give you is words and behaviour, which need careful analysis.
