lessons.title: Qualitative Analysis
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersObservations tell you what people do; questions tell you what they say and feel. Both need structure to analyse.
🧠 Memory hookRaw data → Codes → Themes. Look for patterns, not anecdotes.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Qualitative vs. quantitative dataObservations vs. questionsOpen vs. closed questionsWhat qualitative data is good forTranscribing qualitative dataConverting qualitative data into quantitative dataAI-powered thematic analysis
⚡ At a glance — turning words into numbers
Collect (observe / ask)→Cluster into themes→Code each item→Check inter-coder reliability→Report counts + quotes
📛 Exact names — know these word for word: data and question types
NameWhat it isTell it apart
Qualitative dataDescriptions; analysed for themes and patternsHard to measure
Quantitative dataNumbers; analysed statisticallyEasy to measure
Open questionsQualitative: answered in the participant’s own words“What did you like about the UI?”
Closed questionsQuantitative: answered from fixed options“Is the UI easy or hard to use?”
14.1Qualitative vs. quantitative data
Aspect Qualitative Quantitative
Nature Descriptions Numbers
Measurability Hard to measure Easy to measure
Analysis approach Themes and patterns Statistical analysis
Source Qualitative example Quantitative example
Questions Open-question responses; "further comment" responses; opinions Age, job role, years of experience; closed-question responses
Observations Critical incidents; think-aloud data; participant comments; description of how a task was performed Time spent on a task; number of errors; number of clicks

Complementary data

Qualitative and quantitative data are complementary; scales/ranks give more analysable detail but can still be very subjective.

People often behave differently than they report, but questions remain valuable for prior experiences and expectations. Open questions allow unexpected insights and capture the user's own words. Qualitative data = dynamic information and subjective feelings (e.g. interview/think-aloud transcripts).

Goals: discover root causes, explore unexpected usage patterns, persuade with authentic user voices. Different goals → different methods and data (rich descriptions/contextual evidence vs. numerical measures).

Think-aloud caveat

"If you ask a question, people will always give an answer, even if it has nothing to do with facts" — so thinking aloud does not guarantee correct answers (matches §15.2).

14.2Observations vs. questions

Observations are generally more reliable than self-reported answers, because people are often not fully aware of their own actions, and not always able to put their thoughts into words accurately. Questions remain useful for two things observation can't easily capture: demographics (age, gender, occupation) and subjective assessments (how someone feels).

🧩 Pause & recall — Qualitative data is best for:
Answer: Exploring why problems happen and explaining them with rich description
It reveals causes and persuades with authentic user voices.
14.3Open vs. closed questions
Type Example
Open (qualitative) "What did you like about the UI?" / "What did you dislike about the UI?"
Closed (quantitative) "In your opinion, is the UI easy or hard to use?"

Worked refinement of a closed question, from weakest to strongest:

  1. Bad (binary): "The UI is easy to use. (Agree/Disagree)" — forces an artificially binary choice, losing nuance.
  2. Better (Likert scale): "The UI is easy to use." — Strongly agree / Agree / Neither / Disagree / Strongly disagree — adds graded nuance.
  3. Best (specific + Likert): "The data entry UI is easy to use." — Strongly agree / Agree / Neither / Disagree / Strongly disagree — additionally narrows the vague "the UI" down to a specific named feature, so the answer is actually actionable.
14.4What qualitative data is good for

It helps you understand design problems — discover their underlying causes and identify potential solutions — and it helps you explain problems to others (design-team members, developers, and managers), because rich description communicates more persuasively than a bare number.

14.5Transcribing qualitative data

Transcripts of audio/video/notes are very useful for analysis but time-consuming to fully produce. A practical shortcut: you don't have to transcribe everything — mark the timestamps of interesting events/quotes as you go, and transcribe only those interesting parts later.

Quotes are powerful supporting evidence; short video clips are even more powerful.

The most useful material to capture in a transcript: critical incidents (moments significant to the activity being observed — the slides reference the "selective attention" awareness-test video as an illustration of how easy it is to miss things without deliberate, structured attention), comments made during the task while it's still fresh in the participant's mind, and questionnaire responses.

Video — best use

Too much data to process wholly; best for ~20-second snippets that communicate successes or problems; a clip is very convincing to people who weren't at the study.

14.6Converting qualitative data into quantitative data

Yes, this is possible — via a clustering step followed by a coding step.

Clustering: Group observations/comments/descriptions into "interesting piles" (the number of clusters is not fixed in advance — it emerges from the data) Items within one cluster should have higher similarity/affinity to each other than to items in other clusters

Which groupings count as "interesting" depends on your specific research question.

Once clustered, report summaries — e.g. "7 of 10 participants could not find the 'close' button," "4 of 5 participants said the UI was easy to use," "Participant 1 shouted an expletive 8 times." Worked example: a K-Sketch vs. PowerPoint animation-tool comparison study clustered participant comments around themes like "similarity to sketching," "timeline control," and direct points of comparison with K-Sketch.

Coding (also called indexing): the more formal analytical process of categorising data.

Category type Definition Example
Nominal Categories with no inherent rank/order Colour preference (red, green, blue)
Ordinal Categories with a meaningful rank/order Sketch quality (poor=1, medium=2, good=3)

Process: a coder reviews roughly 5% of the data to generate the category set, then places every observation/comment into a category.

Worked example — K-Sketch animation quality was coded on three ordinal (0–2 point) dimensions: timing (do motions run at the correct speed/duration, do coordinated actions match up in time), location (are objects in the right positions, do they avoid crossing lines they shouldn't, do coordinated actions match up spatially), and overall quality (does it match the given criteria, does the motion look intentional and controlled).

Coding is not an exact science — check inter-coder reliability. Have roughly 5% of the data independently coded by two different coders, then compute a difference score: for ordinal categories, use the average pairwise difference; for nominal categories, use the percentage of observations placed in different categories by the two coders. If the difference exceeds 10%, revise your category set — it's likely too ambiguous or not well-defined.

14.7AI-powered thematic analysis

AI/NLP can automate the coding and clustering of qualitative data, identifying themes across thousands of responses at once (cited figure: 95% of UX researchers reportedly used AI tools regularly by 2026).

Benefits: much faster transcription/coding (minutes vs. hours), analysis at a scale no human team could match manually, and more consistent categorisation (reducing inter-coder variability, the exact problem the reliability check above exists to catch).

As with every other AI-augmentation case in this course (§4.6, §6.5, §10.6, §12.5): human judgement remains essential for interpreting what the themes actually mean in context.

Overall qualitative-analysis procedure and thematic analysis

Highlight significant things → write a short key theme/phrase → map all data into the identified themes/codes → check inter-coder reliability. Worked example (child-protection design workshops): transcribed 10.5 hours of recordings; used thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006); open coding generated >1000 codes; then an affinity-mapping process compared and clustered similar codes into emergent themes.

📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Child-protection design workshops

The setting

A research team ran design workshops about child protection and had to make sense of many hours of conversation.

What happened

They transcribed 10.5 hours of recordings and used thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006): open coding produced more than 1,000 codes, then affinity mapping clustered similar codes into emerging themes.

The lesson

Qualitative data becomes usable through coding and clustering into themes, which is how you turn many words into a few findings.

⚡ Quick examples
When to use qualitative data
PointIt explains causes and gives rich description.
ExampleThink-aloud shows a user misreading 'Save' as 'Send'.
ExplanationNumbers say what happened; words say why.
Capturing data
PointTranscribe only critical incidents; use ~20 s video clips.
ExampleA short clip of a user failing to find 'close' convinces stakeholders.
ExplanationFull transcription is slow; targeted capture saves time.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • It explains causes and gives rich description.
  • Transcribe only critical incidents; use ~20 s video clips.
  • Clustering = informal grouping; coding = formal labels with definitions.
  • Independent coders should classify items the same way.
  • Open coding then affinity mapping into themes.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Nominal vs. Ordinal codingtap to flip
Unranked categories vs. ranked categories
Inter-coder reliabilitytap to flip
Agreement check between two independent coders (<10% difference target)
Clustering vs. Codingtap to flip
Grouping into themes vs. formally labelling into categories
Clustering vs. codingtap to flip
Informal grouping vs. formal categorisation with reliability checks
Inter-coder reliabilitytap to flip
Independent coders reach the same conclusion; iterate until acceptable
➡ Where next? Now we run a proper, controlled usability study step by step.

lessons.title: Laboratory Studies
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersA laboratory study is a controlled usability test. A clear process keeps it fair and useful.
🧠 Memory hookSix steps: Plan · Recruit · Prepare · Run · Analyse · Recommend.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Why "laboratory"?Step 1: PlanStep 2: RecruitStep 3: Prepare materialsStep 4: Run the studyStep 5: Analyse, and Step 6: RecommendAI in usability testing
⚡ At a glance — the six steps
1 Plan→2 Recruit→3 Prepare→4 Run (pilot first)→5 Analyse→6 Recommend
↺ 5–8 users → major problems · 10–12 → rarer ones · 15+ → statistics.
📛 Exact names — know these word for word: where laboratory studies sit
NameWhat it doesTell it apart
Laboratory studiesA usability study in a controlled environment; you control variablesPrecise and repeatable, but may not show natural behaviour
Field studiesObserve users in their real settingRealistic, but little control
ExperimentA study with two or more conditions to test a hypothesisCan be run in a lab, but is defined by its comparison structure

Laboratory studies are one of the four evaluation strategies in §13.2.

This lecture expands the "laboratory studies" row of §13.2's comparison table into a full six-step process.

15.1Why "laboratory"?

A controlled environment lets you control variables for precise, repeatable testing — the defining trade-off (cross-reference §13.2) is higher precision/control at the cost of lower ecological validity (realism) compared to field studies.

flowchart LR
    S1["1. Plan<br/>(goals, method, participants,<br/>environment, data)"] --> S2["2. Recruit"]
    S2 --> S3["3. Prepare<br/>(materials for experimenters<br/>& participants; system setup)"]
    S3 --> S4["4. Run<br/>(pilot, then real sessions)"]
    S4 --> S5["5. Analyse"]
    S5 --> S6["6. Recommend"]

Caption: the six-step laboratory-study pipeline. Step 1 (Plan) itself has five sub-decisions (goals, method, participants, environment, data), detailed below — getting these wrong is the single biggest risk to a laboratory study, since every later step depends on them.

Laboratory study vs. field study

Laboratory studies (usability studies) prioritise control over variables for reliable, repeatable results; disadvantage: may not capture natural behaviour. Controlled environments let you isolate interface elements, measure precise behaviours, collect standardised data, cut distractions and keep conditions consistent.

Controllable variables include which data are collected (time, eye tracking, clicks…). Lab choice: if running a laboratory study, prepare a quiet office with no interruptions Balance control with authenticity — realism elements improve ecological validity.

15.2Step 1: Plan

Goals — should scale with your design stage:

Stage Goal style Example How to measure it
Early Exploratory "Users should be able to do task1 without guidance." Observe signs of confusion; track deviation from the expected navigation path
Early Exploratory "Users should find function1 useful." Analyse user comments; or a simple closed-ended agree/disagree question
Later Specific "Users should be able to do task1 in 5 seconds." A clear, directly measurable time metric
Later Specific "100% of users should find function1 useful." A counted Likert-scale response
Later Specific (harder to measure) "Users should find the design pleasing (average rating 5/7)." A subjective rating scale — harder to interpret than a hard behavioural metric
Later Specific (hardest to measure) "95% of users should interpret UI terminology without errors." Count comments/instances where users got lost specifically due to wording — genuinely difficult to isolate

Rule of thumb: if you have a specific goal, you should be able to explain where the target number came from — an arbitrary number (why 5 seconds and not 8?) isn't a real success criterion.

Method — selecting tasks: Choose realistic, representative tasks that align with your goals and are made as concrete as possible, to avoid uncontrolled variation between participants (this directly parallels the "context/key/validation scenario" specificity progression from §3.4).

Progression from vague to good: (bad) "Try out the UI" → (better) "Search for a movie" → (good) "Search for 'Spider Man 3'." Additional cautions: don't train participants unless training would be normal in real use Don't choose tasks that are secretly biased in favour of your own system

Avoid over-fragmenting a task into disconnected sub-steps — let participants choose their own workflow, and allow later tasks to build naturally on earlier results.

Method — defining the script/procedure: decide the overall event sequence (briefing → consent → training → tasks → questionnaires → debrief) and the task order — natural order (mirrors real-world usage), simple-to-complex (minimises the learning curve confounding later results), or counterbalanced (systematically varying the order across participants to cancel out order effects).

Participants: more participants cost more time/money but catch more issues; fewer participants risk missing important problems, though common/frequent bugs need fewer participants to surface. Use representative sampling, not convenience sampling (cross-reference §2.2), and specifically consider whether some issues will only surface with specialised user groups (expert users, domain specialists, users with disabilities).

Ethical considerations (explicit checklist): Informed consent, clearly communicating that participation is voluntary; avoid any pressure to participate; participants may withdraw at any time; anonymise all collected data using participant IDs (e.g. P01, P02) rather than names. A standard framing line to use with participants: *"We are testing the interface.

This is not a test of your abilities."* — this reduces performance anxiety and encourages honest struggle/feedback rather than face-saving behaviour.

Environment: try to match where and when the real system will actually be used; when a fully realistic environment isn't achievable, you can simulate relevant real-world conditions (ambient noise, distractions, even temperature/humidity where relevant).

Data: decide what qualitative and quantitative data you'll collect, using the same qualitative/quantitative taxonomy from §14.1 (critical incidents, think-aloud data, comments vs. time-on-task, error counts, click counts).

The "Thinking Aloud" method (a specific data-collection technique used during Step 4, introduced here): ask participants to continuously verbalise what they're thinking while performing a task — not just what they're doing, but what they're trying to do, questions that arise, and things they're reading — prompting them to keep talking ("tell me what you're thinking") while avoiding leading, specific questions.

Record it (audio/video or detailed notes) so you can later reconstruct exactly what they were doing when they said each thing.

Problems with thinking aloud: It inflates task-completion times, since verbalising while acting is itself extra cognitive work. A common alternative: record video of the task with no verbal interruption, then afterward review the video with the participant and have them think-aloud retrospectively about what they were doing/thinking at each moment.

A second caution: thinking-aloud data isn't always accurate — people often answer even when they have no real factual basis for the answer (i.e. they may confabulate a plausible-sounding reason after the fact rather than reporting a genuine real-time thought).

Three worked "Plan" examples given directly in the slides, useful as templates:

Aspect Example 1 (no goal, early exploratory) Example 2 (specific goal, guided) Example 3 (specific goal, unguided/realistic)
Goal None Users should do task1 in 5 seconds Users should do task1 in 5 seconds
Method Walk through the design with the same scenarios used for the design Self-guided, low-level (broken-down) steps Self-guided, high-level tasks (not broken down)
Participants 3 representative users ~6 representative users >20 representative users
Environment Conference room Conference room Where the system would normally be used
Data Comments, subjective ratings Comments, ratings, critical incidents & navigation paths Comments, ratings, critical incidents, navigation paths, and task completion times

Note the progression: as the goal becomes more specific and the setting becomes more realistic, both the required participant count and the data collected become richer and more quantitative.

Goals: early vs. later studies

  • Early (non-specific): look for signs users are lost, track path deviations from the expected path, analyse comments during/after tasks, use rating scales (5-point Likert) for usefulness.
  • Mistakes can mean an unclear conceptual model or navigation trouble — find the cause.
  • Later goals become specific and measurable (e.g. a precise task time
  • "users rate the design as pleasing, average ≥5/7"). Verification = meets its specification (building the thing right
  • Objective if specs are precise)
  • Validation = meets what is wanted (the right system
  • Subjective, hard to determine). Claims are best when specific. Subjective ratings are hard to measure accurately.

Task selection

Realistic tasks users would actually do Concrete (reduces variability) Avoid tasks biased toward your system don't fragment tasks ("don't break into steps for them") — let users discover steps, build complex tasks progressively

Later tasks may use earlier results. Procedure: briefing → natural workflow sequence → simple-to-complex → counterbalanced order (rotate to reduce learning/ordering effects — often hard in practice) Write a script for consistency across sessions.

Ethics

Informed consent must be written, before the study, covering what they'll do, right to stop any time, potential risks/discomfort. Privacy: participant numbers (P01) not names, secure storage of recordings/notes, follow data-protection rules; no video without permission.

Tests can distress people — some take poor performance personally ("sometimes participants leave in tears") — so you have a responsibility to alleviate this. "We're testing the design, not you" — essential for a comfortable environment

Keep stressing so users feel like collaborators helping find usability bugs.

Data to collect

Qualitative: "further thoughts" comments, opinions/preferences, critical incidents, think-aloud protocols. Quantitative: responses to scaled questions, ratings, error counts and types.

Think-aloud — details

Reveals cognitive aspects invisible to observation: elements they notice, reasons for decisions.

Use neutral prompts ("What are you thinking now?"), avoid specific/biasing questions, record audio/video, take notes matched to interface elements. Limitations: tasks take 25–100% longer, so time data is distorted (normalise or use separate participants)

Alternative = retrospective think-aloud (record silently, review afterwards) Users may rationalise post-hoc, some processes are hard to verbalise, social-desirability bias.

Three planning examples

Early design: ~6 representative users, conference room, comments + subjective ratings of difficulty/satisfaction. Better design: more structured, medium group, comments + some quantitative. Even better: larger group, more realistic setting, task times and error rates. What to plan: participants, environment, apparatus.

Planning exercise

one specific, measurable goal (e.g. "complete task X in under 5 seconds"), one concrete task tied to it, location/conditions, how to ensure realism, specific qualitative and quantitative measures. copy an existing website's UI in Figma (each member copies one page, 25 min; then add transitions) to learn Figma quickly.

🧩 Pause & recall — What is the correct order of the six laboratory-study steps?
Answer: Plan, Recruit, Prepare, Run, Analyse, Recommend
Plan → Recruit → Prepare → Run → Analyse → Recommend.
15.3Step 2: Recruit

Recruiting channels, ranked roughly from most-convenient/least-representative to more-representative: personal contacts ("call your friends") → email lists (current users, professional groups — more representative) → recruiting from the product's own website → a professional participant panel (e.g. Dynata). Considerations: screening questionnaires (to confirm participants actually match your target profile) and incentives.

Participants — how many

5–8: major, frequent problems; 10–12: less common issues; 15+: quantitative measurement with statistical significance. Match demographics and expertise Include special users (experts, domain experts, people with disabilities) because some problems appear only for them

Fewer participants may miss important problems, though common bugs need fewer. Recruiting channels: personal networks (quick, biased), professional organisations (domain expertise), product website, research panels (pre-screened E.g. Research Now), screening questionnaires

Incentives: money/knick-knacks, appeal to altruism, or required participation (employees, students in a class).

15.4Step 3: Prepare materials
For Materials
Experimenters Script; observation forms
Participants Informed consent form; training materials (if any); task instructions; pre-test/post-test questionnaires (online or hardcopy)
System The deployed system itself (use real content where possible); a data-collection setup — automated time logging, video/audio recorders, screen capture

The six steps (overview)

Plan (goals, methods, participants, environment, data strategy) → Recruit → Prepare (materials, systems, observation protocols) → Run (follow script) → Analyse → Recommend. Each step builds on the last. In practice most tests are lighter/faster than the full process: a few hours of testing every month counts — "if it involves observing real people using your design, it's usability testing" (A List Apart).

Materials checklist & roles

Script, observation forms, deployed system with realistic content, recording/screen capture/analytics, consent forms (+ pen), training materials (give the training real users would get

Usually brief or none), written task instructions (guarantees consistent delivery → internal validity), pre/post questionnaires (e.g. SUS), note-taking forms, folders per participant; templates at usability.gov.

Computer set up with the monitor, resolution and connection speed stated in the plan. Roles: facilitator, note-taker, camera operator, technical support (combine in small studies).

Pilot run before real participants — in a pilot you may help participants; in the main study do not interfere.

15.5Step 4: Run the study

Roles: facilitator, note-taker(s), camera/videographer (requires separate consent), tech support. Pilot study first: a dry run before the real study, ideally run twice — first with colleagues, then with a real (but non-counted) participant — to catch problems with the materials or setup before they cost you real data.

Worked run-script example (a template you can reuse):

  1. Greet & brief: introduce everyone, explain the purpose, explicitly state "This is not a test of your abilities" and "you can stop at any time," obtain signed consent, administer the pre-test/demographics questionnaire, explain thinking-aloud (with a short demo/practice run if that data will be collected), and optionally train the participant (mirroring real-world training conditions — kept brief or omitted if that matches real use).
  2. For each task: the participant works on the scenario while thinking aloud; note-takers record navigation pathways (deviations from the expected path), the outcome (success / failure / success-with-assistance), and critical incidents (points where things went smoothly or roughly). If the participant asks a question, answer only if doing so won't give away exactly what you're trying to learn — otherwise, explain (briefly) why you won't help right now. If a participant gets stuck, decide in advance whether/when to intervene, and document every intervention (when and how) since an assisted completion isn't equivalent to an unassisted one in your later analysis.
  3. Debrief: administer post-test questions, ask "how did it go?", ask for comments on specific features/critical incidents (optionally reviewing the video together), thank the participant, and provide the agreed incentive.

Running the session

  • Intro: introduce the team, welcome, explain roles and how feedback is used, review consent.
  • The facilitator welcomes, seats participant, states the session goal, asks profile questions, gets the release form, explains/demonstrates think-aloud, says where to start. During tasks: present the scenario
  • Deflect help requests with "What would you do normally?"
  • Note when help was requested
  • decide intervention criteria in advance
  • Document any assistance and points of frustration
  • Use standardised recording forms. Critical incidents are moments particularly smooth or bumpy — discuss with the team and later with participants (remind them
  • Ask what they were thinking). Debrief: open-ended ("How did the experience feel overall?", "What worked well / was challenging?"), ask about specific confusion, show video/screens (people forget what they did), mention alternatives they didn't see, thank, explain how input will be used, give the agreed incentive.
15.6Step 5: Analyse, and Step 6: Recommend

Analyse: consolidate all raw data into one place, summarise the findings in a report (with references back to the raw data for traceability), and weigh the evidence against your original plan — did the UI work the way you expected? Did participants follow the pathways you expected? Was anything missing?

Recommend: revisit your design decisions in light of the findings; rate each usability issue by both severity and ease of fixing; prioritise fixing the most severe problems and the "easy wins" first — mirroring the severity-rating logic from heuristic evaluation (§12.4), now applied to real-user findings instead of expert-identified violations.

Analyse & recommend

Organise notes/recordings/metrics; recurring problems; task success/failure; compare actual vs. expected pathways ("Did participants use pathways you expected?"); rate severity (critical → minor) and frequency; fix severe problems first and include quick wins. Always do at least this much after every test — you recall surprisingly little without notes.

15.7AI in usability testing

AI moderators can follow a script, ask follow-up questions, and probe tasks — running many sessions concurrently without the scheduling constraints of human moderators. Automated analysis can extract themes across hundreds of interviews and detect sentiment/emotion in responses.

Cited trend figures (2025–2026): 80% of UX researchers now use AI tools (up 24% year-on-year), and a 60–80% reduction in qualitative-analysis time.

As with every other AI-augmentation topic in this course, human judgement remains essential for interpreting context — an AI-run session scales the mechanics of testing, not the interpretation of what the results mean.

⚡ Quick examples
The six steps
PointPlan → Recruit → Prepare → Run → Analyse → Recommend.
ExamplePlan goals and tasks, recruit 8 users, prepare scripts, run a pilot, analyse, then recommend fixes.
ExplanationEach step builds on the last; skipping planning ruins everything after.
Goals and tasks
PointEarly goals are exploratory; later ones specific and measurable. Tasks should be realistic.
ExampleEarly: 'users can book without help'. Later: 'complete in <5 s'. Task: 'update your phone number', not 'click Settings then Profile'.
ExplanationDon't fragment tasks into steps — let users discover them.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Plan → Recruit → Prepare → Run → Analyse → Recommend.
  • Early goals are exploratory; later ones specific and measurable. Tasks should be realistic.
  • 5–8 users find major problems; 10–12 rarer ones; 15+ for statistics.
  • Informed consent, right to stop, privacy; 'we test the design, not you'.
  • Use neutral prompts; decide intervention criteria in advance; pilot first.
  • Rate severity and frequency; fix severe and quick-win issues first.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Thinking Aloud methodtap to flip
Participant verbalises thoughts while performing a task
Pilot studytap to flip
Dry run of a study before running it with real counted participants
Think-aloud coststap to flip
Tasks take 25–100% longer; use retrospective review for timing
Participant numberstap to flip
5–8 major problems, 10–12 rarer ones, 15+ for statistics
➡ Where next? Good tests need good tools — and the tools you pick shape what you can build.

lessons.title: UI Tools
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersTools and standards speed you up, but each one has strengths and limits.
🧠 Memory hookLow threshold, high ceiling. Easy to start with, powerful enough to finish with.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Standards: why they matter, and the innovation trade-offTypes of UI toolsWhy (and when) to use UI toolsThreshold and ceilingAI trend: Generative UI (tooling angle)
⚡ At a glance — tool trade-offs
Tool typeWhat it isTrade-off
Toolkit / SDKMostly a library of componentsFlexible, more work
FrameworkLibrary + architectureFaster, harder to combine
UI builder / IDEWYSIWYG + code environmentEasy start, can limit non-standard widgets
Low threshold, low ceiling→⟷→High threshold, high ceiling
16.1Standards: why they matter, and the innovation trade-off

A standard fixes one part of a design so everyone can build on it. Thread standard example: the Unified Thread Standard (UTS) makes screws and bolts from different manufacturers interchangeable, so nobody rebuilds fasteners from scratch. Before 1864 each manufacturer made its own threads, until William Sellers began the first successful fight to standardise them.

📍 CASE FILE

William Sellers and the screw thread (1864)

The setting

Before 1864 each manufacturer made its own screw threads, so bolts from different shops were not interchangeable.

What happened

William Sellers began the first successful fight to standardise the screw thread (‘On a Uniform System of Screw Threads’). Today there are nearly 800,000 standards.

The lesson

Standards let designers focus on innovation rather than reinventing basics, just as standard UI patterns let users reuse what they know.

Standards inhibit innovation in one area and enable it in another. With the thread fixed, manufacturers innovate around it (materials, drive types, coatings). UI standards work the same way: a fixed basic interaction pattern, such as the layout of every search engine, lets designers spend their innovation elsewhere, and lets users reuse mental models they already have.

Benefits of standards (one list, learn these six):

  • Efficiency: streamlined processes save time and cost.
  • Compatibility: interoperable parts give wider market access.
  • Competitive pricing: more suppliers keep standardised parts cheap.
  • Compliance: simpler regulation, and compliance builds customer confidence.
  • Benchmarking for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
  • Consumer protection: safety, durability and fair markets.
16.2Types of UI tools
Type Description
Toolkits (SDKs) Mostly a library of components; easily combined with other libraries; examples: Google Web Toolkit (GWT), Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK), Java Development Kit (JDK), Android Studio & SDK tools, SQLite, DirectX
Frameworks Libraries designed to work together as a coherent architecture; can handle most common UI issues out of the box; hard to combine multiple frameworks at once; examples: .NET, Spring, the Android Application Framework, frontend frameworks (React, Angular), backend frameworks (Django, Rails, jQuery), mobile frameworks (Flutter, React Native, Cordova)
IDEs (Integrated Development Environments) Integrate toolkits/frameworks together and often include UI Builders (WYSIWYG editors for the underlying libraries/frameworks) — with powerful UI builders (Microsoft Visual Studio, Atom, IntelliJ IDEA, NetBeans, Eclipse) or more primitive ones (Adobe Dreamweaver, Arduino IDE, Apple Xcode)

Platform interface guidelines exemplify how standards get expressed concretely for a specific device family:

  • iOS Human Interface Guidelines: address display characteristics (medium-sized, high-resolution), ergonomics (one/two-handed use, portrait/landscape switching), inputs (multi-touch gestures, onscreen keyboards, voice, location/accelerometer/gyroscope sensing), typical app-interaction patterns (a minute or two checking updates vs. an hour or more of media/browsing), and system-level features (Widgets, Home Screen, Spotlight, Shortcuts, Activity views). Following such a guideline lets independent apps (e.g. Spotify, Twitter, Airbnb) offer a consistent baseline user experience while still customising within it — consistency with customisation.
  • Android Interface Guidelines: based on Google's Material Design principles, covering icon design/templates (launcher, menu, action, status bar, tab icons), widget design/templates, and tooling (Android Jetpack Compose, Android Studio IDE, Android NDK).

Spectrum, not boxes

toolkits and frameworks are ends of a spectrum. A toolkit/SDK is mostly library; a framework adds architecture and is harder to combine; UI builders (WYSIWYG) are often bundled in IDEs.

Platform ecosystems

Apple: Xcode IDE, Swift, TestFlight (beta testing), governed by the Human Interface Guidelines. Android: Material Design, Jetpack Compose, Android Studio IDE, NDK.

🧩 Pause & recall — UI standards both inhibit and enable innovation. How?
Answer: They fix one dimension (inhibit there) so effort goes elsewhere (enable there)
Like the screw-thread standard: lock the fastener, innovate around it.
16.3Why (and when) to use UI tools

Why use UI tools? A tool is the "path of least resistance" for developers, and it makes interfaces more predictable for users.

Benefit What it means
Consistency Same tool, same behaviour across apps, enforced automatically, so users can predict it
Code reuse UI code is about 50% of an app, so reusing it saves a lot of work
Faster iteration Changes are easier, and WYSIWYG prototypes exist before any application code
Wider participation Non-programmers (domain specialists, users, stakeholders) can join the design
Lower maintenance Less code, UI separated from application logic, complexity hidden, higher reliability
Easier porting Device-specific quirks stay inside the tool

But UI tools can discourage change.

  • Non-standard widgets are harder: you must build or buy them (e.g. speech or sketching input, multi-user and multi-device apps).
  • Hard to fix problems inside the tool: developers rely on its stability, and a fix can break workarounds others depend on.
  • Tools suit particular domains and stages: word processors, CAD, games and ATMs each have their own UI style, and brainstorming, low-fidelity prototyping, high-fidelity prototyping, development, testing and deployment each need different tools.

Choosing a prototyping tool, ask three questions

does it support the intended UX? how easily can you iterate? does it allow user testing?

16.4Threshold and ceiling

Threshold: how hard the tool is to learn or start using. Ceiling: how much it can ultimately do. Making a web page: MS Word has a low threshold and a low ceiling; HTML sits in the middle; JavaScript has the highest threshold and the highest ceiling.

📍 CASE FILE

Word, HTML and JavaScript: threshold vs. ceiling

The setting

Three ways to make a web page.

What happened

MS Word has a low threshold (easy to start) but a low ceiling; raw HTML has a higher threshold and ceiling; JavaScript has the highest threshold and the highest ceiling.

The lesson

Threshold is how hard a tool is to start; ceiling is how much it can ultimately do. The best tools have a low threshold and a high ceiling.

flowchart LR
    A[MS Word<br/>Low threshold, Low ceiling] --> B[HTML<br/>Medium threshold, Medium ceiling] --> C[JavaScript<br/>High threshold, High ceiling]

Caption: threshold and ceiling usually rise together. That is the trade-off to weigh when choosing a tool for a task and skill level.

16.5AI trend: Generative UI (tooling angle)

Generative UI lets AI dynamically create UI components at runtime, replacing static mockups with adaptive layouts. Cited impact: 40–60% faster feature shipping (citing Figma Make). Framed structurally: this lowers the threshold while raising the ceiling — i.e. it breaks the usual threshold/ceiling trade-off from §16.4, making a tool simultaneously easier to start with and more capable, rather than forcing a choice between the two. Key frameworks named: Vercel AI SDK, CopilotKit, Tambo.

📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Epic vs. Apple (August 2022)

The setting

Fortnite's maker Epic offered a direct payment option to avoid the App Store's 30% fee.

What happened

The episode shows that the platform owner sets the rules (fees, payment methods) for everyone building on the platform.

The lesson

UI tools and platforms come with governance: the owner's control shapes what you can build.

⚡ Quick examples
Toolkit vs. framework
PointToolkits are mostly libraries; frameworks add architecture; IDEs include UI builders.
ExamplejQuery as toolkit; a full web framework imposes structure.
ExplanationPick based on how much structure you want.
Threshold and ceiling
PointThreshold = ease of starting; ceiling = what you can ultimately build.
ExampleWord: low threshold, low ceiling; hand-coded HTML/JS: high threshold, high ceiling.
ExplanationChoose by project stage: fast demo → low threshold.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Standards enable innovation elsewhere while limiting it where they apply.
  • Toolkits are mostly libraries; frameworks add architecture; IDEs include UI builders.
  • Reuse, consistency, faster iteration; but non-standard widgets are harder and tools can lock you in.
  • Threshold = ease of starting; ceiling = what you can ultimately build.
  • Apple: Xcode/Swift/HIG/TestFlight. Android: Material Design/Jetpack Compose.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Toolkit / Framework / IDEtap to flip
Component library / architecture-level library set / integrated tool with builders
Threshold / Ceilingtap to flip
Ease of starting with a tool / its maximum ultimate capability
Threshold / ceilingtap to flip
Ease of learning vs. attainable sophistication of a tool
➡ Where next? With a live product you can test at massive scale — web experiments.

lessons.title: Web Experiments
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersWhen you have thousands of users, let data decide between designs.
🧠 Memory hookOne change · random split · measure. That's A/B testing.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Where this sits among evaluation methodsWhy A/B test instead of trusting a "HiPPO"?A/B testing mechanicsGetting valuable insights: conversion and metricsTest populations: assignment and sample sizeToolsDesigning a good web experimentA/B testing vs. multivariate testingAI-powered A/B testing
⚡ At a glance — an A/B test
Hypothesis→Randomly split users→Control (A) vs Treatment (B)→Measure conversion→Ramp up / auto-abort→Decide with data, not HiPPO
📛 Exact names — know these word for word: where web experiments sit
NameWhat it doesTell it apart
A/B testingCompares exactly two whole designs, Control (A) vs Treatment (B)The simplest randomised controlled experiment
Multivariate testingTests every combination of several design variables at onceNeeds significantly more traffic than A/B testing
Laboratory studiesObserve a few users in a controlled settingSmall samples, richer observation, complementary to A/B testing

A/B tests are an experiment run online. They are not one of the four evaluation strategies by themselves: Surveys list a “web experiment”, and Chapter 18 defines the experiment.

17.1Where this sits among evaluation methods

A spectrum of evaluation methods, arranged along two axes — obtrusive vs. unobtrusive to the user, and empirical vs. theoretical: inspection and model/simulation sit toward the theoretical end

Survey/interview, field study/observation, laboratory study, and (web) analytics span the empirical, more-to-less obtrusive range, with web analytics being the least obtrusive empirical method (it observes real behaviour without the user ever knowing they're being studied). This lecture focuses on A/B testing, an unobtrusive-to-moderately-obtrusive, strongly empirical method, distinct from — but complementary to — the laboratory studies of §15.

17.2Why A/B test instead of trusting a "HiPPO"?

HiPPO = Highest Paid Person's Opinion — a decision made by authority/seniority rather than by data. The core course argument, stated repeatedly across worked cases: data trumps intuition, and small changes can have big impact.

Worked cases (real, named companies/products):

📍 CASE FILE

Expedia and the “Company” field

The setting

Expedia's booking form had an optional field asking for a company name.

What happened

Customers often typed their bank's name there, which then failed address verification. After testing, removing the field increased profit by about $12 million.

The lesson

Small changes can have a big impact, and data beats intuition: a field most people did not need was costing real money.

More from the lecture
  • Expedia.com: a "Company" field on a form was removed after testing; removing it increased profit by $12M, because the field was an unnecessary friction point most users didn't need but every user had to consider.
  • Expedia — $12M field: customers clicking "Buy Now" failed to complete purchases; analytics found the optional "Company" field under Name was filled with the bank's name, then the bank's address was entered and failed card address verification. Deleting the field produced an overnight step change worth ~$12M profit a year; Expedia says it found "50 or 60" such issues via analytics.
📍 CASE FILE

Greg Linden and Amazon's cart recommendations

The setting

Amazon engineer Greg Linden had built personalised recommendations shown when an item is added to the cart.

What happened

A senior vice-president (the ‘HiPPO’, highest-paid person's opinion) ordered the project stopped, fearing it would distract from checkout. Linden ran a simple experiment anyway and it was wildly successful.

The lesson

Measured customer data beat a senior executive's intuition, which is the case for A/B testing.

More from the lecture
  • Amazon shopping-cart recommendations: engineer Greg Linden built personalised, cart-content-based recommendations shown when adding an item — good for prompting impulse purchases (pro: cross-sells more items and increases basket size; con: a legitimate risk of distracting from checkout and reducing conversion). A senior VP (the HiPPO in this story) ordered the project stopped, but Linden ran a simple experiment anyway — it was wildly successful, directly demonstrating that measured customer data beat the senior executive's intuition.
  • Amazon cart recommendations (Greg Linden): a senior VP told him to stop (it would distract from checkout); he ran a simple experiment anyway; sales rose massively and the feature shipped — customer data beats executive opinion.
📍 CASE FILE

Checkout A vs. Checkout B (the coupon field)

The setting

A redesigned checkout page (B) looked nicer than the original (A).

What happened

B actually lost about 90% of revenue. When B was tested again without one added feature, a coupon-code field, it increased revenue by 6.5% over A.

The lesson

Do not bundle several changes into one test: one confound can flip a good redesign into a disaster, and you cannot tell which change caused which effect.

More from the lecture
  • A checkout-page redesign ("Checkout A" vs. "Checkout B"): "upgrading" A to the visually nicer B actually lost 90% of revenue; when B was tested again without one specific added feature (a coupon-code field), it instead increased revenue by 6.5%. Lesson: avoid bundling multiple changes into one test — a single confound (the coupon-code field) can flip an otherwise-positive redesign into a catastrophic loss, and you can't tell which specific change caused which effect if you change several things at once.
  • Checkout "upgrade": moving from checkout A to B lost 90% of revenue; the culprit was the coupon-code field (users wondered if they were overpaying). Removing it from B raised conversion 6.5% over A. Lesson: avoid multiple simultaneous changes; behaviour beats intuition. Conversion rate = percentage of visits that include a purchase.

Design choices repeatedly shown to matter a lot (a checklist of things worth testing rather than guessing about): the position and colour of the primary call-to-action; testimonial placement; whether links are text- or image-based; the amount of whitespace; the position/prominence of the main heading; the number of columns; the number of visual elements competing for attention; and even the age/sex/appearance of a person shown in a photo.

📍 CASE FILE

Facebook Japan and Uber India: wording and context

The setting

Companies adapted wording and options to local context and measured the result.

What happened

Facebook Japan used ‘announcement’ rather than the rude-sounding ‘invite’; Instagram-style ‘Promote’ became ‘Boost Post’ and raised engagement; Uber India added a ‘become a driver’ button and a cash payment option (card use was limited), which fuelled rapid growth.

The lesson

Test wording and context, and track a North Star metric (such as monthly active riders) that shows whether the change moved what matters.

More from the lecture
  • Wording and context: Facebook Japan ("announcement" rather than the rude "invite"); Instagram-style "Promote" → "Boost Post" raised engagement; Uber India: "become a driver" button and a cash payment option (limited card use) → exponential growth. Metrics: needle-mover, North Star metric (e.g. Facebook MAU; Uber monthly active riders, weekly trips). Framing tracking as personalisation increases opt-in; negative framing increases opt-outs.
🧩 Pause & recall — HiPPO stands for:
Answer: Highest Paid Person's Opinion
A/B testing replaces opinion with data.
17.3A/B testing mechanics

Definition (reproduced from source): "Evaluate design alternatives via randomised controlled experiments. The simplest form is A/B testing: compare two versions to measure which performs better."

flowchart TD
    P["100% Sample Users"] --> C["50% Users →<br/>Control Condition<br/>(Existing system)"]
    P --> T["50% Users →<br/>Treatment Condition<br/>(Alternative design)"]
    C --> A[User interactions analysed & compared]
    T --> A
    A --> D[Results inform design decisions]

Caption: the basic A/B testing flow — a single user population is randomly split between the existing system (control) and an alternative (treatment); comparing their interactions produces a data-driven design decision, rather than relying on a HiPPO's opinion. The same logic underlies vaccine efficacy trials (comparing a treated group against a control/placebo group), which the slides cite as a familiar, high-stakes real-world analogy for the same controlled-comparison structure.

17.4Getting valuable insights: conversion and metrics

Conversion rate: the percentage of users who take a desired action (e.g. the fraction of visitors who purchase on an e-commerce site), or more generally, task completion rate.

Conversion type Description
Macro conversion The primary success metric — usually the ultimate goal, and relatively infrequent (e.g. completing a purchase)
Micro conversion Frequent smaller actions that lead toward the macro conversion (e.g. adding an item to cart, viewing a product page)

Additional useful behavioural data: total time for one full transaction, or time spent on each individual page — and, for a conversion-rate exercise: did the user complete the purchase, and if not, at what step did they drop off; which interaction step took the longest?

Worked example — three offer-page versions

A = original; B = minor copy changes; C = one-column → two-column layout to bring more content on-screen. C did much worse: two columns use a "menu" pattern (two possible things to do) whereas the page needs a "funnel" pattern guiding the customer through purchase, which A and B do via a top call-to-action. Design choices (e.g. linked elements as text vs. image) affect conversion.

Metrics

Task completion, time metrics; macro conversions (main success, infrequent) vs. micro conversions (smaller, frequent actions leading to macro, e.g. add to wishlist). Typical e-commerce conversion ≈ 3%, but the other 97% of visits still carry information (NN/g).

Track the whole funnel (each step a drop-off point) and time at each stage; faster interaction can raise conversion even if steps are unchanged.

Question: what behavioural data would Amazon value? Web UX analytics tracks traffic: session duration, page-view time, areas of focus (Preece p.264, 514).

17.5Test populations: assignment and sample size
  • Aim for a 50%-50% split between treatment and control, assigning users to groups at random, using methods that guarantee a uniform distribution.
  • Determine minimum sample size needed to reliably detect an effect: bigger true differences are easier to detect with fewer participants (Cohen's d effect size, e.g. d=0.2 needs roughly 193 users at power=0.5, while d=0.8 needs only around 13 users at the same power) — i.e. subtle effects require dramatically more participants to detect reliably than large, obvious effects.

Ramp-up and auto-abort — risk management for live experiments: Start an experiment at a very small treatment percentage (e.g. 0.1% treatment / 99.9% control), run a quick analysis to catch any major problems early, then ramp up gradually (e.g. 99.9%:0.1% → 99.5%:0.5% → 90%:10% → 50%:50%).

Auto-abort the experiment immediately if a significant negative change is detected, before it can do wide-scale damage. This is a direct, practical mitigation for exactly the Expedia/checkout-page kind of catastrophic-regression risk shown in §17.2.

Experiment design vocabulary

  • Process: start with 100% of sample users → randomly divide into equal groups → track interactions on both versions.
  • Benefits: removes confirmation bias, statistical confidence, reveals unexpected behaviours, enables iterative optimisation. Between-subjects: a participant is in treatment or control, never both
  • Each extra treatment needs a new group
  • Avoids carryover effects of within-subjects designs. Control (baseline; "blue pill", status quo
  • Also "placebo") vs. treatment (the change; "red pill"
  • Should vary from control in limited ways). Principles: randomisation and replication (large enough sample)
  • blocking (group by a relevant characteristic, then randomise within blocks → avoid confounds)
  • blinding and placebos to avoid psychological effects. Origin: randomised controlled trials — e.g. vaccine efficacy compares infection rates between placebo and vaccine groups. Choose a randomisation method giving uniform distribution
  • Do a simple analysis early to catch egregious problems.

Sample size and safe roll-out

Detect small effects (0.2 effect size) needs ~193 users per group for power 0.5; big differences need fewer.

Sample size can come from experience, target variance (precision/CI), target power, or confidence level (higher confidence → larger n). Ramp-up: start with ~0.1% in treatment (e.g. 0.1% → 0.5% → 2.5% → 10% → 50%), analyse at each step, and configure auto-abort if significant negative change appears

Small populations catch errors quickly (square factor in the power formula).

17.6Tools
Tool Notes
SMU Qualtrics (recommended) Web-survey delivery; supports A/B testing within surveys via a Randomiser element in the survey flow; free for SMU students; limited ways to measure time
Loop11 (recommended) Task-based testing on live web apps; measures task completion rate, time per task, success/fail analysis, first-click tracking, detailed participant path analysis, page views per task, and video/audio/screen recording; 14-day free trial, academic licence available
Maze Gaining popularity for ease of use; imports Adobe XD/Figma/InVision/Marvel prototypes directly for wireframe and usability testing; supports A/B testing
UserZoom Web survey and usability testing for UX researchers/designers/PMs/marketers; supports think-aloud video, surveys, live intercept, click tests
Web Analytics (Google Analytics, Adobe Analytics, Open Web Analytics) Tracks real user traffic patterns — time on page, navigation source, ad exposure, etc. — without an explicit A/B split

Tools

Qualtrics — structured surveys, logic branches, limited time measurement; best for preference/qualitative feedback. A/B in Qualtrics: add blocks/conditions → place under the Randomiser (with "Evenly Present Elements") so each respondent sees one version only.

Loop11 — remote usability testing on real sites; tracks paths, success/fail pages, page-view counts, time; more behavioural than surveys; SMU enterprise access. Maze — integrates Figma/Adobe XD to test early prototypes (web surveys, wireframe testing).

UserZoom — enterprise research for UX researchers, designers, PMs, marketers (think-aloud video, survey, live intercept, click test; academy resources). Google Analytics — most widely used for live-site behaviour.

17.7Designing a good web experiment

Practical guidance directly targeted at the course's own project: focus on one important part of the problem or the first breakdown — not the whole prototype (e.g. just one screen/view, or just the navigation style); avoid too many simultaneous independent changes between A and B (small changes can have big impact, but only if you can actually attribute the effect to one specific change); and pick two alternatives where it isn't already obvious which one is better, tested fairly with realistic tasks.

17.8A/B testing vs. multivariate testing

Both split live traffic across design variations. A/B testing compares exactly two whole designs. Multivariate testing tests every combination of several design variables at once (layout, copy, navigation, visual design), and can identify which specific change or combination had the greatest impact — but requires significantly more traffic, since all combinations of variants must both occur in the data and make sense together as coherent designs.

HiPPO and the case for testing

Why test instead of relying on the Highest Paid Person's Opinion: A/B testing removes subjective opinion — random assignment + behaviour measurement shows with statistical confidence which design better meets goals.

"An expert's credentials and opinions mean squat" next to live data. Purpose: compare two alternatives using predefined outcomes and estimate how the design change affects outcomes we care about

In a randomised experiment participants are assigned to conditions at random. A/B testing (split testing) also helps choose price points — especially valid for digital goods.

A/B vs. multivariate

A/B: two distinct designs (may differ in many ways — you won't know why one wins), clearer cause–effect, easier to implement/analyse. Multivariate: manipulates several variables simultaneously, can find interaction effects (blue button better in one header, worse in another) but needs significantly more traffic. Both measure which variation yields the highest conversion for set goals and divide live traffic.

17.9AI-powered A/B testing

Machine-learning-driven testing automates hypothesis generation, variant creation, and traffic allocation — testing hundreds of combinations simultaneously rather than a fixed two-variant test — and can steer live traffic toward winning variants in real time (adapting the UI per user segment, i.e. predictive personalisation).

Cited 2026 figures: an 18–34% conversion lift within 60 days, 47% faster design-iteration cycles, and (per McKinsey) 40% more revenue for the strongest personalisation adopters. Framed conclusion: "AI doesn't replace testing — it makes it continuous."

⚡ Quick examples
Safe roll-out
PointRamp-up: expose a tiny share first; auto-abort if harmful.
Example0.1% → 0.5% → 2.5% → 10% → 50%.
ExplanationProtects users and revenue while you learn.
A/B vs. multivariate
PointA/B compares whole designs; multivariate tests combinations and interactions.
ExampleButton colour × header image.
ExplanationMultivariate needs far more traffic.

  • Ramp-up: expose a tiny share first; auto-abort if harmful.

lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersAn experiment is only as good as its design. Poor design gives confident but wrong answers.
🧠 Memory hookIV = what you Vary. DV = what you get (Data). Protect internal and external validity.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
User study vs. experimentIndependent and dependent variablesValidity: internal and externalAssigning participants: between-subjects vs. within-subjectsAI-powered A/B testing (methodology angle)
⚡ At a glance — between vs within subjects
AspectBetweenWithin
Each participant seesOne conditionAll conditions
Participants neededMore (≈2×)Fewer
Ordering effectsNoneYes → counterbalance (Latin square for 3+)
Session lengthShorterLonger
Individual differencesCan confoundControlled
📛 Exact names — know these word for word: experiment vocabulary
NameWhat it isTell it apart
User study (observation study)Measures data from real usersDescriptive, with no comparison
ExperimentA user study with two or more conditions that tests a hypothesisGives the measurement a reference point
Independent variableWhat the experimenter manipulatesThe conditions
Dependent variableWhat is measuredThe outcome
Internal validityDid X really cause Y?About the study’s design and confounds
External validityDo results generalise to other people, designs and contexts?About generalisability
Between-subjectsEach participant sees one conditionNeeds more participants; no ordering effects
Within-subjectsEach participant sees all conditionsNeeds fewer participants; counterbalance the order

The experiment is a type of user study, not one of the four evaluation strategies in §13.2.

This lecture formalises the statistical/methodological vocabulary underlying the A/B testing introduced in §17.

18.1User study vs. experiment
Aspect User study (observation study) Experiment (e.g. A/B testing)
Participants Real users Real users
What it does Measures data (e.g. counts errors) Tests a specific hypothesis — e.g. "People make fewer errors with interface B than interface A."
Key difficulty Interpreting a raw measurement is hard on its own — "how few errors is few enough?" has no obvious answer An experiment is specifically a special type of user study that adds a comparison structure, giving the raw measurement a reference point
Value Descriptive A path to continuous, measurable improvement

Why "experiment"? Because it has two or more conditions, letting you directly compare measurements taken under each — a plain user study of one design in isolation cannot support that comparison.

Deliverables & planning template

One slide: screenshots of Designs A and B, chosen usability metric + justification, study design type. Experiment plan: Prediction (expected improvement and why), Task, Measures (two dependent variables and how recorded), Participants and procedure (within/between, assignment/order), Main risk (what could make the comparison unfair).

18.2Independent and dependent variables

Borrowing the math notation y = f(x) (y depends on x):

Aspect Independent variable Dependent variable
Definition The condition you control — not dependent on user actions The measure you collect — depends on user actions and the condition
Examples UI design choice (icons/labels/lexicon, position/colour of text blocks, layout/whitespace, toolbar location); which search algorithm is used Conversion rate, task completion time, error rate, accuracy, recall, emotional response

First step to verify a hypothesis ("x causes y"): manipulate the independent variable (x) and observe whether it produces a difference in the dependent variable (y). Worked example: Interface A (no instruction text) vs. Interface B (with instruction text) → average task completion times of 4.7 minutes vs. 2.5 minutes → this supports (does not, on its own, definitively prove) the hypothesis that instruction text reduces completion time.

Fuller worked A/B example (N=40, 20 per condition): Control A (no instruction) had 9/20 (45%) task completions; Treatment B (with instruction) had 19/20 (95%) completions — a large, visually obvious gap in completion rate that the experiment's design lets you attribute specifically to the instruction-text change.

🧩 Pause & recall — In y = f(x), x is the ___ variable.
Answer: Independent
x is manipulated; y is measured.
18.3Validity: internal and external
Type Goal What threatens it
Internal validity The measured difference is genuinely caused by the manipulated condition Confounding variables — things that change systematically alongside the independent variable, offering an alternative explanation for the result
External validity The results generalise to other situations beyond this specific study An unrepresentative sample (e.g. results from one specific student population may not generalise to the wider population)

Controlling confounding variables — three strategies:

Strategy How it works Trade-off
Hold constant Fix a variable so it's the same for every case (e.g. everyone gets the same task) Lowers generalisability, increases precision
Randomise Allow the variable to vary randomly across all cases (e.g. randomise participant age) Maintains generalisability, similar precision, may require more participants
Random within blocks Allow the variable to vary randomly, but within set constraints A compromise between the two above

Sampling gotcha, cross-referencing §2.2 and §15.2: A convenience sample — individuals easily accessible and matching the target profile just because they're nearby (friends, family, or a single accessible student population) — is more likely to end up over-represented in your sample, which is precisely why it's generally a bad basis for drawing conclusions about the wider population.

A simple random sample avoids this, though caution is still needed if non-response is high (people who don't respond may differ systematically from those who do).

Worked validity exercise (Tesla map UI):

  • Independent variable = two map UIs
  • Dependent variable = task completion time
  • Version A's task was "Orchard MRT to Bugis MRT," Version B's task was a much longer/more complex real-street-address route
  • Participants were taxi drivers, tested in a conference room; Version A was faster.
  • Conclusion drawn ("People are faster with Version A") is NOT well supported: this is internally invalid, because the task itself is a confounding variable — Version A's task was inherently simpler/shorter than Version B's, so the faster time can't be cleanly attributed to the UI design rather than the easier route.
  • It's also questionably externally valid: testing only taxi drivers (already route-planning experts) in an artificial conference-room setting may not generalise to ordinary drivers navigating their own trip in real driving conditions. This exercise is a direct, worked demonstration of why both internal and external validity must be checked before trusting an experiment's conclusion — a plausible-looking result can fail on either axis independently.

Internal validity — extra

The degree to which changes in X can appropriately be concluded to have caused changes in Y The major threat is confounding variables: testing different versions at different times of day, groups of different skill, differing environments, inconsistent task instructions.

Classic threats: history (e.g. UI changes), maturation, selection, mortality (people in one condition can't finish), testing, statistical regression, interaction with selection.

Study enough people so the result is unlikely chance. Worked scenario: 18 of the Design-B participants had prior task experience but only some in A → confound; randomise assignment to minimise confounds you can't control.

Controlling confounds — three strategies

Strategy Pros Cons Example
Hold constant Higher precision May reduce generalisability Identical tasks for all versions
Randomise Keeps generalisability May need larger samples Random assignment to conditions
Block / random with constraints Balances precision and generalisability More complex Random selection within demographic categories

Controlling a variable can raise internal but lower external validity; in IS211 feel free to control variables as long as they stay at levels seen reasonably often (e.g. a common task). Four key design decisions: Recruitment (who; relevant experience; how the sample differs), Control (task, instructions, device, conditions), Blocking (e.g. prior experience before assignment), plus assignment/ordering. Blocking → higher precision but may require more people.

External validity — extra

Synonymous with generalisability: can the causal relationship transfer to other similar designs and populations? E.g. results from computer-science students may not apply to older adults or children. No study "has" external validity by itself; there is a trade-off with internal validity.

Terminology: the textbook says "scope" for external validity, "validity" for internal validity, and "different participants" for between-subjects (Preece 13.6.2, 14.3). Judging a sample experiment: different tasks for A/B → confound (internal) Taxi drivers → fairly generalisable

Conference room → not very.

Sampling

Random sample: every individual has equal chance → unbiased but hard when non-response is high. Convenience sample (friends, colleagues, only SCIS students for a public website) → often unrepresentative and biased; recruit participants who reflect actual target users.

18.4Assigning participants: between-subjects vs. within-subjects

Core design question: should each participant experience all conditions, or only one?

Design Structure Pros Cons
Between-subjects Each participant experiences only one condition (e.g. half the participants use System A, the other half use System B) Minimises learning/transfer effects across conditions; shorter individual sessions; easier to set up with multiple independent variables May need many more participants overall
Within-subjects Every participant experiences all conditions Requires fewer participants overall (cheaper to run); each participant "controls for themselves," minimising random noise since the same person's individual differences affect every condition equally, making a true difference between conditions less likely to be masked by that noise Ordering effects — fatigue (performance drops in later conditions) or learning (performance improves in later conditions purely from practice, not from the condition itself) 
flowchart TD
    subgraph Between["Between-Subjects (20 people)"]
        B1["Participants 1-10 → Control"]
        B2["Participants 11-20 → Treatment"]
    end
    subgraph Within["Within-Subjects (10 people)"]
        W1["Participants 1-10 → Control, then Treatment"]
    end

Caption: between-subjects needs 20 people to get 10 measurements per condition; within-subjects gets the same 10-per-condition count from only 10 people — at the cost of introducing ordering effects that between-subjects avoids entirely.

Mitigating ordering effects — counterbalancing: for two conditions, have half the participants experience A-then-B, and the other half B-then-A, so any learning/fatigue effect is evenly distributed across both conditions rather than always favouring whichever condition comes second. For three or more conditions, use a Latin Square — a systematic rotation ensuring every condition appears in every position (first/second/third) roughly equally often across participants, e.g.:

A B C
B C A
C A B

Unmoderated remote testing (added note, extends the tools of §17.6): Software (rather than a live researcher) delivers instructions, records actions, and may ask predetermined follow-up questions, with no researcher needing to attend each session. Limitations: early-prototype testing is difficult without a moderator present to explain the prototype or help participants recover from its rough edges

And without a moderator, participants tend to be less engaged and behave less realistically on tasks that depend on imagination, decision-making, or emotional response — plus a practical risk of "cheaters and outliers" in unmoderated remote data that a live moderator would normally catch.

Counterbalancing

Half test A→B, half B→A; keeps the within-subjects advantage with no extra participants — works only if ordering effects are small; it doesn't eliminate every carryover effect; use comparable task versions where repeating a task would reveal the answer. Latin square for ≥3 conditions: each condition appears once in each position and once before/after every other (A-B-C, B-C-A, C-A-B…).

Choosing within vs. between

Within when: carryover is manageable but sessions short, setups complex with many conditions, participants scarce/expensive, individual differences large, direct comparisons needed. Between when: learning/carryover unavoidable, many participants available. Neither is "easy": the IV sometimes dictates the design.

Unmoderated remote testing

Participants work independently; software collects data. Pros: many participants, lower cost, geographic diversity, 24/7 scheduling, no researcher bias. Cons: no help when stuck, less realistic for imaginative tasks, little insight into thought processes. Best for simple, well-defined tasks on stable prototypes. Watch for cheaters/outliers (NN/g).

18.5AI-powered A/B testing (methodology angle)

LLM agents can simulate diverse user personas navigating real webpages to run A/B tests without needing live human traffic Dynamic (rather than fixed 50/50) traffic allocation via multi-armed-bandit algorithms shifts traffic toward the winning variant as evidence accumulates

AI-assisted analysis can reach statistical significance 3–5× faster.

Named validity concern (directly extending §18.3's validity framework to AI methods): AI-simulated participants cannot replace real users, and external validity is limited when the "users" are synthetic — best suited for early-stage hypothesis screening, not final decisions.

Null-hypothesis significance testing preview

Step 1: null and alternative hypotheses; Step 2: choose a test statistic (e.g. "difference in success rates", pA=45% vs. pB=95%, N=40, 20 per design); Step 3: statistical test; the p-value is the probability of observing the results given H0 — low p → H0 unlikely.

📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Worked example: N = 40, two designs

The setting

A small between-subjects study compares two designs with 20 participants each.

What happened

Success rates were 45% on design A and 95% on design B. Each person saw only one design, so the groups are independent and the result can be tested with an appropriate test.

The lesson

Between-subjects means each participant gets one condition; compare group results and check that the difference is unlikely to be chance.

⚡ Quick examples
Variables
PointIndependent = manipulated; dependent = measured; control = held constant; confounding = uncontrolled.
ExampleIV: layout A vs. B; DV: time to complete.
ExplanationConfounds make results ambiguous.
Internal vs. external validity
PointInternal: did X cause Y? External: does it generalise?
ExampleOnly testing students limits external validity; different tasks for A and B threaten internal validity.
ExplanationThere is a trade-off; control can reduce generalisability.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds

  • Internal: did X cause Y? External: does it generalise?
  • Each participant sees one condition.
  • Each participant sees all conditions.
  • Rotate orders; Latin square for 3+ conditions.
  • Participants work alone; software collects data.
