lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersNumbers always vary. Statistics tells you whether a difference is bigger than chance.
🧠 Memory hookCoin-flip test: could luck alone produce this? Pick the test by the type of variable.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Why do statistical analysis at all?The coin-flip intuition for hypothesis testingThe t-testDependent-variable types (levels of measurement)Tests for other variable types (non-parametric alternatives)Choosing the right test (decision structure)AI-powered hypothesis testing
⚡ At a glance — which test?
Dependent variableBetween-subjectsWithin-subjects
Interval / ratio, normalIndependent t-testPaired t-test
Interval/ratio non-normal, or ordinal (Likert)Mann-Whitney UWilcoxon signed-rank
Nominal (yes/no)Fisher’s exact / chi-squareMcNemar
One binary preference (each participant tries both)—Binomial

Decision rule: p < α (usually 0.05) ⇒ statistically significant ⇒ reject H0. Default to two-tailed.

This lecture supplies the statistical machinery for interpreting the A/B and experimental results introduced in §17–18.

19.1Why do statistical analysis at all?

Two branches:

Branch Purpose
Descriptive statistics Summarise the sample data itself — exploratory data analysis (EDA), graphically (histograms, scatter plots) or non-graphically
Inferential statistics Infer patterns about the wider population from a sample — extends to forecasting, prediction, estimation, and testing causality (the effect of an independent on a dependent variable)

Purpose: to understand data (measure, quantify, discover facts) and to quantify your confidence in a prediction/estimate about the population, rather than simply reporting a raw average and guessing whether it's meaningful.

Why statistics

Moves beyond intuition, quantifies confidence, and enables evidence-based decisions: determine whether observed differences are meaningful or random.

Descriptive statistics summarise a sample (mean, median, SD); inferential statistics infer properties of a population (hypothesis tests, estimates); exploratory data analysis summarises main characteristics, often with graphics.

A common goal is investigating causality: effect of independent variables on dependent variables. Qualitative data → thematic coding; quantitative → tests, comparisons, significance. Same stats, different graphs — always plot your data (Anscombe-style warning).

19.2The coin-flip intuition for hypothesis testing

Worked exercise: flip a coin 20 times, count heads — is the coin fair? Framing:

  • Null hypothesis (H₀): "nothing unusual is happening" — the coin is fair (50% heads), and any observed deviation is due to random chance.
  • Alternative hypothesis (Hₐ): the observed difference is real (e.g. caused by a biased coin), not due to random chance.

Under a fair coin, most 20-flip trials cluster near 10 heads (a bell-shaped/normal distribution of outcomes across many repeated trials); a result far in either tail (e.g. 19/20 heads) is possible by chance but unlikely — its probability of occurring purely by chance is exactly what a p-value quantifies.

P-value (formal definition, reproduced from source): "a measure of the probability that an observed difference could have occurred just by random chance." Worked interpretation: if 19/20 heads has p≈.00004 (two-tailed: 19 or more, or 1 or fewer, heads), that means a result this extreme should happen only about 4 times in 100,000 by random chance alone if the coin really were fair.

📍 CASE FILE

The coin-flip intuition

The setting

Before the formal t-test, the course uses a simple coin analogy.

What happened

Flip a fair coin 20 times: getting 19 heads has a probability of about 0.004% (p ≈ 0.00004, two-tailed), so chance is no longer a good explanation. The t-test example reports p = 0.007586.

The lesson

A small p-value means the difference is unlikely to be luck; that is the logic behind hypothesis testing.

Significance level (α) / critical value: the p-value threshold required to reject the null hypothesis — if the observed p-value is below α, the difference is called "significant" (probably not due to chance). Most statisticians conventionally use α = 5% (0.05); other common choices are α = 1% (0.01) and α = 0.1% (0.001) — the choice of α is itself a judgement call about how much false-positive risk you're willing to accept, not a fixed law of nature.

Why a bare average isn't enough (worked visual argument): Given "Interface B completed the task 10 seconds faster than Interface A on average," you initially can't judge whether that's meaningful — you need to see the spread (variance) of the underlying data points, not just the two means, because a 10-second gap could be a real, consistent effect or could easily be noise if both interfaces' individual times overlap heavily.

Confidence that "B is superior to A" depends on both the mean difference AND the spread — this is exactly the intuition a statistical test like the t-test formalises.

Coin-flip intuition for p-values

Flip a fair coin 20 times and record heads. The distribution of # heads is bell-shaped with expected value n/2 (10 = 50%); 8 heads is common; 19 heads is rare — the probability of a result this extreme (≥19 or ≤1) is ≈0.004% (p ≈ 0.00004, two-tailed), so "no longer random chance". Real p-values depend on the estimated mean/SD but are always interpreted the same way: lower p = stronger evidence.

Hypotheses and α

  • H0 = "nothing special is happening" (no difference between variants; presumed true until evidence nullifies it).
  • The decision is either (A) an extremely unlikely event happened (significant) or (B) the sample isn't unusual (chance).
  • If p < α the result is statistically significant.
  • Most statisticians use α = 5% (0.05).
  • Why 0.05?
  • Nothing special — a hangover from pre-computer days of printed tables with p = 0.05/0.01/0.001; journals often mark * for p<0.05 and ** for p<0.01.
  • H0 for A/B: PA − PB = 0. Procedure: choose test → compute how likely H0 explains the results → compare p with α and conclude.
🧩 Pause & recall — If p < α (α = 0.05) you
Answer: Reject the null hypothesis: the result is statistically significant
A small p means the result is unlikely under H0.
19.3The t-test

When to use it: for interval variables (see §19.4) that are (roughly) normally distributed, comparing means between two conditions (A and B) — e.g. task time, number of clicks, money spent.

Inputs: per-participant measurements. Outputs: a t-statistic, degrees of freedom (reflecting sample size), and a p-value. Run in Excel or R.

Checking the normality assumption first: Inspect a histogram of the dependent variable (e.g. via Excel's Analysis ToolPak, choosing bin size carefully). Distribution shapes to recognise: normal (roughly symmetric bell curve), slight skew, heavy skew, and bimodal (two separate peaks — often a sign of two hidden subgroups rather than one homogeneous population).

You can use tests that assume normality (like the t-test) only if the data is roughly normal, or if the sample size is large (n > 30), which makes the test more robust to non-normality Otherwise, do not use tests that assume a normal distribution — use a non-parametric alternative instead (§19.5).

T-test variants — choose based on two independent axes:

Axis Option Use case
Pairing Within-subjects Paired-sample t-test
Pairing Between-subjects Independent-sample (Welch's / "two-sample unequal variance") t-test
Tail Two-tailed Tests for either an increase or a decrease (H₀: A = B); p-value split across both tails; more conservative (lower statistical power); makes no assumption about the direction of any difference
Tail One-tailed Tests for a specific direction only (A > B, or A < B); the entire p-value sits on one tail; higher statistical power, but only valid if you correctly assumed the direction in advance

Reporting format (a template worth memorising verbatim, reproduced from the source example): "A paired-sample t-test showed that task time was significantly longer for A than for B." — reporting A's mean and standard deviation, B's mean and standard deviation, the t-statistic, degrees of freedom, and the p-value (e.g. t = 3.7, df = 7, p < .01).

t-test details

Assesses whether the means of two groups differ, judging the mean difference relative to variability; mathematically equivalent to one-way ANOVA and a form of regression. Assumes normally distributed data (t-test assumes the sample is drawn from a normal distribution).

Run via Excel, R or JASP (open the CSV, Analysis → T-Tests). Degrees of freedom relate to the number of samples. Example output: mean difference 169.6 − 150.3 = 19.4; SD_A = √65.125 = 8.07, SD_B = √121.9286 = 11.04; two-tailed p = 0.007586 → significant at α = 0.01.

Report just "p<.05 / .01 / .001 / .0001" — more detail is uninteresting.

Checking normality

Plot histograms to check bell shape and also spot data-recording errors. Bin size: too few → one bin; too many → sparse bins; use the same bin size when comparing groups. A bimodal histogram suggests two different effects (systematic participant/condition difference) — investigate before testing. Non-parametric Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney work if distributions share the same shape.

Tails and pairing

Two-tailed (A ≠ B): checks both directions, splits α (0.025 per tail), needs no directional assumption — default; one-tailed: more power but requires a prior directional hypothesis, and choosing it after a failed two-tailed test is not legitimate (drug example: you'd miss the possibility the new drug is worse). Paired = same participants use A and B; unpaired = different participants.

19.4Dependent-variable types (levels of measurement)

Extending the nominal/ordinal distinction first introduced in §14.6:

Level Definition Examples
Interval Numeric, ordered, and the exact distance between values is meaningful Temperature, dates, standardised test scores
— Ratio Interval with a meaningful zero point Task completion time, clicks, errors, cost, height, age, income
Ordinal Categorical, ordered, but the distance between values is not meaningful Likert-scale response (1–5), letter grades, rank
Nominal Categorical, unordered Task success (True/False), preferred version (A/B), blood type, race

Why this classification matters: the level of measurement of your dependent variable is the single biggest factor determining which statistical test is even valid to use — see the decision structure in §19.6.

Data-mining model (added structure, referenced as useful for big-data contexts more broadly):

Category Sub-type Description
Descriptive Clustering Grouping comments/observations (cross-reference §14.6's clustering step)
Descriptive Association Finding causal/associative relationships
Predictive Classification Assigning to discrete categories
Predictive Regression Modelling a continuous, linear relationship with dependent variables

Measurement scales — extra examples and rules

Nominal (no natural order; numeric codes arbitrary; mean/median meaningless): blood type, zip code, eye colour, party, interface preference A/B, compass directions. Ordinal (order matters, gaps unequal): education level, income bands, satisfaction ratings, rankings, letter grades, Likert data.

Interval (exact equal distances, no true zero): °C/°F (the 100–90 gap equals 90–80), pH, SAT/credit scores. Ratio (true zero, "none of it"): weight, length, concentration, pulse, survival time, Kelvin.

Examples from the deck: age = ratio, expertise level = ordinal. Independent samples = data from two separate participant groups (control/treatment).

19.5Tests for other variable types (non-parametric alternatives)

Used when the interval/ratio data is not normally distributed, or when the data is ordinal or nominal:

Test Variable type Design
Wilcoxon signed-rank Non-normal interval/ratio, or ordinal (e.g. Likert) Within-subjects (two measurements per participant)
Mann-Whitney U (aka Wilcoxon rank-sum) Non-normal interval/ratio, or ordinal (e.g. Likert) Between-subjects (one measurement per participant)
Fisher's Exact Nominal, small sample size (use Chi-square/G-test for large samples) Between-subjects (one value per participant; assumes independent observations)
McNemar's Exact Nominal Within-subjects (paired values per participant; groups must be mutually exclusive, e.g. can't be both "true" and "false" at once)
Binomial Nominal, comparing preference between two options Within-subjects (each participant tries both versions and gives one preference, e.g. preferred UI version; tested against a 50/50 split)

Both Wilcoxon signed-rank and Mann-Whitney U report a p-value and are written up like a t-test result, but omitting the t-statistic and degrees of freedom (since those are specific to the t-distribution). Example write-ups (reproduced): "A Fisher's exact test showed that significantly more participants completed the task with version B than with version A (p<.05)."; "A binomial test showed participants' preference for version A was significant (p<.05)."

Other tests

Mann-Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum): non-parametric alternative to the independent t-test for skewed/Likert data, reports like a t-test without t and df; Wilcoxon signed-rank for dependent samples. Binomial (two-option nominal, e.g. preference or Yes/No recommend; within-subjects: every participant tries both versions and gives one choice; tests deviation from 50/50). McNemar (paired nominal, e.g. task success: "p<.05, B 90% vs. A 65%"). Fisher's exact (small samples, between-subject success rates; chi-square for larger).

19.6Choosing the right test (decision structure)
flowchart TD
    Q1{What type is the<br/>dependent variable?}
    Q1 -->|Interval / ratio| Q2{Does it satisfy normality<br/>assumptions?}
    Q1 -->|Nominal| Q4{Paired or independent sample?}
    Q1 -->|Ordinal| Q5
    Q2 -->|Yes| Q3{Paired or independent sample?}
    Q2 -->|No| Q5{Paired or independent sample?}
    Q3 -->|Paired| R1[Paired t-test]
    Q3 -->|Independent| R2[Independent-sample t-test]
    Q5 -->|Paired| R3[Wilcoxon signed-rank]
    Q5 -->|Independent| R4[Mann-Whitney U]
    Q4 -->|Paired| R5["McNemar's (task success) / Binomial (preference)"]
    Q4 -->|Independent| R6["Chi-square / Fisher's Exact"]

Caption: the full test-selection tree — the two questions that gate everything are (1) is the dependent variable interval/ratio, ordinal or nominal (ordinal data takes the non-parametric branch, like non-normal interval/ratio data), and (2) is the design paired (within-subjects) or independent (between-subjects); normality only needs checking for interval/ratio data, since ordinal and nominal tests don't assume it.

Steps to perform a non-parametric statistical test: (1) choose the right test based on the experiment's design and the data's characteristics (within- vs. between-subjects); (2) define a sample statistic (e.g. sample mean) plus a null hypothesis (random chance) and an alternative hypothesis (a real dependency); (3) compute the p-value; (4) interpret the result against your chosen significance level (α).

19.7AI-powered hypothesis testing

Automated hypothesis-validation systems are emerging (e.g. POPPER, Stanford 2025 — AI agents that validate hypotheses with rigorous p-value control Google DeepMind's Co-Scientist — AI research partners generating/validating hypotheses in domains like oncology, hepatology, microbiology).

In UX research specifically, NLP can analyse open-ended responses and detect patterns across mixed qualitative/quantitative data.

Why the fundamentals in this lecture still matter: human judgement is still required for choosing the correct test, and for correctly understanding what a p-value and a null hypothesis actually mean — an automated tool can run the numbers, but interpreting them correctly is still the analyst's job.

⚡ Quick examples
Why statistics
PointSeparate real differences from chance.
ExampleB seems 5 s faster — is it luck or real?
ExplanationDescriptive stats summarise; inferential stats generalise.
Measurement scales
PointNominal, ordinal, interval, ratio.
ExampleBlood type (nominal); Likert (ordinal); °C (interval); time (ratio).
ExplanationThe scale determines which tests are valid.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds

  • Nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio.

  • Check histograms; default to two-tailed tests.
  • Report mean, SD, test statistic, df, p.

lessons.title: Presenting Design Work
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersA great design is wasted if nobody understands it. Short, clear stories win.
🧠 Memory hookOne clear story. Problem → people → solution → proof.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
How to make a great pitch videoGeneral design tips for the video/pitch itself
⚡ At a glance — pitch structure
Grab attention (60 s)→Problem & why it matters→Your solution→What’s unique→Leave them wanting more

This lecture's slides are largely visual/example-driven (screenshots and video-example placeholders) with comparatively few text bullets — the points below capture everything stated in text; where a slide showed only an image/example with no accompanying text, it's noted as illustrative rather than reconstructed.

20.1How to make a great pitch video

Two-part structure, given directly: WHAT (the problem) and HOW (the solution).

Question Prompts to answer
What is the problem? State it in one sentence; then explain why it's important, why the audience should care, and how it affects them
How did you solve it? Explain the solution, and explicitly identify what makes your solution/project unique compared to alternatives

Cross-reference — Simon Sinek's "Why/How/What" (Apple example, added context): The slides reference Sinek's well-known "Start With Why" framing (using Apple as the marketing example) as a related storytelling structure — communicate the underlying purpose/belief (Why) before the approach (How) and the product itself (What), rather than leading with product features.

This is offered as a complementary storytelling lens to the "What is the problem / How did you solve it" structure above, not a separate requirement.

20.2General design tips for the video/pitch itself
  • Speak to both logic and emotion — a purely feature-driven ("logic-only") pitch is contrasted with one that also engages emotion; the Creative Zen vs. Apple iPod example is used to illustrate how a technically comparable (or even superior) product can still lose if its story fails to engage the audience emotionally as well as logically.
  • Use powerful visuals — don't just describe the interface in words; show it directly.
  • Show the visual interface at a high level — give the audience an impression of the design rather than a detailed evaluation walkthrough; save the deep evaluation discussion for elsewhere in the presentation/report, not the pitch video itself.
  • Less is more — keep the video short (the summary guideline specifies roughly 60 seconds) and prioritise conveying the core problem/solution/uniqueness clearly over cramming in detail.
  • Leave people hungry for more — end while the audience is still interested, rather than over-explaining until interest fades.

Telling a story

A pitch = telling a story; use visual cues (show the interface/demo); the video must grab attention — you have 60 seconds. Stories need few words: Hemingway's six-word "For sale: baby shoes, never worn." Show off the UI you built (video, or the poster if time is short).

Filling a video/poster with uninteresting words drives audiences away: present the most compelling facts and give them space to stand out

Facts and logic matter but speak to emotions too. Two ways to share UX research insights: let them hear you (talk, don't just post) and no walls of text. Practice: find a short product-pitch video on YouTube and write a critique.

AI's influence on the design process

  • UI beyond GUIs (conversational UI)
  • Defining simulated user behaviours
  • generative design (generate several designs, then choose and edit)
  • Well-established, visually inspectable heuristics will be automated
  • LLMs make large-scale qualitative analysis (affinity diagramming / content analysis) feasible for small teams
  • Algorithms optimise the experimental plan for efficient design-space exploration. Related courses: IS428 Visual Analytics for BI; CS462 IoT
  • CS463 Computer Graphics and VR.
🧩 Pause & recall — A pitch video in this course has about
Answer: 60 seconds to grab attention
Grab attention fast and keep it concise.
📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Sinek's Why–How–What and Hemingway's six words

The setting

Two models of storytelling are used to explain pitch videos.

What happened

Simon Sinek's Golden Circle starts with why you do something (Apple is the example); Hemingway's six-word story ‘For sale: baby shoes, never worn’ shows that a story needs very few words.

The lesson

Lead with why and keep the story short and clear.

⚡ Quick examples
The pitch
PointYou have ~60 seconds to grab attention.
ExampleOpen with the problem a real user faces, not with features.
ExplanationAttention is the scarcest resource.
Visual tips
PointShow the interface; keep text short; speak to logic and emotion.
ExampleA 20 s demo video beats three slides of bullets.
ExplanationVisuals persuade; clutter drives audiences away.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • You have ~60 seconds to grab attention.
  • Problem → why it matters → solution → what's unique.
  • Show the interface; keep text short; speak to logic and emotion.

Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
What/How story structuretap to flip
Problem (what) then solution (how), for a pitch video

A persuasive pitch engages both rational and emotional response

lessons.title: What We Learned (Course Review)
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersThe course is one loop seen from many angles. Review shows how the pieces fit.
🧠 Memory hookThe loop: understand → define → create → test → learn → repeat.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Review structureRefinement: more precise Model Human Processor figuresNew discussion hook: "is there a problem with this process?"AI-powered prototyping — 2026 trend figures

This lecture is an explicit course review, re-walking the Empathy → Prototype → Evaluate cycle (equivalently, the Design Thinking cycle) and revisiting material already covered in depth earlier in this document. Per the "don't re-explain, cross-reference" rule, this section only records what's genuinely new or refined here; everything else is cross-referenced back to its original section.

21.1Review structure

The lecture organises the whole course under four headings, each mapped onto a stage of the Empathy→Prototype→Evaluate / Design Thinking cycle: (1) Design — course values, observation, requirements (persona & scenarios), models/memory/input/mobile

(2) Prototype — quantity vs. quality, colour/font, strategy and parallel prototyping, goals and methods

(3) Test — experts vs. users, field vs. laboratory, study vs. experiment, qualitative vs. quantitative, dependent vs. independent variables. Every concept named in this map has already been covered in full in §1–§19 above See the cheat-sheet for a fast index back to each one.

21.2Refinement: more precise Model Human Processor figures

The review lecture gives more granular timing figures for the memory stores first introduced in §7.1 — treated here as a refinement/correction of that section rather than a new topic:

Store Size Decay
Visual image store 7–17 letters 70–1000 msec
Auditory image store 4.4–6.2 letters 900–3500 msec
Working (short-term) memory 5–9 "chunks" 73–226 sec for 1 chunk, or 5–34 sec for 3 chunks
Long-term memory Unlimited (associative) None (stable)

Corrected/refined note: §7.1 gave rounder approximate figures (e.g. "100–1000 ms," "~4±1 chunks"); these more precise ranges are the authoritative version. The key qualitative point from §7.1 stands unchanged: working memory is the clear bottleneck (smallest capacity, fastest decay relative to how much information passes through it), which is why §7.4's "avoid taxing working memory" design implication matters.

🧩 Pause & recall — According to the course review, systems appear when
Answer: A vision meets reality; quality depends on both the vision and its adaptation to reality
The design cycle is fundamental to everything in the course.
21.3New discussion hook: "is there a problem with this process?"

After re-presenting the standard Empathy→Prototype→Evaluate cycle and the Design Thinking cycle, the lecture poses an open, unanswered discussion question: "But wait! Is there a problem with this process?", immediately followed by a slide on 2026 AI prototyping trends.

This is best read as a deliberate bridge into Lecture 22: the implied "problem" is that the classical, fully-human-driven Design Thinking cycle doesn't yet account for AI acting as an active participant (ideator, prototyper, evaluator) rather than a passive tool — exactly the gap §22 addresses.

The design cycle is fundamental

The iterative cycle underlies everything in the course: used to establish requirements; systems appear when a vision meets reality — quality depends on how beautiful the vision is and how well it adapts to reality; many techniques exist at varying cost. Closing debate: is all this user-centred work really necessary — could it be harmful? (Fast Company, "user-led innovation can't create breakthroughs — just ask Apple and IKEA").

21.4AI-powered prototyping — 2026 trend figures

New figures not given back in §5.5: 50–70% faster iteration cycles from lo-fi to hi-fi Designers reportedly shifting from creators to curators of AI output And an explicit reminder that human-centred empathy and evaluation are still required regardless of how much of the prototyping itself is AI-assisted.

The lecture poses this as an open question rather than a settled answer: does AI help us iterate more (quantity) or better (quality)? — directly echoing the quantity-vs-quality ceramics-class lesson from §4.2, now applied to AI-assisted iteration specifically.

⚡ Quick examples
Key contrasts
PointExperts vs. users; field vs. lab; study vs. experiment; qualitative vs. quantitative; dependent vs. independent variables.
ExampleExperts via heuristics; users via laboratory studies; experiments via A/B.
ExplanationChoosing the right contrast is choosing the right method.
Human limits
PointMemory, attention, motor control and colour perception shape interface design.
ExampleFitts's Law for buttons; chunking for forms.
ExplanationDesigning within human limits is what makes interfaces usable.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test is the backbone.
  • Experts vs. users; field vs. lab; study vs. experiment; qualitative vs. quantitative; dependent vs. independent variables.
  • Memory, attention, motor control and colour perception shape interface design.
➡ Where next? AI now touches every stage of that loop.

lessons.title: AI-Powered Design Thinking (full treatment)
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersAI can speed up each stage of design thinking, but people still own the judgement.
🧠 Memory hookAI proposes, humans decide.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
The full mapNew material not previously covered: named AI design tools in…New caution not previously stated: sycophancy
⚡ At a glance — AI across the cycle
Empathise: synthetic users (supplement only)→Define: goals & constraints→Ideate: AI partner (watch fixation)→Prototype: prompt-to-UI→Test: AI heuristics, moderation, analysis
↺ Human judgement stays essential at every stage.

This lecture is the consolidated version of the AI-augmentation material previewed piecemeal throughout the course (§1.4, §2.2, §3.5, §4.6, §5.5, §6.5, §10.6, §12.5, §14.7, §15.7, §17.9, §18.5, §19.7). Rather than repeating each stage's content in full, this section presents the consolidated map and adds only what's genuinely new here — full detail on the named AI tools, and a few extra caution phrases not given earlier.

    E[Empathise] --> D[Define]

    P --> T[Test]

    E -.-> E1["Synthetic Users<br/>(Empathy)"]

Caption: the complete AI-augmentation map across all five Design Thinking stages. Every branch has already been explained in depth at its cross-referenced section — this diagram exists purely to show how the pieces fit together as one coherent picture, per the lecture's own framing (and the same diagram opens and closes the lecture, emphasising it as the throughline).

22.2New material not previously covered: named AI design tools in full

Extending §5.5's brief mention with the full detail this lecture gives:

Tool Maker What it does Workflow Export / handoff
Claude Design Anthropic Labs AI-powered visual creation: prototypes, wireframes, decks, marketing collateral; frontier capabilities extending toward voice, video, shaders, and 3D Describe → generate → refine → export; auto-applies an existing brand system pulled from the codebase/design files; refine via chat, inline comments, direct edits, or sliders Canva, PDF, PPTX, HTML — or hand off directly to Claude Code
Google Stitch (beta) + Design.md Google AI-native "vibe design" canvas: prompts, wireframes, or screenshots → editable UIs + production code Describe → generate → iterate → export; includes a voice canvas and a design agent for real-time critiques; free tier (350 generations/month), no subscription Figma, HTML/CSS, React — or Google AI Studio; the DESIGN.md file format encodes portable design rules with built-in WCAG accessibility validation
Figma Make Figma AI-powered "prompt-to-app" tool Text-to-App (a plain-language prompt generates both UI and underlying logic from scratch); Design-to-Code (paste existing Figma design frames directly in — the AI analyses auto-layout, typography, and colour schemes to build a functioning, responsive coded interface); Iterative Prompting (refine interactively via natural language or point-and-edit); Design System Integration (reference published design libraries/guidelines to keep AI-generated elements on-brand) Outputs real frontend code (e.g. React and CSS), directly bridging designers and engineers

All three tools are explicitly positioned as comparable alternatives to each other, aimed at the same underlying "prompt/sketch → working design" workflow, differing mainly in ecosystem (Anthropic/Claude Code, Google/Figma/React, Figma's own native pipeline) and specific export targets.

AI in ideation

AI as a "naïve expert" (outsider asking unexpected questions) can reduce early fixation, but teams may latch onto the first reasonable AI output (convergent homogeneity). Role shift: idea generator → creative curator; humans define problems/constraints and evaluate/select/refine. Prompt: if ideas become cheap, which design skill is most valuable?

Generative UI

  • AI creates and adapts layout, colour, typography and component arrangement per user at runtime
  • Links AI tool calls to real components (e.g. itinerary cards instead of text)
  • lowers the threshold while raising the ceiling (see threshold/ceiling in Chapter 16)
  • Still relies on design-system standards (Material, HIG) as constraints
  • Example: a fintech replaced six report views with one adaptive view and support tickets fell 27%.
  • Personalisation reshapes whole flows (navigation, hierarchy).
  • AI can audit contrast and colour-blind-safe palettes (WCAG 2.1 AA/AAA).
  • Fundamentals — Gestalt, colour theory, typography, grids — remain what lets designers evaluate AI output.
  • "AI slop" = mass-produced, low-effort generated content. AI eye tracking can estimate fatigue/cognitive load from gaze dynamics; NL chart creation in AI data-viz tools.
🧩 Pause & recall — Synthetic (AI-generated) users should be treated as
Answer: Hypotheses to be tested with real users
They can supplement but not replace real user empathy; watch for sycophancy.
22.3New caution not previously stated: sycophancy

Extending §2.2's synthetic-user caution with a specific named failure mode: synthetic users carry a key caution around sycophancy — a tendency to agree with or flatter the prompt/premise rather than push back — and they do not always model real human behaviour well, which is exactly why they're restricted to a supplementary role (desk research, hypothesis generation) rather than being trusted for final decisions.

📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Baymard UX-Ray and AgentA/B

The setting

Two AI tools cited on the slides for evaluating designs.

What happened

Baymard's UX-Ray 2.0 reports about 95% accuracy over 207 heuristics (a claim from the slide); AgentA/B simulates A/B tests with 1,000 LLM persona agents.

The lesson

AI can scale evaluation, but treat vendor claims with caution and keep real users in the loop.

⚡ Quick examples
Synthetic users
PointAI-generated users are hypotheses, not evidence.
ExampleAn AI persona says it loves the feature, but real users don't.
ExplanationTest with real people; watch for sycophancy.
Goals over screens
PointWhen UI is generated dynamically, goals and constraints matter most.
ExampleA travel app composes a different layout per user.
ExplanationDefine goals clearly; interfaces may change.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • AI-generated users are hypotheses, not evidence.
  • When UI is generated dynamically, goals and constraints matter most.
  • AI widens ideas and speeds prototypes but risks convergent output.
  • AI heuristic checks, AI-moderated tests, AI thematic analysis.
  • Multi-armed bandits shift traffic to winning variants.

Human-in-the-looptap to flip
Keeping a human able to review/correct AI output as a default safety pattern

➡ Where next? The last step: designing the interaction with AI itself.

lessons.title: Human–AI Interaction (Optional, supplementary)
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersDesigning for AI is new: its answers are probabilistic and can surprise users.
🧠 Memory hookOld mental models strain. Users need new ones for AI behaviour.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
From traditional HCI to Human-AI InteractionNielsen's 10 Heuristics, reimagined for Human-AI InteractionPossible new heuristics for Human-AI Interaction (beyond…
⚡ At a glance — four mental-model shifts
Deterministic → Probabilistic→Rule-based → Learning-based→Transparent → Opaque→Fixed → Adaptive

This entire lecture is explicitly marked in the source as supplementary material: "This supplementary material is optional and not tested for IS211 final examination." It's included here for completeness, but should be deprioritised relative to §1–§22 when studying for the exam.

23.1From traditional HCI to Human-AI Interaction
Aspect Traditional HCI Modern Human-AI Interaction
Character Deterministic, rule-based, transparent Probabilistic, learning-based, adaptive
Interactions Fixed Requires new mental models from the user

Why this matters (cited research): users who misperceive an AI system as deterministic (i.e. expect it to always behave the same predictable way, like traditional software) struggle with trust and with comprehending the system's explanations (Kulesza et al., 2013) — this is a direct extension of the mental-models material from §6.1: an outdated conceptual model of "how software behaves" actively harms a user's ability to use an AI system well.

Four key mental-model shifts (reproduced from source, each paired with a plain-language reframing the interface should help the user adopt):

Shift User's needed reframing
Deterministic → Probabilistic "This AI gives likely answers — it might be wrong sometimes."
Rule-based → Learning-based "Its strengths and blind spots depend on what it was trained on."
Transparent → Opaque "It may not show how it decided, but it should offer understandable reasons."
Fixed → Adaptive "As I interact, it changes and my behaviour shapes its responses."

Worked real-world examples: probabilistic outputs — Gmail Smart Compose shows text completions in light grey (visually signalling "this is a suggestion, not committed text") Medical AI tools display explicit confidence scores (e.g. "85% certainty").

Learning-based interactions — Netflix/Spotify's like/dislike buttons and "Match %" indicators

Language-learning apps that adjust difficulty based on the learner's performance. AI as collaborator — GitHub Copilot integrates into the IDE, offering code suggestions the developer can accept, modify, or reject (echoing the "human-in-the-loop" pattern from §22).

Transparency & explanations — IBM Watson includes "how it works" explanations of its underlying model and data sources.

Mental-model shift

Interacting with AI is fundamentally different from traditional software; treating AI as fixed/deterministic causes confusion — users who wrongly assume AI is deterministic struggle to trust it and understand its explanations (Kulesza et al., 2013).

Four core assumptions change as you move to AI systems; good AI interfaces make uncertainty and adaptation visible, and effective AI acts as a partner while being open about how it reaches outputs.

Nielsen's ten heuristics still apply to AI and are re-walked across three slides (three, three, then the final set).

23.2Nielsen's 10 Heuristics, reimagined for Human-AI Interaction

Directly extends §12.4's heuristics with an AI-specific reading of each:

# Heuristic AI-specific reading Worked example
1 Visibility of system status Display progress, typing indicators, or model confidence ChatGPT shows a "typing..." indicator; Gemini (at time of writing) lacked this feedback
2 Match between system and real world Use a conversational tone and correct domain context ChatGPT uses natural conversational language; Copilot sometimes misuses technical jargon
3 User control and freedom Provide undo, retry, and corrective flows ChatGPT allows editing a prompt; Copilot lets you reject a suggestion
4 Consistency and standards Maintain a consistent tone, controls, and invocation method for the AI ChatGPT and Copilot both follow conversational norms consistently
5 Error prevention Flag low-confidence outputs and possible hallucinations Gemini's image-generation errors, at time of writing, went unmarked; Copilot lacked uncertainty indicators
6 Recognition rather than recall Include suggestion history, past prompts, and inline hints Many tools, at time of writing, still lack these features
7 Flexibility and efficiency of use Provide power-user features while keeping the default UI simple Copilot's snippet support
8 Aesthetic and minimalist design Clean UI with progressive disclosure Both ChatGPT and Copilot's interfaces
9–10 Help with errors & documentation Explain failures, suggest fixes, and integrate help Many AI tools, at time of writing, still show only a generic "failed to generate" error rather than a constructive explanation

Gotcha: this table is explicitly framed as an evaluation snapshot, not a permanent scorecard — the examples cite specific tool behaviours "at time of writing" which are exactly the kind of fast-moving product details likely to change. Treat the heuristic reinterpretation itself (column 3) as the durable, examinable content, and the specific tool examples (column 4) as illustrative only.

🧩 Pause & recall — Which mental-model shift is NOT among the four?
Answer: Cheap → expensive
The four are probabilistic, learning-based, opaque and adaptive.
23.3Possible new heuristics for Human-AI Interaction (beyond Nielsen's original 10)
Proposed new heuristic What it covers
Transparency & Explainability Expose reasoning, data sources, and confidence metrics to support user trust
Human-in-the-Loop Provide actionable feedback flows so the user can correct or help train the AI over time
Ethics, Bias & Fairness Detect and communicate biases; allow user flagging and adjustable filters
Privacy & Data Control Include consent settings, data visibility, and deletion tools
Customisation & Value Alignment Offer settings for tone, risk level, and domain preferences

These five are presented as candidate additions to Nielsen's classic 10 (§12.4), reflecting usability concerns that simply didn't exist for the largely deterministic, rule-based interfaces Nielsen's heuristics were originally written for.

📍 Real-life case files
Cases that are not told in the lecture text above.
📍 CASE FILE

Kulesza et al. (2013): users and non-deterministic AI

The setting

Researchers studied how people form mental models of intelligent systems.

What happened

Users who wrongly assume AI behaves deterministically struggle to trust it and to understand its explanations.

The lesson

Designing for AI means helping users build a correct mental model of probabilistic behaviour.

⚡ Quick examples
Heuristics for AI
PointNielsen's 10 still apply but are reinterpreted.
ExampleShow confidence indicators; provide undo/retry; flag possible hallucinations.
ExplanationVisibility and control matter more when behaviour is uncertain.
New AI heuristics
PointTransparency, human-in-the-loop, fairness, privacy, value alignment.
ExampleLet users review and correct AI actions before they take effect.
ExplanationBuilds trust and safety.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Deterministic → probabilistic; rule-based → learning; transparent → opaque; fixed → adaptive.
  • Nielsen's 10 still apply but are reinterpreted.
  • Transparency, human-in-the-loop, fairness, privacy, value alignment.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Deterministic→Probabilistic (AI mental model shift)tap to flip
