L23

This entire lecture is explicitly marked in the source as supplementary material: "This supplementary material is optional and not tested for IS211 final examination." It's included her…

1.q: Which sequence lists the five Design Thinking stages in order?
o: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test
Define, Empathise, Prototype, Ideate, Test
Empathise, Ideate, Define, Test, Prototype
Research, Design, Build, Test, Launch
1.e: Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test, with iteration looping back from Test.
w: Define comes after Empathise, and Prototype comes before Test, so this order is wrong.
Test comes last, and Define comes before Ideate.
That is a generic project pipeline, not the Design Thinking stages.

1.q: During Ideate, participants are told to 'defer judgement'. Why?
o: Criticism is rude, so teams should avoid it at every stage of the project
Early critique makes people self-censor, shrinking the number and variety of ideas
Ideas should be ranked by the most senior person before others add more
Judging ideas on the spot saves time by dropping weak ones immediately
1.e: Ideation aims for quantity and variety. Critical judgement is not banned; it is postponed to the selection and Test stages, once there are enough ideas to choose between.
w: Critique is valuable. The rule only postpones it until after ideas have been generated, when you converge on the best ones.
Ranking by seniority is not part of ideation. It would anchor the group on one view and make juniors hold back ideas.
Dropping ideas early does not save time. It shrinks the pool before there is enough choice, and people stop offering ideas.

1.q: Which law says that the time to reach a target depends on its distance and its size?
o: Power Law of Practice
Fitts's Law
Hick's Law
Gestalt closure
1.e: Fitts's Law: bigger and closer targets are acquired faster, so the key action should be large and near.
w: The Power Law of Practice is about improvement with repetition, not target size or distance.
Hick's Law is about decision time rising with the number of choices.
Closure is a Gestalt idea about completing partial shapes, not about reaching targets.

1.q: Which is one of the course's design-philosophy values?
o: Trust designer intuition and skip user feedback to save time
Iterate and improve, compare alternatives and prototype for feedback
Perfect a single design in private and ship it as early as possible
Make it look attractive first and research the users once it is built
1.e: The course stresses principles-based, human-centred design: iterate, compare alternatives and prototype early to get feedback while change is cheap.
w: Designers' intuition is often wrong about real users. The course asks for evidence from feedback, not assumptions.
One polished design shipped early tests nothing. The course prefers several cheap alternatives that feedback can improve.
Research comes first. A good-looking design built on untested assumptions has to be reworked once users react.

1.q: What does the Power Law of Practice state?
o: Performance improves predictably but with diminishing gains as practice accumulates
Experts reach perfect accuracy after enough practice, so errors vanish
The more options a menu has, the slower people choose between them
After the first few trials, extra practice has no further effect
1.e: The Power Law of Practice says time per task falls steeply at first and then flattens. It also explains why users resist change: they have already invested in learning the old interface.
w: Practice cuts both time and errors, but never to zero. Even experts slip.
That describes Hick's Law, which links decision time to the number of choices, not to practice.
Gains do not stop. They shrink, so the curve flattens but keeps improving.

2.q: Which kind of knowledge does interviewing alone tend to miss?
o: Explicit, documented procedures that users can easily state
Tacit knowledge such as workarounds, hacks and undocumented practices
Legal and regulatory requirements written in policy documents
Hardware specifications listed in the product's technical sheet
2.e: Tacit knowledge is what people do without being able to articulate it. Interviews only capture what people say, so you also need observation and immersion.
w: Explicit knowledge is exactly what people can say, so an interview captures it well.
Legal requirements are written down, so they can be found by reading.
Hardware specifications are documented facts about the product.

2.q: Which is the best interview question?
o: Don't you think the checkout is confusing?
Do you like the new design? (yes/no)
Tell me about the last time you bought something online
Wouldn't a bigger button help you?
2.e: Open, neutral questions that ask for a story avoid steering the participant, and they bring out behaviour, context and reasons.
w: This is leading: 'Don't you think...' signals the answer you expect, so people agree to be polite.
This is closed. A yes/no answer gives no reasons, no context and no story to learn from.
This is leading and solution-first. It suggests a bigger button before you have learned what the real problem is.

2.q: Learning the work by doing it alongside an expert user is called:
o: A diary study, where participants record events themselves over time
Lead-user innovation, studying advanced users who build their own solutions
Master–apprentice (contextual) learning, where you learn the work by doing it
A Likert survey that collects ratings on a fixed scale
2.e: Master–apprentice learning is an immersion technique: the researcher learns the task from the expert, in the real setting, by doing it alongside them.
w: In a diary study the participants record events themselves. The researcher does not take part in the work.
Lead-user innovation studies advanced users' own inventions and workarounds. It does not mean learning by working beside them.
A Likert survey gathers ratings on a scale. It involves no shared work or observation.

2.q: Why does the course value silence in interviews?
o: Silence ends the interview sooner so more users can be fitted in
Pauses give participants room to elaborate and surface unprompted detail
Silence stops the recording from picking up the interviewer's voice
Silence removes the need to transcribe the interviewer's questions
2.e: People often add the most useful detail after a pause. Filling every gap pushes your own framing onto the conversation.
w: The aim is richer answers, not shorter sessions. Silence usually makes an interview longer.
Silence has no effect on what the recording captures. It is about how the participant responds.
Transcription depends on what is said, not on pauses. Silence is a technique for getting better answers.

2.q: Why are users’ workarounds and hacks valuable to researchers?
o: They show that users follow the manual exactly
They reveal needs the current design fails to meet
They prove that the product has no usability problems
They measure how satisfied users are through ratings
2.e: Hacks and workarounds expose needs the system fails to meet, because people invent their own fix where the design lets them down.
w: Following the manual exactly shows no gap between the design and how people really work.
A workaround is evidence of a problem, not proof that there is none.
Ratings are opinions. Workarounds are behaviours that show unmet needs.

2.q: What is the main weakness of relying only on a convenient sample of friends for user research?
o: It costs too much compared with other recruiting methods
It may not represent real users, so findings can be biased
It makes each interview run far longer than planned
It rules out observing people in their own context
2.e: Convenience samples risk systematic bias because friends differ from your target users. Recruit people who reflect the real user population.
w: Friends are usually the cheapest participants to recruit, so cost is not the problem.
Interview length depends on the questions and the facilitator, not on who is recruited.
You can still observe friends. The problem is that what you see may not apply to your real users.

o: Uploading a photo is something the system does on request
The page must load in under 2 seconds
Logging out is something the user can do in the app
Sending confirmation emails is something the system does automatically
3.e: Functional requirements say what the system does. Non-functional requirements describe qualities and constraints such as speed, security, reliability and usability.
w: Uploading a photo is a function the system performs, so it is functional.
Logging out is a behaviour the system provides, so it is functional.
Sending emails is a system behaviour. Non-functional would describe how fast or how securely it does so.

o: A detailed profile of one real interviewee, kept under their real name
A famous person chosen to stand in for the typical user
A synthesised archetype whose behaviour patterns are supported by observed data
A list of the UI components the design will need
3.e: Personas are not real individuals. They are archetypes synthesised from patterns in your research, so the team designs for evidence, not assumption.
w: A persona is built from many participants. Using one real person over-weights a single voice and raises privacy issues.
A celebrity has no basis in your research, so you would be designing for assumptions.
A component list describes the interface, not a user.

3.q: What is a common pitfall when creating personas?
o: Choosing just one primary persona to design for first
Creating too many personas, or making each one too detailed
Grounding every persona in observed research data
Giving each persona clear goals and frustrations
3.e: Too many or over-detailed personas dilute focus and become hard to use. A small set of data-backed personas works best.
w: Focusing on one primary persona is sound practice. It gives the team a clear target.
Basing personas on data is the goal, not a pitfall. Invented personas are the problem.
Goals and frustrations are what make a persona useful for design decisions.

3.q: Scenarios are most useful early in design because they:
o: They specify the exact pixel layout of each screen
They focus on goals and context while keeping the UI abstract
They replace the need for user testing later on
They list the database tables the system will need
3.e: A scenario narrates how a persona achieves a goal in context and deliberately leaves the interface open, so early design is not locked into one solution.
w: Pixel layouts are far too concrete for a scenario. They belong to later, detailed design.
Scenarios organise design thinking, but they are not evidence from real users. Testing is still needed.
Database tables are technical design. A scenario is a story about a person and a goal.

3.q: Which pair correctly maps requirement categories?
o: System side: user and contextual; user side: functional, non-functional, data
System side: functional, non-functional, data; user side: user and contextual
System side: functional and data; user side: non-functional and contextual
System side: persona and scenario; user side: functional and data
3.e: Functional, non-functional and data requirements describe the system. User and contextual requirements describe the people and the setting.
w: The sides are swapped. Functional, non-functional and data describe the system; user and contextual describe people and settings.
Non-functional requirements (speed, security) are qualities of the system, so they belong on the system side.
Persona and scenario are tools for communicating users and goals. They are not requirement categories.

3.q: In the Define stage you should:
o: Choose the final colour palette and typography
Synthesise findings into a clear problem statement and requirements
Run an A/B test to choose between two live designs
Write the production code for the first release
3.e: Define turns the findings from Empathise into a focused problem statement and requirements that guide ideation.
w: Colour and type are detailed design choices made much later, after the problem is defined.
An A/B test compares live designs, so it needs a built design that Define comes before.
Production code comes after ideation and prototyping. Define is about framing the problem.

3.q: “The page must load in under 2 seconds” is which type of requirement?
o: Functional
Data
Contextual
Non-functional
3.e: Non-functional requirements say how well the system does something, and are measurable.
w: A functional requirement says what the system does.
A data requirement says what data is stored and how.
A contextual requirement concerns the context of use.

4.q: Which statement best captures 'quantity leads to quality' in ideation?
o: Commit to the first good idea to save time
Generate many ideas first, then converge on the strongest
Keep every idea alive and never discard any
Leave ideation to experts who know the domain best
4.e: Ideation alternates divergence (many options) with convergence (selection). Quantity gives you more to choose from, and quality comes from choosing well.
w: Sticking to the first idea is fixation. It skips the exploration that produces better ideas.
Converging means discarding weaker ideas. Keeping everything defeats the purpose.
Anyone can contribute, and diverse perspectives usually produce a wider range of ideas.

o: Locking onto early or supplied concepts and failing to explore alternatives
Quickly fixing bugs found during testing before the next iteration
Restricting a design to a single typeface for consistency
Running a usability test with only one participant
4.e: Fixation narrows exploration. It shows up when people stay with an early idea or the example they were given, which is why pursuing several alternatives reduces it.
w: Fixing bugs is routine maintenance and has nothing to do with how people think about ideas.
A single typeface is a style decision, not a pattern of thinking.
Test size is a sampling choice. Fixation is about how people generate ideas.

o: Critique ideas immediately to save time
Entertain wild ideas and defer judgement
Stay on one idea only
Do it alone silently
4.e: Focus on the topic, encourage wild ideas, go for quantity, defer judgement, use sticky notes.
w: Immediate critique blocks idea flow.
Staying on one idea narrows the search.
Brainstorming works through building on others' ideas.

4.q: Showing teams an example before they ideate tends to:
o: Always increases originality, since examples spark new angles
Increases fixation on the example, though inspiration can still help
Eliminates fixation, since teams see the full solution space
Has no measurable effect on the ideas produced
4.e: Studies show that a sample solution makes people copy its features, which increases fixation. Existing designs are still valuable as inspiration if used carefully.
w: Examples often reduce originality, because teams copy features from what they were shown.
Examples increase fixation. They do not remove it.
The effect is measurable: groups shown an example produce more similar ideas.

4.q: What is a risk of using AI as a brainstorming partner?
o: It cannot generate usable ideas at all
Teams latch onto the first plausible output, producing similar convergent ideas
It removes fixation completely, so human judgement is no longer needed
It always costs more than running a human workshop
4.e: AI can widen the range of ideas but also create its own fixation: people anchor on the first reasonable output, which leads to convergent, similar results.
w: AI can produce a large number of ideas quickly. The risk is not an absence of ideas.
AI does not remove fixation. It can add a new anchor, and human judgement is still needed.
Cost is not the main risk. The concern is the narrowing of ideas, not price.

o: To impress stakeholders with a polished look
To expose known and unknown unknowns while change is cheap
To avoid having to test with real users
To lock in the final code before testing
5.e: Prototypes are a strategy for dealing with things that are hard to predict: they answer known questions and reveal problems nobody thought to ask about.
w: Impressing stakeholders is a side effect at best. The purpose is to learn.
Prototypes exist to be tested with users, so they do not replace testing.
Code is not final at this stage. Prototypes are meant to be thrown away or changed.

5.q: Which prototyping strategy tends to give better designs and less fixation?
o: Serial prototyping
Parallel prototyping
One perfect prototype
No prototyping
5.e: Parallel prototyping yields better results, more divergence and increased confidence in the final design.
w: Serial prototyping tends to cause more fixation.
One perfect prototype invites fixation.
Not prototyping leaves unknowns.

o: Complete, polished and permanent
Incomplete, easy to change and short-lived
Built only in code
Hidden from users
5.e: Keep them cheap and disposable so learning is maximised and time minimised.
w: Complete and polished is expensive to change.
Prototypes need not be built in code.
Prototypes should be tested with users.

o: Paper prototype or storyboard
A fully coded app with a working backend
A production database with real customer records
A Figma mock-up populated with real data
5.e: Navigation diagrams, storyboards and paper prototypes are low fidelity: quick and cheap to make and easy to change.
w: A fully coded app is high fidelity. It takes real effort to build and change.
A production database is real infrastructure, not a prototype of any kind.
A realistic Figma mock-up with real data looks near-final, which makes it high fidelity.

o: A person behind the scenes secretly acts as the system
The app is fully automated using a finished speech engine
No real user takes part, only expert reviewers
It is only used for A/B tests on live traffic
5.e: In Wizard of Oz, a human simulates the system so you can test an interaction before building it, while the participant believes it is automatic.
w: If the system were really automated, it would not be Wizard of Oz. The point is that a human plays the system.
Real users take part. It is the user who must believe the system works.
It is used early, before the system exists, not to run live A/B tests.

5.q: When should you prototype a part of the design early?
o: When the cost of changing that part will rise over time
When the part is purely cosmetic and easy to restyle
When the part is already final and signed off
Never, because prototypes are only for the whole product
5.e: Prototype early the parts whose cost of change will increase, so you learn about them while there is still time to change them cheaply.
w: Cosmetic changes stay cheap, so there is little to gain from prototyping them early.
If a part is final, there is nothing left to learn from a prototype.
Prototypes can cover a single risky part. They are not only for whole products.

6.q: Which model is the designer's/system's view of how it actually works?
o: User's mental model
Implementation model
Persona
Scenario
6.e: The implementation model is how the system really works; the user holds a mental model; the conceptual model is what you present.
w: The user's mental model is what users believe.
A persona is a user archetype.
A scenario is a story of use.

o: Did I get what I wanted?
How do I specify what I want?
Who built this?
Is it fast?
6.e: Execution = how to turn intention into actions; evaluation = understanding the outcome.
w: That is the Gulf of Evaluation question: did I get what I wanted?
Not a design question about interaction.
Speed is unrelated.

6.q: A progress bar and a confirmation message primarily reduce which gulf?
o: Gulf of Evaluation
Gulf of Execution
Both equally by definition
Neither
6.e: Feedback helps users judge whether the result matches their goal.
w: The Gulf of Execution is about specifying actions.
They do not reduce both equally.
They clearly help evaluation.

6.q: A desktop 'trash can' is an example of:
o: A metaphor that borrows a familiar object but can mislead when stretched too far
A command-line interface that accepts typed text instructions
A persona describing a typical user of the system
A heuristic evaluation of the interface by expert reviewers
6.e: Metaphors help people learn by borrowing a familiar object, but they mislead where the metaphor breaks, such as dragging a disk to the trash to eject it.
w: A command line is text-based and uses no visual metaphor at all.
A persona is a research artefact about users, not part of the interface.
A heuristic evaluation is an inspection method used to find problems, not an interface element.

6.q: A slip is best defined as:
o: A wrong plan chosen because of a flawed understanding
A right goal carried out with the wrong action
A user's failure to interpret the system's response
A metaphor that breaks down when overextended
6.e: A slip is an execution error: the intention was correct but the action went wrong. A mistake comes from a wrong goal or plan.
w: That is a mistake. The error is in the plan, not the execution.
That is the gulf of evaluation, about interpreting feedback.
That is a metaphor failure, which concerns how the interface suggests it works.

6.q: Which interaction style is a two-way verbal or textual exchange?
o: Instructing
Manipulating
Conversing
Exploring
6.e: Conversing covers chat interfaces and voice assistants. Instructing is one-way.
w: Instructing is one-way commands.
Manipulating means acting directly on represented objects.
Exploring means moving around within a represented space.

7.q: In the Model Human Processor, which store has very limited capacity and short duration?
o: Long-term memory
Working memory
Sensory memory only
Cloud storage
7.e: Working memory is small and brief; long-term is large and durable.
w: Long-term memory has huge capacity and long duration.
Sensory memory is brief but not the key bottleneck here.
Cloud storage is not part of the model.

o: Increases the effective capacity of working memory by grouping items into meaningful units
Moves information straight into long-term memory with no rehearsal
Speeds up reading by hiding the less important items
Makes users hold more separate items in mind at once
7.e: Experts chunk information into meaningful units, which effectively expands what working memory can hold. Phone numbers are written in groups for this reason.
w: Moving information to long-term memory takes rehearsal and repetition. Chunking only organises items already in view.
Chunking groups items. It does not hide them, and its aim is understanding, not reading speed.
Chunking does the opposite. It reduces the number of separate items users must hold.

7.q: According to the Yerkes–Dodson idea in the notes, performance is best at:
o: Very low arousal, when nothing competes for attention
Moderate attentional load
Maximum load, when the task demands all of the person's capacity
Zero load, when there is nothing to attend to
7.e: Performance follows an inverted U: it peaks at a moderate level of load, and too little or too much degrades it.
w: At very low arousal people under-engage and make careless errors.
At maximum load people are overwhelmed and performance drops.
With zero load there is nothing to engage attention, so performance is poor.

7.q: Which design choice avoids taxing working memory?
o: Asking users to remember a code from one screen to the next
Showing the options visibly so users recognise them instead of recalling them
Hiding commands behind keyboard shortcuts users must remember
Presenting long, unstructured forms with no grouping
7.e: Recognition over recall: keep needed information visible so users do not have to hold it in working memory.
w: Remembering a code across screens loads working memory, and the code is lost if attention drifts.
Shortcuts demand recall of commands, unless they are also shown on screen.
Ungrouped long forms force people to track many items at once, which overloads memory.

7.q: Using colour, size or position to highlight the key element is an example of:
o: Using representations to direct attention
Increasing working-memory load by adding more visual elements
A dark pattern that manipulates the user
Chunking related items into meaningful groups
7.e: Design implication 1 from the notes: use representations such as colour, size and position to direct attention to what matters.
w: Highlighting one element reduces the search effort, so it lowers the load.
Highlighting what matters is helpful guidance. A dark pattern would steer users against their interests.
Chunking is grouping items for memory. Highlighting is guiding attention to one item.

8.q: Fitts's Law predicts that pointing time depends on:
o: Target colour and how strongly it contrasts with the background
Distance to the target and the size of the target
How many other targets are on the screen (the number of choices)
The user's age and how long they have used computers
8.e: Fitts's Law: pointing time grows with distance to the target and shrinks as the target gets bigger.
w: Colour affects visibility and search, but it does not appear in the movement-time equation.
The number of choices is Hick's Law, which predicts decision time, not pointing time.
Age affects speed in general, but the law itself relates time to distance and size only.

8.q: Which pointing device is generally the fastest?
o: Trackball
Pointing stick
Mouse
Touchpad
8.e: In the notes, the mouse remains the fastest general-purpose pointing device.
w: Trackballs are precise but slower, because long moves need repeated rolling.
A pointing stick controls cursor speed by pressure, which makes fast, accurate pointing harder.
A touchpad has a small surface, so long moves need clutching, which makes it slower.

8.q: The 'fat-finger' problem on touchscreens refers to:
o: Occlusion and imprecision when touching small targets
Network lag that delays the response to each tap
Battery drain caused by a large touchscreen
Colour blindness making buttons hard to tell apart
8.e: A finger is large and hides the target while touching, so small targets are hard to hit. Larger targets and techniques such as Shift help.
w: Lag delays the response, but fat-finger errors happen at the moment of the tap.
Battery use has nothing to do with whether a finger hits the intended target.
Colour blindness affects perception of colour, not whether a tap lands on the right target.

o: The fastest possible layout, proven by typing studies
Dominant and familiar, but not the fastest
Obsolete, replaced by Dvorak on most computers
Used only on touchscreens, never on desktops
8.e: Familiarity and years of practice keep QWERTY dominant even though alternatives such as Dvorak are faster.
w: Alternatives such as Dvorak are faster. QWERTY survives because people already know it.
QWERTY remains by far the most widely used layout, not obsolete.
QWERTY is used on desktops, laptops and phones alike.

8.q: Why are screen-edge/corner targets easy to hit with a mouse?
o: The cursor stops at the screen edge, giving an effectively infinite target depth
Edge targets are drawn larger on screen than other targets
Edge targets are always closer to where the cursor starts
The operating system gives edge targets a faster cursor speed
8.e: Because the cursor cannot move past the edge, you can fling the mouse and still land on the target, so the edge acts as an infinitely deep target.
w: They are not drawn bigger. Their effective depth is larger because the cursor cannot overshoot.
Distance still matters, and edges are no closer than other points. The cursor simply stops.
Cursor speed does not change at edges. The edge only stops the movement.

9.q: Why use DP (Android) or PT (iOS) instead of raw pixels?
o: It keeps sizes consistent across screens with different pixel densities
It makes the app run faster on slower hardware
It is required by app-store policy for every release
It adjusts colours for different screen brightness
9.e: Density-independent units (dp on Android, pt on iOS) keep a button about the same physical size on screens with different pixel densities.
w: Units affect layout size, not execution speed.
Neither store requires these units. They are used because they make layouts robust.
Colour is unrelated to size units.

9.q: Mobile use is best characterised as:
o: Long uninterrupted sessions at a desk
Contextual and frequently interrupted
Always one-handed
Identical to desktop
w: Mobile sessions are short and fragmented.
Mobile use is not always one-handed.
Mobile differs from desktop in context and input.

9.q: Touch differs from click because touch:
o: Touch is more precise than a mouse pointer
Touch has no hover and suffers from occlusion and imprecision
Touch is slower than a mouse for every task
Touch lets you hover a finger to preview items
9.e: A finger covers the target and cannot hover, so touch needs larger targets and no hover-only features.
w: A fingertip is wider than a cursor, so touch is less precise.
Touch can be quick. Its defining differences are no hover and finger occlusion.
Touchscreens cannot detect a hovering finger, so hover-based previews do not work.

9.q: Which testing practice does the notes recommend for device diversity?
o: Test on one emulator
Test on real devices
Skip testing
Test only on newest phone
9.e: Expect device diversity and test on real hardware.
w: One emulator misses real hardware differences.
Skipping testing leaves problems unseen.
Only the newest phone ignores most users' devices.

9.q: Which is a sensible design response to small, dense screens?
o: Shrink all text so the desktop layout fits
Prioritise content, use large touch targets and reveal detail progressively
Copy the desktop layout and let users zoom in
Hide all navigation behind a single icon on every screen
9.e: Small, dense screens need prioritised content, large targets and progressive disclosure. Shrinking the desktop layout does not work.
w: Shrinking makes text and targets too small to read or tap.
Zooming a desktop layout forces constant panning and ignores touch precision.
Hiding all navigation hurts discoverability. Navigation should stay visible where it matters.

10.q: How do most people read web content?
o: Word by word, reading every line in full
They scan the page, often in F- or Z-patterns
They read only the headings and ignore all body text
They look only at the images and skip the text
10.e: Eye tracking shows that people scan web pages, so write concisely and make text scannable with headings, lists and keywords.
w: Reading every word is rare online. Eye-tracking studies show scanning is the norm.
Most people read some body text too, usually the first words of lines and paragraphs.
Images get attention but people also scan text, especially headings and the first words of lines.

o: Cues that help users judge whether a path leads to their goal
How quickly a page loads once the user clicks
The visual contrast between a link and its background
The total number of links on a page
10.e: People forage for information by following scent. Strong cues keep them on the path, and weak scent makes them leave.
w: Speed affects patience, but information scent concerns whether labels signal the right destination.
Contrast makes a link visible, but scent is about what the label tells you about where it leads.
The count of links is a different matter. A page with many links can have strong or weak scent.

o: Truncating a bar chart's y-axis to exaggerate differences
Labelling both axes with units
Using the same scale across charts that are meant to be compared
Citing the source of the data
10.e: A distorted scale makes differences look larger than the data supports, which is design-driven rather than data-driven variation.
w: Labelling axes with units helps readers interpret values accurately, so it supports integrity.
Using the same scale allows fair comparison across charts, which supports integrity.
Citing sources lets readers check the data, which supports integrity.

o: Show many similar charts side by side so they can be compared
Replace all text labels with a single colour legend
Show one big headline number with a trend arrow
Decorate a dashboard so it looks more complete
10.e: Repeating the same chart structure makes comparisons easy, because the eye only needs to spot differences.
w: They are charts, not a substitute for labels or explanation.
A single large number with a trend is a KPI tile, a different display.
Small multiples are analytical. Decoration adds clutter and weakens integrity.

o: Where attention goes first and how the eye travels over the page
How much information memory can hold at once
How many colours a palette should include
Which page loads first when a user opens the app
10.e: Size, contrast and position set a reading order, so users notice the most important items first.
w: Memory capacity is a cognitive limit. Hierarchy helps work within it but does not describe it.
Palette size is a colour decision. Hierarchy uses size, contrast and position to rank importance.
Load order is a technical matter, unrelated to how the eye ranks what it sees.

11.q: Which colour property should encode ordered quantitative values?
o: Distinct hues for each value
Lightness steps (tints and shades)
Random colours chosen for contrast
A different font for each value
11.e: Use lightness for ordered data, since light-to-dark has a natural order. Use distinct hues for unordered categories.
w: Hues have no natural order, so they suit categories, not ordered quantities.
Random colours imply no order, so readers cannot tell which value is bigger.
Fonts do not encode quantity, and mixing fonts hurts readability.

11.q: Roughly how many hues should you limit qualitative categories to?
o: About 2 hues
About 6 hues
About 20 hues
There is no practical limit
11.e: Beyond about six hues, people struggle to tell categories apart and to remember which colour is which.
w: Two hues can separate only two categories, so it is too few for most charts.
Twenty hues cannot be told apart reliably, especially under colour-blindness.
There is a practical perceptual limit, which is why charts with many categories need another approach.

11.q: To accommodate colour blindness you should:
o: Use colour alone as the signal
Supplement colour with shape, position or size
Remove all colour from the interface
Use only red and green for status
11.e: Colour should never be the only cue. Adding shape, position, size or labels keeps information accessible.
w: Colour alone excludes users who cannot tell the colours apart.
Removing all colour throws away useful cues for the many users who can see it.
Red and green are the classic pair that red-green colour-blind users confuse.

11.q: The Gestalt principle where we group items inside a shared border is:
o: Closure
Common region
Figure/ground
Proximity
11.e: Common region groups elements enclosed in the same area, such as cards or boxes, so they read as related.
w: Closure is about seeing a complete shape from incomplete parts.
Figure/ground concerns how we separate an object from its background.
Proximity groups by closeness. No border is needed.

11.q: Which pair is correct about colour models?
o: RGB is additive (screens) and CMYK is subtractive (print)
RGB is subtractive (print) and CMYK is additive (screens)
Both are additive models used mainly on screens
Both are subtractive models used mainly in print
11.e: RGB adds light, so mixing all colours gives white on screens. CMYK inks absorb light, so mixing them subtracts.
w: This reverses them. Screens emit light (additive RGB) and print uses inks (subtractive CMYK).
CMYK is not additive. Inks absorb light on paper.
RGB is not subtractive. Screens add light.

11.q: Why is consistent font use important?
o: It aids recognition and keeps reading easy on the eyes
It makes designs look more expensive and polished
It hides small layout errors from users
It increases creativity across the team
11.e: Consistency helps recognition, so readers do not have to adjust to new letterforms, which reduces strain.
w: Looks are secondary. The main benefit is readability.
Consistency does not hide errors. It makes inconsistency stand out.
Consistency serves clarity. It does not make the team more creative.

11.q: Which Gestalt principle describes filling in small gaps to see a complete shape?
o: Proximity
Closure
Common region
Figure/ground
11.e: Closure: we prefer complete shapes and mentally fill in small gaps.
w: Proximity groups elements that are close together.
Common region groups elements that share a bounded area.
Figure/ground separates a stable figure from the background.

o: Learnability for a first-time user
How well the server handles heavy load
Whether brand colours are used consistently
How many sales the design generates
12.e: A cognitive walkthrough steps through a task asking four questions from a first-time user's point of view.
w: Server performance is a technical test, not a walkthrough question.
Brand colours are a style matter, not what the walkthrough evaluates.
Sales are a business outcome. A walkthrough checks whether users can complete the task.

12.q: Which is NOT one of the walkthrough's concerns?
o: Will users try to achieve the right effect?
Will they notice the action is available?
Will they associate it with their goal?
Will the database scale?
12.e: The four questions are about goal, visibility, recognising the right action and understanding the feedback.
w: This is a walkthrough question: does the user form the right goal?
This is a walkthrough question: is the correct action visible?
This is a walkthrough question: does the user connect the action with what they want?

o: Visibility of system status
Consistency and standards
Error prevention
Help and documentation
12.e: Keep users informed about what is going on through timely feedback.
w: Consistency and standards is heuristic #4. It says to follow conventions.
Error prevention is heuristic #5. It says to design so mistakes are less likely.
Help and documentation is heuristic #10. It says to support users when the interface is not enough.

12.q: A hidden exit that leaves users feeling trapped violates:
o: Visibility of system status
User control and freedom
Aesthetic and minimalist design
Recognition rather than recall
12.e: Users need clearly marked exits, undo and redo so they can escape from mistakes or unwanted states.
w: Visibility is about showing what the system is doing, not about being able to leave.
Aesthetic and minimalist design is about not cluttering the interface with irrelevant information.
Recognition rather than recall is about reducing memory load.

o: Different experts find different problems, with diminishing returns as evaluators are added
One experienced expert finds every problem
Several evaluators cost less than testing with users
Severity ratings become unnecessary once there are several evaluators
12.e: No single evaluator finds everything, so combining several finds more. Each extra person adds fewer new problems.
w: No evaluator finds everything, however experienced, because each notices different things.
Evaluators cost time and money. Cost is not why you use several.
Severity ratings are still needed to prioritise the problems that are found.

12.q: Severity of a usability problem depends on:
o: Frequency, impact and persistence
Colour, size and position of the affected control
Seniority of the evaluator who reports it
How soon the release date is
12.e: Nielsen rates severity by how often the problem occurs, how serious it is when it does, and whether it persists.
w: Visual attributes may describe the problem but do not determine its severity.
Who reports a problem does not change how much it harms users.
The release date affects planning, not how bad the problem is.

12.q: Which heuristic is violated when users can perform destructive actions with no confirmation and no undo?
o: User control and freedom (and error prevention)
Aesthetic and minimalist design only
Consistency and standards only
Visibility of system status only
12.e: Irreversible destructive actions without safeguards take away the user's control and invite errors, so they are likely severity 4.
w: The problem is not visual clutter, so aesthetics do not explain it.
Consistency is not the issue. The problem is the lack of any safeguard.
Visibility is not the main issue. The harm comes from being unable to reverse the action.

12.q: A weakness of inspection is that:
o: It cannot be done until a working product exists
Experts may miss problems real users hit, and bring their own biases
It needs thousands of participants to be reliable
It always costs more than a field study
12.e: Inspections are cheap and quick but cannot replace real users, who run into problems that experts do not anticipate.
w: Inspection can be done early, even on paper prototypes.
Inspections use a handful of experts, not thousands of participants.
Inspections usually cost less than field studies, so they are good for early checks.

12.q: Which two inspection methods does the course name?
o: Heuristic evaluation and Cognitive walkthrough
Field studies and Laboratory studies
A/B testing and Multivariate testing
Think-aloud and Surveys
12.e: Both are inspection methods: heuristic evaluation compares the UI with Nielsen's 10 heuristics, and a cognitive walkthrough steps through a scenario.
w: These are two of the four evaluation strategies, not inspection methods.
These are two web experiment designs.
Think-aloud is a technique, and Surveys is a strategy.

13.q: Which evaluation method offers the highest realism but least control?
o: Laboratory study
Field study
Survey
Inspection
13.e: Field studies observe people in real contexts, which gives high realism, but researchers can control little of what happens.
w: A lab gives control over the setting, but the artificial setting lowers realism.
A survey collects self-reports, not behaviour in context, so it is low in realism.
An inspection is done by experts, not by users in real use.

13.q: Which is easiest to run at scale but least behaviourally accurate?
o: Survey
Field study
Laboratory study
Cognitive walkthrough
13.e: A survey can reach many people cheaply, but it captures opinions and recalled behaviour, not what people actually do.
w: Field studies need travel and observation time, so they are costly and hard to scale.
Laboratory studies use few participants run one at a time, so they are small scale.
A walkthrough is an inspection and does not use a large participant sample.

13.q: Why combine methods ('triangulate')?
o: Each method has different blind spots in realism, control and cost
To increase the budget so the study seems more serious
To avoid having to state hypotheses in advance
Because ethics rules require at least three methods
13.e: No single method maximises realism, control and generalisability, so combining methods lets the strengths of one cover the weaknesses of another.
w: Triangulation increases confidence in findings, not cost for its own sake.
Hypotheses still matter. Using more methods does not remove the need to state what you expect.
No rule requires three methods. Triangulation is good practice for stronger evidence.

13.q: Which is a well-formed usability success criterion?
o: Users like it
Users complete the transfer in under 60 seconds with at most 5 steps
It looks modern and consistent with the brand
The team agrees that it is good enough
13.e: A good success criterion is objective, measurable, tied to the goal and set before testing.
w: 'Like' is subjective and cannot be measured against a clear threshold.
Looking modern is a matter of taste and cannot be tested objectively.
Team agreement is opinion, not evidence from users.

13.q: A usability task card contains:
o: Goal, Task, Data, Apparatus
Persona, Scenario, Prototype, Budget
Colour, Font, Layout, Logo
Only the task wording
13.e: A task card says what you want to find out (Goal), what the participant does (Task), what you will record (Data) and what equipment is needed (Apparatus).
w: Those are design and planning items. A task card does not describe personas or budget.
Colour, font, layout and logo are visual design properties, not parts of a test task card.
The task alone omits the goal, data to collect and equipment, so the test cannot be planned properly.

13.q: Which is a quantitative usability metric?
o: A participant quote about their experience
Task completion time
A description of a critical incident
An observer's note that a user looked frustrated
13.e: Quantitative metrics are numbers such as time, errors and success rate. Quotes, incidents and observed emotion are qualitative.
w: A quote is words, so it is qualitative.
An incident description is a narrative account, so it is qualitative.
Frustration noted by an observer is a qualitative observation.

13.q: McGrath's taxonomy says evidence trades off:
o: Generalisability, precision and realism
Cost, speed and attractiveness
Colour, size and shape of stimuli
Users, tasks and tools
13.e: McGrath's taxonomy says no method can maximise generalisability, precision and realism at the same time, so every choice trades one for another.
w: Cost and speed matter in practice, but they are not the three McGrath trade-offs.
Visual properties of stimuli are not part of the taxonomy.
Users, tasks and tools describe a study's ingredients, not the trade-off between types of evidence.

13.q: Which list gives the four evaluation strategies exactly as the course names them?
o: Inspection, Field studies, Laboratory studies, Surveys
Inspection, Field studies, Laboratory studies, Experiments
Heuristic evaluation, Cognitive walkthrough, Surveys, Interviews
Inspection, Field studies, A/B tests, Surveys
13.e: The four strategies in §13.2 are Inspection, Field studies, Laboratory studies and Surveys.
w: Experiments are a type of user study (Chapter 18), not one of the four strategies.
Heuristic evaluation and cognitive walkthrough are two inspection methods, and interviews belong under Surveys.
An A/B test is an experiment, not a separate evaluation strategy.

13.q: Which strategy observes users in their real context, with little experimental control?
o: Inspection
Field studies
Laboratory studies
Surveys
13.e: Field studies are realistic because they happen in the real context, but they lack experimental control.
w: Inspection has experts analyse the system. It does not observe users.
Laboratory studies use a controlled environment, so they are more precise but less realistic.
Surveys ask questions instead of observing tasks.

13.q: Which strategy observes users in a controlled environment, giving precise but less realistic data?
o: Field studies
Surveys
Inspection
Laboratory studies
13.e: Laboratory studies trade realism for precision and control.
w: Field studies happen in the real context, with little control.
Surveys ask people questions instead of observing them.
Inspection uses experts, not users.

13.q: Which strategy has experts, not users, analyse the system?
o: Inspection
Laboratory studies
Field studies
Surveys
13.e: Inspection is expert analysis, so it is easy to run but less reliable because experts are not real users.
w: Laboratory studies observe users in a controlled environment.
Field studies observe users in their real context.
Surveys ask people questions.

o: Computing a t-test to compare two means
Exploring why problems occur, with rich descriptions and user voices
Measuring exact task times in seconds
Counting events from server logs
14.e: Qualitative data reveals causes and meaning, and authentic user voices make findings persuasive.
w: A t-test works on numbers, so it needs quantitative data.
Exact seconds are numerical measurements, which are quantitative.
Server-log counts are quantitative. They show what happened, not why.

14.q: Which question type gives richer, unexpected insights?
o: Closed yes/no questions
Open-ended questions
Binary choices between two options
Ranking a fixed list
14.e: Open questions let people answer in their own words, which can surface things the researcher did not think to ask.
w: Yes/no questions restrict answers to what you already expected.
A binary choice limits responses to two options and gives no reasons.
Ranking only gives an order of the options you supplied.

14.q: Clustering differs from coding in that clustering is:
o: Informal grouping of similar items; coding uses formal categories with defined criteria
Automated by software, while coding is done by hand
Numeric, while coding is always verbal
The same thing as coding under a different name
14.e: Both turn qualitative data into something countable. Coding adds explicit definitions and reliability checks.
w: Clustering is usually done by people, for example with sticky notes or affinity mapping.
Neither is inherently numeric. Both start from words or observations.
They are different. Coding is more formal and has defined criteria and checks.

o: Whether independent coders classify the same items the same way
Whether the data follow a normal distribution
Whether the sample was chosen at random
Whether the interface is consistent across screens
14.e: If independent coders agree, the coding scheme is reliable. If they disagree, the categories are refined and coding is repeated.
w: Normality is a check for statistical tests on numeric data, not coding agreement.
Randomness concerns how the sample was selected, not how coders classify.
UI consistency is a design property and has nothing to do with coding.

14.q: To save time with long recordings you should:
o: Transcribe everything word for word
Timestamp the video and transcribe only key segments
Skip analysis and rely on memory of the session
Delete the video once notes have been taken
14.e: Mark timestamps and critical incidents, then transcribe only what matters, because full transcription rarely pays for itself.
w: Full transcription takes a long time and most of it is rarely needed.
Memory is unreliable, so skipping analysis loses evidence.
Deleting the recording removes the evidence you may need to check or revisit later.

14.q: Which Likert scale response is better than a binary easy/hard question?
o: Strongly agree … strongly disagree
Yes / No
True / False
A free-text comment box only
14.e: A Likert scale gives graded responses that can be compared and analysed, so it carries more information than a two-way choice.
w: A binary answer says nothing about how strongly someone feels.
True/False is also binary, so it has the same limitation.
Free text gives rich but unstructured data. It cannot be compared as easily as scale ratings.

15.q: What is the correct order of the six laboratory-study steps?
o: Plan, Recruit, Prepare, Run, Analyse, Recommend
Recruit, Plan, Run, Prepare, Recommend, Analyse
Prepare, Plan, Run, Recruit, Analyse, Recommend
Run, Plan, Prepare, Recruit, Analyse, Recommend
15.e: Plan what you want to learn, then recruit participants, prepare materials, run sessions, analyse the data and recommend changes.
w: You cannot recruit before the plan says who you need, and analysis must come before recommendations.
Preparing materials before planning has no goal to prepare for, and running before recruiting has no participants.
Running comes after the plan, recruiting and preparation, not first.

o: 'Click Settings, then Profile, then Edit.'
'Update your phone number in your account.'
'Try out our new feature.'
'Explore the app and tell us what you think.'
15.e: Good tasks give a realistic goal without telling the participant how to do it, so you can see how they find the path.
w: It tells users the exact path, so you learn nothing about whether they could find it.
It is too vague. Participants do not know what to do, and you cannot measure success.
It has no goal or success criterion, so you cannot compare participants.

15.q: Roughly how many participants usually find major, frequent problems?
o: 1–2 participants
5–8 participants
50–60 participants
Hundreds of participants
15.e: About 5–8 users usually find the major, frequent problems. Use 10–12 for rarer problems and 15 or more when you need statistics.
w: One or two give too little to see patterns, so you may mistake a personal quirk for a problem.
Fifty or more are for statistical comparison, not for finding the major problems.
Hundreds are for surveys or analytics. Qualitative testing does not need them.

15.q: The statement 'We are testing the design, not you' is important because:
o: It reduces defensiveness and encourages natural behaviour
It is legally required before any session begins
It makes participants finish tasks faster
It allows recording without consent
15.e: People who feel judged behave unnaturally, so reminding them that the design is being tested keeps them relaxed and honest.
w: It is good ethical practice, not a legal requirement.
It does not speed tasks. It affects how comfortable participants feel.
Recording always needs informed consent. This statement does not replace it.

15.q: A drawback of thinking aloud is that it:
o: Slows tasks by 25–100%, distorting timing measures
Hides the participant's thoughts
Prevents sessions from being recorded
Requires at least 100 participants to be valid
15.e: Talking while working slows people down. Use retrospective review if timing matters.
w: Thinking aloud is used precisely to reveal thoughts.
Think-aloud sessions can be recorded like any other.
It works with a small sample. It does not need 100 participants.

15.q: In a pilot study you may help participants; in the main study you should:
o: Always step in when participants struggle
Follow the protocol and intervene only by pre-set criteria
Leave the room so participants are not influenced
Skip note-taking so the participant is not distracted
15.e: Decide the intervention criteria in advance and note any help you give, so every participant is treated the same way.
w: Constant intervention biases results because participants stop trying to solve problems themselves.
Leaving the room defeats observation, and participants may need guidance on safety or ethics.
Notes are still essential. Skipping them risks losing observations.

15.q: When prioritising fixes after a study you should:
o: Fix severe problems first and include quick wins
Fix cosmetic issues first because they are easiest
Ignore frequency and rely on severity alone
Wait for more data before fixing anything
15.e: Rate severity and frequency, then fix the most serious problems first and add easy improvements that are cheap to implement.
w: Cosmetic issues are low priority. Severe problems harm users more.
Frequency matters. A problem that affects many users deserves attention.
Waiting delays improvements, and usability studies already give enough evidence to act.

15.q: Informed consent must make clear that participants:
o: Must finish every task they start
Participate voluntarily and can stop at any time
Cannot ask questions during the session
Will be named in the published report
15.e: Informed consent means voluntary participation, the right to stop at any time, and clear information about how data are used and protected.
w: Participants are never forced to finish. They may stop whenever they want.
Participants may ask questions. Consent requires that they understand the study.
Reports are normally anonymised, using participant numbers and secure data storage.

16.q: UI standards both inhibit and enable innovation. How?
o: They fix one dimension, which inhibits there but frees effort to innovate elsewhere
They ban innovation in all interface design
They replace the need for usability testing
They apply only to hardware controls
16.e: Like the screw-thread standard: lock the fastener, then innovate around it. A standard limits one dimension but frees effort for others.
w: Standards do not ban innovation. Innovation moves to dimensions the standard leaves open.
Standards help consistency, but they do not remove the need to test whether designs work.
UI standards apply to software as well as hardware.

16.q: A toolkit/SDK versus a framework: a framework has
o: More architecture, so it is harder to combine with others
Fewer features than a toolkit
No code for developers to write
Only visual components with no logic
16.e: Toolkits are mostly libraries you call, while frameworks impose an architecture that your code must fit into, which makes frameworks harder to combine.
w: Frameworks typically offer more built-in structure and features, not fewer.
Frameworks are made of code. Developers still write code that plugs in.
Frameworks cover logic and structure as well as visuals.

16.q: Threshold and ceiling: a tool that is hard to learn but can build complex things has
o: High threshold and high ceiling
Low threshold and low ceiling
Low threshold and high ceiling
High threshold and low ceiling
16.e: Threshold = difficulty of learning; ceiling = sophistication achievable.
w: Low threshold and low ceiling is easy but limited.
Low threshold with high ceiling is the ideal, and rare.
High threshold with low ceiling is the worst combination.

16.q: For a demo tomorrow, which tool profile fits best?
o: Low threshold, even with a low ceiling
High threshold and high ceiling
No tool, writing everything by hand
A custom framework built from scratch
16.e: Threshold is how hard a tool is to start with, and ceiling is what it can do. For a quick demo, getting to a clickable prototype fast matters more than capability.
w: A high threshold means a long learning curve, which does not suit a demo tomorrow.
Without a tool nothing is clickable in time for the demo.
Building a framework is far too much work for a one-day deadline.

16.q: A main drawback of UI tools is that they
o: Make non-standard widgets harder and can discourage change
Prevent code from being reused
Make interfaces less consistent across screens
Remove the need for user testing
16.e: Tools give reuse and consistency, but their standard parts make the path of least resistance the default, which discourages unusual designs.
w: Tools encourage reuse through shared components.
Tools tend to increase consistency, because designers use the same widgets.
Tools do not tell you whether designs work, so testing is still needed.

16.q: Generative UI frameworks still depend on:
o: Design-system standards such as Material and HIG as constraints
No standards, since the AI invents its own
Only hand-drawn mock-ups supplied by designers
Paper prototypes made for every screen
16.e: Generative UI automates assembly of interfaces but works within the constraints of established design systems.
w: Without standards, generated interfaces would be inconsistent. Constraints are still needed.
Hand-drawn mock-ups are not what generative systems depend on.
Paper prototypes are not part of how generative UI works.

17.q: In A/B testing culture, ‘HiPPO’ refers to:
o: The Highest Paid Person's Opinion overriding data
A High-Priority Product Objective set by management
A Hierarchical Page Prioritisation Order for navigation
A Hypothesis-Informed Prototype Outcome from a test
17.e: HiPPO stands for Highest Paid Person's Opinion. A/B testing replaces opinion with data about what users actually do.
w: This is not what the term means. HiPPO is about opinion versus data, not objectives.
This is not what the term means. HiPPO has nothing to do with navigation.
This is not what the term means. HiPPO describes decisions made without data.

17.q: In an A/B test the 'control' is:
o: The unchanged baseline version
The new design being tested
A survey sent to users
A random mix of old and new
17.e: The control is the existing version, which provides the baseline for comparison. The changed version is the treatment or variant.
w: The new design is the variant, also called the treatment.
A survey is a different method, not a version of the design.
The control is a single unchanged version, not a mixture.

17.q: Why is changing many things at once in a single test a problem?
o: You cannot tell which change caused the result
It guarantees that the new version will lose
It makes random assignment impossible
It removes the control group
17.e: Bundled changes are confounded: if the result moves, you cannot tell which change was responsible.
w: A bundle of changes can win or lose. The problem is that you cannot attribute the outcome.
Random assignment is still possible. The issue is the interpretation of the result.
The control group is still there. The difficulty is separating the effects of the changes.

17.q: Why can removing an unnecessary form field raise conversion?
o: It cuts friction and confusion, so more users complete the form
It makes the page load more slowly
It forces users to create an account
It lowers the price shown to users
17.e: Every field adds effort and a chance for confusion or error, so removing one that is not needed can lift completion rates.
w: One removed field does not slow page load. The effect comes from reduced effort.
Removing a field does not change whether an account is required.
Removing a field does not change prices.

17.q: Macro vs. micro conversions: which is a micro conversion?
o: Completing a purchase
Adding an item to a wishlist
Revenue per quarter
Returning customer rate
17.e: Micro conversions are smaller steps leading to the macro goal.
w: A purchase is the macro conversion.
Revenue is a macro outcome.
Returning rate is a macro outcome.

o: Start with a tiny share of users and stop automatically if results turn harmful
Send all users to the new design instantly
Run the test indefinitely until someone stops it
Run the test only during off-peak hours
17.e: Ramp-up limits risk by exposing few users first. Auto-abort ends the test if the metrics get worse, which protects users and revenue.
w: Sending everyone at once removes the safeguard against a harmful change.
A test must end. Auto-abort stops it early if needed.
Time of day does not define the safeguard. Gradual exposure and automatic stopping do.

17.q: Multivariate testing compared with A/B testing:
o: Tests several variables and interactions, but needs much more traffic
Needs less traffic because it tests fewer ideas
Cannot detect interactions between variables
Is always simpler to design and analyse
17.e: A/B compares whole designs, while multivariate tests combinations of variables. This finds interactions but needs far more users.
w: More combinations to test means more traffic is needed, not less.
Finding interactions is what multivariate testing is for.
It is more complex, since the number of combinations grows quickly.

17.q: Which assignment best supports a valid A/B test?
o: Random assignment of users to A or B
Putting freshmen in A and seniors in B
Letting users choose their version
Putting high-GPA students in A
17.e: Random assignment spreads unknown differences evenly between groups, which avoids selection bias.
w: Year of study is a difference between groups that could affect the result.
Self-selection means the groups differ in motivation or preference.
Grades are a difference that may influence the outcome, so the groups would not be comparable.

18.q: In an experiment, the independent variable is:
o: The factor the experimenter manipulates
The outcome that is measured
An uncontrolled factor that varies with the conditions
A factor held constant across conditions
18.e: The independent variable is what the experimenter changes between conditions. The dependent variable is what is measured.
w: The measured outcome is the dependent variable.
An uncontrolled factor that varies with conditions is a confound.
A factor held constant is a control variable.

o: Internal validity, because you cannot tell what caused the effect
Only the number of participants you can recruit
Only the cost of running the study
Nothing, provided the sample is large enough
18.e: If a confound varies with the conditions, you cannot attribute the effect to the design, so the claim that X caused Y is weakened.
w: Sample size is a separate issue. A confound can ruin a study of any size.
Confounds affect what you can conclude, not what the study costs.
A larger sample does not remove a confound. It makes the biased estimate more precise.

o: Do the results generalise beyond this experiment's people, designs and settings?
Did the manipulated factor actually cause the change in the outcome?
Is the user interface visually appealing to participants?
Was the sample large enough to detect an effect?
18.e: External validity is about generalisability to other people, designs and situations.
w: That is internal validity: whether X really caused Y within the study.
Visual appeal is not a validity concept.
Sample size relates to statistical power, not to generalisability.

18.q: In a within-subjects design where every participant sees condition A first and then B, the main risk is:
o: Ordering (learning/fatigue/carryover) effects
Selection bias only
No risk
Mortality
w: Selection is about who is chosen.
There is a clear risk.
Mortality is dropout.

18.q: Counterbalancing three conditions is done with a
o: Latin square
Pie chart
Random font
Single order
18.e: Each condition appears in each position and before/after others.
w: A pie chart is a display.
Random fonts are irrelevant.
A single order is the problem.

o: Fewer participants are needed and individual differences are controlled
Sessions are shorter because each participant does less
There are no ordering effects, because everyone sees every condition
There is no learning, because the designs are different
18.e: Each person acts as their own control, so fewer people are needed and differences between people drop out. The cost is ordering effects and longer sessions.
w: Each participant does more, so sessions are longer, not shorter.
Within-subjects designs do have ordering effects, so counterbalancing is needed.
Learning from one condition can carry over to the next, even if the designs differ.

18.q: Why does testing a public-facing website with only university students threaten validity?
o: It limits external validity, because results may not generalise to other users
It threatens internal validity only
It makes timing measurements unreliable
It has no effect on the study
18.e: A convenience sample limits generalisability. Results may not apply to the wider user population.
w: The main limitation is generalisation beyond the sample, which is external validity.
Timing measurement is unaffected. The issue is who the participants are.
The sample matters because findings may only apply to people like them.

18.q: Holding the task constant across conditions generally
o: Raises internal validity but may lower external validity
Lowers both internal and external validity
Raises both internal and external validity
Has no effect on either
18.e: Tight control removes noise so you can attribute effects to the design, but a narrow, artificial task may not represent real use.
w: Holding the task constant removes alternative explanations, which raises internal validity.
Control tends to reduce generalisability, since the task becomes artificial.
Control matters, since it changes both what can be concluded and how widely it applies.

18.q: How does the course define an experiment?
o: A fifth evaluation strategy alongside Inspection, Field studies, Laboratory studies and Surveys
A special type of user study with two or more conditions that tests a hypothesis
Any study that takes place in a laboratory
A survey that is sent to many people
18.e: An experiment adds a comparison structure to a user study, so measurements have a reference point.
w: It is not one of the four strategies. It is a type of user study.
Where it is run does not define it. The two or more conditions do.
A survey asks questions. An experiment compares conditions.

o: Reject the null hypothesis; the result is statistically significant
Accept the null hypothesis, because the difference is small
Prove that the new design is better
Collect more data before deciding anything
19.e: A small p means a result this extreme would be unlikely if H0 were true, so you reject H0.
w: When p < α you reject H0. Failing to reject is a different outcome.
Significance does not prove a design is good. It only says the difference is unlikely to be chance.
You may be able to conclude now. More data is not always needed.

o: If H0 were true, a result this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
The new design is 97% likely to be better
3% of users failed the task
The effect size is small (3%)
19.e: p is the probability of data at least this extreme if H0 is true. It is not the probability that H0 is true, and it is not an effect size.
w: p does not give the probability that a design is better.
p is not a rate of failure among users.
p describes how surprising the data are under H0, not how big the effect is.

19.q: Likert-scale data is usually treated as
o: Ordinal
Ratio
Nominal
Interval with a true zero
19.e: Likert responses are ordered, but the gaps between points are not necessarily equal, so they are ordinal.
w: Ratio data has a true zero and equal spacing, which Likert items do not have.
Nominal categories have no order, but Likert responses are ordered.
Interval data does not have a true zero, so that description is contradictory.

19.q: Between-subjects, interval data, not normal: which test?
o: Mann–Whitney U
Independent t-test
McNemar's test
Paired t-test
19.e: Mann–Whitney U is the non-parametric alternative to the independent t-test, so it is used when data are not normal.
w: The independent t-test assumes roughly normal data, which this data does not meet.
McNemar's test is for paired nominal (yes/no) data.
A paired t-test is for within-subjects data, but this design is between-subjects.

19.q: Paired nominal task success (yes/no) before vs after:
o: McNemar's test
Independent t-test
Wilcoxon rank-sum
ANOVA
19.e: McNemar's test compares paired yes/no outcomes, such as the same users' success before and after a change.
w: A t-test needs interval data, and yes/no data is nominal.
Wilcoxon rank-sum compares independent groups on ordinal data, but these data are paired.
ANOVA compares several groups on interval data, not paired yes/no outcomes.

19.q: Why prefer a two-tailed test by default?
o: It tests both directions; one-tailed needs a justified direction
It is always more powerful than a one-tailed test
It ignores the chosen alpha level
It can only be used with normal data
19.e: A two-tailed test detects an effect in either direction. A one-tailed test needs a directional hypothesis justified in advance.
w: A one-tailed test is more powerful in its direction, so this is not the reason.
A two-tailed test still uses alpha, split across both tails.
Normality is a separate assumption, and it is not what makes a test two-tailed.

19.q: Which level has a true zero?
o: Ratio
Interval
Ordinal
Nominal
19.e: A ratio scale has a true zero, such as time, weight or length. Temperature in °C is interval because its zero is arbitrary.
w: Interval has equal spacing but an arbitrary zero.
Ordinal data has order only, so there is no meaningful zero.
Nominal data are labels, so zero has no meaning.

o: Two different effects or groups; investigate before testing
Perfect normality, so a t-test is safe
A bug in the statistical software
Nothing worth investigating
19.e: Two peaks suggest two subgroups or conditions behaving differently, so the average may hide an important difference.
w: A bimodal shape is not normal, so a t-test may not be valid.
The software is computing the histogram correctly. The data have that shape.
A bimodal histogram usually signals something real, such as subgroups or a condition effect.

20.q: A pitch video in this course has about
o: 60 seconds to grab attention
10 minutes to explain every feature
2 seconds to show the logo
No limit, as long as it is engaging
20.e: A pitch video has very little time, so it has to grab attention fast and stay concise.
w: Ten minutes is far too long. Audiences lose interest and the message gets diluted.
Two seconds is too short to say what the product does or why it matters.
There is a limit. Pitches are short because attention is limited.

o: State the problem and why it matters, then the solution and what is unique
List every feature first, then the price
Introduce the team members, then tell a joke
Show the code first, then the demo
20.e: Tell a story: the problem and why it matters come first, then your solution and what makes it different.
w: A feature list is not a story and gives no reason to care.
Team introductions and jokes do not explain the problem or the solution.
Code is not what an audience needs first. They need to understand the problem.

o: Fill slides with text so nothing is missed
Show the interface with powerful visuals; speak to logic and emotion
List every feature so the audience sees the full scope
Read the script word for word so nothing is forgotten
20.e: Less is more: show the real interface with strong visuals and speak to both logic and emotion, so people want to know more.
w: Text-heavy slides make people read instead of listen, so they lose the audience.
Listing every feature dilutes the message, so the key point gets lost.
Reading a script flattens delivery and loses the audience's attention.

o: Few, and given space to stand out
Packed into dense paragraphs so none is missed
Left out, so the story stays simple
Placed in the footer to avoid distraction
20.e: Do not dilute your best evidence. A few strong facts, given room, are remembered.
w: Facts buried in dense text are not noticed.
Leaving them out removes the evidence that makes the pitch persuasive.
Footers are rarely read, so the facts would go unnoticed.

21.q: According to the course review, systems appear when
o: A vision meets reality, and quality depends on how it adapts to reality
The code is finished and released
The budget is approved by management
A manager makes the final decision
21.e: A system appears when a vision meets reality. Quality depends on both the vision and how well it adapts, which is why the design cycle is central.
w: Finished code is not the criterion. The question is whether the vision works in the real world.
Budget approval is a business step and does not determine quality.
A manager's decision does not decide quality. Evidence from reality does.

21.q: Where does the course review place the GUI's impact?
o: It empowered mainstream users beyond computer experts
It reduced the need for larger screens
It made usability testing unnecessary
It slowed adoption by making computers harder to use
21.e: Graphical interfaces made computers accessible to everyone, not just experts, which changed who uses them.
w: GUIs did not aim to shrink screens. They changed how people interact.
GUIs raise the need for testing, since more kinds of people use them.
GUIs sped adoption because they made computers easier to learn.

21.q: Working memory is best described as
o: A small, temporary workspace that holds and manipulates information
Permanent storage for everything we have learned
A brief sensory buffer that holds raw input
A hard drive that stores unlimited data
21.e: Working memory constantly takes in, holds and releases a small amount of information while we work on it.
w: Permanent storage is long-term memory, not working memory.
A sensory buffer holds raw input briefly. Working memory goes beyond this by manipulating information.
Working memory is small and temporary, so the hard-drive comparison fails.

21.q: Which pairs of ideas are recapped in the evaluation part?
o: Experts vs users, field vs lab, study vs experiment, qualitative vs quantitative
Serif vs sans-serif and warm vs cool colours
Hardware vs software and native vs web
Functional vs non-functional and persona vs scenario
21.e: These four contrasts structure the evaluation lectures and help you choose a method.
w: Serif vs sans-serif and warm vs cool are visual design ideas, not evaluation contrasts.
Hardware vs software and native vs web are technology choices, not evaluation contrasts.
Functional vs non-functional and persona vs scenario belong to requirements, not evaluation.

22.q: Synthetic (AI-generated) users should be treated as
o: Hypotheses to be checked against real users
A full replacement for recruiting real users
Ground truth about real users' behaviour
Valid evidence for regulatory approval
22.e: Synthetic users can supplement but not replace real-user empathy, and models may flatter or agree too easily.
w: AI personas lack real emotion and context, so they cannot replace real users.
They are generated by a model, not observed, so they are not ground truth.
They are not accepted evidence in a regulatory context.

o: Goals and constraints
Exact screen mock-ups
Brand colour
Server speed
22.e: 'The only stable thing left is the user's goal.'
w: Exact mock-ups are not what matters.
Brand colour is not what matters.
Server speed is not what matters.

o: Teams fixating on the first reasonable output, so ideas converge
AI producing no ideas at all
The cost of running the model being too high
Designers' typing speed slowing the session
22.e: AI can produce many ideas, but people anchor on the first reasonable output. The designer's role shifts from idea generator to creative curator.

Typing speed does not affect the quality of ideas.

Replacing all human researchers
Reading participants' body language
Running pure A/B tests on live traffic
22.e: AI moderation trades nuance for scalability and consistency, so it suits structured questions and leaves open exploration to people.
w: Researchers are still needed to interpret, explore and decide.
Current AI moderation cannot read body language or subtle reactions.
A/B testing compares versions on live traffic. It is a different method.

Without any human review, to save time
Only for numeric data such as ratings
Never, because it always produces wrong themes
22.e: AI can speed up first-pass coding, but hallucination, bias and over-reliance mean people must check the results.

o: Shifting traffic towards better-performing variants during the test
Using only a single user as the test sample
Ignoring metrics and picking a random winner
Removing the control version from the experiment
22.e: A bandit adapts as results come in, so fewer users are exposed to the losing variants.
w: A bandit still uses many users. It only changes how traffic is allocated.

The control remains one of the arms, so it is not removed.

o: Early hypothesis screening, not as final proof
Replacing every real-user experiment
Demonstrating legal compliance
Judging the visual polish of a design
22.e: Simulated agents lack real emotion and context, which limits external validity. They are useful for screening ideas before real tests.

Visual polish needs human judgement.

Transparent → opaque
Cheap → expensive

Avoid asking users for feedback

The AI acts alone once it has been trained
No users take part in the interaction
AI replaces usability testing

w: An AI acting alone has no human check, which is the opposite of human-in-the-loop.

Consistency and standards
Visibility of system status
Recognition rather than recall
23.e: AI-specific heuristics include transparency and explainability, human-in-the-loop, ethics and fairness, privacy and value alignment.

Recognition rather than recall is a classic Nielsen heuristic.

selfq:
(Q1–Q34 from the original notes; Q35–Q48 added from the Kahoot quizzes and the additional section material.)

Q1 (recall). Name the five Design Thinking stages in order.

Answer

Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test, with iteration looping back from Test to either Prototype or Empathise as needed.

Q2 (explain why). Why does the "Ideate" stage explicitly tell participants to "defer judgement" and "encourage wild ideas," when the later "Test" stage is all about critical judgement?

Answer
