Deferring judgement during ideation protects the volume and diversity of candidate ideas — critiquing too early causes people to self-censor and the group converges on safe, obvious ideas before exploring the wider possibility space. Critical judgement is deliberately postponed to the Test stage, where you have concrete prototypes to evaluate against real user data rather than untested opinions.

Q3 (application). A team designs a checkout kiosk where the "Confirm Payment" button is small and placed in a corner far from where the user's hand naturally rests, while the "Cancel" button is large and centrally placed. Using a course value/principle from this lecture, explain what's wrong and how you'd fix it.

Answer

This violates Fitt's Law: the button used most often / that matters most for task completion (Confirm Payment) should be the large, close, easy-to-hit target, not the rarely-used one. Fix: enlarge "Confirm Payment" and move it to a natural resting position (e.g. thumb zone on a touchscreen); the low-priority "Cancel" action can be smaller/farther away since accidentally triggering it is worse than requiring slightly more effort to reach it.

Q4 (compare/contrast). Contrast a low-fidelity and a high-fidelity prototype in terms of purpose, not just appearance.

Answer

Low-fidelity: rough, fast, cheap to build and throw away; purpose is to test whether the concept/flow is right before investing effort — mistakes here are cheap to fix. High-fidelity: detailed and realistic; purpose is to test the actual look, feel, and fine interaction details close to what will ship — mistakes found here are more expensive to fix, which is why low-fidelity work should happen first (course value #4, "Iterate").

Q5 (recall). What is the difference between a "slip" and a "mistake" as error types, and what's the recommended fix for each?

Answer

A slip is an execution error — the user's plan was correct but something went wrong carrying it out (e.g. pressing the wrong icon); fix with small physical/interface design improvements. A mistake is a planning error — the user's underlying plan/understanding was wrong and they can't self-correct (e.g. misunderstanding what "Clear cache" does); fix by providing clearer information and aligning the interface with the user's actual mental model.

Q6 (explain why). Why is "Do you like the UI?" a poor interview question for a project team to ask, and how would you improve it?

Answer

It's a leading/biased question: because it comes from the project team itself, it invites polite agreement rather than honest feedback, and a yes/no format discourages elaboration. Improve it by neutralising the wording and making it open-ended and specific — e.g. ask the user to recall a specific recent interaction with the UI and describe what they thought or felt, without signalling what answer is hoped for.

Q7 (application). A team observes users of a library self-checkout kiosk and notices several kiosks have a hand-written "press green button twice" note taped next to the scanner. Using concepts from §2.1, what does this artifact reveal, and what should the team do next?

Answer

The taped note is a workaround/hack — physical evidence of tacit knowledge and undocumented practice: the official process doesn't require pressing green twice, but users have learned informally (and taught each other) that it's necessary, likely because of a slip-prone or unreliable first press. The team should treat this as a design signal, not just a curiosity: investigate why a single press is unreliable (an execution/slip problem) and redesign the button/scanner response so the workaround becomes unnecessary, rather than leaving users to keep discovering and re-teaching the hack.

Q8 (compare/contrast). Contrast a scenario and a use case for the same delivery-app situation, and say which one you'd write first and why.

Answer

A scenario is an informal narrative focused on the user's goals and context, deliberately keeping the UI and system details abstract (e.g. "Jason imports his deliveries and follows a suggested route, adjusting along the way"). A use case is the formal, concrete version of the same situation, spelled out as a numbered sequence of system displays and user actions (e.g. "1. System displays options to input orders. 2. User imports orders. 3. System displays recommended route…"). Write the scenario first — it supports early requirements discovery, when you're still confirming what problem you're solving — and only formalise it into a use case once the goal and flow are settled and you're ready for software design/implementation.

Q9 (application). Your team has only interviewed 3 users so far and isn't confident it has covered the full range of user behaviour. Should you build 5 fully detailed personas now? Why or why not?

Answer

No — with limited data, the recommended move is to create provisional personas rather than fully detailed ones, and use them to guide further research rather than to finalise design decisions. Building 5 fully detailed personas from only 3 interviews risks two of the course's named pitfalls at once: too many personas, and personas that are more detailed than the evidence actually supports.

Q10 (explain why). Why does showing a team a sample/example solution before brainstorming tend to make their ideas more fixated, not less, even though the intent was to "inspire" them?

Answer

Study evidence shows participants given a sample solution anchor on that specific example, producing designs that resemble it more than a control group who saw no sample at all — the example itself becomes the fixation point. (The control group still shows some fixation, but on their own first self-generated idea rather than a shared external one.) The lesson isn't "never use examples," but that examples should come after independent ideation, and combined with an explicit instruction to diverge from them, not as a starting template.

Q11 (application). Your team is choosing between two prototyping strategies for an app redesign: (a) build one wireframe and refine it through 6 rounds of feedback, or (b) build 3 different wireframes and refine each through 2 rounds of feedback. Which does the evidence favour, and what specific risk does the other option carry?

Answer

Evidence favours (b), parallel prototyping — in the cited ad-design study it beat serial prototyping on click-through rate, time on site, and expert rating, while producing more distinct (less similar) final designs. Option (a), serial prototyping, carries a specific risk of design fixation: because each round builds on the same single idea, the team is very likely to lock onto that first concept rather than discover a stronger alternative, as illustrated by the serial participant's own account of "sticking with the same idea."

Q12 (application). A ride-hailing app's "cancel ride" button and "confirm ride" button are identically sized and placed right next to each other. A user means to confirm but taps cancel by mistake. Using Norman's model (§6.4), classify this error and name two design fixes.

Answer

This is a slip, not a mistake: the user's intention was correct (confirm the ride), but the physical action went wrong due to poor mapping/affordance — the two buttons are too easy to conflate. Fixes targeting the Gulf of Execution: (1) increase the size/distance/visual distinction between the two buttons (larger, more separated targets reduce the Fitts's-Law-driven chance of a mis-tap, §8.3); (2) add a confirmation step or undo window after "cancel" is tapped, and/or clearer visual/colour differentiation (e.g. destructive red vs. affirmative green) so the affordance itself signals the difference before the tap happens.

Q13 (compare/contrast). Contrast why chess experts outperform novices on a real game board but not on a randomly arranged one, and state the general design implication this supports.

Answer

Experts have built up chunked, structured patterns from meaningful game configurations through practice — recognising a familiar arrangement lets them encode it as a few large chunks rather than many individual pieces. A random arrangement doesn't match any of their learned patterns, so their chunking advantage disappears and they perform like novices. General implication (Design Implication 1, §7.3): good interface representations should reveal real, meaningful structure, because users' pattern-recognition/chunking ability only helps when the structure shown is genuine, not arbitrary.

Q14 (application). Redesign brief: a train-line map currently shows the entire national rail network in full geographic accuracy on a phone screen. Using §7.4 and §9.1, list two concrete changes and explain the memory-related reasoning behind each.

Answer

(1) Replace the geographically accurate map with an abstracted schematic diagram showing only station order and interchange points — this offloads working-memory load (§7.4) by removing irrelevant real-world scale/shape detail the rider doesn't need to complete their journey. (2) Show only the current/nearby portion of the line rather than the whole network at once, consistent with mobile's "show only what you need now" principle (§9.1) — on a small, interruption-prone screen, forcing the rider to locate their relevant segment within a large, memory-taxing map compounds both the working-memory limits from §7.1 and mobile's already-scarce attention.

Q15 (recall). State Fitts's Law's Index of Difficulty formula and explain, in plain language, what larger D and larger W each do to pointing time.

Answer

ID = log₂(D/W + 1), where D is the distance to the target and W is the target's size (width). Increasing D (moving the target farther away) increases the Index of Difficulty and therefore pointing time; increasing W (making the target bigger) decreases the Index of Difficulty and therefore pointing time. In short: closer and bigger targets are faster to point at, which is why screen corners (effectively infinite W, since the cursor can't overshoot) are the fastest possible targets.

Q16 (explain why). A dashboard chart uses ten distinct, arbitrarily assigned colours (red, blue, green, purple...) to represent ten sales regions ranked by revenue. Why is this a poor colour choice, and what should replace it (§7.3)?

Answer

Hue does not imply order, so an arbitrary colour assignment gives no visual cue about which region ranks higher or lower — the viewer has to cross-reference a legend for every single value, adding unnecessary cognitive/working-memory load. Since revenue is a quantitative, ordered value, the fix is to use a single-hue intensity scale (e.g. light-to-dark blue) instead of many arbitrary hues — intensity is easy to compare visually and directly encodes the ordering.

Q17 (recall). Name the four Gestalt principles covered in Lecture 11 and give a one-line description of each (§11.5 lists two more: similarity and continuity).

Answer

Closure — we prefer complete shapes and mentally fill in small gaps. Common region — we group elements that share the same enclosed/bordered area. Figure/ground — we seek a stable, unambiguous "figure" against a background rather than tolerating visual ambiguity. Proximity — we group elements that sit physically closer together, separating them from more distant elements.

Q18 (application). A data dashboard needs to show both (a) which of 5 product categories a sale belongs to, and (b) how large each sale was, in the same colour-coded chart. Using §11.3, how should colour be assigned to each variable?

Answer

Product category is qualitative with no inherent order, so assign a distinct hue to each of the 5 categories (well under the ~6-hue readability limit). Sale size is quantitative/sequential, so encode it using lightness within each hue (lighter = smaller sale, darker = larger sale) rather than a second set of arbitrary hues — this keeps the categorical split (hue) and the ordered magnitude (lightness) each mapped to the colour property that's actually suited to it.

Q19 (compare/contrast). Contrast a cognitive walkthrough and a heuristic evaluation: what does each one specifically catch that the other might miss?

Answer

A cognitive walkthrough is scenario-driven and specifically targets problems a new, first-time user would hit at each step of a task (via the 4 fixed questions about wanting/seeing/recognising/interpreting an action) — it's strong on learnability issues but only examines the specific scenarios walked through. A heuristic evaluation applies broad, general usability principles (Nielsen's 10) across the whole interface, independent of any one scenario — it's strong at catching consistency, error-prevention, and aesthetic issues across the whole system, but doesn't specifically simulate a first-time user's step-by-step reasoning the way a cognitive walkthrough does. Using both together covers more ground than either alone.

Q20 (application). During a heuristic evaluation, an expert flags: "Users can accidentally delete a file with no confirmation dialogue and no way to undo it." Which heuristic number does this violate, and what's its severity rating likely to be?

Answer

This primarily violates Heuristic #3, User control and freedom (no undo/redo, no "emergency exit" from an unwanted state), and arguably also #5, Error prevention (no confirmation check before an error-prone, irreversible action). Given that permanent, unrecoverable data loss is a serious real-world consequence, this would likely be rated a 4 (catastrophic) — imperative to fix before release.

Q21 (explain why). Why does the course recommend triangulating multiple evaluation methods (e.g. a laboratory study and a survey) rather than relying on just one?

Answer

Each method has a distinct, non-overlapping blind spot on the realism/control/cost trade-off (§13.2): inspections are cheap but miss real user behaviour; field studies are realistic but uncontrolled; laboratory studies are precise but less naturalistic; surveys are easy to run but the least behaviourally reliable. Combining methods lets the strengths of one compensate for the blind spots of another, producing a more complete and more trustworthy picture than any single method alone.

Q22 (application). A researcher has 200 open-ended survey comments about a new checkout flow and wants a quantitative summary for a stakeholder report. Walk through the two-step process from §14.6 they should use, and name one risk to watch for.

Answer

First, cluster the 200 comments into a set of interesting themes based on similarity (e.g. "confusion about shipping cost," "praise for one-click checkout," "complaints about form length") — the number of clusters isn't fixed in advance. Second, code/index each comment into a category from that set (nominal if the themes have no inherent order, ordinal if they do, e.g. rating severity of complaint). Risk to watch: coding is not an exact science — the researcher should have a second, independent coder code a 5% sample and check inter-coder reliability; if more than 10% of items are coded differently between the two coders, the category definitions need revising before trusting the full-dataset summary.

Q23 (application). You're planning a laboratory study for a food-delivery app's new address-entry screen, still early in the design process. Write one exploratory goal and one specific (later-stage) goal for the same feature, and explain what would need to be true before you could actually use the specific one.

Answer

Exploratory (early-stage) goal: "Users should be able to enter a delivery address without guidance" — measured by observing signs of confusion or by tracking deviation from the expected entry flow. Specific (later-stage) goal: "Users should be able to enter a delivery address in under 15 seconds" — measured with a simple timer/task-completion metric. Before using the specific version, per the "explain where the target number comes from" rule (§15.2), the team would need a justified baseline for what "under 15 seconds" means — e.g. a competitor benchmark, an existing version's current average time, or a business requirement — rather than picking a number arbitrarily.

Q24 (explain why). Explain how a UI standard can simultaneously "inhibit" and "enable" innovation, using the screw-thread analogy from §16.1.

Answer

The Unified Thread Standard fixes the fastening mechanism itself — manufacturers can't innovate on thread compatibility, since that's exactly what the standard locks down. But by removing that entire design dimension from consideration, it frees manufacturers to focus their innovation effort on everything else around the fastener (materials, coatings, drive types, tools). The same logic applies to UI standards: fixing a baseline interaction pattern (e.g. platform navigation conventions) inhibits variation in that one dimension while enabling designers to spend their creative effort elsewhere in the product.

Q25 (application). You're choosing a tool to build a quick clickable prototype for a stakeholder demo tomorrow, vs. a tool to build the final production app over the next 6 months. Using §16.4 (threshold/ceiling), how should these two choices differ?

Answer

For tomorrow's demo, prioritise a low-threshold tool (fast to learn/use) even if its ceiling is low, since you only need it to demonstrate a look/flow, not to ship a finished product — e.g. a medium-fidelity tool like Balsamiq or Marvel POP. For the 6-month production build, a higher-threshold, higher-ceiling tool (e.g. a proper frontend framework) is worth the steeper learning investment, because the project has enough time to pay off that upfront cost and will need the tool's full capability by the end.

Q26 (application). A team redesigns a checkout page, changing the button colour, moving the testimonials, and adding a new coupon-code field, all in the same A/B test. The treatment loses significant revenue. What is the methodological problem here, and how should the test have been designed instead?

Answer

This bundles multiple independent changes into a single treatment, so even though the test correctly detects that something went wrong, it can't tell which specific change caused the revenue loss — this directly mirrors the course's own Checkout A/B case, where adding a coupon-code field alone (isolated from the rest of the redesign) was the culprit. The test should isolate one change at a time (or use a proper multivariate test designed to disentangle multiple simultaneous variables), so that each change's individual effect can be attributed correctly.

Q27 (compare/contrast). Contrast a between-subjects and a within-subjects design for testing two versions of a search interface, and explain which ordering-effect risk applies to which design.

Answer

Between-subjects: each participant uses only one version (half use A, half use B) — this avoids ordering effects entirely, since no participant experiences both, but requires roughly twice as many participants to get the same per-condition sample size. Within-subjects: every participant uses both versions — this needs fewer total participants and reduces random noise (since each person acts as their own control), but introduces ordering effects: fatigue (performance degrades in whichever condition comes second) or learning (performance improves in the second condition purely from practice with the underlying task, not because that version is actually better). Only the within-subjects design needs counterbalancing (or a Latin square, for 3+ conditions) to cancel out this risk.

Q28 (application). A researcher collects task-completion times for two versions of an app (within-subjects, 8 participants) and finds the data is heavily skewed (not normally distributed). Which statistical test should they use, and why not a paired-sample t-test?

Answer

They should use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test — it's designed for within-subjects (paired) comparisons of interval/ratio data that is not normally distributed (or for ordinal data), which is exactly this situation. A paired-sample t-test assumes the dependent variable is roughly normally distributed; running it anyway on heavily skewed data (with a small sample of only 8, well under the n>30 threshold that makes t-tests more robust to non-normality) risks an unreliable p-value and a wrong conclusion about significance.

Q29 (recall). What does a p-value of 0.03 mean in plain language, and would it be considered "significant" at the conventional α = 0.05 threshold?

Answer

A p-value of 0.03 means that, if the null hypothesis were actually true (i.e. if there really were no real effect and any observed difference were just due to random chance), a result this extreme (or more extreme) would occur only about 3% of the time. Since 0.03 is less than the conventional significance level α = 0.05, this result would be called "significant" — there is enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis and conclude the observed difference likely isn't just random chance.

Q30 (application). A dependent variable records whether each of 100 users completed a task or not (True/False), tested between-subjects (50 in each of two conditions). Which statistical test from §19.5 fits, and why not a t-test?

Answer

Fisher's Exact test (or Chi-square, given the reasonably large sample) fits: the dependent variable (task success, True/False) is nominal and unordered, and the design is between-subjects. A t-test is inappropriate here because t-tests require an interval/ratio dependent variable that can meaningfully have a mean and standard deviation computed on it — a binary True/False outcome is nominal, not interval/ratio, so its "average" doesn't have the same statistical meaning a t-test relies on.

Q31 (application). Your team's pitch video for the course project spends 45 of its 60 seconds listing every single feature of the prototype. Using §20, what's wrong with this approach and how should the time be reallocated?

Answer

This violates the "What/How" story structure and the "less is more" guideline: a feature list skips straight past establishing why the problem matters and doesn't foreground what makes the solution unique — and packing in maximum feature detail contradicts the explicit "less is more" and "leave people hungry for more" guidance for a ~60-second video. Reallocate time to briefly and clearly state the problem and why it matters (a few seconds), show the solution with powerful visuals (the bulk of the time), and explicitly call out what's unique about it — engaging both logic and emotion rather than only listing features.

Q32 (explain why). Why does the Q&A-style "But wait, is there a problem with this process?" question at the end of Lecture 21's course review function as a bridge into Lecture 22, specifically?

Answer

The review lecture re-presents the classical Empathy→Prototype→Evaluate / Design Thinking cycle as a purely human-driven process. The immediately following slide introduces 2026 AI prototyping trends, implying the "problem" is that this classical framing doesn't account for AI acting as an active participant (generating ideas, prototypes, and evaluations) rather than a passive tool the human wields — which is exactly the gap Lecture 22's full AI-augmentation map (§22.1) is built to fill.

Q33 (compare/contrast). Compare Claude Design, Google Stitch, and Figma Make (§22.2) on one dimension: what each tool exports to, or hands off to next.

Answer

Claude Design exports to Canva, PDF, PPTX, or HTML, or can hand off directly to Claude Code for further development. Google Stitch exports to Figma, HTML/CSS, or React, or can hand off to Google AI Studio. Figma Make outputs real, working frontend code directly (such as React and CSS), positioning itself as bridging designers and engineers within Figma's own native pipeline rather than exporting outward to another company's tool.

Q34 (recall — flagged non-examinable). Name the four "mental model shifts" from Lecture 23 that traditional-HCI users need to make when interacting with modern AI systems. (Reminder: Lecture 23 is explicitly marked optional/non-examinable — this question is included only for completeness.)

Answer

(1) Deterministic → Probabilistic: the AI gives likely answers that might sometimes be wrong. (2) Rule-based → Learning-based: its strengths and blind spots depend on its training data. (3) Transparent → Opaque: it may not show its exact decision process but should offer understandable reasons. (4) Fixed → Adaptive: it changes as you interact with it, and your own behaviour shapes its responses.

Q35 (compare/contrast). A user means to press "L" but hits "K"; another user deletes a file by dragging only its desktop shortcut to the bin, believing the file itself is gone. Classify each error and justify.

Answer

The K-for-L keystroke is a slip — the goal was right, the execution was wrong. Deleting only the shortcut is a mistake — the user's mental model (shortcut = file) was wrong, so the goal/plan itself was flawed. Mis-clicking "minimise" when meaning "maximise" is a slip too. ⟦Kahoot wk1–3, wk1–10⟧

Q36 (recall). What is the key principle at the start of brainstorming, and what should not happen while ideas are being offered?

Answer

Focus on quantity first (many ideas, not one polished idea); critique is deferred, so nobody should critique each idea immediately "to save time". ⟦Kahoot wk1–10⟧

Q37 (recall). What makes a good persona, and what does a context scenario describe?

Answer

A persona has a distinct set of behaviour patterns supported by observed data — it is not a single interviewee and not a recognisable celebrity. A scenario narrates how the persona achieves goals using the system (not a list of UI components, a navigation map, or performance/database specs). ⟦Kahoot wk1–3, wk1–10⟧

Q38 (application). Google Drive shows the progress of a file upload; an installer asks "Default or Custom installation?". Which Nielsen heuristic does each illustrate?

Answer

The upload progress indicator = #1 Visibility of system status. Default-vs-custom install = #7 Flexibility and efficiency of use (a fast path for novices, a configurable path for experts). ⟦Kahoot wk5–6⟧

Q39 (application). According to Fitts' Law, which target is fastest to click, and why does consistent font use matter in UI design?

Answer

A large target close to the pointer is fastest (time depends on distance and size). Consistent fonts prevent eye strain and improve readability/recognition; they do not exist to look expensive or hide layout mistakes. ⟦Kahoot wk1–10⟧

Q40 (application). In y = f(x), which variable is independent and which dependent? What goes wrong if confounding variables are not controlled?

Answer

x (the manipulated condition) is independent; y (the measured outcome) is dependent. Uncontrolled confounds threaten internal validity — you can't say the design caused the change. Also, A/B tests are not "experiments with aliens": both observe behaviour, but an A/B test compares conditions experimentally. ⟦Kahoot wk10⟧

Q41 (explain why). In a study every participant uses Design A first and then Design B. What is the risk, and how do you mitigate it? Contrast with between-subjects.

Answer

It is prone to ordering (learning/fatigue/carryover) effects; mitigate by counterbalancing (half A→B, half B→A; Latin square for ≥3). Between-subjects has no learning transfer and shorter sessions, but needs more participants and individual differences may confound. ⟦Kahoot wk1–10, wk10⟧

Q42 (application). A 1–7 Likert response is which level of measurement? For a between-subjects design with interval data that is not normal, which test replaces the independent-samples t-test?

Answer

Likert data = ordinal. For between-subjects non-normal data use Mann-Whitney U (the independent t-test assumes normality). ⟦Kahoot wk10⟧

Q43 (recall). If p < α, what does that mean?

Answer

The result is statistically significant: the observed difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone, so you reject the null hypothesis. ⟦Kahoot wk1–10⟧

Q44 (recall). What small change gave Expedia ~$12M extra profit per year? What does the control condition in an A/B test mean?

Answer

Removing the optional "Company" field from checkout. The control is the unchanged baseline version; the treatment is the new/modified version. ⟦Kahoot wk9⟧

Q45 (application). A booking app has a blue button at the bottom. Which treatment tests button position? How should students be assigned to versions A and B of a room design?

Answer

Change one thing (e.g. only the position, keep the colour) — moving the button to the top and recolouring it confounds two changes (cf. Q26). Assign participants randomly; assigning by year, GPA or self-selection introduces selection bias. ⟦Kahoot wk9⟧

Q46 (explain why). What is one key advantage of UI tools, and how do threshold and ceiling describe a tool's trade-off?

Answer

Tools give consistency and code reuse (and faster iteration); downsides include harder non-standard widgets. Threshold = how hard to learn; ceiling = how sophisticated the output can be — "hard to learn but can do complex things" = high threshold, high ceiling. ⟦Kahoot wk9⟧

Q47 (reading). In the Tullis & Albert IVR study (§13.4): how many participants, which satisfaction questionnaires, and how is a problem's severity score computed?

Answer

6 participants; ASQ after each task and PSSUQ after all tasks. Severity = frequency (% of participants affected) × impact weight (Level 1 = 10, 2 = 5, 3 = 2, 4 = 1; max 1,000). ⟦L13⟧

Q48 (compare/contrast). Compare cognitive walkthrough vs. heuristic evaluation in terms of what they assess and who is needed.

Answer

Cognitive walkthrough: learnability for a new user, scenario-driven four questions, no users needed. Heuristic evaluation: analytic "discount" review against Nielsen's 10, independent evaluators; severity from frequency, impact and persistence; use several evaluators; use in addition to (not instead of) user testing. ⟦L12⟧

(This self-check set is now complete across all 23 lectures — 48 questions spanning recall, explain-why, compare/contrast, and application types, per §9's mixed-question-type requirement.)

mcq.q: What is/are the benefit(s) of video recording your interview sessions with users?
o: The video recordings collect richer qualitative data than taking notes.
The video recording can ensure the interviewee's privacy is preserved.
The video recording and analysis takes less time than identifying and recording critical incidents during observation.
Video recordings can capture subtle emotional reactions and non-verbal cues that are difficult for an interview facilitator or note-taker to capture.
The video recording can support remote asynchronous interviews with remote participants.
mcq.e: The notes list video as ‘rich data (captures everything)’ but ‘time-consuming to review and transcribe’, so C is false; recording also raises privacy concerns, so B is false. E is the less certain one: recordings do make remote, asynchronous review possible.
w: True: video keeps richer qualitative detail than notes.
False: recordings put privacy at risk, not protect it.
False: reviewing video takes longer than noting critical incidents.
True: video captures emotion and non-verbal cues an observer may miss.
True: recordings allow remote and asynchronous sessions.

mcq.q: Which of the following practice(s) correctly describe(s) empathising with users?
o: Ask users to elaborate on their experiences in detail to collect rich qualitative data instead of prompting short, concise answers.
Prioritise asking direct questions over observing users in their natural environment.
An unstructured interview is more encouraged to reduce the risk of interviewer bias than a structured interview.
Perform contextual inquiry in controlled environments to discuss users' challenges.
Provide hints on the step-by-step procedures of a task to facilitate collecting thoughts from users.
mcq.e: Empathy favours rich detail and observation in context. Contextual inquiry is done in the user's real setting (not a controlled one); hints and leading steer the user; unstructured interviews increase, not reduce, variability.
w: True: invite detailed stories rather than prompting with answers.
False: observing in context is at least as valuable as asking.
False: unstructured interviews carry more interviewer bias, not less.
False: contextual inquiry belongs in the user's real setting.
False: hints bias what users tell you.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about different methods of usability testing?
o: Inspection-based testing is more theoretical than a laboratory study.
Heuristic evaluation involves target users.
In contrast to heuristic evaluations, usability testing collects qualitative data.
A laboratory study has more interventions than an observational field study.
A field study is more obstructive than an interview.
mcq.e: Inspections use experts and theory, not users. Labs control and intervene more than field observation. Both methods can yield qualitative data, and field observation is less obtrusive than an interview.
w: True: inspection is more theoretical than a laboratory study.
False: heuristic evaluation uses experts, not target users.
False: usability testing and inspection can both give qualitative data.
True: a laboratory study intervenes more than field observation.
False: a field study is less obstructive than an interview.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE about brainstorming?
o: Critique ideas to help refine ideas for better outcomes.
Foster an open environment to ensure all participants feel comfortable sharing their ideas.
Encourage wild ideas during brainstorming to make innovative solutions.
Avoid having a facilitator to make everyone feel equal.
Brainstorming should be focused on generating a lot of ideas instead of identifying a few good ideas.
mcq.e: Defer judgement during brainstorming (A is false), and a facilitator keeps the session on track (D is false). B, C and E are true brainstorming guidelines.
w: False statement: critique is deferred in brainstorming.
True statement: an open environment helps participation.
True statement: wild ideas are encouraged.
False statement: a facilitator keeps the session working fairly.
True statement: aim for quantity first.

mcq.q: Which of the following is/are true about addressing fixation when brainstorming?
o: Attach to the initial idea and refine it to improve the designs.
As long as brainstorming has an open environment, we do not have to consider fixation.
Encourage designers to focus on how to solve the problem without thinking about the functional features of an application.
Provide sample example solutions that are relevant to our application before brainstorming.
Encourage participants to draw inspiration from existing products and solutions.
mcq.e: Fixation means locking onto the first idea or familiar function, so reframe away from features and look widely for inspiration. Sample solutions given beforehand increase fixation (Dow et al.).
w: False: attaching to the first idea is fixation.
False: an open environment does not remove fixation.
True: focus on the problem, not on existing functional features.
False: example solutions increase fixation.
True: drawing on diverse existing products widens the search.

mcq.q: Which of the following suggestion(s) help(s) to improve the design during the prototyping phase?
o: The use of an online low/mid-fidelity prototyping tool should be avoided.
We should wait until we have a finalised application before conducting user testing to ensure comprehensive feedback.
High-fidelity prototypes are essential for gathering accurate user feedback during the early design process.
Utilise iterative cycles of prototyping and testing to continuously refine the design based on feedback from users.
We should implement all ideas that we come up with to gain valuable insights from users.
mcq.e: Fail early, fail cheap: low-fidelity prototypes early, iterate with user feedback. Waiting for a finished product or building everything wastes effort.
w: False: low/mid-fidelity tools suit early prototyping.
False: waiting for a finished app is too late for cheap changes.
False: early feedback does not need high fidelity.
True: iterating between prototype and test improves design.
False: building every idea wastes effort.

mcq.q: Which of the following scenario(s) illustrates a ‘slip’?
o: While completing a form halfway, you press ‘Back’ to retrieve information from the previous page but your entered information has disappeared.
You accidentally click ‘Delete’ on an email when you meant to click the ‘ARCHIVE’ button next to it.
You visit the SMU Admin building for your regular weekly meeting without realising the meeting place was changed to SCIS 1 SR 4.1.
Using a restaurant recommendation app, you press an icon with food images to show types of food but it shows a list of restaurants.
You aim to copy with CTRL+C but mistakenly press CTRL+X and cut the contents.
mcq.e: A slip is a correct intention executed wrongly (adjacent button, wrong key). A, C and D are mistakes: the plan itself was wrong because of a wrong or outdated mental model.
w: False: expecting something and getting something else is a mistake, not a slip.
True: right goal, wrong action on an adjacent control is a slip.
False: wrong plan from outdated information is a mistake.
False: misreading an icon is a mistake.
True: intended CTRL+C but pressed CTRL+X is a slip.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) correctly describe(s) empathy with users?
o: Empathy can be avoided in later stages when we focus on technical implementations.
Ask users to use your systems over an extended period and write a note on their experiences to identify pain points.
Empathy focuses on emotional reactions to design and does not require a deep understanding of user tasks or contexts.
Apply quantitative surveys alone to effectively understand user preferences and behaviours.
Observe how technical engineers interact with the system to identify potential improvements.
mcq.e: Diary-style, longitudinal self-reporting is a recognised empathy method. Empathy needs context and tasks, is not just surveys, and concerns the real target users, not engineers.
w: False: empathy matters in every stage.
True: diaries over time reveal problems you would otherwise miss.
False: empathy requires understanding tasks as well as feelings.
False: surveys alone miss why people behave as they do.
False: engineers are not the target users.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) correctly describe(s) user-centred design (UCD) practices?
o: Test with your target users to identify directions for improvement.
Ideation is a critical step to understand users' needs.
Avoid observational testing as we do not have direct interactions with users.
Specify a persona of the target users during the Define phase.
Prototype requires having full functionalities before testing it with users.
mcq.e: Understanding needs is the Empathise stage, not Ideate. Observation is valuable, and prototypes can be partial.
w: True: test with target users to find directions for improvement.
False: ideation is not how you understand needs; Empathise is.
False: observation is a key way to learn from users.
True: personas are defined in the Define phase.
False: prototypes can be partial before testing.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about unstructured interviews?
o: Learn about the user by preparing the questions in advance and ad hoc during the session.
It is more suitable for experienced interviewers as they can follow pre-defined questions.
An interviewer has complete control over a session and decides which questions to be asked.
Provide rich insights into things that are difficult to articulate.
Reduce the variability of the collected data due to the interviewer's experience.
mcq.e: The notes: unstructured = interviewer has full control and chooses questions on the fly; maximum depth and flexibility but least comparability (so E is false, and ‘pre-defined questions’ describes structured interviews).
w: False: preparing questions in advance describes semi-structured interviews.
False: experienced interviewers suit unstructured ones; pre-defined questions are structured.
True: the interviewer decides the questions freely.
True: it yields rich insight into hard-to-articulate things.
False: unstructured interviews increase variability.

mcq.q: When designing an AI-assisted clinical decision-making application for healthcare professionals, which user characteristics is/are critical to consider?
o: Openness to use AI in practice.
Technology literacy.
Age of the health professionals.
Whether the health professional is in a control group or a treatment group.
Experience of practising medical conditions.
mcq.e: Attitude to AI, technology literacy and clinical experience shape how they use the tool. Age alone is a weak proxy, and control or treatment group is an experiment label, not a user characteristic.
w: True: openness to AI affects adoption.
True: technology literacy affects use.
False: age is not a key characteristic here.
False: control or treatment group is an experiment assignment, not a user characteristic.
True: clinical experience affects how they judge decisions.

mcq.q: Which of the following options are NOT commonly used as a metaphor in user interface design?
o: Shopping cart icon to present items a user intends to purchase.
Folder icon to organise files and documents.
Scissor icon for cutting contents in the document.
Trash can icon for discarding unwanted files or items.
Speed limits to indicate the performance of websites.
mcq.e: Cart, folder, scissors and trash are standard metaphors; speed limits for website performance are not.
w: False: the cart icon is a common metaphor.
False: folder is a common metaphor.
False: scissors for cut is a common metaphor.
False: trash can is a common metaphor.
True: speed limits for performance are not commonly used.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE about inspections?
o: Design experts during inspections are the best people to provide feedback as they are unbiased.
Inspection procedures do not require specifying realistic actions or tasks if design experts are involved.
Design experts are difficult to recruit because there are fewer ethical and practical issues to consider.
Inspections are more theoretically oriented than user testing.
Design experts can miss important problems in a system.
mcq.e: Experts are not unbiased and are not users; inspections still need realistic tasks or scenarios; and recruiting is hard for other reasons, not because there are fewer ethical issues. D and E are true.
w: False statement: experts are biased and miss problems.
False statement: inspection still needs realistic tasks.
False statement: experts are not hard to recruit because of fewer issues.
True statement: inspection is more theoretical than user testing.
True statement: experts can miss problems.

mcq.q: Which strateg(ies) can you employ to gather the requirements of developers, marketing officers and product managers and align everyone with the user requirements?
o: Hold regular cross-team meetings to gain consensus on user needs and create scenarios.
Define which data will be collected from users before specifying personas and scenarios.
Utilise prototypes to discuss and gather feedback from team members on how an application would benefit target users.
Specify multiple personas based on the requirements of each team member.
Compile a document of comprehensive requirements based on the perspectives of stakeholders without involving target users.
mcq.e: Align through shared artefacts (scenarios, prototypes) tied to real users. Personas represent users, not team members, and requirements without users miss the point.
w: True: cross-team meetings build consensus and scenarios.
False: personas and scenarios come before deciding data to collect.
True: prototypes help stakeholders see user benefit.
False: separate personas for each team member fragments focus.
False: ignoring stakeholders misses requirements.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE about personas and scenarios?
o: Personas should be generic to make your system applicable to a wide range of users.
Personas should be updated frequently to reflect changing user needs and market conditions.
Scenarios describe the context and functions of an application through a narrative story.
Personas should not be defined without real data.
Personas should outline the demographic characteristics of the target audience without considering their goals or challenges.
mcq.e: Good personas are specific and include goals, pain points and context, not just demographics. They should be based on real data.
w: False statement: personas should be specific, not generic.
True statement: personas should be updated.
True statement: scenarios are narrative stories of context and function.
True statement: personas need real data.
False statement: personas need behaviours and goals, not just demographics.

mcq.q: Which of the following statements is/are a closed-ended and unbiased interview question?
o: “What do you look for when you do online shopping?”
“Why do you think that AI could assist your practice?”
Rate on a scale of 1 to 5, “How well does this application assist your tasks?”: (1) Strongly assist … (5) Strongly does not assist.
“How much more or less time do you spend on your WhatsApp versus Telegram?”
“Which of the two interface versions do you like more?”
mcq.e: Closed-ended questions give fixed response options (a rating scale, a choice between two). A is open-ended, B is leading (assumes AI could assist), D invites a free numeric estimate.
w: False: open-ended, not closed.
False: leading and open-ended.
True: a rating scale is closed and neutral.
False: it is comparative and odd, not a clean closed question.
True: two options with neutral wording are closed.

mcq.q: You are designing an app for a bike rental service. Which scenario(s) represent(s) an edge case that the design must account for?
o: A user reviews a map with available bikes around the current location.
A user inspects images and descriptions of a bike to ensure its quality.
A user utilises filters to specify a type and years of bikes.
A user needs to extend the rental period, which is different from the standard process of renting a bike.
A user reviews detailed feedback on a previous bike user to assess the quality of a bike.
mcq.e: An edge case departs from the standard (‘happy path’) flow, such as extending a rental. The others are normal flows.
w: False: viewing a map is a standard flow.
False: inspecting a bike is a standard flow.
False: filtering is a standard flow.
True: extending a rental differs from the standard flow.
False: reading reviews is a standard flow.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) best reflect(s) UCD practices?
o: Prototypes should always be high-fidelity from the beginning to ensure accurate feedback.
Once a prototype has been reviewed and tested with the internal team, the design is considered final and moves to production.
After testing with users, it is not necessary to empathise with different users.
Observational testing should be avoided due to lack of direct user feedback.
Prototypes are revised iteratively based on feedback, requiring revisiting ideation, prototyping and testing phases multiple times.
mcq.e: UCD is iterative: testing with real users sends you back to earlier stages.
w: False: early prototypes can be low-fidelity.
False: internal review does not make a design final.
False: you still empathise with different users after testing.
False: observational testing is valuable.
True: UCD is iterative based on feedback.

mcq.q: Which sequence(s) correctly execute(s) the user-centred design process as discussed in class?
o: Ideate, prototype, and test.
Prototype, test, ideate, prototype, and test.
Define, prototype, and test.
Empathise, define, ideate, prototype, and test.
Empathise, define, ideate, prototype, evaluate, ideate, prototype, and test.
mcq.e: The full cycle is Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test, and iteration can loop back (E). A–C skip stages.
w: False: it skips Empathise and Define.
False: it starts with Prototype.
False: it skips Empathise and Ideate.
True: the standard five-stage order.
True: iteration back to Ideate after evaluation is allowed.

mcq.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE about the benefits of personas and scenarios?
o: Personas and scenarios can assist the team to scope the problem to the target audience and their needs.
Personas should be updated frequently to reflect changing user needs and market conditions.
Making multiple personas can make the problem applicable to a wide range of target users.
Facilitate communications with diverse stakeholders.
Personas can assist a team in maintaining focus throughout the user-centred design process by representing specific user needs and behaviours.
mcq.e: Personas are meant to narrow focus on specific users; creating many personas just to cover everyone defeats the purpose. (B also appears as an option in Q15, where it is treated as true.)
w: True statement: personas scope the target audience.
True statement: update personas.
False statement: too many personas dilute focus.
True statement: personas aid communication.
True statement: personas help keep focus.

mcq.q: Which of the following scenario(s) illustrates a ‘mistake’?
o: Expecting to find a list of nearby eateries, you click a burger icon in an app but are surprised when it displays a menu of food items.
You head to your usual meeting spot at Starbucks, not realising the meeting point was changed to Coffee Bean today.
You install Google Drive because you misunderstand its purpose, thinking it will provide post-office locations.
You aim to save a file but accidentally click an adjacent ‘exit’ button, closing the program without saving.
You click ‘reply all’ when you had intended to click ‘reply’ to respond only to the sender.
mcq.e: A mistake comes from a wrong plan or mental model (wrong expectation, outdated information, misunderstanding). D and E are slips: correct intention, wrong action.
w: True: a wrong understanding of the icon is a mistake.
True: a wrong plan from outdated information is a mistake.
True: misunderstanding the purpose is a mistake.
False: clicking an adjacent button by accident is a slip.
False: reply-all when you meant reply is a slip.

mcq.q: What does the term ‘typography’ refer to in visual design?
o: To design a grid layout of web pages.
To design text for software development.
To determine font size to create emphasis.
To create images and styles for visual appeal.
To arrange and style text for readability.
mcq.e: Typography is the arrangement and styling of text so that it is readable and communicates well.
w: False: layout grids are layout, not typography.
False: typography is not about software text.
False: font size alone is only part of typography.
False: visual appeal is broader.
True: typography arranges and styles text for readability.

mcq.q: You are designing a flight training simulator with a physical mock cockpit and simulation software, for training airline pilots. Which statement(s) is/are true?
o: Despite the blinking red signal, a user unknowingly crashed while landing without the gears out. This is a problem with bridging the gulf of evaluation.
A user cannot remember where the cockpit light switch is located even though he used it 10 minutes ago. This indicates that he has a poor working memory.
It would be appropriate to evaluate the simulator with participants who frequently travel by air.
A user confused the aileron control stick with the throttle stick when attempting to gain speed. This is a problem with bridging the gulf of execution.
The simulator's lexicon should contain common words that can be understood by its users.
mcq.e: Not noticing or understanding the signal is an evaluation problem; confusing controls is an execution problem; use the users' own language. B blames the user for what is a design issue, and C uses the wrong participants: test with trainee or airline pilots.
w: True: not noticing or understanding the signal is a gulf of evaluation problem.
False: this blames the user; forgetting a switch location is a design issue.
False: evaluate with the intended users, such as pilots or trainees.
True: confusing controls is a gulf of execution problem.
True: use words the users understand.

mcq.q: Direct manipulation is one of the user interaction styles. Which of the following is/are true?
o: It is faster than a command-line interface if the user needs to perform a large number of actions on many objects.
It focuses on physical actions instead of complex syntax in a ‘programming’ language.
It allows the user to interact with visible objects of interest in the user interface environment.
It works well for users with motor skill impairments, especially if it is heavily based on physical actions.
It allows physical, reversible and incremental actions that receive immediate feedback.
mcq.e: Direct manipulation = visible objects, physical actions, reversible incremental actions with immediate feedback. It is not necessarily faster for bulk operations (command lines can batch) and is hard for people with motor impairments.
w: False: command lines are faster for repetitive batch actions.
True: direct manipulation uses physical actions rather than syntax.
True: users act on visible objects.
False: it can be hard for users with motor impairments.
True: actions are physical, reversible and incremental with feedback.

mcq.q: Which scenario(s) illustrate(s) a mismatch between the designer's conceptual model and the user's mental model?
o: A search bar that displays relevant results as soon as the user begins typing.
A ‘Save’ icon in a document editor that requires clicking ‘Save As’ each time instead of just ‘Save’ to update the current document.
Clicking ‘Add to Cart’ directs the user to a page that recommends related items instead of adding the item directly to the cart.
A mobile banking app that uses a password prompt to verify each transaction.
A music app where the play button starts playing a song when clicked.
mcq.e: The system behaves differently from what the user expects. A, D and E behave as expected.
w: False: that matches user expectation.
True: needing Save As each time mismatches expectation.
True: Add to Cart not adding is a mismatch.
False: a password prompt is intended design.
False: play playing is expected.

mcq.q: Which statement(s) about colours is/are FALSE?
o: Blue is sometimes associated with calmness and stability.
Analogous colours are directly opposite to each other on the colour wheel.
Red is always regarded as good luck and celebration.
Complementary colour scheme creates a high-contrast effect.
A triadic colour scheme uses colours that are evenly spaced around the colour wheel.
mcq.e: Analogous colours sit next to each other; complementary colours are opposite. Colour meanings are cultural: red is lucky in Chinese culture but signals danger or ‘stop’ in the West.
w: True statement: blue suggests calm.
False statement: analogous colours are neighbours.
False statement: red is not always lucky; meaning varies.
True statement: complementary schemes give contrast.
True statement: triadic colours are evenly spaced.

mcq.q: Which statements describe strategies to get information into long-term memory?
o: Creating a to-do list of items in a mobile application.
Practising using a QWERTY keyboard multiple times to improve typing speed.
Reading instructions repeatedly to be familiar with the steps.
Splitting a sixteen-digit credit card number into sets of four.
Copying out the contents of a script multiple times.
mcq.e: Repetition and practice move information into long-term memory. A to-do list is an external aid; splitting digits is chunking (helps working memory).
w: False: a to-do list offloads memory instead of storing it.
True: repeated practice builds long-term memory.
True: repetition aids memorisation.
False: splitting numbers is chunking for working memory.
True: copying repeatedly rehearses material.

mcq.q: Which statement(s) about input devices is/are true?
o: Input using a touch screen is better than a mouse for accuracy and speed.
There are drawbacks in using on-screen keyboards compared to physical keyboards, since they can be redesigned to fit any user's hand size.
Typing on the keyboard is slower than dictation in general.
Mouse is frequently used to enter text into the system.
QWERTY is designed to be the fastest keyboard format, which is why it is so popular and currently the most used format.
mcq.e: Dictation is generally faster than typing. QWERTY persists through network effects and training inertia, not speed, and touch is not better than a mouse for accuracy.
w: False: touch is less accurate than a mouse.
False: on-screen keyboards can be redesigned, which is an advantage.
True: dictation is generally faster than typing.
False: a mouse is not the main text-entry device.
False: QWERTY is not the fastest.

mcq.q: Which statement(s) is/are FALSE for using UI tools and design guidelines?
o: Reduce the learning curve to interact with an application.
Require higher development costs to import existing libraries.
UI tools offer features to easily compare the usability of prototype applications.
Support a highly flexible development environment to create customised features.
Maximise compatibility of a prototype application with widely accepted design conventions.
mcq.e: Libraries lower development cost, and UI tools do not automatically compare usability. (D is also debatable: flexibility is limited by a tool's ceiling.)
w: True statement: tools reduce learning curves.
False statement: libraries lower development cost.
False statement: UI tools do not compare usability for you.
True statement: tools allow flexible environments.
True statement: tools help maintain conventions.

mcq.q: Which of the following is/are true about Fitts' Law?
o: Apple menu bars (fixed at the top of the screen) are faster to target than Windows' menu bars because the screen edge creates a virtually infinite target height.
Magic pixels (pixels at each corner of the screen) defy Fitts' Law because the screen frame stops the cursor from moving past them.
Microsoft toolbars offer the option of displaying a label below each tool. This makes the labelled tool accessed faster, because of Fitts' Law.
In a car's dashboard design, placing the most frequently used buttons far from the driver will make them easier to reach quickly.
Fitts' Law is useful when reaching a target object faster would make a UI easier to use.
mcq.e: Time falls as targets are larger and nearer; edges and corners act as very large targets (so magic pixels obey Fitts' Law, B false), and labels enlarge the target. Frequent controls should be close, not far.
w: True: edge-fixed menus are infinitely tall targets.
False: magic pixels obey Fitts's Law via infinite size.
True: labels enlarge the clickable target.
False: far placement makes frequent buttons slower.
True: Fitts's Law helps when reaching faster improves use.

mcq.q: Which is/are true about drag-and-drop interfaces in UI tools?
o: It results in consistent behaviour across devices and platforms.
Visual feedback during drag-and-drop helps prevent mistakes.
It increases the amount of manual coding required.
It incurs higher costs as customisations are needed.
A high level of competency is required to be able to use it.
mcq.e: Drag-and-drop tools have a low threshold and reduce coding; their cost is limited customisation. Immediate visual feedback helps prevent errors.
w: False: behaviour is inconsistent across platforms.
True: drag feedback helps avoid mistakes.
False: it reduces manual coding.
False: it reduces cost.
False: it lowers the competency needed.

mcq.q: Why should we maintain UI consistency in a project?
o: It increases the development time.
It presents a professional design.
It ensures a seamless and predictable user experience.
It makes the application look monotonous.
It reduces the application's performance.
mcq.e: Consistency (Nielsen's heuristic 4) makes interfaces predictable and professional.
w: False: consistency reduces development time.
True: consistency looks professional.
True: consistency makes it predictable.
False: consistency is not monotony.
False: it does not reduce performance.

mcq.q: Which do you AVOID in terms of colour design strateg(ies)?
o: Use only one colour for the entire contents even when there are keywords to be highlighted.
Apply a complementary colour scheme to highlight two contrastive pieces of information.
Use six colour combinations to show creative designs.
Choose colour schemes carefully to make information accessible for people with colour blindness.
Consider different meanings of colours by countries, regions or other contexts.
mcq.e: Avoid one colour when emphasis is needed, and avoid too many colours. B, D and E are good practice.
w: Avoid: one colour cannot highlight keywords.
Do: complementary colours contrast two pieces of information.
Avoid: too many colours confuse.
Do: design for colour blindness.
Do: respect colour meanings by culture.

mcq.q: Identify the item(s) NOT commonly used as a metaphor in user experience (UX) design.
o: Stove controls in digital interfaces.
Bin icon for word processor.
Tree branches for user navigation paths.
Traffic lights for progress indicators.
Desktop as a virtual workspace.
mcq.e: The bin, tree view and desktop are standard metaphors (notes: desktop, trash bin, file cabinet, tree view). Stove controls and traffic lights for progress are not standard.
w: True: stove controls are not a common metaphor.
False: bin is a common metaphor.
False: tree branches are a common metaphor.
True: traffic lights are not a common progress metaphor.
False: desktop is a common metaphor.

mcq.q: Which statements describe steps in the Gulf of Evaluation in Don Norman's Action Cycle?
o: A user assesses the result of a calculation done using a spreadsheet.
A user interprets an error message in a dialogue box.
A user intends to click on the ‘Home’ icon on a mobile application.
A user sees the screen rotate from portrait to landscape mode.
A user decides to click the ‘Send’ button to submit an email.
mcq.e: The evaluation side is perceive → interpret → evaluate. Forming an intention and deciding on an action belong to the gulf of execution.
w: True: assessing the result is evaluation.
True: interpreting an error message is evaluation.
False: forming the intention is execution.
True: perceiving the state change is evaluation.
False: deciding to act is execution.

mcq.q: You are designing a virtual reality basketball game on a mobile phone. The game begins by choosing your team and players before a training session. Which statement(s) is/are FALSE?
o: The virtual players and basketball are objects in the conceptual model.
The game should use virtual reality terminology (e.g., rotate) to represent the actions performed on the objects, such as the basketball.
The interaction style that best describes this game is direct manipulation.
Touching an object in this virtual world launches a pop-up menu. However, most users expect some form of interaction. This indicates a gap between the user's mental model and the conceptual model.
Users are complaining that aiming the basketball into the net does not ‘feel’ right. This indicates a problem with bridging the gulf of evaluation.
mcq.e: Use the users' own language rather than technical terminology (B). Aiming that doesn't feel right is more about how the action maps to the result (execution/feedback), so E is the weaker claim. These two are my best reading; E is the less certain.
w: True statement: players and ball are objects in the conceptual model.
False statement: use the users' own language, not technical VR terms.
True statement: acting directly on objects is direct manipulation.
True statement: expecting some interaction shows a gap with the user's mental model.
False statement: an off aiming feel is about mapping the action to the result, not evaluating feedback.

mcq.q: Human working memory can only hold a limited amount of information for a short period. Which UI design choice(s) might help reduce memory overload?
o: Differentiating new data entries from defaults or pre-existing data with visual cues in a form.
Consolidating all data fields onto a single, complex page in a data entry form.
Using new terminology so that the user can remember in order to complete tasks.
Displaying the number of unread items in the notifications bell with an icon indicator.
Implementing a breadcrumb trail to indicate the user's navigation path through a website visually.
mcq.e: Recognition cues and visible state (badges, breadcrumbs) offload memory; cramming everything onto one page or inventing terms raises memory load.
w: True: visual cues reduce recall load.
False: one complex page overloads memory.
False: new terminology adds learning load.
True: an unread badge supports recognition.
True: breadcrumbs show the path.

mcq.q: You are writing an article ‘Creating Content on Social Media’ aimed primarily at readers over 60. Which advice should be AVOIDED?
o: Consider including a summary page that outlines key tips for enhancing the appeal of social media content.
Break down information into short, manageable sections. Use headings to organise content logically.
Restrict the vocabulary to slang and phrases to keep the content exclusive to those who can understand it.
Involve social media content creation experts to evaluate the relevance and quality of the article.
Limit the use of alternative text and descriptive captions for images as they are redundant.
mcq.e: Use plain language, and keep alt text and captions for accessibility.
w: Fine: a summary page helps.
Fine: short sections and headings help.
Wrong: slang excludes readers.
Fine: experts can review quality.
Wrong: alt text and captions are not redundant.

mcq.q: Which of the following reduce(s) the information scent of documents?
o: Break down the contents to describe one idea per paragraph.
Enumerating options in a paragraph instead of using bulleted lists.
Deliver more content than conventional writing to provide details.
Include overly promotional writing to catch the reader's attention quickly.
Highlight keywords with different text styles (e.g. bold) and colours.
mcq.e: Scannable writing (one idea per paragraph, lists, highlighted keywords) strengthens scent; burying options in paragraphs, adding more text and promotional language weaken it.
w: False: one idea per paragraph raises scent.
True: enumerating options in a paragraph reduces scent.
True: bloated content reduces scent.
True: promotional writing reduces scent.
False: highlighting keywords raises scent.

mcq.q: Which is/are true to improve users' information foraging?
o: Apply Gestalt's principles effectively to organise the UI's visual elements.
Use small multiples to organise visual data for quick data exploration.
Improve affordance to increase accessibility.
Follow heuristics of strong information scent to improve document scannability.
Use Treemap design to visualise data for quick information exploration.
mcq.e: All five support finding information quickly: organisation by Gestalt, visualisation types (small multiples, treemap), clear affordances and strong scent.
w: True: Gestalt organises visuals.
True: small multiples aid exploration.
True: affordances aid accessibility.
True: scent improves scannability.
True: treemaps support exploration.

mcq.q: You are conducting an experiment to determine whether adding a personalised greeting on the homepage increases learning motivation on an online learning platform. What should you consider?
o: Excluding data from users who engage with the platform frequently to reduce bias.
Measuring learning motivation using metrics, such as time spent on the platform and number of clicks.
Changing the layout of the homepage along with the greeting to test multiple factors at once.
Use a random number generator to allocate users to either see the personalised greeting or the standard homepage.
Ensuring the greeting is displayed to all users, but only some users are aware of it.
mcq.e: Operationalise the dependent variable and randomise assignment. Change only one thing (C is a confound) and do not drop users selectively.
w: False: excluding frequent users biases the sample.
True: clicks and time are suitable proxies.
False: changing layout too confounds the test.
True: random allocation controls bias.
False: awareness differences confound the test.

mcq.q: You are conducting a laboratory study to evaluate the usability of a new navigation system for an online store. Which best practice(s) improve the validity of your laboratory study?
o: Ensuring that all participants are given the same tasks to perform.
Avoiding any form of assistance or hints during tasks that impact measurements when users encounter difficulties.
Allowing participants to freely explore the website without a defined task structure to observe natural behaviour.
Allowing participants to perform tasks at their own pace, with some using a mobile device and others using a desktop.
Recruiting participants who are familiar with online shopping to ensure faster data collection.
mcq.e: Standardise tasks and procedure (internal validity). Mixed devices and free exploration add confounds, and convenient recruiting hurts representativeness.
w: True: same tasks keep conditions comparable.
True: no hints keeps measurements valid.
False: no task structure removes comparability.
False: mixed devices confound results.
False: recruiting only experienced shoppers biases the sample.

mcq.q: You are conducting an inspection of a new e-commerce website using Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics. Which finding(s) would align with these heuristics?
o: The checkout process lacks clear confirmation messages, leaving users uncertain if their transaction was successful.
Users are unsure whether their search request was processed.
Users prefer the website over a competitor's due to its advanced features.
The website uses different icons for the same action across pages.
The homepage takes more than 5 seconds to load, frustrating users.
mcq.e: A and B = visibility of system status; D = consistency and standards. C is a preference, not a violation; E is a performance issue rather than a named heuristic.
w: True: missing confirmation violates visibility of system status.
True: unsure whether search ran is also status.
False: preference for features is not a heuristic issue.
True: inconsistent icons violate consistency and standards.
False: load time is performance, not one of the ten heuristics.

mcq.q: You are evaluating a new feature in a video streaming app using heuristic evaluations, observational studies and A/B testing. Which best describe(s) how these methods complement each other?
o: Heuristic evaluations are done by experts to identify usability issues, while observational studies gather quantitative and qualitative data from real users, and A/B testing compares across different design versions.
A/B testing provides insights into users' thought processes, while heuristic evaluations and laboratory studies focus on statistical performance comparisons.
Heuristic evaluations and laboratory studies are both used to compare different design versions, while A/B testing focuses only on task completion times.
Heuristic evaluations provide quantitative data, while A/B testing and observational studies are best suited for identifying specific design violations.
Observational studies help measure user performance quantitatively, while heuristic evaluations and A/B testing rely on qualitative insights to identify user preferences.
mcq.e: Experts find rule violations, observation shows how real users behave, and A/B testing compares versions: triangulation uses each method's strengths.
w: True: experts find issues while observation shows behaviour.
False: A/B testing does not reveal thought processes.
False: the methods do not compare as stated.
False: heuristic evaluation is mostly qualitative.
False: observation is not mainly quantitative.

mcq.q: You collected open-ended comments from users about their experience and measured task completion times. Which best describe(s) the correct analysis of the user feedback?
o: Using user comments to statistically measure the likelihood of errors.
Analysing the correlation between users' comments and their task completion times to identify performance bottlenecks.
Identifying common themes in users' comments to understand their experiences with the interface.
Converting user feedback into qualitative satisfaction ratings by assigning numerical values to each comment.
Using task completion times to calculate the average time taken by the user using the interface.
mcq.e: Comments → themes (qualitative); completion times → averages (quantitative). Do not force comments into numbers.
w: False: comments are not statistical measures.
False: that mixes data types poorly.
True: theming comments finds experience insights.
False: forcing numbers loses qualitative value.
True: averaging times is quantitative analysis.

mcq.q: You want to measure both user satisfaction and task completion times for a new mobile app feature. Which consideration(s) would ensure your experiment captures the data effectively?
o: Conducting post-task interviews with users to gather detailed feedback about their experience with the app.
Assigning each participant to either the new feature or the old version of the app and measuring which version they prefer.
Recording user interactions during the experiment and coding their behaviours into numerical categories for subsequent qualitative analysis.
Using a survey with Likert scale questions to measure user satisfaction after completing tasks.
Measuring the time it takes for users to complete each task and comparing averages across different user groups.
mcq.e: Use a satisfaction instrument (Likert, interviews) and time the tasks. B (preference without exposure to both) and C (coding for ‘qualitative’ analysis) don't fit the goals.
w: True: interviews give detailed satisfaction feedback.
False: that compares versions but is not a satisfaction/time measure by itself.
False: coding behaviours is about observation, not these measures.
True: Likert measures satisfaction.
True: timing measures completion.

mcq.q: You are running a web experiment to determine which landing page converts more visitors into paying customers, using A/B testing with a between-subjects design. Which statement(s) is/are true?
o: Analysing data after a significant amount of traffic has visited both versions.
Assigning each visitor to test both version A and version B.
Ensuring that both versions of the landing page are identical in every detail.
Measuring conversion rate as one of the dependent variables.
Running the experiment for a few hours to get quicker results.
mcq.e: Wait for enough traffic; the conversion rate is the dependent variable. Between-subjects means each visitor sees one version, and the versions differ in the variable under test.
w: True: wait for enough traffic.
False: each visitor sees one version.
False: identical versions test nothing.
True: conversion is a dependent variable.
False: a few hours gives noisy results.

mcq.q: You are evaluating two versions of a homepage redesign. Which statement(s) correctly describe the laboratory study and the A/B test?
o: Laboratory studies focus on measuring conversion rates over time, while A/B testing collects qualitative feedback.
Laboratory studies require large sample sizes to detect statistically significant differences, while A/B testing can be conducted with a small number of users in a short period.
A/B testing is always conducted in live environments, not in controlled settings.
A/B testing involves random assignment of users to different versions, while laboratory study emphasises evaluation of how real users interact with one version of the design in a controlled setting.
Both laboratory studies and A/B testing allow users to freely explore multiple versions to compare preferences.
mcq.e: A/B tests randomly assign many live users to versions and measure behaviour; laboratory studies observe real users in detail in a controlled setting.
w: False: reversed; lab is qualitative and A/B is conversion.
False: A/B needs larger samples.
False: A/B can run in controlled settings.
True: A/B randomises users; labs evaluate behaviour in depth.
False: users do not freely explore both in A/B.

mcq.q: You are analysing feedback from a usability study of a fitness tracking app that collected numerical ratings and open-ended feedback. Which option(s) about qualitative and quantitative data is/are true?
o: User comments describing their frustrations with the app's interface are considered quantitative data.
A 5-point satisfaction rating scale provides qualitative insights into their overall experience.
Counting how many users encountered the same issue during the test is an example of qualitative data.
User comments and feedback about their experience with the app are examples of qualitative data.
Measuring the average time it took users to complete a task is an example of qualitative data.
mcq.e: Comments are qualitative; ratings, counts and times are quantitative.
w: False: comments are qualitative.
False: ratings are quantitative.
False: counting issues is quantitative.
True: comments are qualitative data.
False: time is quantitative.

mcq.q: You are conducting an A/B test of two product recommendation versions. You want to understand users' feelings about the relevance of the recommendations. Which approach(es) allow you to gather the QUALITATIVE data required?
o: Randomly assigning users to each version and recording the number of purchases made from recommended items.
Tracking the number of clicks on recommended items to assess the effectiveness of each version.
Interviewing selected users after the A/B test to gather in-depth feedback about their experience with the recommendations.
Measuring the time users spend reviewing recommendations before making a purchase.
Using a post-task survey with open-ended questions to ask users how relevant they found the recommended items.
mcq.e: Interviews and open-ended survey questions are qualitative. Purchases, clicks and time are quantitative.
w: False: that measures purchases, not why.
False: clicks measure behaviour, not reasons.
True: interviews give in-depth understanding.
False: time spent does not reveal why.
True: open-ended survey questions explain relevance.

mcq.q: You are evaluating the impact of a new navigation system on a travel booking website. You need both internal and external validity and are using a between-subjects design. Which best practice(s) help?
o: Recruiting only participants who are experienced with using travel booking websites to ensure consistent results.
Use variations of device types (e.g., iPhone 14 Pro, Galaxy Tab S8, MacBook Air) and screen sizes.
Focusing only on quantitative measures, such as task completion time and number of clicks, to minimise subjective bias.
Randomly assigning participants to either the new navigation system or the old one to control for differences between users.
Allowing participants to freely explore both versions of the navigation system to compare their preferences without restricting their choices.
