mcq.e: Random assignment protects internal validity; varied devices help external validity (generalisation). Only experienced users limits generalisation; both versions contradicts between-subjects.
w: False: only experienced users limits generalising.
True: varied devices improve generalising.
False: ignoring qualitative data loses insight.
True: random assignment controls differences.
False: free exploring of both biases preference.

mcq.q: You are running a web experiment to determine if changing the colour of a ‘Buy Now’ button improves click-through rates throughout the day for users globally. What should you focus on to ensure internal and external validity?
o: Changing multiple elements of the page to see if the colour change works better with other adjustments.
Using visitors from a specific region to control the results.
Randomly assign visitors to see either the original or new button colour.
Restricting the experiment to one specific time of day to minimise variables.
Including a diverse sample of visitors from different demographics.
mcq.e: Random assignment supports internal validity; a diverse sample supports external validity. Changing several elements, or restricting region or time, undermines one or the other.
w: False: changing multiple elements confounds the colour effect.
False: one region limits generalising.
True: random assignment controls bias.
False: one time of day limits generalising.
True: a diverse sample supports generalising.

mcq.q: You are evaluating whether adding personalised product recommendations to an e-commerce site increases user engagement, measured by number of items added to the cart. Which statement(s) is/are true?
o: The independent variable is user engagement.
The independent variable is the presence of personalised recommendations.
The dependent variable is the number of personalised recommendations shown.
The dependent variable is the time users spend browsing the website.
The confounding variable could be the user's familiarity with online shopping.
mcq.e: IV = what you vary (presence of recommendations); DV = what you measure (items added to cart). Familiarity is a plausible confound.
w: False: engagement is the dependent variable (items added to cart), not the IV.
True: the IV is what you vary: whether recommendations are shown.
False: the DV is items added to cart, not how many recommendations are shown.
False: the DV here is items added to cart, not browsing time.
True: prior familiarity with online shopping is a plausible confound.

mcq.q: You are considering heuristic evaluation or cognitive walkthrough for a mobile payment app. Which statement(s) correctly distinguish(es) between the two?
o: Inspections are less formal and are typically done during the early stages of development, while heuristic evaluations are performed after product launch.
Cognitive walkthrough focuses on detecting violations of Nielsen's 10 heuristics, while heuristic evaluations assess general user satisfaction.
Heuristic evaluations require larger sample sizes of users, while inspections can be performed with just a few experts.
Heuristic evaluations are conducted by real users, while cognitive walkthroughs are carried out by usability experts.
Heuristic evaluations are structured around specific usability principles, while cognitive walkthrough relies on expert judgement by asking a set of questions from the perspective of the user.
mcq.e: Heuristic evaluation = principles; cognitive walkthrough = step-by-step questions from the user's perspective. Both are done by experts.
w: False: both are formal inspections.
False: it is the other way round.
False: neither needs large user samples.
False: both use experts.
True: heuristic evaluation uses principles, a walkthrough uses tasks.

mcq.q: Your team first conducts an inspection and then usability testing in a lab. Which statement(s) accurately describe(s) the key difference(s)?
o: Usability testing is less structured than inspections, allowing users to explore the app freely and provide qualitative feedback.
Inspections rely on expert evaluators, while usability testing requires real users to interact with the app.
Usability testing focuses more on detecting design inconsistencies, while inspections are mainly used to measure task performance metrics.
Both use similar evaluation frameworks, but laboratory studies are less reliable due to user variability.
Inspections focus on identifying high-level user interface design issues, while usability testing provides detailed insights into how real users perform tasks.
mcq.e: Experts versus real users, and breadth versus detailed behaviour.
w: False: inspections are not less structured.
True: inspections use experts, testing uses real users.
False: that reverses the strengths.
False: laboratory studies are not simply less reliable.
True: inspection finds high-level issues, testing gives user evidence.

mcq.q: You are designing an experiment to test a new feature in a task management app, gathering data on how users interact with it and how they feel about it, while ensuring validity. Which best practice(s) help?
o: Ensuring that participants are given the same tasks in the same order to eliminate variability.
Using a survey with a 5-point Likert scale to measure user satisfaction and conducting follow-up interviews to gather in-depth feedback.
Recruiting participants who are familiar with the task management app to increase the reliability of the data collected.
Randomly assigning participants to different experimental groups and measuring only task completion times to compare performance across groups.
Focusing only on recording and analysing the number of errors made by users, as qualitative feedback introduces subjective bias.
mcq.e: Mix quantitative and qualitative measures to cover both interaction and feeling. Same order creates order effects; measuring only one metric misses the second goal.
w: False: same order introduces order effects.
True: Likert plus follow-up interviews give mixed data.
False: familiar users bias the sample.
False: measuring only time ignores satisfaction.
False: ignoring qualitative feedback loses insight.

mcq.q: You are deciding between a between-subjects and within-subjects design for two onboarding processes. Which statement(s) is/are true?
o: A within-subjects design helps to control for participant variability since each participant experiences both versions.
A between-subjects design avoids the risk of learning effects between versions.
A within-subjects design increases the risk of carryover effects, where experiences with one version influence performance on the other.
A between-subjects design requires each participant to only experience one version of the onboarding process.
A between-subjects design requires fewer participants than a within-subjects design to achieve statistical power.
mcq.e: Within-subjects uses each person as their own control but risks order and carryover effects (use counterbalancing); between-subjects needs more people. B is also commonly stated as true, since each person sees only one version, but A, C and D are the clearest.
w: True: each person sees both, controlling variability.
False: between-subjects avoids learning effects across versions.
True: within-subjects risks carryover.
True: between-subjects: one version each.
False: between-subjects needs more participants.

mcq.q: Your team is conducting an inspection with heuristic evaluation on a new mobile app. Which action(s) is/are true for this inspection method?
o: Interviewing users to gather subjective opinions about the app's design.
Observing real users interact with the app in a controlled environment.
Using a panel of usability experts to evaluate the app based on established usability principles.
Analysing user behaviour data to identify patterns in app usage.
Gathering feedback from a large group of real users to identify common usability issues.
mcq.e: Inspection is done by experts using principles; the other options involve real users.
w: False: interviewing users is not an inspection.
False: observing users is user testing.
True: expert panel with principles.
False: analysing behaviour data is analytics.
False: large user feedback is not an inspection.

mcq.q: During a heuristic evaluation of a mobile banking app, users struggle to locate the logout button, hidden in a submenu under ‘Settings’, and the app shows technical error codes like ‘Error 404’ when connectivity is lost. Which usability issue(s) is/are observed?
o: The app violates ‘Error prevention’ by allowing errors like ‘404’ to occur.
The app violates ‘User control and freedom’ by placing the logout option in a submenu, making it hard to exit.
The app violates ‘Match between system and the real world’ by using technical jargon like ‘Error 404’.
The app violates ‘Help and documentation’ by not offering a guide for finding the logout button.
The app violates ‘Flexibility and efficiency of use’ by not offering shortcuts to frequently used functions like logout.
mcq.e: The hidden exit is a user control and freedom issue; the jargon is a mismatch with the real world. A, D and E are weaker fits for the described issues.
w: False: 404 is not error prevention.
True: hidden logout reduces control and freedom.
True: jargon like Error 404 violates match with the real world.
False: help is not the issue.
False: shortcuts are not the issue.

mcq.q: You want to assess how quickly users complete a new onboarding process in a mobile banking app. Which step(s) should you take to capture QUANTITATIVE data?
o: Recording the time it takes for users to complete each step of the onboarding process.
Conducting think-aloud sessions where users verbalise their thoughts while interacting with the app.
Using open-ended survey questions after the experiment to gather detailed feedback on emotional reactions.
Limiting the study to open-ended survey questions to avoid introducing subjective bias.
Assigning participants to control and treatment versions of the onboarding process randomly.
mcq.e: Timing steps gives quantitative data. Think-aloud and open-ended questions are qualitative. (E is an experiment-design step, not a data-capture step.)
w: True: step times measure speed.
False: think-aloud slows tasks.
False: emotions are not speed.
False: open questions do not measure speed.
False: random assignment is a design choice, not a measure.

wr.q: Define direct and indirect pointing methods in user interfaces. For each type, provide an example and explain why it is classified as direct or indirect pointing.
wr.a:
Direct pointing: the user touches or points at the object itself, so the input and the display are in the same place (control–display ratio 1:1). Example: a touchscreen — the finger lands on the on-screen button, so the mapping is direct.

Indirect pointing: the user moves a separate device and a cursor on the screen moves in response. Example: a mouse or touchpad — the hand moves on the desk but the cursor moves on the display, so the mapping is indirect and the C-D ratio can vary with speed/gain.

wr.q: Using the ‘shopping cart’ as a metaphor in an e-commerce shopping app, describe three benefits of using this metaphor. What are two potential drawbacks?
wr.a:
Benefits: (1) it leverages users' existing, familiar knowledge of shopping, so they know what to do; (2) it maps actions neatly — ‘add product’ = put it in the cart, ‘check out’ = calculate the total and pay; (3) it makes it easier to explain and discuss complex functionality across the team and with users.

Drawbacks: (1) it can mislead or does not scale: a real cart is for imminent purchase, but people use an online cart as a ‘save for later’ list; (2) it degrades across contexts and over time, e.g. on small touch screens cart abandonment rises and mobile carts need extra animation or clearer cues.

wr.q: Define triangulation in UI/UX research design and explain its key benefit. Support your answer with an example.
wr.a:
Definition: combining more than one method (e.g. observation and an experiment, or a laboratory study and a survey) to study the same question.

Key benefit: each method has a different, non-overlapping blind spot (realism, control, cost), so combining them covers the gaps and gives more trustworthy conclusions.

Example: evaluate a checkout redesign with an expert heuristic evaluation (finds rule violations cheaply), a laboratory study with think-aloud (shows why users struggle) and an A/B test (measures conversion with real traffic).

wr.q: Define the concepts of threshold and ceiling in gentle slope systems. Provide one example of a low-threshold, high-ceiling system.
wr.a:
Threshold: how hard the tool is to learn and start using. Ceiling: how much it can ultimately do. A gentle-slope system lets people start easily and keep growing in capability.

Example: a low-threshold, high-ceiling system is a tool people can begin using immediately yet extend into advanced work — for instance a web-page tool that starts with simple drag-and-drop and can be extended with HTML/JavaScript. (From the notes: MS Word has a low threshold but low ceiling, raw HTML higher threshold and ceiling, JavaScript highest of both.)

wr.q: You are designing a user study to test a new e-commerce website and want both internal and external validity. List five steps to ensure the validity of the study. State if each is for internal or external validity.
wr.a:
1. Randomly assign participants to conditions — internal validity.
  2. Give all participants the same tasks, instructions and equipment (standardised procedure) — internal.
  3. Control confounds such as time of day, device, prior experience (hold constant or counterbalance) — internal.
  4. Recruit a representative sample of the real target users — external.
  5. Use realistic tasks and settings (e.g. real shopping scenarios, varied devices and contexts) — external.

wr.q: You are evaluating a new learning platform to measure student engagement and experience. Describe five methods you would adopt. State if the data collected is quantitative or qualitative.
wr.a:
1. Usage analytics (time on platform, lessons completed, clicks) — quantitative.
  2. Likert-scale survey / SUS after use — quantitative.
  3. Semi-structured interviews with students — qualitative.
  4. Observation or think-aloud usability sessions — qualitative (with quantitative timing if recorded).
  5. A/B test of a feature, measuring completion or retention — quantitative; combine with open-ended comments (qualitative) to triangulate.

wr.q: Describe five strategies for designing a high-quality mobile version of an existing website originally designed for desktop.
wr.a:
1. Design for thumbs and one hand: bottom-oriented, thumb-reachable navigation and large targets (Fitts' Law).
  2. Use device-independent units (DP/PT) so the design is consistent across screen densities.
  3. Prioritise and simplify content: overview → scan → detail and minimal clutter for small screens.
  4. Give immediate visual feedback because mobile interaction is easily interrupted.
  5. Ask for permissions in context, make search/filters prominent, and test with real users on real devices.

wr.q: State the three stages of the gulf of evaluation and provide two examples of how you would reduce the gulf of evaluation to indicate whether Bluetooth is on or off.
wr.a:
Stages: (1) Perceive the system state, (2) Interpret what it means, (3) Evaluate whether it matches the goal.

Examples: (1) Show a clear, persistent status icon whose colour/fill changes (e.g. a solid highlighted Bluetooth icon when on, greyed or crossed out when off) so state is perceivable at a glance. (2) Give immediate feedback with text and motion when toggled (e.g. toggle switch that slides plus a label ‘On — connected to Headphones’), so the user can interpret the result.

wr.q: Explain how a laboratory study differs from a field study in the context of usability testing.
wr.a:
Laboratory study: carried out in a controlled setting with set tasks and measurement, so you can control variables and compare reliably (stronger internal validity), but behaviour may be less natural.

Field study: carried out in the users' real environment, observing natural use, so it is more realistic (stronger external validity) but you have less control, more noise and it can be harder to record and replicate.

wr.q: You are evaluating a new mobile banking app using Nielsen's 10 heuristics. List five potential usability issues. State clearly the heuristic violated and an example of the issue.
wr.a:
1. Visibility of system status: no confirmation or progress after a transfer, so users do not know if it succeeded.
  2. Match between system and the real world: jargon such as ‘Error 404’ or ‘insufficient liquidity’.
  3. User control and freedom: no way to cancel or undo a payment, or the logout is buried.
  4. Consistency and standards: different icons or labels for the same action on different screens.
  5. Error prevention: no confirmation or format check before sending money to a new payee. (Others: recognition rather than recall, help and documentation.)

wr.q: Case: a startup is developing a mobile app for household energy usage (real-time consumption, usage alerts, historical comparison, personalised recommendations). The team (a) wants to explore design concepts quickly through lo-fi prototyping and (b) worries about functional fixation among members who previously worked on other energy monitoring systems. (a) Describe two lo-fi prototyping techniques that could help the team explore novel solutions. (b) For each, explain how it could help rapidly come up with UI and interaction methods. (c) Explain what ‘functional fixation’ is, and explain with an example how each technique can help combat it.
wr.a:
(a) Two lo-fi techniques: paper sketching / paper prototyping (hand-drawn screens that can be rearranged) and storyboarding (a comic-style sequence of how a user checks and reduces energy use). Wizard of Oz is another option.

(b) How they speed up exploration: sketches are very cheap and quick, so the team can draw many alternatives (several layouts for real-time usage and alerts) in minutes and discard weak ones without emotional cost; paper pieces let you act out interaction (tap, swipe, swap screens) with a teammate or user and see which flows work. Storyboards explore the sequence and context (alert arrives → user checks usage → adjusts the thermostat), revealing missing interaction steps.

(c) Functional fixation: the tendency to see an object or concept only in terms of its familiar use or form, which blocks alternatives (Duncker's candle problem; design fixation = locking onto the first workable idea). Example: team members used to line charts of kWh might only imagine dashboards. Parallel sketching forces many different representations (e.g. a ‘traffic light’ home status, a game with a neighbourhood leaderboard). A storyboard focused on the user's goal (‘lower the bill tonight’) rather than on features can lead to ideas like a one-tap ‘eco mode’ or proactive suggestions instead of yet another chart.

wr.q: Consider a simple messaging app with a traditional chat UI (typed messages, bubbles in chronological order, text input, basic emoji reactions). The team wants to improve it using principles of direct manipulation. (a) List two principles of direct manipulation interfaces, (b) explain what each means in UI design, (c) for each, identify a current limitation in the app and suggest a specific improvement. Explain how it enhances the user experience (you may use features of popular apps such as Telegram).
wr.a:
Principle 1 — Continuous representation of objects of interest. Meaning: the objects and actions are visible and you act on them directly. Limitation: messages can only be reacted to with a few emoji, and replying to an earlier message is awkward. Improvement: let users drag or swipe a message to reply (as in Telegram), pin or move messages directly. Benefit: the user acts on the visible object, so there is no need to learn a command and context is kept.

Principle 2 — Physical, reversible, incremental actions with immediate feedback. Meaning: actions are done by gestures or clicks rather than complex syntax; each step gives instant feedback and can be undone. Limitation: sending is final, with no way to undo or edit a message and no preview of attachments. Improvement: add undo-send and edit, press-and-hold to record or cancel a voice note by sliding, and live previews. Benefit: fewer errors, more control and confidence.

wr.q: Case: a fitness tracking app added a gamification system (achievements, badges, weekly challenges). The company ran an A/B test: (a) gamified experience vs (b) standard experience, assessing engagement by completed workout lessons. Identify and explain five distinct threats that could undermine the study's internal validity. Each should represent a different category of validity concern.
wr.a:
1. Selection: if users are not randomly assigned (e.g. keen users opt into gamification), the groups differ from the start.
  2. History: an outside event (New Year resolutions, a competing app, an app update, a holiday) affects one group more than the other or changes behaviour over time.
  3. Maturation: users naturally become fitter or more motivated (or bored) over the test period regardless of condition.
  4. Mortality (attrition): people drop out of one condition more than the other (for example, users who find challenges stressful leave), leaving a biased sample.
  5. Testing / instrumentation: being measured changes behaviour, or the way ‘completed lessons’ is logged differs between versions; also confounds such as differing devices or differing tasks and instructions.

(Other categories from the notes: statistical regression and interaction with selection.)
